title: When is Routing Meaningful? Diversity and Robustness in Language Model Societies
summary: Routing policies for multi-model systems are evaluated almost exclusively on task accuracy and inference cost. We argue that two properties, orthogonal to performance, determine whether routing is meaningful. First, the society of actors must be behaviourally differentiated: if all actors respond identically, routing is vacuous. Second, the routing policy must be stable: surface-form variants of a query should be assigned to the same actor. High task accuracy is compatible with violating both properties, since a router can operate over a redundant society or assign queries inconsistently, preventing specialisation regardless of performance. We adapt Hierarchic Social Entropy (HSE) to language-model societies and introduce a perturbation-based robustness metric to diagnose these failure modes. Applied to EmbedLLM and RouterBench, we find that HSE exhibits strong diminishing returns, suggesting that a curated subset of fewer than ten agents recovers most available diversity in a large pool -- a practical coreset heuristic for society design. We further find that KNN routers gain accuracy from specialist societies but collapse in robustness under perturbation, while prompted routing remains stable across all perturbation types -- illustrating that accuracy and meaningfulness can sharply diverge.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that evaluating routing policies solely on accuracy and cost is insufficient. It introduces two orthogonal criteria—behavioural differentiation (actors must respond differently) and routing stability (queries with the same intent must route to the same actor)—and proposes metrics (Hierarchic Social Entropy and perturbation-based robustness) to diagnose failures in multi-model routing systems. Applying these to EmbedLLM and RouterBench reveals diminishing diversity returns beyond ~10 agents and a divergence between KNN routers (accurate but perturbation-unstable) and prompted routers (stable).
AI.motivation: Current evaluation of multi-model routing policies focuses exclusively on task accuracy and inference cost, ignoring whether the routing is actually meaningful. A router can achieve high accuracy even when the underlying society of models is redundant (no behavioural differentiation) or when semantically equivalent queries are routed inconsistently (instability), both of which defeat the purpose of specialization.
AI.method: The authors adapt Hierarchic Social Entropy (HSE) from ecology/sociology to quantify behavioural differentiation among language-model actors in a society. They also introduce a perturbation-based robustness metric: surface-form variants of the same query (paraphrases, typos, etc.) are generated, and routing consistency across variants is measured. These diagnostics are applied to two benchmark systems—EmbedLLM and RouterBench—to assess differentiation and stability across different router architectures (KNN-based vs. prompt-based).
AI.result: HSE exhibits strong diminishing returns: a curated subset of fewer than 10 agents recovers most of the available behavioural diversity in a large pool, providing a practical coreset heuristic for society design. KNN routers achieve higher accuracy when using specialist societies but collapse in robustness under perturbation, while prompted routing remains stable across all perturbation types—demonstrating a sharp divergence between accuracy and meaningfulness.
AI.conclusion: Accuracy and cost alone are insufficient to evaluate routing policies. Meaningful routing requires both a behaviourally differentiated society of models and a stable routing policy. The proposed HSE and perturbation-robustness metrics provide practical diagnostics, and the findings suggest that small, curated model societies with stability-focused routers offer a better path toward genuine specialization in multi-model systems.

title: Mosaic: Runtime-Efficient Multi-Agent Embodied Planning
summary: LLM-based multi-agent embodied planning remains impractical due to prohibitively high execution latency. We identify failed actions as the dominant bottleneck, stemming from two core challenges: inaccurate state tracking under partial observability and inefficient coordination that produces redundant or conflicting actions. We introduce Mosaic, a runtime-efficient multi-agent planning framework that addresses both challenges. Mosaic maintains accurate yet lightweight state tracking through agent-centric semantic memory that stores objects in relative coordinates, enabling geometric transformations and coordination. It ensures efficient coordination through Integer Linear Programming that allocates actions at every planning step, enforcing physical feasibility and inter-agent coordination constraints. Across AI2-THOR and search-and-rescue benchmarks, Mosaic achieves 27-32% faster execution, 30-33% fewer LLM calls, 25-31% fewer steps, and 4-10% points higher success rates. These results demonstrate that efficient memory and constraint-guided coordination are critical for scalable, low-latency multi-agent planning.

AI.tldr: Mosaic is a runtime-efficient multi-agent embodied planning framework that reduces execution latency by using agent-centric semantic memory for accurate state tracking and Integer Linear Programming for coordination, achieving up to 32% faster execution with fewer LLM calls and higher success rates.
AI.motivation: LLM-based multi-agent embodied planning suffers from prohibitively high execution latency, primarily caused by failed actions due to inaccurate state tracking under partial observability and inefficient coordination leading to redundant or conflicting actions.
AI.method: Mosaic introduces two key components: (1) agent-centric semantic memory that stores objects in relative coordinates, enabling geometric transformations and accurate state tracking; and (2) Integer Linear Programming (ILP)-based action allocation at each planning step to enforce physical feasibility and inter-agent coordination constraints.
AI.result: On AI2-THOR and search-and-rescue benchmarks, Mosaic achieves 27-32% faster execution, 30-33% fewer LLM calls, 25-31% fewer steps, and 4-10 percentage points higher success rates compared to baselines.
AI.conclusion: Efficient memory representations and constraint-guided coordination are critical for enabling scalable, low-latency multi-agent embodied planning.

title: SolarChain-Eval: A Physics-Constrained Benchmark for Trustworthy Economic Agents in Decentralized Energy Markets
summary: As agentic AI systems are increasingly applied to cyber-physical environments, their evaluation requires assessment of both task performance and trustworthiness. In decentralized energy markets, autonomous agents may improve market utility, but may also exploit invalid physical data, create artificial liquidity, and produce unstable governance decisions. Therefore, we propose SolarChain-Eval, a physics-constrained benchmark for evaluating trustworthy economic agents. It formulates market governance as a Gymnasium-compatible Markov Decision Process, where agents make hourly decisions. SolarChain-Eval evaluates each policy across multiple dimensions, including market utility, physical safety, slippage, action smoothness, spatial fairness, and auditability. To support agentic evaluation, SolarChain-Eval incorporates an LLM-based Planner/Auditor layer. The Planner defines episode-level action bounds and audit rules, while the Auditor reviews and revises high-risk actions. All interventions are recorded through structured logs, including trigger signals, proposed actions, revised actions, and audit rationales. Experiments with static, random, myopic, RL, and RL+LLM policies reveal a clear utility-safety trade-off. RL agents improve market utility but can still produce unsafe behavior. When the physics penalty is removed, reward-maximizing agents exploit invalid generation and increase artificial liquidity. The LLM Planner/Auditor improves auditability and mitigates selected risks, but it cannot fully compensate for a misspecified reward function. These results indicate that trustworthy agentic AI evaluation requires both physical constraints and transparent intervention traces. We release data and code as open access on GitHub for replicability.

AI.tldr: SolarChain-Eval is a physics-constrained benchmark for evaluating trustworthy economic agents in decentralized energy markets, integrating LLM-based planning/auditing layers with RL policies, and revealing a fundamental utility-safety trade-off where reward misspecification leads to exploitative agent behavior.
AI.motivation: As agentic AI systems are deployed in cyber-physical domains like decentralized energy markets, existing evaluation methods focus narrowly on task performance while neglecting trustworthiness dimensions. Autonomous agents may exploit invalid physical data, create artificial liquidity, and destabilize governance. There is a need for benchmarks that jointly assess task performance and trustworthiness under realistic physical constraints.
AI.method: The authors propose SolarChain-Eval, which formulates market governance as a Gymnasium-compatible Markov Decision Process with hourly decision steps. It evaluates policies across six dimensions: market utility, physical safety, slippage, action smoothness, spatial fairness, and auditability. An LLM-based Planner/Auditor layer is incorporated, where the Planner sets episode-level action bounds and audit rules, while the Auditor reviews and revises high-risk actions. All interventions are logged with structured traces (trigger signals, proposed/revised actions, audit rationales). Experiments compare static, random, myopic, RL, and RL+LLM policies.
AI.result: A clear utility-safety trade-off emerges: RL agents improve market utility but still produce unsafe behavior. When the physics penalty is removed, reward-maximizing agents exploit invalid generation and increase artificial liquidity. The LLM Planner/Auditor improves auditability and mitigates selected risks but cannot fully compensate for a misspecified reward function.
AI.conclusion: Trustworthy agentic AI evaluation requires both physical constraints and transparent intervention traces. The LLM-augmented auditing layer provides partial safeguards but is insufficient when the underlying reward function is poorly specified. Datasets and code are released open-access on GitHub.

title: Secret Scanner Agent: Extracting Secrets and Access Context from Unstructured Documents
comment: Submitted to the Conference on Applied Machine Learning for Information Security (CAMLIS) 2026
summary: Exposed documents such as emails, chat threads, tickets, and incident notes routinely leak credentials, but during incident response a leaked secret is only half the story. Responders also need to identify the ``door'' the secret opens: the account, tenant, endpoint, database, cloud resource, or other system that the credential could allow an attacker to access. Traditional secret scanners rely on regular expressions or trained classifiers which work well on well-formatted code, yet they struggle when a credential is fragmented, reformatted, or far from the resource it unlocks, and they report the secret string without naming what it opens. We present Secret Scanner Agent (SSA), a multi-agent large-language-model system that extracts both the secret and its associated door, together with supporting evidence, from unstructured exposed documents. SSA pairs a detection agent that favors recall with a review agent that filters false positives and recovers missing context. Because real credential data is sensitive, we evaluate SSA on synthetic benchmarks we generated that span 23 secret types and multiple document formats, scored with a three-step pipeline of programmatic matching, an LLM judge, and human review. Across six models, multi-agent SSA improves extraction precision over a single-agent variant, with the largest gains on door extraction, by up to 16 percentage points. SSA matches a regular-expression scanner's precision while more than tripling its recall, and against thirteen security analysts it is more precise, recovers nearly twice as many secret--door pairs, and runs five to seventeen times faster. By returning the secret, its door, and supporting evidence in one result, SSA turns credential detection into an actionable finding for triage and remediation.

AI.tldr: Secret Scanner Agent (SSA) is a multi-agent LLM system that not only detects leaked credentials in unstructured documents but also identifies the associated "door" (account, tenant, endpoint, etc.) the secret unlocks, outperforming regex-based scanners and human analysts in both precision and recall.
AI.motivation: Traditional secret scanners using regex or classifiers detect credential strings but fail to identify the "door" — the specific resource (account, database, cloud resource, etc.) the credential grants access to. They also struggle with fragmented, reformatted, or contextually distant secrets. Incident responders need both the secret and its door to make findings actionable for triage and remediation.
AI.method: SSA employs a multi-agent LLM architecture with two agents: a detection agent optimized for high recall, and a review agent that filters false positives and recovers missing context. The system extracts both the secret string, its associated door, and supporting evidence from unstructured documents. Evaluation uses synthetic benchmarks spanning 23 secret types and multiple document formats, scored via a three-step pipeline of programmatic matching, an LLM judge, and human review.
AI.result: Multi-agent SSA improves extraction precision over a single-agent variant by up to 16 percentage points, with largest gains on door extraction. SSA matches regex-scanner precision while more than tripling recall. Against 13 security analysts, SSA is more precise, recovers nearly twice as many secret-door pairs, and runs 5–17× faster.
AI.conclusion: By jointly returning the secret, its door, and supporting evidence, SSA transforms credential detection from a passive alert into an actionable finding, significantly improving incident response workflows.

title: MemeBuddy: Dialog-Style Audio Representations for Engaging Non-Visual Meme Experiences
summary: Image memes are a pervasive form of online communication, widely used to convey humor, opinions, and cultural references. Prior work has explored making memes accessible to blind users, primarily through auto-generated descriptive captions. While these approaches improve comprehensibility and sometimes incorporate prosodic or emotional cues, they often fail to capture the humor, narrative structure, and contextual nuances that make memes engaging. We present MemeBuddy, a system that models memes as dialog, generating structured, multi-turn audio representations using role-based speakers. MemeBuddy reinterprets a meme as a conversation between two speakers, integrating extracted meme text with contextual knowledge implicitly inferred by a multimodal LLM (e.g., recognition of common meme templates and cultural references) to convey intent, timing, and implicit meaning through conversational interaction. We evaluate MemeBuddy in a user study with 14 blind participants. Results show that dialog-style meme representations consistently improve engagement and user satisfaction compared to caption-style descriptions, while maintaining comparable comprehension.

AI.tldr: MemeBuddy transforms image memes into multi-turn dialog between two speakers using a multimodal LLM, improving blind users' engagement and satisfaction over traditional caption-based descriptions while maintaining comprehension.
AI.motivation: Existing meme accessibility solutions rely on descriptive captions that, while comprehensible, fail to convey the humor, narrative structure, timing, and contextual nuances that make memes engaging for sighted users. There is a need for richer, more engaging representations.
AI.method: MemeBuddy models memes as dialog by reinterpreting each meme as a conversation between two role-based speakers. It extracts meme text and leverages a multimodal LLM to infer contextual knowledge (e.g., meme templates, cultural references), generating structured, multi-turn audio representations that convey intent, timing, and implicit meaning through conversational interaction.
AI.result: A user study with 14 blind participants demonstrated that dialog-style meme representations consistently improved engagement and user satisfaction compared to caption-style descriptions, with comparable levels of comprehension.
AI.conclusion: Dialog-based representations offer a promising direction for making visual internet humor more accessible and engaging for blind users, suggesting that conversational framing can capture the social and narrative dimensions of memes that descriptive captions miss.

title: Programmers Are Poor and Overconfident Judges of LLM-Generated Assertions
summary: Code comprehension and code review are already critically important software engineering tasks, and the rising use of AI code generation tools is only increasing that importance. Generative AI has the possibility of supporting these activities, for example by augmenting code with assertions and natural-language explanations describing code behavior. However, little is known about how effective such support may be. We conduct a controlled experiment with 86 Python programmers and a follow-up think-aloud study to examine developers' ability to assess the correctness and completeness of generated assertions of varying quality, and to investigate how natural-language explanations influence these assessments. While programmers can somewhat accurately judge correct assertions (74% accuracy), they perform poorly when shown incorrect assertions (49% accuracy), despite reporting similar levels of confidence in both judgments. This difference in judgment accuracy is statistically significant (p < 0.001): the odds of a developer accurately judging a correct assertion was nearly three times higher than the odds of accurately judging an incorrect assertion (OR = 2.94). Surprisingly, natural-language explanations of assertions provided no overall benefit. Furthermore, low-quality explanations could impair specification assessment accuracy (p = 0.037, OR = 0.58) while simultaneously increasing developer confidence (p = 0.005, 3.99/5 vs. 4.25/5). Our findings suggest that, contrary to common assumptions, AI assistance may not improve the reliability of code comprehension and review. More broadly, our findings highlight the importance of helping developers evaluate machine-generated reliability artifacts, in addition to generating them.

AI.tldr: An experiment with 86 Python programmers found that while developers can judge correct AI-generated assertions reasonably well (74% accuracy), they struggle with incorrect ones (49% accuracy). Natural-language explanations provided no overall benefit; low-quality explanations actually impaired accuracy while boosting confidence. Results challenge the assumption that AI assistance improves code comprehension and review reliability.
AI.motivation: AI code generation tools are increasingly prevalent, and there is growing interest in using generative AI to support code comprehension and review through assertions and natural-language explanations. However, little empirical evidence exists on how effective such AI assistance actually is for developers assessing code correctness.
AI.method: The authors conducted a controlled experiment with 86 Python programmers, followed by a think-aloud study. Participants assessed the correctness and completeness of machine-generated assertions of varying quality, both with and without natural-language explanations. Statistical analyses included odds ratios and significance testing.
AI.result: Developers achieved 74% accuracy judging correct assertions versus only 49% for incorrect assertions (p < 0.001, OR = 2.94). Natural-language explanations yielded no overall benefit; low-quality explanations significantly reduced specification assessment accuracy (p = 0.037, OR = 0.58) while paradoxically increasing developer confidence (p = 0.005, from 3.99/5 to 4.25/5).
AI.conclusion: Contrary to common assumptions, AI assistance may not improve the reliability of code comprehension and review. The findings emphasize the need to help developers evaluate machine-generated artifacts critically, rather than focusing solely on generating them.

title: A Seed for Privacy -- semi-automatic privacy-revealing data reminder in databases and data streams
summary: Sharing databases and data streams imposes the danger of revealing private information in the form of complex events which can comprise individual data elements and their combinations. Identifying these privacy-revealing complex events is crucial for preserving privacy while maintaining data utility. However, data producers often lack the expertise to comprehensively identify these events, which undermines many state-of-the-art privacy-preserving mechanisms that rely on accurate event labeling. To address this challenge, we developed pArborist - a tool that can semi-automatically create a set of queries to identify and label privacy-revealing complex events in both static datasets and dynamic data streams, guided by the privacy requirements of the data producer. pArborist uses the schema of the database or data stream combined with initial input from the data producer, i.e., seed queries. From each seed query, pArborist grows a tree containing all possible syntactically correct queries, constrained by an upper limit on computational resources. Following this growing phase, the tree is refined by eliminating queries that lack correlation to the seed or are conditionally independent of the seed. Our evaluation indicates that pArborist achieves overall recall of 90% and precision of 93% in finding privacy-revealing queries, and this significantly surpasses the state-of-the-art approach FQID. In data stream processing experiments, pArborist introduces a delay of approximately 1.3 ms following an average warm-up period of 920 ms. The experiments also show that pArborist can automatically detect privacy-revealing complex events according to GDPR.

AI.tldr: pArborist is a tool that semi-automatically identifies privacy-revealing complex events in static databases and data streams by growing and refining query trees from user-provided seed queries, achieving 90% recall and 93% precision.
AI.motivation: Data producers often lack the expertise to comprehensively identify privacy-revealing complex events (combinations of individual data elements), which undermines privacy-preserving mechanisms that depend on accurate event labeling. Existing approaches are insufficient for this task.
AI.method: pArborist takes the database/data stream schema and seed queries from the data producer. For each seed, it grows a tree of all syntactically correct queries within computational resource limits. The tree is then refined by pruning queries that are uncorrelated with or conditionally independent of the seed query.
AI.result: pArborist achieved 90% recall and 93% precision in identifying privacy-revealing queries, significantly outperforming the state-of-the-art FQID approach. In stream processing, it introduces ~1.3 ms delay after a ~920 ms warm-up period, and successfully detects GDPR-relevant privacy-revealing complex events.
AI.conclusion: pArborist provides an effective semi-automated solution for labeling privacy-revealing complex events, bridging the expertise gap of data producers and enabling robust privacy preservation without sacrificing data utility.

title: Beyond Topicality: A Conceptual Analysis of Societal Relevance and Its Application to Search Results and AI Responses
summary: This paper examines "societal relevance," a concept introduced by Haider and Sundin to address the limitations of traditional relevance models in web search. While topical and user relevance are foundational to information science, they are insufficient for managing harmful content such as misinformation or discrimination found on the uncontrolled web. This study investigates three analytical questions: the definition of societal relevance, its practical application in search systems, and its distinction from information quality measures. By analyzing various combinations of system, user, and societal relevance, the paper explores how search outputs can be optimized for the "greater good". Although the concept remains theoretically underdeveloped, it provides a vital framework for developing value-driven search engines that prioritize ethical outcomes and societal interests over mere keyword matching.

AI.tldr: This paper explores "societal relevance," a novel concept proposed by Haider and Sundin that extends traditional topical/user relevance models to address harmful web content. It examines the definition, practical application, and distinction from information quality measures, arguing for value-driven search engines that prioritize ethical outcomes and the greater good over keyword matching.
AI.motivation: Traditional relevance models in web search — topical relevance and user relevance — are insufficient for managing harmful content (e.g., misinformation, discrimination) prevalent on the uncontrolled web. A new framework is needed to incorporate ethical and societal considerations into search systems.
AI.method: The study adopts a conceptual-analytical approach, investigating three questions: (1) defining societal relevance, (2) its practical application in search systems, and (3) distinguishing it from information quality measures. It analyzes various combinations of system, user, and societal relevance to explore how search outputs can be optimized for the "greater good."
AI.result: Societal relevance remains theoretically underdeveloped, yet it offers a vital framework for designing value-driven search engines. The analysis reveals that search outputs can be optimized by balancing system, user, and societal relevance, moving beyond mere keyword matching toward ethically-oriented results.
AI.conclusion: Though still nascent, the concept of societal relevance provides an essential lens for rethinking search engine design. It advocates for prioritizing ethical outcomes and societal interests, laying groundwork for future development of search systems aligned with the public good.

title: Interval Certifications for Multilayered Perceptrons via Lattice Traversal
summary: In this work we present a rigorous theoretical framework to a foundational problem of AI safety, namely adversarial robustness. In particular, we show that the adversarial robustness problem can be reduced to a lattice traversal problem. Each element of this lattice corresponds to an interval, i.e., an axis-aligned hyper-rectangle, containing an input point $\mathbf{x}$. Consider a multilayered perceptron classifier (MLP). An interval $I$ constitutes a sound certification if $\mathbf{x} \in I$ and $\mathbf{x}$ can be freely perturbed in $I$ without changing the MLP's prediction. Complementarily, an interval $I$ constitutes a complete certification if $\mathbf{x} \in I$ and when $\mathbf{x}$ moves outside of $I$ the MLP's prediction is guaranteed to change. While the sound certification problem corresponds to the well-studied adversarial robustness, complete certifications have not been examined in the literature. We develop lattice traversal operators, which we apply in a refine & verify iterative scheme. Using formal MLP verifiers, sound maximality and complete minimality are guaranteed. Moreover, we examine objective optimization problems. There we discover some interesting asymmetries. For complete certifications, the minimum solution is obtained in polynomial oracle calls. This does not hold for sound certifications, where we prove strong intractability results. Additionally, we examine optimization problems in symmetric intervals (i.e., $\ell_\infty$-spheres), where we provide logarithmic algorithms. Finally, we present an empirical evaluation, using the novel ParallelepipedoNN system.

AI.tldr: The paper frames adversarial robustness as a lattice traversal problem, where intervals (axis-aligned hyper-rectangles) serve as certification regions. It introduces the novel concept of complete certification alongside traditional sound certification, develops iterative refine-and-verify operators, proves polynomial-time solutions for complete minimality but strong intractability for sound maximality, and provides logarithmic algorithms for symmetric ℓ∞-sphere optimization problems.
AI.motivation: Existing work on adversarial robustness focuses almost exclusively on sound certification (guaranteeing no prediction change within a region). The paper identifies a gap: complete certification, which guarantees prediction change when leaving a region, has been entirely unexamined. The authors aim to build a rigorous theoretical framework unifying both certification types through lattice theory, and to understand the fundamental computational complexity differences between them.
AI.method: The paper reduces adversarial robustness to a traversal problem on a lattice of intervals (axis-aligned hyper-rectangles). Each lattice element is an interval containing an input point. The authors develop lattice traversal operators used in a refine-and-verify iterative scheme, employing formal MLP verifiers to guarantee sound maximality and complete minimality. They analyze objective optimization problems for both certification types and for symmetric intervals (ℓ∞-spheres). The empirical evaluation uses a novel system called ParallelepipedoNN.
AI.result: Key results include: (1) For complete certifications, the minimum solution is obtainable in polynomial oracle calls. (2) For sound certifications, strong intractability results are proven — the optimization problem is significantly harder. (3) Logarithmic-time algorithms exist for optimization in symmetric ℓ∞-spheres. These findings reveal fundamental asymmetries between sound and complete certification problems.
AI.conclusion: The lattice-theoretic framework provides a principled foundation for both sound and complete certification in adversarial robustness. The asymmetry between tractable complete minimality and intractable sound maximality has significant implications for practical robustness verification, and the logarithmic algorithms for ℓ∞-spheres offer efficient solutions for a practically relevant special case.

title: A Unified Approach to Interpreting Knowledge Distillation for Large Language Models via Interactions
summary: Despite the success of knowledge distillation (KD) in Large Language Models (LLMs), the underlying mechanism behind its efficacy remains unclear. In this paper, we propose a unified approach to explore the common mechanism of various KD methods using interactions. Specifically, we decompose the output score of the LLM into the sum of numerous interactions. Each interaction represents a nonlinear relationship involving a set of input variables (e.g., words). Based on the decomposed interactions, we discover that the common mechanism underlying various KD methods is the sparsification of interactions, i.e., student models retain fewer interactions for inference while suppressing other interactions to zero effects. Furthermore, we discover that the performance variance across different KD methods arises from their capabilities in handling complex interactions. A KD method typically yields better performance if it enables the student model to achieve higher sparsity of complex interactions. Motivated by these insights, we propose a plug-and-play loss function called Complex Interaction Penalty (CIP) to explicitly enforce the sparsity of complex interactions during the distillation process. Extensive experiments demonstrate that integrating CIP consistently improves the performance of diverse KD methods on both in-domain and out-of-distribution benchmarks.

AI.tldr: This paper reveals that the common mechanism behind knowledge distillation in LLMs is the sparsification of interactions—student models retain fewer nonlinear interactions while zeroing out others. The authors propose a Complex Interaction Penalty (CIP) loss to explicitly enforce sparsity of complex interactions, which consistently improves KD performance across methods and benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Despite the empirical success of knowledge distillation in LLMs, the underlying mechanism driving its effectiveness remains poorly understood. The authors aim to uncover a unified explanatory framework that reveals what various KD methods have in common at a mechanistic level.
AI.method: The authors decompose the LLM's output score into a sum of interactions, where each interaction captures a nonlinear relationship among a subset of input variables. Using this decomposition, they analyze how different KD methods alter interaction structures. Based on the finding that KD works by sparsifying interactions—particularly complex, high-order ones—they propose a plug-and-play Complex Interaction Penalty (CIP) loss function that explicitly penalizes complex interactions during distillation to enforce higher sparsity.
AI.result: The interaction-based analysis reveals that all effective KD methods share the mechanism of interaction sparsification. Performance differences across KD methods correlate with their ability to handle complex interactions—methods yielding higher sparsity of complex interactions perform better. Integrating the proposed CIP loss consistently boosts the performance of diverse KD methods on both in-domain and out-of-distribution benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The unified mechanism behind KD in LLMs is interaction sparsification. Explicitly enforcing sparsity of complex interactions via CIP provides a simple, effective, and method-agnostic way to improve knowledge distillation, bridging mechanistic interpretability with practical performance gains.

title: Communication-Efficient Digital-Twin Coordination for Heterogeneous LLM Embodied Agents over Computing Power Networks
summary: Embodied agent teams powered by heterogeneous large language models (LLMs) are being widely deployed in physical artificial intelligence such as smart factories, warehouses, and service robotics. To enable collaboration among such an agent team, efficient coordination mechanisms that operate reliably under limited network resources are required. However, existing heterogeneous LLM-agent coordination frameworks that rely on multi-round natural-language-based conversations introduce three coupled challenges. First, inter-agent dialogue incurs communication overhead that grows rapidly with team size. Second, the quality of coordination is constrained by the heterogeneous capabilities of the agent team's LLMs. Third, agents may suffer from action delays due to iterative negotiation. To address these challenges, we propose LDT-Coord, a networked coordination framework built upon a lightweight digital twin (DT). Specifically, each agent independently selects its intended action and reports both the action decision and a structured temporal constraint over shared resources to the DT server, thereby decoupling coordination performance from natural-language reasoning ability. Then, DT executes a training-free, rule-based orchestrator algorithm to resolve cross-agent conflicts and returns coordination instructions to prevent such conflicts. To further reduce communication overhead, we formulate agent reporting control as a constrained partially observable Markov decision process (C-POMDP) and solve it with the PPO-Lagrangian algorithm. Simulation results show that LDT-Coord achieves a task success rate comparable to conventional coordination methods while reducing communication overhead by more than 70x and maintaining robustness under LLM heterogeneity.

AI.tldr: LDT-Coord proposes a lightweight digital twin (DT) based coordination framework for heterogeneous LLM-agent teams that decouples coordination from natural-language reasoning, achieving comparable task success rates while reducing communication overhead by 70x and maintaining robustness under LLM heterogeneity.
AI.motivation: Existing heterogeneous LLM-agent coordination frameworks rely on multi-round natural-language conversations, which introduce three coupled challenges: (1) communication overhead growing rapidly with team size, (2) coordination quality constrained by heterogeneous LLM capabilities, and (3) action delays from iterative negotiation. A more efficient, reliable coordination mechanism is needed for resource-constrained physical AI deployments.
AI.method: LDT-Coord introduces a lightweight digital twin (DT) server architecture where: (1) each agent independently selects intended actions and reports structured temporal constraints over shared resources to the DT, rather than engaging in multi-round natural-language dialogue; (2) a training-free, rule-based orchestrator on the DT resolves cross-agent conflicts and issues coordination instructions; and (3) agent reporting control is formulated as a constrained partially observable Markov decision process (C-POMDP) and optimized via the PPO-Lagrangian algorithm to further reduce communication overhead.
AI.result: Simulations demonstrate that LDT-Coord achieves a task success rate comparable to conventional multi-round conversation-based coordination methods, while reducing communication overhead by over 70x and maintaining robustness across heterogeneous LLM capabilities.
AI.conclusion: LDT-Coord effectively decouples coordination performance from natural-language reasoning ability, enabling efficient and robust coordination for heterogeneous LLM-agent teams under limited network resources, making it well-suited for real-world physical AI deployments such as smart factories and service robotics.

title: Micro-level AI Feedback Features and Student Responses in Consecutive LLM Tutoring Interactions
summary: AI-assisted feedback research has shown that micro-level feedback features, such as concrete elaboration, affective language, and response length, are associated with learning outcomes. Existing studies have primarily examined these features using session- or task-level measures. We examine how feedback provided in one user-AI interaction is associated with student confusion and understanding in the immediately following interaction in a naturalistic tutoring setting. We focus on three micro-level features of AI feedback: concrete elaboration (analogies, comparison-based explanations, or worked examples), affective language (encouragement, empathy, or apology), and response length. We analyzed 16,851 conversational user-AI interactions from the StudyChat dataset, a naturalistic record of student interactions with an LLM tutor in an undergraduate AI course, and identified 1,718 cases in which students expressed confusion and continued to a subsequent interaction. Using chi-square tests and Generalized Estimating Equations (GEE), we found that concrete elaboration was associated with higher understanding and lower re-confusion in the student's next interaction. Empathetic language showed no significant association with either outcome, while longer responses were independently associated with lower understanding. These findings highlight the value of examining feedback across consecutive user-AI interactions and suggest that concrete elaboration may play an important role in supporting immediate student understanding.

AI.tldr: Analyzing 16,851 conversational turns from an LLM tutoring dataset, this study finds that concrete elaboration (analogies, comparisons, worked examples) in AI feedback predicts higher student understanding and lower re-confusion in the immediately following interaction, while empathetic language shows no significant effect and longer responses independently predict lower understanding.
AI.motivation: Prior AI-assisted feedback research has examined micro-level features (concrete elaboration, affective language, response length) only at session- or task-level granularity. The authors argue that understanding how feedback in one interaction shapes the very next interaction is critical for designing effective conversational tutoring systems, yet this fine-grained, turn-by-turn relationship remains unexplored.
AI.method: The authors analyzed the StudyChat dataset — 16,851 conversational user-AI interactions from an undergraduate AI course where students interacted with an LLM tutor. They identified 1,718 instances where students expressed confusion and then continued to a subsequent interaction. Three micro-level feedback features were coded: concrete elaboration (analogies, comparisons, worked examples), affective language (encouragement, empathy, apology), and response length. Statistical analyses used chi-square tests and Generalized Estimating Equations (GEE) to model the association between these AI feedback features and two outcomes in the next student turn: understanding and re-confusion.
AI.result: Concrete elaboration was significantly associated with higher understanding and lower re-confusion in the subsequent student interaction. Empathetic language showed no significant association with either outcome. Longer AI responses were independently associated with lower student understanding in the next turn.
AI.conclusion: The findings underscore the value of analyzing feedback at the level of consecutive user-AI interactions rather than aggregated measures. Concrete elaboration emerges as a potentially important design principle for LLM-based tutoring systems aiming to support immediate student comprehension, while empathy and response brevity warrant further investigation.

title: Better Harnesses, Smaller Models: Building 90% Cheaper Agents via Automated Harness Adaptation
summary: Frontier LLM agents are automating many business tasks, but their high inference cost makes large-scale deployment unsustainable. Small language models (SLMs) offer a cheaper alternative, yet they typically fall short when swapped into a harness designed for a frontier LLM. We show that for many routine business tasks, SLM agents can match LLM performance at 90% lower cost, when paired with an adapted harness that can be automatically discovered by a meta agent. The key insight is that much of the task difficulty is shared across instances and can be lifted from the model into the harness via tailored instructions, tools, and orchestration loops. To study this systematically, we create a framework that maps agent failure modes to harness adaptation strategies, and build a harness optimizer that automatically discovers effective adaptations from failure trajectories. Across seven business-oriented agentic tasks and three SLM families, we found optimized harnesses significantly improve performance on 16 of 21 task-SLM pairs, with seven pairs closing the SLM-LLM performance gap and the best SLM agent recovering 89.7% of LLM performance at 4% of the cost. Our analysis further shows that adaptation works best for tasks with more repetitive workflows and for SLMs with sufficient base capabilities. Together, these results suggest that harness adaptation can expand the practical deployment range of SLM agents in routine business tasks.

AI.tldr: SLM agents can match frontier LLM performance on routine business tasks at ~90% lower cost when paired with automatically discovered, task-adapted harnesses. A meta-agent optimizes instructions, tools, and orchestration loops by learning from failure trajectories. Across 7 business tasks and 3 SLM families, optimized harnesses closed the SLM-LLM gap on 7 of 21 pairs, recovering 89.7% of LLM performance at 4% cost.
AI.motivation: Frontier LLM agents are too expensive for large-scale deployment in business automation. SLMs are cheaper but perform poorly when used as drop-in replacements in harnesses designed for large models. The authors hypothesize that task difficulty can be shifted from the model into the harness (instructions, tools, orchestration) to enable SLMs to perform competitively.
AI.method: The authors create a framework mapping agent failure modes to harness adaptation strategies (instructions, tools, orchestration loops). They build a meta-agent harness optimizer that automatically discovers effective adaptations by analyzing failure trajectories. The approach is evaluated across seven business-oriented agentic tasks and three SLM families.
AI.result: Optimized harnesses significantly improved performance on 16 of 21 task-SLM pairs. Seven pairs fully closed the SLM-LLM performance gap. The best SLM agent recovered 89.7% of LLM performance at only 4% of the inference cost. Adaptation works best for tasks with repetitive workflows and for SLMs with sufficient base capabilities.
AI.conclusion: Harness adaptation via automated meta-agent optimization can substantially expand the practical deployment range of SLM agents for routine business tasks, offering dramatic cost savings with minimal performance degradation.

title: Privacy-Preserving Intent Fulfilment and Assurance for 6G RAN
summary:
Intent-based network management is the emerging paradigm for 6G service lifecycle automation, with the 3GPP intent management framework (TS~28.312) defining creation, translation, fulfilment, and assurance stages. Existing fulfilment and assurance approaches require deep packet inspection, per-flow state tracking, or access to vendor-internal node telemetry to verify that provisioned resources satisfy expressed intents. These requirements conflict with regulatory constraints (GDPR, ePrivacy Directive) in multi-tenant networks and with vendor opacity in multi-vendor O-RAN deployments.
  We present an architecture for privacy-preserving intent fulfilment and assurance in which a coordinator provisions resources from declared intent categories without traffic inspection, and verifies fulfilment using only aggregate standardised PM counters at the O1 interface. A data-processing inequality argument shows that the resource allocation reveals at most $\log_2 K$ bits about traffic content, where $K$ is the number of intent categories. We define two architectural privacy properties, intent-traffic unlinkability and node-opaque verification, and show that both hold by construction. Node-opacity does not sacrifice detection power: the aggregate verifier weakly dominates the per-agent verifier under a homogeneity condition.
  We map the architecture to the 3GPP intent lifecycle and the O-RAN Non-RT RIC, identifying the concrete interfaces, data objects, and deployment points at which the mechanism operates. On production PM counter data from four operator networks, increasing intent-category granularity sharpens provisioning but weakens assurance, consistent with the theoretical prediction that the privacy ceiling is a structural side effect of the detection constraint rather than a separate design parameter.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a privacy-preserving architecture for 3GPP intent-based network management. It provisions resources using only intent categories (not traffic inspection) and verifies fulfilment via aggregate standardised O1 PM counters. A data-processing inequality bounds information leakage to log₂K bits, where K is the number of intent categories. Two architectural privacy properties (intent-traffic unlinkability and node-opaque verification) are proven, and the approach is validated on production PM data from four operator networks.
AI.motivation: Existing intent fulfilment and assurance methods rely on deep packet inspection, per-flow state tracking, or vendor-internal telemetry — practices that conflict with GDPR and the ePrivacy Directive in multi-tenant networks, and with vendor opacity in multi-vendor O-RAN deployments. A privacy-compliant alternative is needed that neither inspects traffic nor depends on proprietary node internals.
AI.method: The authors design an architecture with a coordinator that maps declared intent categories to resource allocations without inspecting traffic content. Fulfilment verification uses only aggregate, standardised PM counters collected via the O1 interface. A data-processing inequality formalises the privacy guarantee: resource allocation reveals at most log₂K bits about traffic. Two formal properties are defined — intent-traffic unlinkability and node-opaque verification — and proven to hold by construction. The aggregate verifier is shown to weakly dominate the per-agent verifier under a homogeneity condition. The architecture is mapped concretely to the 3GPP intent lifecycle (TS 28.312) and O-RAN Non-RT RIC, specifying interfaces, data objects, and deployment points. Empirical evaluation uses production PM counter data from four operator networks, varying intent-category granularity to probe the privacy–assurance trade-off.
AI.result: The two privacy properties (intent-traffic unlinkability, node-opaque verification) hold by construction. The aggregate verifier weakly dominates the per-agent verifier under homogeneity, so node-opacity does not sacrifice detection power. On production PM data, increasing intent-category granularity sharpens provisioning but weakens assurance, confirming the theoretical prediction that the privacy ceiling is a structural consequence of the detection constraint, not a tunable parameter.
AI.conclusion: Privacy-preserving intent fulfilment and assurance is feasible within the standardised 3GPP/O-RAN framework using only aggregate O1 PM counters. The log₂K privacy bound is inherent to the approach, and the trade-off between provisioning precision and assurance fidelity is structurally determined by the detection constraint. The architecture is directly deployable at identified 3GPP and O-RAN Non-RT RIC integration points.

title: From Raw IDs to Semantic Planning: How Recommender Systems Utilize Information at Scale
summary: The evolution of recommender systems can be explored by asking how they utilize information at scale. Throughout most of the historical period under consideration during the past two decades, industrial systems have relied on raw IDs, which are discrete, globally unique, and semantically opaque identifiers that enable exact lookup, logging, and item-specific memorization at scale. Over time, however, recommender systems have sought to utilize richer sources of information, including item content, context, multimodal signals, and cross-domain structure. This development has led to a new stage in which part of such information is no longer used solely as auxiliary features around item identity, but is increasingly encapsulated in semantic IDs that provide a more structured, model-facing form of identity. We argue that this shift goes beyond the rise of generative recommendation over traditional methods. Indeed, it reflects a broader evolution in how recommender systems utilize information under industrial-scale constraints. This paper looks at the past, present, and future to examine three connected questions: why raw IDs dominated the early development of recommender systems, why semantic information is increasingly being encapsulated in IDs today, and what may come next once recommendations move beyond semantic retrieval. In particular, we introduce semantic planning as a possible future direction in which the system first predicts the semantic target of the next exposure, and only then instantiates that target as a specific item or generated creative. We further argue that such a shift may require changes not only in model design but also in evaluation and in the way recommender systems coordinate the objectives of users, platforms, and providers.

AI.tldr: This paper traces the evolution of recommender systems through their use of identifiers: from raw, opaque IDs to increasingly semantic ones, and speculates on a future "semantic planning" paradigm where systems first predict what to communicate before instantiating it as an item.
AI.motivation: To understand the fundamental shift in how recommender systems utilize information at scale — moving from raw ID-based memorization toward semantic IDs and beyond — and to provide a coherent historical narrative that explains why each paradigm emerged under industrial constraints, while also charting possible future directions.
AI.method: This is a position/survey paper that adopts a historical-analytical approach. It examines the evolution of recommender systems across three eras (past, present, future) through the lens of how identifiers encode and convey information. The authors introduce the concept of "semantic planning" as a speculative future paradigm and discuss its implications for model design, evaluation protocols, and multi-stakeholder objective coordination.
AI.result: The paper identifies three stages: (1) raw ID dominance driven by exact lookup, logging fidelity, and item-specific memorization at scale; (2) the current transition to semantic IDs that encapsulate content, context, multimodal signals, and cross-domain structure as first-class identity rather than auxiliary features; (3) a proposed future of semantic planning where systems decouple semantic target prediction from item instantiation, potentially enabling generated creatives. It argues this evolution necessitates changes in evaluation methodology and stakeholder alignment.
AI.conclusion: The shift from raw IDs to semantic IDs represents more than just the rise of generative recommendation — it reflects a deeper reconfiguration of how recommender systems structure information under scale constraints. The next frontier, semantic planning, may fundamentally alter not only model architecture but also how success is measured and how user, platform, and provider objectives are reconciled.

title: CogniConsole: Externalizing Inference-Time Control as a Formal Abstraction for Reliable LLM Interactions
comment: Revised version focusing on the CogniConsole system architecture and empirical evaluation of inference-time control probes (N=489)
summary: Reliability in large language model (LLM) systems is typically framed as a function of model capability. We challenge this by demonstrating that reliability is significantly influenced by \emph{inference-time control} -- the computational layer governing task framing and context selection. We introduce \emph{CogniConsole}, an architectural instantiation that externalizes this control into a structured interface combining programmatic coordination with bounded prompt-based reasoning. Through \emph{controllability-oriented probes} ($N=489$) in a multi-step interactive environment, we show that increasing structural scaffolding -- from unstructured to fully scaffolded -- \textbf{systematically reduces output variance and failure rates under a fixed model architecture}. Our results indicate that many observed failure modes, such as context drift and inconsistent constraint adherence, arise from under-specified control rather than insufficient capability. This work provides an empirical basis for treating inference-time control as a first-class abstraction, opening new directions for designing and evaluating LLM systems beyond scaling alone.

AI.tldr: Challenges the view that LLM reliability is purely a function of model capability, demonstrating instead that inference-time control (task framing and context selection) is a critical determinant. Introduces CogniConsole, a structured interface combining programmatic coordination with bounded prompt-based reasoning, and shows through controllability probes (N=489) that increased structural scaffolding systematically reduces output variance and failure rates under a fixed model.
AI.motivation: The dominant framing treats LLM reliability as primarily a function of model capability (scaling). The authors challenge this, arguing that many observed failure modes — context drift, inconsistent constraint adherence — stem from under-specified inference-time control rather than insufficient model capability. They seek to establish inference-time control as a first-class design abstraction.
AI.method: Introduction of CogniConsole, an architectural instantiation that externalizes inference-time control into a structured interface combining programmatic coordination with bounded prompt-based reasoning. Evaluation via controllability-oriented probes (N=489) in a multi-step interactive environment, comparing performance across a spectrum from unstructured to fully scaffolded control configurations under a fixed model architecture.
AI.result: Increasing structural scaffolding systematically reduces output variance and failure rates under a fixed model architecture. This confirms that many failure modes arise from under-specified control rather than insufficient capability.
AI.conclusion: Inference-time control should be treated as a first-class design abstraction in LLM systems, opening new directions for system design and evaluation beyond model scaling alone.

title: iLENS: Interpretable LLM-Guided Mixture-of-Experts for Neuroimaging Survival Analysis
summary: Alzheimer's Disease (AD) is a complex neurodegenerative disorder that continues to impact millions of people worldwide. Predicting AD conversion during the prodromal stage remains critical for disease understanding and patient care. As such, survival models are widely used for AD risk prediction, yet they are typically static predictors with limited interpretability and no capacity for natural language reasoning. In this work, we propose iLENS, an interpretable large language model (LLM) guided framework based on mixture-of-experts (MoE) for survival prediction in AD conversion. Our approach uses LLM to synthesize structured neuroimaging measurements and unstructured information to guide expert routing. Our framework demonstrates competitive predictive performance and capability in patient subtyping. Furthermore, our framework provides transparent, biologically grounded rationales for its routing decisions, bridging the gap between high-performance survival analysis and interpretable clinical decision support.

AI.tldr: iLENS is an interpretable LLM-guided mixture-of-experts framework for Alzheimer's Disease conversion prediction that combines structured neuroimaging with unstructured clinical data, offering competitive survival analysis with transparent, biologically grounded routing rationales.
AI.motivation: Existing survival models for AD conversion prediction are static, lack interpretability, and cannot perform natural language reasoning, limiting their clinical utility during the critical prodromal stage.
AI.method: The authors propose iLENS, which leverages an LLM to synthesize structured neuroimaging measurements with unstructured clinical information. This synthesized representation guides a mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture for survival prediction, where the LLM routes input cases to specialized expert submodels.
AI.result: iLENS achieves competitive predictive performance on AD conversion survival analysis and demonstrates effective patient subtyping capabilities.
AI.conclusion: By providing transparent, biologically grounded rationales for routing decisions, iLENS bridges the gap between high-performance survival analysis and interpretable clinical decision support in AD prognostics.

title: Shared Selective Persistent Memory for Agentic LLM Systems
summary: Agentic LLM systems that generate code through multi-turn tool use face a fundamental context problem: each session starts from zero, discarding the configuration choices, domain constraints, data schemas, and tool-use patterns that made previous sessions productive. Naively persisting entire conversation histories is token-inefficient and counterproductive: irrelevant context degrades generation quality. We introduce shared selective persistent memory, an architecture that identifies and retains four categories of reusable context (task specifications, data schemas, tool configurations, and output constraints) while discarding session-specific reasoning traces. Crucially, this memory is shared: workspaces encapsulating selective memory can be transferred across users with role-based access control, enabling collaborative reuse without redundant specification. We implement it in a deployed collaborative workspace platform where LLM agents produce, edit, and maintain git-versioned artifacts (dashboards, reports, and data-driven documents) from heterogeneous sources (CSV, SQL, REST APIs, and MCP servers). A complementary zero-token data refresh mechanism decouples generated programs from runtime data, enabling artifact reuse without re-invocation. Across three enterprise scenarios, shared selective persistent memory achieves 96% task completion (vs. 79% without memory and 71% with full history). Zero-token refresh eliminates LLM re-invocation for recurring updates (14x task-time reduction), while summary-driven generation cuts per-invocation token cost by 97x versus raw data injection. A replication on four public datasets confirms generalizability, with zero-token refresh succeeding in 12/12 trials. Notably, naive full-history persistence actively degrades completion by biasing the agent with stale traces, while selective memory outperforms both extremes.

AI.tldr: Proposes shared selective persistent memory for agentic LLM systems that retains only reusable context (task specs, schemas, tool configs, output constraints) while discarding session traces. Implemented in a collaborative workspace platform with zero-token data refresh, achieving 96% task completion vs. 79% (no memory) and 71% (full history), with 97x token cost reduction and 14x task-time improvement.
AI.motivation: Agentic LLM systems for code generation suffer from a "cold start" problem: each session begins with zero context, wasting prior configuration, domain constraints, schemas, and tool-use patterns. Naively persisting full conversation histories is both token-inefficient and harmful — irrelevant context degrades generation quality. There is a need for an architecture that selectively retains valuable context while enabling collaborative reuse across users.
AI.method: The authors introduce shared selective persistent memory, which identifies and retains four categories of reusable context: (1) task specifications, (2) data schemas, (3) tool configurations, and (4) output constraints, while discarding session-specific reasoning traces. Memory is organized into shareable workspaces with role-based access control. A complementary zero-token data refresh mechanism decouples generated programs from runtime data, allowing artifact reuse without LLM re-invocation. The system is deployed on a collaborative workspace platform where agents produce git-versioned artifacts from heterogeneous sources (CSV, SQL, REST APIs, MCP servers).
AI.result: Shared selective persistent memory achieves 96% task completion across three enterprise scenarios, compared to 79% without memory and 71% with full history persistence. Zero-token refresh yields 14x task-time reduction for recurring updates. Summary-driven generation reduces per-invocation token cost by 97x versus raw data injection. Replication on four public datasets confirms generalizability (12/12 trials for zero-token refresh). Notably, full-history persistence actively degrades performance by biasing the agent with stale traces.
AI.conclusion: Selective persistent memory strikes an optimal balance: retaining configuration-level context improves task completion substantially, while discarding ephemeral reasoning traces prevents degradation seen with full-history approaches. The shared workspace architecture enables collaborative reuse, and zero-token refresh decouples generation from data, making the system practical for recurring enterprise workflows.

title: Living Inside the Black Box: Behavioral Probing and Adaptation in Mandatory Wearable Sensing
summary: Wearable sensing systems in high-stakes institutional contexts translate behavioral data into consequential judgments, yet wearers have little access to how those judgments are made. We present a qualitative study of 24 individuals who experienced mandatory electronic monitoring in China's community corrections system. We show that participants built what we term sensor literacy under constraint, a practical form of risk-oriented knowledge developed through uncertainty, behavioral probing, and adaptation. We identify two orientations across rule domains. Where participants had mapped system behavior, they sometimes regained limited flexibility. Where uncertainty remained costly, they contracted movement and discretionary activity beyond formal rules. Some former wearers described residual habits of calculation after device removal. We discuss design implications for making institutional sensing intelligible to wearers, including sensor uncertainty, usable documentation, and evaluation after device wearing.

AI.tldr: A qualitative study of 24 individuals under mandatory electronic monitoring in China's community corrections system reveals how wearers develop "sensor literacy under constraint" — a risk-oriented knowledge built through uncertainty, behavioral probing, and adaptation. Participants either regained limited flexibility where they mapped system behavior, or contracted their activities beyond formal rules where uncertainty remained. Residual habits of calculation persisted after device removal.
AI.motivation: Wearable sensing systems in high-stakes institutional contexts make consequential judgments about wearers' behavior, yet wearers have little understanding of how those judgments are formed. This opacity creates significant power asymmetries and practical challenges for individuals whose freedom depends on complying with poorly understood sensing systems.
AI.method: The authors conducted a qualitative study involving semi-structured interviews with 24 individuals who experienced mandatory electronic monitoring (e.g., ankle bracelets or GPS trackers) as part of China's community corrections system. Data were analyzed to identify patterns in how participants learned about, adapted to, and were affected by the sensing technology.
AI.result: Participants developed "sensor literacy under constraint" — a practical, risk-oriented form of knowledge built through uncertainty, behavioral probing, and adaptation. Two orientations emerged: (1) where system behavior was successfully mapped, participants sometimes regained limited flexibility; (2) where uncertainty remained and its costs were high, participants over-compiled by contracting movement and discretionary activity beyond formal requirements. Some former wearers described residual calculation habits persisting after device removal.
AI.conclusion: The study highlights the need for design interventions to make institutional sensing systems more intelligible to wearers. The authors propose implications including communicating sensor uncertainty, providing usable documentation, and offering post-wearing evaluation to mitigate the lasting behavioral impacts of opaque monitoring.

title: Toward Inferring Accurate Context-free Grammars for Big Languages in a Black-box Setting
summary: Black-box context-free grammar inference is crucial for program analysis, reverse engineering, program understanding, fuzzing, and security. But existing approaches such as Arvada, TreeVada, Kedavra, and Cucio struggle with scalability, accuracy, and grammar readability, especially on larger languages. To address this challenge, Xvada introduces several new techniques for deterministic inference of context-free grammars. In an empirical comparison that avoids several pitfalls of recent studies, Xvada improves on the highest-scoring competitor (TreeVada) both in grammar accuracy and grammar compactness. Xvada also found a CVE in the widely used Python Liquid engine. Fuzzing based on the XVada-inferred grammar found five more bugs, which the Python Liquid developers fixed based on our bug reports. XVADA and all experimental data and scripts are freely available.

AI.tldr: Xvada is a new deterministic context-free grammar inference tool that outperforms existing approaches (Arvada, TreeVada, Kedavra, Cucio) in accuracy and compactness, scales to larger languages, discovered a CVE in Python Liquid, and found five additional bugs via grammar-based fuzzing.
AI.motivation: Existing black-box context-free grammar inference tools suffer from scalability, accuracy, and readability issues, particularly when applied to larger languages, limiting their practical utility for program analysis, reverse engineering, fuzzing, and security applications.
AI.method: Xvada introduces several novel techniques for deterministic context-free grammar inference. The paper includes an empirical evaluation designed to avoid common pitfalls in prior benchmarking studies.
AI.result: Xvada surpasses the previous best competitor (TreeVada) in both grammar accuracy and compactness. It identified a CVE in the Python Liquid template engine, and fuzzing with the inferred grammar uncovered five additional bugs that were subsequently fixed by the developers.
AI.conclusion: Xvada advances the state of the art in black-box grammar inference, demonstrating practical impact through vulnerability discovery and developer-confirmed bug fixes. The tool and all experimental artifacts are publicly available for reproducibility.

title: Entropy Bootstrapping for Wireless Embedded Systems
summary: Weak randomness has broken deployed cryptography through implementation bugs, boot entropy scarcity, and backdoored generators. Inexpensive wireless sensors concentrate the risk because many boot or operate in highly deterministic conditions while relying on basic, rudimentary, or opaque RNGs. On ESP32-class boards, RF-disabled wireless device RNG register (WDEV) output is pseudorandom by specification yet passes the same statistical screens as RF-active states, showing that output tests cannot replace source-state admission. We propose a defense-in-depth boot path for ESP32-class IoT nodes that combines SRAM startup material, radio burst extraction, and asymmetric entropy capsules under explicit source-state admission. In radio burst extraction, a trusted node in the local IoT network, such as a gateway or dedicated entropy node, sends a public packet burst to open a measurement window. The client samples its own WDEV output and packet timing during that window, then credits only the local response. Capsules cover the cold-start case with a pre-provisioned asymmetric key pair. The trusted node encrypts fresh seed material to the client's public key and signs the capsule; the client verifies, decapsulates, and hashes before it has local entropy. We benchmark the ESP32 RNG under several radio operating modes, the fixed-burst extraction window, the deterministic capsule client path, and SRAM startup reads. Together, these measurements support an admission policy in which each root is credited only when its required source state and protocol checks hold.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a defense-in-depth boot-time entropy architecture for ESP32-class IoT devices that combines SRAM startup material, radio burst extraction, and asymmetric entropy capsules, all governed by explicit source-state admission policies to mitigate weak randomness risks.
AI.motivation: Weak randomness in IoT devices—due to implementation bugs, boot entropy scarcity, and backdoored RNGs—breaks cryptographic guarantees. ESP32-class devices are especially vulnerable because they operate in deterministic conditions and the WDEV RNG register produces pseudorandom output that passes statistical tests even when RF is disabled, rendering output-only testing insufficient.
AI.method: Three-layer defense-in-depth boot path: (1) SRAM startup material harvested from uninitialized memory; (2) radio burst extraction where a trusted local node sends a public packet burst, the client samples WDEV output and packet timing during the window, crediting only local response; (3) asymmetric entropy capsules pre-provisioned with a key pair, where a trusted node encrypts and signs fresh seed material to the client's public key for cold-start scenarios. All sources are subject to explicit source-state admission checks.
AI.result: The ESP32 RNG was benchmarked across multiple radio modes, fixed-burst extraction windows, deterministic capsule client paths, and SRAM startup reads. Measurements demonstrate that each entropy root can be credited only when its required source state and protocol checks hold, supporting a verifiable admission policy.
AI.conclusion: Statistical output testing cannot replace source-state admission for IoT RNGs. The proposed three-layer boot path provides a practical, verifiable entropy architecture for ESP32-class devices that resists weak-randomness attacks through explicit per-source credentialing.

title: Automatic Thematic Indexing of Large Literary Corpora: A Machine Learning Approach to Voltaire's Complete Works
summary: Thematic indexing -- the practice of assigning structured conceptual labels to sections of text -- is essential to scholarly access in large-scale literary and historical editions, yet it remains a largely manual, labour-intensive process. This paper explores the application of machine learning to automatic thematic indexing, using two substantial sub-corpora of the Complete Works of Voltaire as a test case: the Essai sur les mœurs et l'esprit des nations and the Questions sur l'Encyclopédie. The task is framed as a multi-label classification problem, in which a model must assign the set of index entries that a professional indexer would apply to a given page of text. We compare a range of approaches -- from encoder-based models with classification heads to generative large language models (LLMs) fine-tuned via Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) -- spanning model sizes from approximately 3 to 120 billion parameters. Our best-performing model, from the Mistral family in a 4-bit quantised configuration, achieves F1 scores of up to 0.67; we argue that these figures represent lower bounds, given the inherent subjectivity of professional indexing and the frequency with which model predictions prove semantically valid despite diverging from the print index. We further evaluate cross-corpus generalisation and conduct a detailed qualitative analysis of model behaviour on literary and rhetorical features of the source texts that prove particularly resistant to automated treatment. Our findings have implications for the broader challenge of providing structured thematic access to large-scale literary and historical corpora.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates using machine learning — from encoder-based classifiers to fine-tuned LLMs — for automatic thematic indexing of Voltaire's works, achieving F1 scores up to 0.67 with a quantised Mistral model and arguing these are lower bounds due to indexer subjectivity.
AI.motivation: Thematic indexing in large-scale literary and historical editions is essential for scholarly access but remains a labor-intensive, manual process. Automating this task could significantly accelerate digital humanities scholarship.
AI.method: Framed as multi-label classification: predicting index entries per page. Compared encoder-based models with classification heads against generative LLMs fine-tuned with LoRA, spanning ~3B to ~120B parameters. Used two Voltaire sub-corpora (Essai sur les mœurs, Questions sur l'Encyclopédie). Evaluated via F1 score, cross-corpus generalisation, and qualitative error analysis.
AI.result: Best model: 4-bit quantised Mistral-family model achieving F1 ≤ 0.67. Authors interpret scores as lower bounds due to indexer subjectivity; many "incorrect" predictions were semantically valid. Cross-corpus generalisation was evaluated, and qualitative analysis identified literary/rhetorical features resistant to automation.
AI.conclusion: ML-based automatic thematic indexing is viable for large literary-historical corpora. Current performance, while moderate, likely underestimates real utility. Findings inform broader efforts to provide structured thematic access to such collections.

title: GATS: Graph-Augmented Tree Search with Layered World Models for Efficient Agent Planning
summary: Large Language Model (LLM) agents have shown promise in multi-step planning tasks, but existing approaches like LATS (Language Agent Tree Search) and ReAct rely heavily on LLM inference during planning, leading to high computational costs and stochastic behavior. We present \textbf{GATS} (Graph-Augmented Tree Search), a planning framework that combines systematic UCB1-based tree search with a layered world model to eliminate LLM calls during inference while achieving superior planning performance. Our three-layer world model integrates: (L1) exact symbolic action matching, (L2) statistics learned from execution logs, and (L3) LLM-based prediction for unknown actions. On synthetic planning tasks with branching paths and dead-ends, GATS achieves \textbf{100\% success rate} compared to 92 % for LATS and 64\% for ReAct. On a comprehensive stress test spanning 12 challenging scenarios -- including coding workflows, web navigation, and long-horizon tasks -- GATS maintains \textbf{100\% success} while LATS drops to 88.9 % and ReAct to 23.9%. GATS requires \textbf{zero LLM calls per task} during planning (vs. 37 per task for LATS) and produces deterministic plans with zero variance across runs. Our results demonstrate that systematic search with learned world models can substantially outperform LLM-guided exploration for agent planning.

AI.tldr: GATS (Graph-Augmented Tree Search) is a planning framework that replaces costly LLM inference during agent planning with systematic UCB1-based tree search guided by a three-layer world model (symbolic matching, execution statistics, and LLM fallback). It achieves 100% success rates on synthetic and challenging real-world planning tasks while requiring zero LLM calls during inference, outperforming LATS and ReAct both in success rate and deterministic consistency.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agent planning methods like LATS and ReAct incur high computational costs and exhibit stochastic behavior because they depend on repeated LLM inference during planning. The authors aim to eliminate these LLM calls at inference time while maintaining or improving planning performance through systematic search and learned world models.
AI.method: GATS combines UCB1-based tree search with a layered world model comprising three levels: (L1) exact symbolic action matching for known transitions, (L2) statistical knowledge learned from execution logs to guide exploration, and (L3) LLM-based prediction reserved only for unknown actions encountered during training. During inference, the framework operates deterministically with zero LLM calls, using the world model to simulate outcomes and UCB1 to balance exploration-exploitation in the search tree.
AI.result: On synthetic planning tasks, GATS achieves 100% success (vs. 92% LATS, 64% ReAct). On a stress test of 12 challenging scenarios including coding, web navigation, and long-horizon tasks, GATS maintains 100% success while LATS drops to 88.9% and ReAct to 23.9%. GATS uses zero LLM calls per task during planning (vs. 37 for LATS) and produces fully deterministic plans with zero variance across runs.
AI.conclusion: Systematic search augmented with learned world models can substantially outperform LLM-guided exploration for agent planning.
