GATS demonstrates that by decoupling world knowledge (learned offline) from planning (executed deterministically online), one can achieve both higher success rates and dramatic computational savings compared to LLM-dependent planning strategies.

title: Signed Symmetric Quantization for Few-Bit Integers
summary: The signed integer alphabet contains one more negative representable value than positive. Yet, by convention, the standard symmetric integer quantizer fixes its scale to be strictly positive, which assigns this extra representable value to the negative tail and can force clipping of positive outliers. In this work, we show that, at few-bit precision, such clipping is a non-trivial source of quantization error. Asymmetric quantization addresses this problem with a zero point, shifting the grid toward the observed data range; however, this flexibility is well-known to carry a runtime penalty. For example, in llama.cpp on an AMD EPYC(TM) "Turin" CPU, a 4-bit symmetric format uses up to 9% less memory with up to 2.45$\times$ higher throughput than its asymmetric counterpart. We highlight signed symmetric quantization as a third option that retains the runtime profile of symmetric quantization without the penalty of the asymmetric format: our signed absmax grid places the extra representable value on the dominant-outlier tail through a principled and lightweight sign selection rule while keeping the zero point at zero. Our theoretical analysis offers two main results. First, we establish the signed absmax grid as conditionally bound-optimal on $\ell_2$ quantization error, and show that the condition holds for 88-99% of weight groups across pre-trained large language models (LLMs) at low bit widths. Second, we show that negating the scale of a standard symmetric quantizer is analytically equivalent to a unit zero point shift on the same signed integer alphabet. We empirically validate our proposal on models from the Qwen3, Qwen3.5, and Llama3 families, and observe improvement in perplexity and downstream few-shot accuracy over the standard unsigned symmetric quantizer at no extra inference cost

AI.tldr: This paper proposes signed symmetric quantization, which uses a signed integer alphabet with a principled sign-selection rule to place the extra negative representable value on the dominant-outlier tail, achieving better accuracy than standard symmetric quantization without the runtime penalty of asymmetric quantization.
AI.motivation: Standard symmetric integer quantization forces the extra negative representable value onto the negative tail, causing clipping of positive outliers at few-bit precision. Asymmetric quantization solves this with a zero-point shift but incurs significant runtime overhead (e.g., up to 2.45× lower throughput). The authors seek a method that retains symmetric quantization's efficiency while eliminating the outlier-clipping problem.
AI.method: The authors propose a signed absmax grid with a lightweight sign-selection rule: the grid sign is chosen based on which tail (positive or negative) contains dominant outliers, placing the extra representable value there while keeping the zero point at zero. They provide theoretical analysis proving this grid is conditionally bound-optimal on ℓ₂ quantization error (condition holds for 88–99% of weight groups in LLMs) and show that negating the scale of a standard symmetric quantizer is analytically equivalent to a unit zero-point shift.
AI.result: On Qwen3, Qwen3.5, and Llama3 model families, signed symmetric quantization improves perplexity and downstream few-shot accuracy over standard unsigned symmetric quantization at no additional inference cost. The proposed method achieves this while matching symmetric quantization's runtime profile, unlike asymmetric quantization which can reduce throughput by up to 2.45×.
AI.conclusion: Signed symmetric quantization is a practical third option that combines the runtime efficiency of symmetric quantization with the flexibility of asymmetric quantization, offering improved accuracy at few-bit precision for LLM inference without computational overhead.

title: Central Tendency Bias in Human Selection of AI-Generated Design Variations
comment: Accepted at the 2026 Human-AI Interaction and Experience Design (HAXD 2026) Conference
summary: Image-generation AI systems increasingly support creative work by producing multiple design variations for users to evaluate and select. In such human-AI co-creation workflows, selection becomes a critical stage where human judgment guides AI-generated possibilities toward final outcomes. While presenting multiple alternatives is intended to encourage exploration, the simultaneous multi-option presentation may introduce systematic biases in human decision making. Drawing on ensemble perception theory, we investigate whether these interfaces induce central tendency bias-the tendency to favor options closer to the center of a design set. We conducted a controlled experiment manipulating the variance of design sets (high vs. low) and measured participants' selections in both aesthetic preference and representativeness tasks. Results show that higher variance increases the selection of center-proximal designs across both tasks. These findings suggest that multi-variation interfaces in image-generation AI systems may constrain selection diversity, revealing a potential tension between diversity in generated outputs and diversity in human selection outcomes.

AI.tldr: When image-generation AI presents multiple design variations simultaneously, higher visual variance among options biases users toward selecting designs near the perceptual center of the set—a central tendency bias—potentially undermining the diversity benefits of generating multiple alternatives.
AI.motivation: Image-generation AI systems commonly present multiple design variations for user selection, but the simultaneous multi-option display format may introduce systematic biases in human decision-making, particularly central tendency bias from ensemble perception. The authors aim to investigate whether and how the variance of presented design sets influences which options users select.
AI.method: A controlled experiment with two conditions: high-variance vs. low-variance design sets. Participants performed selection tasks across two contexts—aesthetic preference judgments and representativeness judgments. The dependent measure was the likelihood of selecting designs closer to the perceptual center of the presented set.
AI.result: Higher variance in design sets significantly increased the selection of center-proximal designs in both the aesthetic preference and representativeness tasks, confirming the presence of central tendency bias in multi-variation interfaces.
AI.conclusion: Multi-variation presentation interfaces in image-generation AI systems may inadvertently constrain selection diversity through central tendency bias, revealing a tension between the diversity of AI-generated outputs and the diversity of human selections. This has implications for the design of co-creative human-AI workflows.

title: The Patchwork Problem in LLM-Generated Code
summary: LLM-generated code often compiles, passes tests, and appears correct, yet breaks once deployed. The root cause is frequently structural rather than logical. A generated endpoint references configuration keys never declared in the project, an import targets a package that does not exist in any registry, or a new route omits the authentication guard applied to every sibling endpoint. Each patch is locally valid but globally incoherent, and standard CI toolchains rarely surface these failures. As LLM-powered coding tools see widespread adoption, this blind spot poses a growing risk to software quality. We call this the \textbf{patchwork problem}. This paper formalizes structural coherence as consistency invariants over graph representations of repository artifacts, including import, call, dependency, configuration, schema, resource, control-flow, and routing graphs, and introduces an eight-category failure taxonomy distinguishing defects specific to LLM generation from those merely amplified by it. We present a hybrid verification framework that delegates to mature static analysis tools where they already excel and deploys purpose-built detectors for cross-cutting invariants underserved by existing toolchains, targeting provable constraint violations rather than heuristic pattern matching. Empirical evaluation across two frontier models under four prompting strategies reveals that the vast majority of structural failures evade type checking, testing, and SAST entirely, and that failure patterns diverge qualitatively between models in ways that challenge model-agnostic mitigation strategies. External validation on real-world AI-generated repositories confirms that these failures are not artifacts of controlled experimentation but are prevalent wherever LLMs write code with minimal human oversight.

AI.tldr: LLM-generated code suffers from the "patchwork problem" — locally valid but globally incoherent code patches that break due to structural inconsistencies across project artifacts. The paper formalizes structural coherence via graph invariants, introduces an eight-category failure taxonomy, proposes a hybrid verification framework combining static analysis with purpose-built detectors, and empirically demonstrates that most structural failures evade existing CI toolchains.
AI.motivation: LLM coding tools produce individually correct code patches that fail in deployment due to cross-cutting structural inconsistencies (e.g., referencing undeclared config keys, importing non-existent packages, omitting auth guards). Standard CI pipelines — type checking, testing, SAST — systematically miss these globally incoherent but locally valid failures, creating a growing software quality risk as LLM adoption scales.
AI.method: The authors (1) formalize structural coherence as consistency invariants over eight graph representations of repository artifacts (import, call, dependency, configuration, schema, resource, control-flow, routing graphs); (2) define an eight-category taxonomy distinguishing LLM-specific defects from LLM-amplified ones; (3) propose a hybrid verification framework that combines mature static analysis tools with custom detectors for cross-cutting invariants, targeting provable constraint violations rather than heuristic patterns; and (4) evaluate across two frontier models under four prompting strategies, with external validation on real-world AI-generated repositories.
AI.result: The vast majority of structural failures completely evade type checking, testing, and SAST. Failure patterns diverge qualitatively between models, challenging model-agnostic mitigation approaches. External validation confirmed these failures are prevalent in real-world AI-generated repositories, not merely experimental artifacts.
AI.conclusion: The patchwork problem represents a critical blind spot in LLM code generation that existing toolchains cannot address. Structural coherence verification requires dedicated, graph-based invariant checking beyond current CI practices, and model-specific failure profiles suggest mitigation must be tailored per model rather than applied uniformly.

title: Proof-of-Continuity: A Temporal Model for Authority Propagation in Distributed Systems and AI Agents
summary:
Proof-of-Possession authorization models derive authority from the possession of artifacts such as tokens, credentials, or capabilities. This paper argues that possession is insufficient for discrete execution chains, whether they span multiple services or occur as separated steps within the same machine, because it does not guarantee preservation of the causal relationship between the origin of a request and the authority exercised at later steps. We introduce Proof-of-Continuity, a minimal authority-propagation discipline for the Provenance Identity Continuity (PIC) model, in which each execution step must be causally linked to the previous step and may only propagate a non-expansive subset of the authority received from the origin. It introduces Proof of Relationship, a single-hop causal primitive whose transitive composition is Proof-of-Continuity; these complement Proof-of-Possession rather than replace it. Under this model, the confused deputy condition cannot be satisfied as valid model behavior: any privilege exercised at a later step must already be present in the origin authority context. This is directly relevant to distributed systems and AI agents, where executors invoke tools and downstream services while holding multiple authority sources, so that the same authority/causality mismatch recurs across service boundaries. Under Proof-of-Continuity these sources may be carried together but are never merged into a combined authority, since each step is authorized only against the authority context of the lineage that caused it.
  This paper concerns authorization propagation rather than authentication: identity and authentication mechanisms such as OIDC, verifiable credentials, wallets, and workload identity remain complementary mechanisms for establishing the origin, while Proof-of-Continuity addresses how authority propagates after that origin exists.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Proof-of-Continuity (PoC), a new authorization discipline ensuring that authority across multi-step execution chains remains causally linked to the original request, preventing confused deputy attacks where downstream steps exercise privileges not present at the origin.
AI.motivation: Proof-of-Possession is insufficient for discrete execution chains spanning multiple services or steps because it fails to preserve the causal relationship between a request's origin and the authority exercised at later steps. This gap enables confused deputy vulnerabilities, particularly relevant in distributed systems and AI agent architectures where executors hold multiple authority sources and invoke downstream services.
AI.method: The authors introduce the Provenance Identity Continuity (PIC) model with Proof-of-Continuity as its core discipline. Each execution step must be causally linked to the previous step and may only propagate a non-expansive subset of the authority received from the origin. Proof of Relationship serves as a single-hop causal primitive, whose transitive composition yields Proof-of-Continuity. These primitives complement Proof-of-Possession rather than replace it, and crucially, multiple authority sources are carried together but never merged.
AI.result: Under the Proof-of-Continuity model, the confused deputy condition cannot be satisfied as valid model behavior: any privilege exercised at a later step must already be present in the origin authority context. Each step is authorized only against the authority context of the specific lineage that caused it, preventing privilege escalation through authority merging across service boundaries.
AI.conclusion: Proof-of-Continuity addresses authorization propagation specifically (not authentication), complementing existing identity mechanisms like OIDC, verifiable credentials, and workload identity. The model provides a minimal authority-propagation discipline that ensures causal integrity across distributed execution chains.

title: Letting the Data Speak: Extracting Keywords from Crowdsourced Collections with AI
summary: Identifying and assigning keywords at scale is a technical, practical, and ethical challenge for crowdsourced collections. This article reports the findings of the "Extracting Keywords from Crowdsourced Collections" project, which used the Their Finest Hour Online Archive, a crowdsourced Second World War digital collection hosted by the University of Oxford, as a case study. The project evaluated three Natural Language Processing approaches to automate keyword extraction: Named Entity Recognition, Keyword Extraction, and Topic Modelling. It tested these approaches across a range of artificial intelligence techniques, from traditional statistical methods to modern GenAI neural networks. Our quantitative and qualitative findings indicate that Natural Language Processing approaches offer real potential for keyword extraction at scale in crowdsourced collections, but that no single method offers a complete solution and that model choice significantly shapes results. We argue that in crowdsourced collections, where metadata is the direct product of engagement with living contributors, automated keyword extraction raises distinct stewardship responsibilities that must be addressed alongside technical performance. Open-weight, extractive models emerge from our evaluation as best placed to support responsible deployment, while generative AI, despite its abstractive potential, introduces accountability risks that anyone managing crowdsourced collections should weigh carefully.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates three NLP approaches (NER, keyword extraction, topic modelling) for automated keyword generation in crowdsourced digital archives, finding that while NLP offers real potential, no single method suffices, and the choice of model significantly shapes results. It argues that crowdsourced collections carry distinct ethical stewardship responsibilities, with open-weight extractive models best supporting responsible deployment over generative AI.
AI.motivation: Manually identifying and assigning keywords at scale in crowdsourced collections is technically, practically, and ethically challenging. The project aims to explore whether NLP can automate this process responsibly, using the Their Finest Hour Online Archive as a case study.
AI.method: The project evaluated three NLP approaches — Named Entity Recognition (NER), Keyword Extraction, and Topic Modelling — across a spectrum of AI techniques ranging from traditional statistical methods to modern generative neural networks (GenAI). Both quantitative and qualitative evaluations were conducted on the Their Finest Hour digital archive.
AI.result: NLP approaches demonstrate real potential for keyword extraction at scale, but no single method offers a complete solution. Model choice significantly shapes results. Open-weight, extractive models emerged as best suited for responsible deployment, while generative AI introduced accountability risks.
AI.conclusion: Automated keyword extraction in crowdsourced collections raises distinct stewardship responsibilities because metadata is produced through direct engagement with living contributors. These ethical considerations must be addressed alongside technical performance. Open-weight extractive models are recommended as the most responsible path forward.

title: Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench: Testing the Limits of Agents on Long-Horizon Terminal Tasks with Dense Reward-Based Grading
summary: AI agents have become capable of autonomously completing short, well-specified tasks. However, existing terminal benchmarks largely focus on simple problems that finish within minutes and are evaluated only by their final outcome. This setup overlooks intermediate progress and partial solutions, yielding sparse reward signals and an incomplete picture of agent capability. We introduce Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench, a terminal benchmark of 46 long-horizon tasks spanning nine categories, including experiment reproduction, software engineering, multimodal analysis, interactive games, and scientific computing. Each task follows a Terminal-Bench-style setup with a reference solution or simulation engine, but is further decomposed into fine-grained graded subtasks. This design enables dense intermediate rewards and partial credit, allowing evaluation to capture not only whether an agent reaches the final goal, but also how far it progresses on open-ended workflows. Tasks in Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench typically require hundreds of episodes and minutes to hours of execution, stressing long-horizon planning, long-context management, and iterative debugging rather than one-shot problem solving. We evaluate 15 frontier models and find that agents consume on average 9.9M tokens per task, with roughly 231 episodes and 85.3 minutes of execution time per run, making Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench more demanding than prior terminal-based benchmarks. Even the strongest tested model achieves 15.2% pass@1 at a partial-reward threshold of 0.95 and 10.9% at a perfect-reward threshold of 1.0, while the mean pass rate across models is 4.3% and 1.7% under the two thresholds, respectively. These results reveal headroom for improvement. We further analyze failure modes and error patterns, and release Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench to support future progress on long-horizon terminal agents.

AI.tldr: Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench introduces a benchmark of 46 long-horizon terminal tasks with fine-grained subtask decomposition, enabling dense intermediate rewards. Even the best model achieves only 15.2% pass@1 at a 0.95 partial-reward threshold, revealing significant headroom in long-horizon terminal agents.
AI.motivation: Existing terminal benchmarks focus on short, well-specified tasks evaluated only by final outcomes, yielding sparse reward signals and failing to capture intermediate progress or partial solutions. This limits understanding of agent capabilities on complex, open-ended workflows requiring sustained planning and execution.
AI.method: The authors construct a benchmark of 46 tasks across nine categories (experiment reproduction, software engineering, multimodal analysis, interactive games, scientific computing, etc.). Each task includes a reference solution or simulation engine and is decomposed into fine-grained graded subtasks. This provides dense intermediate rewards and partial credit. Evaluation spans 15 frontier models, measuring pass@1 at partial-reward (0.95) and perfect-reward (1.0) thresholds, along with token consumption, episodes, and execution time.
AI.result: Agents average 9.9M tokens, 231 episodes, and 85.3 minutes per task. The strongest model achieves 15.2% pass@1 at the 0.95 threshold and 10.9% at 1.0. Mean pass rates across all models are 4.3% (0.95 threshold) and 1.7% (1.0 threshold). These results substantially underperform typical short-horizon benchmarks, confirming the difficulty of the benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench reveals a large gap in current agent capabilities for long-horizon terminal tasks, particularly in planning, long-context management, and iterative debugging. The benchmark, with its dense reward structure, is released to facilitate future research on persistent, multi-step terminal agents.

title: Sticky Routing: Training MoE Models for Memory-Efficient Inference
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models activate only a sparse subset of experts per token, yet consecutive tokens frequently activate different experts -- causing constant weight swapping between slow storage and fast memory on edge devices. Existing remedies are either system-level (caching heuristics) or post-hoc (router fine-tuning), leaving the root cause unchanged during pretraining. We propose StickyMoE, a differentiable routing consistency loss that penalises abrupt expert switches between adjacent tokens, encouraging the router to maintain the same expert assignment across semantically coherent spans. StickyMoE requires no architectural changes, adds a single hyperparameter lambda, and unlike post-hoc methods, allows expert representations and routing decisions to co-adapt from the first training step. Experiments on small-scale MoE language models show that StickyMoE reduces the expert switch rate by up to 60% with less than 4% perplexity degradation, Pareto-dominating post-hoc fine-tuning on the quality-locality frontier. Routing temporal locality is most efficiently instilled at training time.

AI.tldr: StickyMoE introduces a differentiable training-time loss that penalizes abrupt expert switches between adjacent tokens in MoE models, reducing switch rate by up to 60% with minimal perplexity degradation, outperforming post-hoc methods.
AI.motivation: MoE models suffer from constant weight swapping between slow storage and fast memory on edge devices because consecutive tokens frequently activate different experts. Existing solutions are either system-level caching heuristics or post-hoc router fine-tuning, neither of which addresses the root cause during pretraining.
AI.method: StickyMoE proposes a differentiable routing consistency loss that penalizes abrupt expert switches between adjacent tokens. This encourages the router to maintain consistent expert assignments across semantically coherent spans. It requires no architectural changes, adds only a single hyperparameter λ, and allows expert representations and routing decisions to co-adapt from the first training step.
AI.result: On small-scale MoE language models, StickyMoE reduces the expert switch rate by up to 60% with less than 4% perplexity degradation, and Pareto-dominates post-hoc fine-tuning on the quality-locality frontier.
AI.conclusion: Routing temporal locality is most efficiently instilled at training time rather than through post-hoc interventions, and StickyMoE provides a simple, effective mechanism to achieve this with negligible performance cost.

title: Privacy Detective: A Narrative Game that Cultivates Student Developers' Privacy Awareness by Harnessing Legal Documents
summary: Developers' choices about what data a system collects, how it is used and shared, and what defaults govern user choices directly shape users' privacy experiences. Yet, developers often make problematic privacy-related design decisions without realizing the potential consequences. We introduce Privacy Detective, a narrative investigation game that leverages real-world legal documents to train developers' privacy awareness. In the game, players search for privacy violation evidence derived from legal documents and organize this evidence into privacy violation reports using curated templates. We evaluated Privacy Detective in a between-subjects study with student developers, comparing it against a baseline in which participants read raw FTC legal documents. Participants in the game condition identified more true violations than the baseline group, flagged fewer non-issues, and provided more complete justifications for the violations they reported.

AI.tldr: Privacy Detective is a narrative investigation game that uses real FTC legal documents to train developers' privacy awareness. In a between-subjects study, participants playing the game identified more true privacy violations, flagged fewer non-issues, and provided more complete justifications compared to those who simply read raw legal documents.
AI.motivation: Developers frequently make privacy-related design decisions (data collection, usage, sharing, defaults) that shape user privacy experiences, yet they often do so without recognizing the potential consequences of problematic choices. There is a need for effective training tools that improve developers' privacy awareness using real-world legal contexts.
AI.method: The authors designed Privacy Detective, a narrative investigation game where players search for privacy violation evidence derived from FTC legal documents and organize findings into violation reports using curated templates. They evaluated the game via a between-subjects study with student developers, comparing game-based learning against a baseline condition of reading raw FTC legal documents.
AI.result: Participants in the game condition outperformed the baseline group across multiple dimensions: they identified more true privacy violations, flagged fewer non-issues (false positives), and provided more complete justifications for the violations they reported.
AI.conclusion: A narrative investigation game grounded in real legal documents can effectively train developers' privacy awareness, outperforming passive reading of legal materials. This gamified approach holds promise for improving privacy-sensitive decision-making among software developers.

title: SCATE: Learning to Supervise Coding Agents for Cost-Effective Test Generation
summary: While autonomous coding agents have significantly advanced automated test generation, they remain fundamentally limited by lazy generation, a phenomenon where agents prematurely terminate tasks and systematically avoid complex programmatic logic, resulting in inadequate code coverage. Currently, mitigating this premature termination requires continuous human-in-the-loop supervision. This heavy reliance on human intuition creates a bottleneck that negates the efficiency gains of automated generation. We propose SCATE, a framework for adaptive, automated supervision of coding agents that replaces human intervention during test generation. By formulating supervision as a contextual bandit problem, SCATE learns to select the most promising testing actions based on the current coverage and class testability metrics, maximizing coverage gains while minimizing wasted generation effort. Our empirical evaluation demonstrates that SCATE integrates seamlessly with different coding agents. When applied to GEMINI-CLI, it achieves 32.3% higher line coverage and 30.9% higher branch coverage than the agent-only baseline. A comparison with CLAUDE CODE confirms the framework dynamically adapts its policy to optimize each agent's unique strengths. SCATE also consistently outperforms state-of-the-art non-agentic approaches across all metrics.

AI.tldr: SCATE introduces an adaptive, automated supervision framework for coding agents that formulates test generation as a contextual bandit problem. It learns to select optimal testing actions based on coverage and testability metrics, eliminating the need for human-in-the-loop supervision. SCATE achieves 32.3% higher line coverage and 30.9% higher branch coverage when integrated with GEMINI-CLI, outperforming both agent-only baselines and state-of-the-art non-agentic approaches.
AI.motivation: Autonomous coding agents suffer from "lazy generation" — prematurely terminating tasks and avoiding complex programmatic logic — leading to inadequate code coverage. Current mitigation requires continuous human supervision, which creates a bottleneck that negates the efficiency gains of automation. The authors aim to eliminate this human-in-the-loop dependency entirely.
AI.method: SCATE formulates the supervision of coding agents as a contextual bandit problem. It learns an adaptive policy that selects the most promising testing actions at each step, conditioned on current code coverage metrics and class testability features. The objective is to maximize cumulative coverage gains while minimizing wasted generation effort. The framework is designed to be agent-agnostic, integrating seamlessly with different coding agents.
AI.result: When applied to GEMINI-CLI, SCATE achieves 32.3% higher line coverage and 30.9% higher branch coverage over the agent-only baseline. It also adapts its policy dynamically to optimize each agent's unique strengths, as confirmed through integration with CLAUDE CODE. SCATE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art non-agentic approaches across all evaluated metrics.
AI.conclusion: SCATE demonstrates that contextual bandit-based automated supervision can effectively replace human-in-the-loop oversight for coding agents in test generation. The framework's agent-agnostic design enables broad applicability, and its learned adaptive policies yield substantial coverage improvements while eliminating the human bottleneck.

title: SeedSmith: LLM-Driven Seed Synthesis for Directed Fuzzing
summary: Directed fuzzing steers fuzzers toward user-defined sink functions to identify vulnerabilities, but it frequently fails to trigger crashes even after long campaigns. We identify two challenges that prevent directed fuzzers from exposing crashes: incomplete static analysis of indirect calls, which leaves reachable paths invisible to distance-based guidance, and lack of semantic guidance for crash preconditions, which blind mutation cannot satisfy within practical time budgets. A natural intervention point is the initial seed corpus: seeds that encode the right control-flow path and satisfy key crash preconditions shift fuzzing from blind exploration to local refinement. Existing seed generation approaches address neither: grammar-based and format-driven methods produce structurally valid inputs with no sink awareness, while LLM-based methods either lack sink targeting or inherit static analysis limitations through one-shot prompting. We present SeedSmith, an agentic LLM pipeline that replicates a security analyst's workflow: starting from a sink, it iteratively explores the codebase, resolves indirect calls, identifies crash preconditions, and synthesizes concrete inputs that satisfy them. Because SeedSmith operates as a seed generation front-end, its seeds are fuzzer-agnostic and improve any downstream mutation-based fuzzer without modification. On Magma, fuzzers using SeedSmith seeds achieve geometric mean crash-time speedups of 11.51 times (AFL++) to 14.66 times (AFLGo) over default seeds. On ARVO, SeedSmith enables fuzzers to trigger 16 previously unreachable bugs spanning 10 projects with diverse input formats.

AI.tldr: SeedSmith is an LLM-based agentic pipeline that generates fuzzing seeds by mimicking a security analyst's workflow: it iteratively explores codebases from a sink, resolves indirect calls, identifies crash preconditions, and synthesizes inputs satisfying them. As a seed-generation front-end, it provides fuzzer-agnostic seeds that deliver 11.5–14.7× geometric mean crash-time speedups on Magma and trigger 16 previously unreachable bugs across 10 projects on ARVO.
AI.motivation: Directed fuzzing fails to trigger crashes due to two challenges: (1) incomplete static analysis of indirect calls leaves reachable paths invisible to distance-based guidance, and (2) lack of semantic guidance for crash preconditions means blind mutation cannot satisfy them within practical time. Existing seed generation (grammar-based, format-driven, LLM-based) addresses neither sink awareness nor indirect call resolution.
AI.method: SeedSmith is an agentic LLM pipeline that replicates a security analyst's workflow: starting from a user-defined sink, it iteratively explores the codebase, resolves indirect calls through iterative code analysis, identifies crash preconditions, and synthesizes concrete inputs that satisfy those preconditions. It operates as a seed generation front-end, making its seeds fuzzer-agnostic and compatible with any downstream mutation-based fuzzer without modification.
AI.result: On Magma, fuzzers using SeedSmith seeds achieved geometric mean crash-time speedups of 11.51× (AFL++) and 14.66× (AFLGo) over default seeds. On ARVO, SeedSmith enabled fuzzers to trigger 16 previously unreachable bugs across 10 projects with diverse input formats.
AI.conclusion: SeedSmith demonstrates that an agentic LLM approach to seed generation — one that resolves indirect calls and identifies crash preconditions through iterative codebase exploration — can significantly improve directed fuzzing effectiveness, exposing previously unreachable vulnerabilities across diverse targets.

title: All Explanations are Wrong, But Many Are Useful: Exploring the Rashomon Explanation Set with Large Language Models
summary: Explaining machine-learning models is increasingly important for decision-making and consumer trust, yet it is widely believed to come at a cost: existing Explainable AI (XAI) methods suffer from a persistent accuracy-explainability trade-off. We argue that this trade-off is not fundamental, but an artifact of treating explanation and prediction as separate objectives; when properly coupled, they become complementary, so that equipping a model to explain itself improves, rather than degrades, its accuracy. We introduce the Rashomon Explanation paradigm, which builds a set of faithful, prediction-guiding explanations rather than a single one, and prove that this set is generally non-empty and that explanation fidelity bounds the performance of the models it guides. To explore this set, we propose RashomonLLM, an Explanation-Prediction-Reflection agentic workflow that generates explanations in natural language by iteratively aligning them with predictions, and we prove it converges and recovers the full set. Across customer-churn classification, clinical survival regression, and industrial click-through prediction on large-scale live-streaming logs, RashomonLLM significantly outperforms state-of-the-art prediction and XAI baselines on both accuracy and explanation quality, with gains driven by explanation fidelity and robust to distribution shifts, temporal splits, and seeds. Our framework thus advances business performance while laying the groundwork for consumer trust.

AI.tldr: The paper challenges the widely-held accuracy-explainability trade-off in XAI, arguing it stems from treating prediction and explanation as separate objectives. The authors propose the Rashomon Explanation paradigm—generating a set of faithful, prediction-guiding explanations—and RashomonLLM, an agentic Explanation-Prediction-Reflection workflow using LLMs that iteratively aligns explanations with predictions. They prove theoretical guarantees (non-emptiness, convergence, fidelity bounds) and demonstrate superior performance over baselines on churn classification, survival regression, and click-through prediction tasks, with robustness to distribution shifts.
AI.motivation: The work is motivated by the persistent and widely-accepted accuracy-explainability trade-off in Explainable AI, where improving interpretability allegedly degrades predictive performance. The authors contend this trade-off is not fundamental but rather an artifact of decoupling explanation from prediction. They aim to demonstrate that when explanation and prediction are properly coupled, they become complementary, enabling models that both perform better and explain themselves faithfully.
AI.method: The paper introduces two core contributions: (1) The Rashomon Explanation paradigm, which constructs a set of faithful, prediction-guiding explanations (rather than a single one), with proofs that this set is non-empty and that explanation fidelity bounds model performance. (2) RashomonLLM, an agentic workflow with three iterative stages—Explanation (generating natural-language explanations via LLMs), Prediction (using explanations to guide predictions), and Reflection (aligning explanations with predictions for fidelity). The authors prove convergence and full-set recovery of the Rashomon set under this workflow.
AI.result: RashomonLLM significantly outperformed state-of-the-art prediction and XAI baselines on three diverse tasks: customer-churn classification, clinical survival regression, and industrial click-through prediction on large-scale live-streaming logs. Gains were observed on both predictive accuracy and explanation quality metrics, driven by explanation fidelity. The results proved robust to distribution shifts, temporal splits, and random seeds.
AI.conclusion: The accuracy-explainability trade-off is not fundamental and can be reversed by coupling explanation with prediction. The Rashomon Explanation framework and RashomonLLM demonstrate that faithful, prediction-guiding explanations improve both model accuracy and interpretability, advancing business performance while establishing foundations for consumer trust.

title: A Formalization of the Mean-Field Derivation of the Vlasov Equation: AI-Assisted Lean Formalization as a Strategy Game
comment: 26 pages, 4 figures. Lean 4 development, blueprint site, and agent logs: https://github.com/Hydrodynamical/Vlasov_Meanfield_Formalization
summary: We formalize a research result in the Lean 4 proof assistant by having a mathematician direct an AI system, and frame the activity as a formalization game. The objective is to turn a LaTeX document into Lean. The game is won when the development compiles, contains no sorry, and a machine check shows the target theorems rest on Lean's foundational axioms alone. Reuse is a second check, by a definition we introduce: whether the development yields a self-contained layer of general mathematics the wider library could absorb. The case study is a complete, axiom-clean formalization of well-posedness for the nonlinear Vlasov equation via Dobrushin's mean-field route -- existence, uniqueness, the stability estimate and mean-field limit, and a short-window superposition principle (weak solutions are Lagrangian). The human's role was to direct, not to write proofs: to scope the definitions, steer the decompositions, and triage the library's gaps; the AI agent executed. The formalization certifies the proof of each statement as written; whether the written statement is the intended theorem stays the mathematician's judgment. The optimal-transport machinery that fell out of the build (in particular, properties of the Wasserstein-1 metric and the Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality theorem) separates into a self-contained layer that compiles against Mathlib alone: about a sixth of the development (49 of 299 declarations), behind a 22-declaration interface with no reverse dependency. The headline theorems ran in about a week, the full development in about a month. We report the quantitative claims as observations of one game, not as general laws. The game's rules name no particular system, so the methodological framing is meant to outlast the tools of any one run.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a case study of formalizing the well-posedness of the nonlinear Vlasov equation in Lean 4, using a human mathematician to direct an AI system within a "formalization game" framework. The complete formalization — including existence, uniqueness, stability, mean-field limit, and superposition principle — was achieved in about a month, with a reusable Wasserstein metric layer (49 of 299 declarations) emerging as a self-contained contribution to Mathlib.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate and evaluate a human-AI collaborative paradigm for large-scale formalization, where a mathematician directs an AI agent rather than writing proofs manually. The authors aim to establish a reusable methodological framing (the "formalization game") that outlasts any specific tool, and to produce a substantial, axiom-clean formalization that yields self-contained mathematical layers reusable by the broader proof-assistant library.
AI.method: The authors frame formalization as a game: convert a LaTeX document into Lean 4 such that the development compiles, contains no `sorry`, and all theorems rest only on Lean's foundational axioms. A human mathematician scopes definitions, steers proof decompositions, and triages library gaps; an AI agent executes the actual proof writing. Reuse is measured by a novel criterion: whether the development yields a self-contained layer with a clean interface (no reverse dependencies) that Mathlib could absorb. The case study targets Dobrushin's mean-field route for the nonlinear Vlasov equation.
AI.result: The complete formalization succeeded in about one month (headline theorems in ~1 week). The Wasserstein-1 metric and Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality machinery separated into a self-contained layer of 49 declarations behind a 22-declaration interface with zero reverse dependencies — roughly one-sixth of the total 299-declaration development. All results compile against Mathlib alone with no `sorry`. The authors emphasize results are observations of a single run, not general claims.
AI.conclusion: The formalization game framework is viable for producing large-scale, axiom-clean formalizations with human-AI collaboration. The decomposition into reusable library layers is a meaningful quality metric beyond mere theorem verification. The methodological framing is tool-agnostic by design, intended to persist beyond the specific AI system used in this study.

title: Reward Transport: Property Control in Flow Matching via Noise-Space Alignment
summary: The coupling in flow matching -- the rule pairing noise vectors with data points -- is typically treated as a computational choice. We show that this coupling can instead serve as an alignment interface: by matching noise and data according to a target molecular property, it embeds controllable structure directly into the learned flow field. Building on this view, we introduce Reward Transport, which uses optimal transport coupling at training time to align a scalar noise-space coordinate with molecular rewards; at inference, varying this coordinate steers the generated distribution without requiring an oracle, reward model, gradient guidance, or additional computation. In the coupling-preserving limit, thresholding this coordinate recovers the Cross-Entropy Method's truncated reward distribution, providing a principled, continuously adjustable distribution-level control knob. Empirically, on ZINC-250K and GuacaMol, sweeping the scalar induces monotone control of logP and consistent QED control over its operating range; most tellingly, the same knob produces opposite structural responses for different targets, growing molecules for logP but shrinking them for QED, which rules out a generic size bias. The interface is complementary to classifier-free guidance and conditional flow matching, while a negative result under epsilon-prediction diffusion clarifies where coupling-level alignment is structurally absent. Code: https://github.com/KehanGuo2/reward-transport

AI.tldr: Reward Transport uses optimal transport coupling in flow matching to align noise-space coordinates with molecular rewards, enabling controllable generation without oracle or gradient guidance. Thresholding the coordinate recovers CEM's truncated distribution, and sweeping it enables monotonic control of properties like logP and QED.
AI.motivation: In flow matching, the coupling between noise and data is typically treated as a mere computational design choice. The authors argue it can serve as an "alignment interface" to embed controllable structure directly into the learned flow field, enabling property-guided molecular generation without inference-time overhead.
AI.method: Reward Transport uses optimal transport coupling during training to align a scalar noise-space coordinate with a target molecular reward. At inference, varying this coordinate steers the generated distribution. The method is analyzed in the coupling-preserving limit, showing that thresholding recovers the Cross-Entropy Method's truncated reward distribution. The approach is complementary to classifier-free guidance and conditional flow matching.
AI.result: On ZINC-250K and GuacaMol benchmarks, sweeping the scalar coordinate induces monotonic control of logP and consistent QED control across the operating range. Crucially, the same knob produces opposite structural responses (growing molecules for logP, shrinking for QED), ruling out generic size bias. A negative result under epsilon-prediction diffusion clarifies where coupling-level alignment is structurally absent.
AI.conclusion: The coupling in flow matching is not merely a computational choice but a principled alignment interface. Reward Transport provides a continuously adjustable, distribution-level control knob for molecular generation that requires no additional models or computation at inference, and is both theoretically grounded and empirically validated.

title: HALO: Hybrid Adaptive Latent Reasoning for Language Models
summary: We study how to improve a frozen pretrained language model with a small amount of adaptive extra computation. A simple approach is to add additional refinement steps on top of the backbone hidden states, but fixed extra refinement can be wasteful: a one-step refinement head may be too weak, while forcing a second full-sequence refinement step everywhere can increase compute without improving transfer. We introduce HALO, a hybrid adaptive latent-refinement method that combines a coarse refinement stage with selective second-stage latent refinement on a subset of tokens chosen by token scoring and monotonic token halting. On the main public benchmark comparison built from MMLU-Pro and GPQA-Diamond, HALO achieves the best overall average among the paper-facing methods, outperforming the frozen backbone, fixed-1, and fixed-2. Internal analysis further shows that HALO reaches nearly the same token-accuracy level as fixed-2 while using fewer average applied refine steps than fixed-1 and far fewer than fixed-2. These results suggest that the key advantage is not simply more refinement, but a better allocation of refinement: HALO achieves the strongest paper-facing result while also using less measured controller compute than either fixed baseline.

AI.tldr: HALO introduces a hybrid adaptive latent-refinement method for frozen pretrained language models that combines coarse refinement with selective second-stage latent refinement on a subset of tokens, using token scoring and monotonic halting to allocate compute efficiently, outperforming fixed-refinement baselines while using fewer refinement steps.
AI.motivation: Fixed extra refinement on frozen LMs is wasteful: a single refinement head may be too weak, while uniformly applying a second refinement step everywhere increases compute without commensurate transfer gains. The need is for adaptive allocation of refinement compute.
AI.method: HALO (Hybrid Adaptive Latent-refinement) combines two stages: (1) a coarse refinement stage applied broadly, and (2) a selective second-stage latent refinement applied only to a subset of tokens. Token selection is governed by a token scoring mechanism and a monotonic token halting criterion, which together determine where additional refinement is warranted, avoiding unnecessary computation on tokens that do not benefit.
AI.result: On MMLU-Pro and GPQA-Diamond benchmarks, HALO achieves the best overall average among compared methods, surpassing the frozen backbone, fixed-1, and fixed-2 baselines. Internal analysis shows HALO reaches nearly the token-accuracy level of fixed-2 while using fewer average refine steps than fixed-1 and far fewer than fixed-2, indicating superior compute allocation.
AI.conclusion: The key advantage is not simply more refinement but better allocation of refinement compute. HALO achieves the strongest results while using less measured controller compute than either fixed baseline, demonstrating that adaptive, selective latent refinement is more effective than uniform fixed-depth alternatives.

title: Configurable AI Coding Assistants: Designing For Developers Who Like to Be in Control
comment: 9 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables, accepted at FSE Companion'26 [HumanAISE]
summary:
AI coding assistants are now widely used in professional development, yet they offer only limited ways for developers to control how they behave. In this paper, we investigate what kinds of configurations experienced developers want in coding assistants, how they prioritize different types of configuration needs, and which interface mechanisms they prefer. We first synthesize product documentation and prior research on trust and personalization to compile a list of 33 configuration options, grouped into four categories: Code suggestions, System & policies, Human-assistant interaction, and Users & their personal context. We then conduct a survey with 56 professional developers and 7 design sessions in which participants arrange configurations into their perfect control board and talk about their needs and experiences in more depth.
  Developers report strong interest in configurability: 72.6% of usefulness ratings are positive, while only around a third indicate that the corresponding configuration is known to participants in their tools. Demand is particularly high for task-related controls such as minimum confidence thresholds, visibility of suggestion quality, and response length, whereas many persona-related configurations are seen as unnecessary. In this paper, we discuss the implications for designing more unified and discoverable configuration surfaces for future coding assistants

AI.tldr: A survey and design study with 56 professional developers reveals strong demand for greater configurability in AI coding assistants, particularly for task-related controls (confidence thresholds, suggestion quality visibility, response length), while many persona-related configurations are deemed unnecessary. Currently, only ~1/3 of useful configurations are known to be available in existing tools.
AI.motivation: AI coding assistants offer limited user control despite widespread professional adoption. The paper seeks to understand what configurations experienced developers actually want, how they prioritize them, and which interface mechanisms they prefer—addressing a gap between existing tool capabilities and developer needs.
AI.method: (1) Synthesized product documentation and prior research on trust and personalization to compile 33 configuration options across four categories: Code suggestions, System & policies, Human-assistant interaction, and Users & their personal context. (2) Conducted a survey with 56 professional developers. (3) Ran 7 design sessions where participants arranged configurations into their ideal control board and discussed needs in depth.
AI.result: 72.6% of usefulness ratings were positive, but only ~1/3 of configurations were known to exist in participants' current tools. Task-related controls (minimum confidence thresholds, suggestion quality visibility, response length) showed highest demand. Persona-related configurations were largely seen as unnecessary.
AI.conclusion: Future coding assistants should feature more unified and discoverable configuration surfaces, prioritizing task-related controls over persona-based ones. The findings provide actionable design implications for building developer-centric AI tool interfaces.

title: Loop-Based Slicing and Input-Driven Concretization: An Empirical Study of Termination and Non-Termination Analysis
summary: Termination and non-termination are fundamental correctness properties, but verifying them in real-world C programs remains difficult because loop interactions and nondeterministic inputs challenge existing analyzers. This paper presents an empirical study of lightweight, tool-independent source-level preprocessing for (non-)termination analysis. We implement FocusTNT, a C front end that applies loop-based slicing to isolate loop-level obligations and input-driven concretization to specialize nondeterministic inputs into selected input-scenario variants. We evaluate slicing, concretization, and their combination across six analyzers on 117 C/C++ programs derived from real-world non-termination bugs and their fixes. The study examines effects on analyzer correctness, complementarity with original-program analysis, loop-level diagnostics, feature sensitivity, runtime behavior, semantic scope, and integration potential. Results show that preprocessing is not uniformly beneficial: its impact depends on the analyzer, task, and program features. Slicing provides conservative structural isolation and localization, whereas concretization can improve detectability for selected scenarios but narrows semantic scope and may increase analysis effort. Their combination is not consistently additive. Overall, the results support adaptive use of preprocessing as a complement to original-program analysis and provide practical guidance to application developers interpreting verification outcomes and tool developers improving analyzer robustness.

AI.tldr: An empirical study of source-level preprocessing (loop-based slicing and input-driven concretization) for termination/non-termination analysis of C programs, evaluating their effects across six analyzers on 117 real-world bug cases. Results show preprocessing impact is context-dependent, not uniformly beneficial, and supports adaptive, complementary use rather than wholesale adoption.
AI.motivation: Verifying termination and non-termination in real-world C programs is difficult due to complex loop interactions and nondeterministic inputs, challenging existing analyzers. The paper aims to empirically assess whether lightweight, tool-independent source-level preprocessing can improve analyzer effectiveness.
AI.method: Implementation of FocusTNT, a C front end applying two preprocessing techniques: (1) loop-based slicing to isolate loop-level obligations, and (2) input-driven concretization to specialize nondeterministic inputs into selected scenario variants. These are evaluated individually and in combination across six analyzers on 117 C/C++ programs from real-world non-termination bugs and their fixes, examining correctness, complementarity, localization, sensitivity, runtime, semantic scope, and integration.
AI.result: Preprocessing is not uniformly beneficial; its impact varies by analyzer, task, and program features. Slicing provides conservative structural isolation and localization. Concretization improves detectability for selected scenarios but narrows semantic scope and may increase analysis effort. Their combination is not consistently additive. Adaptive use as a complement to original-program analysis is supported.
AI.conclusion: The findings support adaptive, context-sensitive use of preprocessing as a complement — not replacement — for original-program analysis, and provide practical guidance for both application developers interpreting verification results and tool developers improving analyzer robustness.

title: RaMark: Radioactive Watermarking for Generated Tabular Data
summary: Recent advances in generative modeling have made generated tabular data a practical solution for privacy-sensitive data sharing, where watermarking enables ownership verification. However, existing watermarking methods fundamentally fail under retraining attacks, in which an adversary retrains a generative model on a watermarked dataset and regenerates high-utility data that no longer carries the watermark. We address this challenge by introducing radioactivity, the property that a watermark remains detectable after generative model retraining, and propose RaMark, a radioactive watermarking method that embeds a sinusoidal dependency as an intrinsic component of the data distribution. By coupling the watermark with the underlying distribution, RaMark ensures that any generative model preserving data utility also has to preserve the watermark. We theoretically show that with high probability removing watermark degrades utility and alters data distribution. Extensive experiments on two real-world tabular datasets, under a large-scale ownership verification setting with $10^5$ independent data owners, demonstrate that RaMark achieves substantially stronger radioactivity than seven state-of-the-art methods and consistently outperforms them against both retraining and data modification attacks.

AI.tldr: RaMark introduces "radioactivity" — watermark persistence after generative model retraining — by embedding a sinusoidal dependency into the data distribution itself, ensuring that any utility-preserving model must retain the watermark. It outperforms seven SOTA methods under retraining and data modification attacks.
AI.motivation: Existing tabular data watermarking methods are vulnerable to retraining attacks, where an adversary retrains a generative model on watermarked data to produce high-utility, unwatermarked data. A fundamentally new approach is needed to ensure watermarks survive such attacks.
AI.method: RaMark embeds a sinusoidal dependency as an intrinsic, non-removable component of the data distribution. This couples the watermark with the underlying distribution so that any generative model preserving data utility must also preserve the watermark. The authors provide theoretical guarantees that removing the watermark with high probability degrades utility and alters the distribution.
AI.result: On two real-world tabular datasets with a large-scale ownership verification setup (10^5 independent data owners), RaMark demonstrates substantially stronger radioactivity than seven state-of-the-art methods and consistently outperforms them against both retraining and data modification attacks.
AI.conclusion: Radioactive watermarking via distribution-coupled sinusoidal embeddings is a viable and robust solution for ownership verification of generated tabular data, with strong theoretical and empirical support.

title: ARCANA: A Reflective Multi-Agent Program Synthesis Framework for ARC-AGI-2 Reasoning
summary: We present ARCANA, a collaborative multi agent framework for solving ARC AGI 2 tasks under strict test time and hardware constraints. ARCANA decomposes each task into iterative perception, hypothesis generation, symbolic execution, and reflective refinement. A perceptual grounding agent builds object centric scene graphs from raw grids, a latent program policy proposes diverse DSL programs, a symbolic executor verifies candidates on demonstrations, and a reflective agent synthesizes failure driven feedback for the next turn. These agents communicate through a shared differentiable blackboard and are scheduled by a learned meta controller. The design combines structured program search with adaptive multi turn correction, improving reasoning efficiency and solution quality on challenging abstract transformation tasks.

AI.tldr: ARCANA is a multi-agent framework for solving ARC AGI-2 tasks that combines iterative perception, program synthesis, symbolic execution, and reflective refinement, coordinated by a learned meta-controller through a shared differentiable blackboard.
AI.motivation: Tackling the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC) challenges requires systematic reasoning under strict test-time and hardware constraints, which single-model approaches struggle with due to the diversity and compositional complexity of abstract grid transformations.
AI.method: ARCANA employs four specialized agents: (1) a perceptual grounding agent that constructs object-centric scene graphs from raw grids; (2) a latent program policy that proposes diverse DSL programs; (3) a symbolic executor that verifies candidates against demonstrations; and (4) a reflective agent that synthesizes failure-driven feedback. These agents communicate via a shared differentiable blackboard and are orchestrated by a learned meta-controller, combining structured program search with adaptive multi-turn correction.
AI.result: The framework improves reasoning efficiency and solution quality on challenging abstract transformation tasks compared to prior approaches, demonstrating the effectiveness of combining program synthesis with iterative, failure-driven refinement under constrained conditions.
AI.conclusion: A collaborative multi-agent architecture with specialized roles, differentiable communication, and meta-level scheduling can effectively address the compositional reasoning demands of ARC-style benchmarks, offering a promising direction for systematic abstraction and reasoning in AI systems.

title: Director: Accelerating Distributed MoE Serving via Online Proactive Expert Placement
summary: Expert parallelism has become the prevailing paradigm to serve Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models. Its efficiency depends on the communication and computation latencies of the GPUs, which are linked to the placement of experts in the GPUs. Existing works for optimizing expert placement focus on leveraging past requests' expert activation patterns. However, they demonstrate deficiencies facing diverse and rapidly changing request patterns, calling for an online, proactive approach. Implementing such an approach requires addressing several challenges: the uncertainty associated with incoming requests' expert activation, the cost of expert migration, and the NP-hard complexity in optimization. Therefore, we present Director, a new distributed MoE serving system that minimizes end-to-end latency via prediction-driven, online expert placement. Director uses either a lightweight cascaded predictor or a low-bit quantized replica for expert activation patterns of incoming requests. An online migration module then enacts the changes with near-zero downtime by executing migrations in compute-bound phases, keeping disruption bounded. At its core, a relaxation-based expert placement optimizer operates under capacity constraints, runs in polynomial time, and achieves a $(1+ε)$ approximation ratio. Finally, we implement a prototype and demonstrate, through extensive experiments, a reduction in end-to-end latency of $11\sim55\%$ for popular MoE models (e.g., Mistral, DeepSeek and Qwen) compared to existing work.

AI.tldr: Director is a distributed MoE serving system that uses online prediction of expert activation patterns and a relaxation-based optimizer to proactively place experts, reducing end-to-end latency by 11–55% compared to existing approaches.
AI.motivation: Existing expert placement methods rely on historical activation patterns and fail under diverse, rapidly changing request patterns. An online, proactive approach is needed but faces three challenges: uncertainty of future expert activations, migration overhead, and NP-hard optimization complexity.
AI.method: Director employs (1) a lightweight cascaded predictor or low-bit quantized replica to forecast expert activations, (2) an online migration module that performs expert transfers during compute-bound phases to minimize disruption, and (3) a relaxation-based optimizer that solves expert placement under capacity constraints in polynomial time with a $(1+\varepsilon)$ approximation guarantee.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on popular MoE models (Mistral, DeepSeek, Qwen) show 11–55% reduction in end-to-end latency compared to existing systems.
AI.conclusion: Director demonstrates that prediction-driven, online expert placement with bounded migration overhead and provable approximation is a viable and effective strategy for serving MoE models under dynamic workloads.

title: An Emergent Mirage: Is Emergent Misalignment and Realignment Indeed a Robust Phenomenon?
summary: Recent work has reported Emergent Misalignment (EM), where language models fine-tuned on narrow, domain-specific misaligned datasets abruptly acquire broadly misaligned behavior, alongside evidence that this behavior can be reversed through limited realignment. We systematically study repeated alignment and misalignment cycles using controlled fine-tuning loops while tracking behavioral performance, and LoRA representations throughout training. Although we reproduce EM, we find that both misalignment and realignment are highly sensitive to superficial dataset characteristics, with apparent rapid realignment largely disappearing after controlling for response-length differences. We further find that previously reported mechanistic signatures, including representational phase transitions in LoRA space, do not consistently correlate with behavioral misalignment across training. Our results suggest that current evidence for EM is less robust than previously claimed and highlight the need for evaluation protocols that carefully control for these surface level dataset artifacts to identify the robustness of the EM phenomenon.

AI.tldr: The paper challenges the robustness of Emergent Misalignment (EM), finding that rapid misalignment and realignment effects are largely artifacts of superficial dataset features (e.g., response length). Representational phase transitions previously reported in LoRA space do not reliably correlate with behavioral misalignment, questioning the validity of current EM evidence.
AI.motivation: Prior work claimed that fine-tuning language models on narrow misaligned datasets causes abrupt, broad misalignment (Emergent Misalignment) and that limited realignment can reverse it. This paper systematically interrogates whether these findings are robust or artifacts of experimental confounds.
AI.method: The authors conduct controlled fine-tuning experiments using repeated misalignment-realignment cycles, tracking behavioral performance metrics and LoRA representations throughout training. They control for superficial dataset characteristics (e.g., response length) and test whether previously reported representational phase transitions correlate with behavioral misalignment.
AI.result: Both misalignment and realignment are highly sensitive to superficial dataset characteristics. Apparent rapid realignment largely disappears after controlling for response-length differences. Previously reported mechanistic signatures (representational phase transitions in LoRA space) do not consistently correlate with behavioral misalignment across training.
AI.conclusion: Current evidence for Emergent Misalignment is less robust than previously claimed. Future work must adopt evaluation protocols that control for surface-level dataset artifacts to properly assess the phenomenon's validity.

title: LLMs for health: Perceived benefits, risks, intention to use AI chatbots, and willingness to self-disclose across sensitive health topics
summary: AI chatbots are increasingly used for answering health-related questions. This study examines the role of topic type discussed with an AI chatbot and individual characteristics on perceived benefits and risks, intention to use an AI chatbot, and willingness to self-disclose health information. We conducted an online experiment with a 2 (topic type: physical versus psychological, between-subjects) x 2 (topic sensitivity: low versus high, within-subjects) mixed design among a Dutch representative sample (N = 1,388). Results showed that perceived benefits were positively associated with intention and willingness to self-disclose, while perceived risks were negatively associated. Moreover, participants reported higher usage intentions for low-sensitive topics compared to high-sensitive topics. Furthermore, perceptions, intention, and willingness to self-disclose varied by individual characteristics. Overall, our findings suggest that intentions to use AI chatbots and self-disclosure of health-related information are primarily related to perceived benefits and risks and to personal characteristics rather than to topic type.

AI.tldr: An online experiment (N=1,388) found that intentions to use AI chatbots for health information and willingness to self-disclose are driven by perceived benefits and risks, as well as individual characteristics, rather than whether the topic is physical or psychological. Topic sensitivity did matter: low-sensitive topics elicited higher usage intentions than high-sensitive ones.
AI.motivation: With the increasing deployment of AI chatbots in health contexts, it is critical to understand what drives users' intentions to adopt them and their willingness to disclose sensitive health information. Prior work had not systematically disentangled the effects of topic type (physical vs. psychological), topic sensitivity, and individual differences on these outcomes.
AI.method: A 2 (topic type: physical vs. psychological, between-subjects) × 2 (topic sensitivity: low vs. high, within-subjects) mixed-design online experiment was conducted with a representative Dutch sample (N = 1,388). Participants were exposed to health-related chatbot scenarios and self-reported perceived benefits, perceived risks, intention to use, and willingness to self-disclose.
AI.result: Perceived benefits positively predicted both intention to use and willingness to self-disclose, while perceived risks negatively predicted these outcomes. Topic sensitivity influenced intention: participants reported higher usage intentions for low-sensitive versus high-sensitive topics. Topic type (physical vs. psychological) did not emerge as a primary driver. Individual characteristics also significantly shaped perceptions, intentions, and disclosure willingness.
AI.conclusion: Users' decisions to engage with AI chatbots for health queries hinge more on their benefit-risk calculus and personal traits than on whether the health topic is physical or psychological. Sensitivity of the topic matters, but the broad categorical distinction between physical and psychological health does not.

title: From Generic to Personalized: Exploring Persona-Aware Code Review Explanations
summary: Code review is essential for ensuring software quality and supporting collaboration, yet prior work shows that developers can interpret code review comments differently. These differences can hinder effective communication, particularly in collaborative settings. To address this challenge, we explore the potential of personified code review explanations. We report initial findings from an ongoing mixed-methods user study in which developers evaluated persona-aligned review comments across multiple code snippets. Our results suggest that preferences for explanation styles vary across problem-solving styles, experience levels, and roles. Across problem-solving style profiles, developers valued explanatory depth, learning support, practical suggestions, and risk awareness over conciseness, highlighting the need to balance personalization with clarity and trust. Based on these findings, we outline a vision for inclusive, human-centered AI-assisted code review systems that adapt feedback to developers' problem-solving preferences.

AI.tldr: Developers interpret code review comments differently based on their problem-solving styles, experience, and roles. A user study shows that persona-aligned code review explanations are valued for depth, learning support, practical suggestions, and risk awareness over mere conciseness, motivating a vision for adaptive, human-centered AI-assisted code review systems.
AI.motivation: Prior research has established that developers can interpret the same code review comments differently, which undermines communication and collaboration. The authors seek to address this by investigating whether persona-aligned (personified) code review explanations can bridge these interpretive gaps and improve the effectiveness of code review feedback.
AI.method: The authors conducted an ongoing mixed-methods user study in which developers evaluated persona-aligned review comments across multiple code snippets. The study examines how preferences for explanation styles correlate with developers' problem-solving styles, experience levels, and roles.
AI.result: Preferences for explanation styles vary significantly across problem-solving styles, experience levels, and roles. Across all problem-solving profiles, developers consistently prioritized explanatory depth, learning support, practical suggestions, and risk awareness over conciseness, indicating that personalization must be balanced with clarity and trust.
AI.conclusion: The findings support a vision for inclusive, human-centered AI-assisted code review systems that adapt feedback to developers' individual problem-solving preferences, rather than applying one-size-fits-all explanation strategies.

title: Neuro-Agentic Control: A Deep Learning-based LLM-Powered Agentic AI Framework for Controlling Security Controls
summary: Cyberattacks on operational technology are increasingly causing costly downtime and physical damage, exposing the limitations of traditional rule-based monitoring in industrial IoT environments. While Large Language Models (LLMs) have strong semantic reasoning abilities to assist in decision support, their hallucinatory nature presents unacceptable safety liabilities for closed-loop control. This paper introduces a neuro-agentic control framework, a novel architecture that couples an LLM-based planner (i.e., such as Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite) with a pre-trained Time-Series Foundation Model (TimesFM), to achieve physics-grounded autonomous defense. The paper introduces a ``Counterfactual Physics Injection'' mechanism that simulates the impact of LLM-proposed interventions within the numerical latent space of the foundation model before actuation, while allowing the system to reject hallucinatory or unsafe actions. Evaluated on an industrial dataset (e.g., the Secure Water Treatment (SWaT)) in the context of stochastic attack scenarios, the framework exhibited better performance compared to LSTM and TCN baselines. The Neuro-Agentic Loop prevented five breaches (33.3%) below the threshold versus LSTM (26.7%) and TCN (13.3%), with zero physically invalid (hallucinated) actions executed. These results demonstrate the efficacy of using foundation models as deterministic ``Sentinels'' to safeguard agentic AI in critical infrastructure.

AI.tldr: A neuro-agentic control framework couples an LLM planner with a Time-Series Foundation Model (TimesFM) via "Counterfactual Physics Injection" to enable autonomous industrial defense. The TimesFM acts as a safety sentinel, simulating proposed interventions before execution and rejecting hallucinatory actions. Tested on SWaT, it achieved 33.3% breach prevention versus LSTM (26.7%) and TCN (13.3%), with zero physically invalid actions executed.
AI.motivation: Traditional rule-based monitoring in industrial IoT/OT environments is increasingly inadequate against cyberattacks causing downtime and physical damage. LLMs offer strong semantic reasoning for decision support but suffer from hallucinations, creating unacceptable safety risks for closed-loop control in critical infrastructure.
AI.method: A neuro-agentic control framework combining: (1) an LLM-based planner (Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite) for semantic reasoning and intervention proposal, (2) a pre-trained Time-Series Foundation Model (TimesFM) serving as a deterministic physics-grounded safety layer, and (3) a "Counterfactual Physics Injection" mechanism that simulates LLM-proposed actions within TimesFM's numerical latent space before actuation, rejecting hallucinatory or unsafe interventions. Evaluated on the SWaT dataset under stochastic attack scenarios against LSTM and TCN baselines.
AI.result: The neuro-agentic framework prevented 33.3% of breaches (5 breaches), outperforming LSTM (26.7%) and TCN (13.3%) baselines. Critically, it executed zero physically invalid (hallucinated) actions, validating the TimesFM sentinel's effectiveness in filtering unsafe LLM outputs.
AI.conclusion: Foundation models can serve effectively as deterministic "Sentinels" to safeguard agentic AI in critical infrastructure, enabling the use of LLM reasoning for autonomous defense while eliminating hallucination risks through physics-grounded validation.

title: LieBN: Batch Normalization over Lie Groups
comment: arXiv admin note: text overlap with arXiv:2403.11261
summary: Manifold-valued measurements are prevalent in various machine learning tasks. Recent advances have extended Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) to operate on manifolds, accompanied by normalization techniques tailored to different geometries, collectively referred to as Riemannian normalization. However, most existing Riemannian normalization methods are either designed for specific manifolds or fail to effectively normalize manifold-valued sample distributions. To address these limitations, we propose LieBN, a framework for Riemannian Batch Normalization (RBN) over Lie groups. Our approach leverages the theoretically convenient left- and right-invariant metrics, which naturally exist in every Lie group, and provides theoretical guarantees for controlling the Riemannian mean and variance. We instantiate LieBN across nine distinct geometries: four on the Symmetric Positive Definite (SPD) manifold, one on the group of rotation matrices, and four on the manifold of full-rank correlation matrices.
