Notably, among the SPD metrics, we introduce a novel right-invariant metric and extend three existing Lie group structures via matrix power deformation. Extensive experiments on different manifolds validate the effectiveness of our framework. The code is available at https://github.com/GitZH-Chen/LieBN.git.

AI.tldr: LieBN is a Riemannian Batch Normalization framework for Lie groups that leverages left- and right-invariant metrics, providing theoretical guarantees on controlling Riemannian mean and variance. It is instantiated across nine geometries spanning SPD manifolds, rotation matrices, and full-rank correlation matrices, demonstrating effectiveness through extensive experiments.
AI.motivation: Existing Riemannian normalization methods are either restricted to specific manifolds or ineffective at normalizing manifold-valued sample distributions. A general, theoretically grounded normalization framework applicable across diverse Lie group geometries is needed.
AI.method: LieBN exploits the left- and right-invariant metrics inherent to every Lie group. It provides theoretical guarantees for controlling the Riemannian mean and variance of normalized distributions. The framework is instantiated on nine geometries: four SPD metrics (including a novel right-invariant metric and three extended via matrix power deformation), one on rotation matrices (SO(n)), and four on full-rank correlation matrices.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across multiple manifolds validate the effectiveness of the LieBN framework, showing consistent performance improvements for deep neural networks operating on manifold-valued data.
AI.conclusion: LieBN offers a unified, theoretically grounded Riemannian Batch Normalization framework applicable to arbitrary Lie groups, overcoming the specificity and ineffectiveness limitations of prior Riemannian normalization methods.

title: AgentKGV: Agentic LLM-RAG Framework with Two-Stage Training for the Fact Verification of Knowledge Graphs
summary: Knowledge graphs (KGs) are often automatically constructed from large-scale corpora, but they inevitably contain factual errors due to noisy sources and extraction failures, and verifying them reliably at industrial scale remains a critical challenge. To address this, we propose AgentKGV, the Agentic LLM-RAG framework for KG fact Verification, that integrates dynamic routing and iterative query rewriting, which handles surface-form mismatch in document-level retrieval. To make this framework more accurate and cost-efficient for industrial deployment, we further introduce a two-stage training strategy: turn-level distillation-based SFT that transfers reasoning ability from a large teacher model into a small model for stable query rewriting and reasoning, and trajectory-level GRPO that optimizes the search policy to reduce unnecessary retrieval at scale. On the long-tail-predicate split of the open-domain T-REx benchmark, our framework improves macro-F1 over single-turn RAG by 5.5 \%p, and two-stage training does it further by 9.4 \%p. GRPO also cuts the average number of search calls from 3.24 to 1.63 without lowering accuracy.

AI.tldr: AgentKGV combines iterative query rewriting with two-stage training (distillation SFT + GRPO) to verify KG facts efficiently, improving macro-F1 by 9.4% points over single-turn RAG while halving retrieval calls.
AI.motivation: Automatically constructed knowledge graphs contain factual errors from noisy sources, and existing verification methods struggle with document-level surface-form mismatch and are too costly for industrial-scale deployment.
AI.method: An agentic LLM-RAG framework with dynamic routing and iterative query rewriting to handle surface-form mismatches. A two-stage training strategy: (1) turn-level distillation SFT transfers reasoning from a large teacher to a small student model, and (2) trajectory-level GRPO optimizes search policy to reduce unnecessary retrievals.
AI.result: On the long-tail-predicate split of T-REx, the framework improves macro-F1 by 5.5 pp over single-turn RAG; two-stage training adds a further 9.4 pp gain. GRPO reduces average search calls from 3.24 to 1.63 without accuracy loss.
AI.conclusion: AgentKGV with two-stage training enables accurate, cost-efficient industrial-scale KG fact verification, significantly outperforming single-turn RAG baselines while minimizing retrieval overhead.

title: Learning When to Intervene on Habitual Behaviors: A Case Study in Oral Health Care
summary: A central challenge for digital health interventions aimed at improving habitual behaviors is deciding when to deliver an intervention prompt. For many daily habits, such as tooth brushing or eating, individuals tend to act around a usual time of day, but this timing is not fixed and can shift as routines evolve. When intervention timing is selected in advance and held constant throughout a study, it can gradually become misaligned with behavior, causing interventions to potentially arrive after the behavior has already occurred or too early to be effective. In this work, we address this habitual timing misalignment in digital health interventions by proposing an online decision-making framework that continuously adapts intervention timing as individual behavior patterns change. Rather than treating intervention timing as a static design choice, our framework adapts it over time and integrates it into a sequential process that determines both when and whether to deliver an intervention. Using data from a deployed oral health intervention trial as a case study, we evaluate our approach using both observed data and simulated settings to assess how well different intervention timing strategies align with the timing of brushing events. Across these evaluations, we measure performance using a coverage-based metric that captures whether an intervention is delivered sufficiently close to a subsequent brushing event. We find that adaptive intervention timing consistently improves coverage compared to fixed intervention times based on user-provided input. The proposed framework is currently deployed in an ongoing randomized controlled trial of a digital oral health intervention, with preliminary results that are consistent with and further support our prior evaluations.

AI.tldr: Adaptive intervention timing in digital health outperforms static scheduling by continuously aligning prompts with users' shifting habitual behaviors, evaluated via coverage metrics on oral health data and validated in an ongoing RCT.
AI.motivation: Fixed intervention schedules in digital health interventions become misaligned with habitual behaviors (e.g., tooth brushing) because individuals' routines shift over time, causing prompts to arrive too early or too late. This timing misalignment undermines intervention effectiveness.
AI.method: An online decision-making framework that jointly adapts both when and whether to deliver an intervention, continuously updating timing as behavioral patterns change. Evaluated using observed data from a deployed oral health trial and simulated settings, with performance measured via a coverage-based metric (whether intervention delivery occurs sufficiently close to a subsequent brushing event). Compared against fixed timing based on user-provided input.
AI.result: Adaptive intervention timing consistently achieved better coverage than fixed intervention times based on user-provided input across both observed and simulated evaluations. Preliminary results from an ongoing randomized controlled trial further support these findings.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive, data-driven intervention timing is superior to static scheduling for habitual health behaviors. The framework is practical for real-world deployment and is currently active in an ongoing oral health RCT.

title: Shadow-Based Noise Fingerprinting of Simulated Quantum Noise Models
summary: Accurate noise classification is essential for operating near-term quantum processors, yet existing approaches, such as quantum process tomography, scale exponentially with system size, limiting their practicality for routine calibration. We propose a scalable noise fingerprinting pipeline that combines structured classical shadow tomography with physics-informed feature engineering to identify noise channels from a fixed set of 3-qubit probe circuits. Each sample is represented by a 279-dimensional feature vector constructed from randomized Pauli measurements and derived observables, designed to resolve physically similar noise channels that produce overlapping signatures under generic measurement sets. We evaluate three classifiers, i.e., random forest, extra trees, and a multilayer perceptron, on a dataset of 14,000 labeled samples spanning 10 noise types. The random forest classifier achieves the highest test accuracy of 0.8426 with a macro F1 score of 0.8437, outperforming both baselines. Confusion analysis reveals that many noise types are classified with high reliability, with the remaining confusions occurring between channels sharing similar physical decay mechanisms, motivating future work on richer probe states and noise parameter estimation.

AI.tldr: A scalable noise fingerprinting pipeline using 3-qubit probe circuits, classical shadows, and physics-informed features achieves 84.26% accuracy in classifying 10 quantum noise types with a random forest, outperforming extra trees and MLP baselines.
AI.motivation: Quantum process tomography scales exponentially with system size, making it impractical for routine calibration of near-term quantum processors. A scalable, efficient method for accurate noise classification is needed.
AI.method: A pipeline combining structured classical shadow tomography with physics-informed feature engineering. Each sample uses a fixed set of 3-qubit probe circuits, yielding a 279-dimensional feature vector from randomized Pauli measurements and derived observables. Three classifiers (random forest, extra trees, MLP) are evaluated on 14,000 labeled samples across 10 noise types.
AI.result: Random forest achieves the highest test accuracy (0.8426) and macro F1 score (0.8437). Many noise types are classified with high reliability; residual confusions occur between channels with similar physical decay mechanisms.
AI.conclusion: The proposed pipeline offers a scalable alternative to full process tomography for noise identification. Future work should explore richer probe states and noise parameter estimation to resolve remaining confusions between physically similar noise channels.

title: SLBench: Evaluating How LLM Agents Follow Logical Relations in Skills
summary: Agent skills extend LLM agents with reusable procedures, tools, and domain-specific workflows, but their safety depends on resolving dependencies among interacting instructions. We introduce SkillLogic, a framework for analyzing logical relations in skill files and constructing executable tests from them. Our taxonomy covers eight relation types, including preconditions that gate valid actions, constraints that limit how allowed actions may be performed, and fallbacks that specify recovery behavior after failure. Using SkillLogic, we scan over 5000 public skills and find that 70% contain at least one logical relation. We then construct SLBench, an 86-case executable benchmark from high-confidence, high-impact, and locally testable relations. Evaluating Codex and Claude Code across six LLM backbones shows unsafe rates up to 70%, with violations leading to privacy leaks, unsafe configuration changes, and incomplete cleanup. The human audit attributes failures to both agent capability gaps and low-salience skill text. We further show that SLGuard, a lightweight inference-time scaffold, reduces violations by 63% on targeted cases. Our results establish logical-relation following as a distinct reliability challenge for skill-guided agents.

AI.tldr: SkillLogic introduces a taxonomy of eight logical relation types in LLM agent skills and an analysis framework that scans skills, constructs executable tests (SLBench), and evaluates agent safety. Scanning 5000+ public skills reveals 70% contain logical relations. Testing with SLBench shows unsafe rates up to 70% across LLMs, with violations causing privacy leaks and unsafe config changes. The SLGuard inference-time scaffold reduces violations by 63%.
AI.motivation: LLM agents increasingly rely on reusable skills (procedures, tools, workflows), but the safety of these skills hinges on correctly resolving logical dependencies among interacting instructions — such as preconditions, constraints, and fallbacks. Prior work lacks systematic analysis of these logical relations and their safety implications for skill-guided agents.
AI.method: The authors propose SkillLogic, a framework that: (1) defines a taxonomy of eight logical relation types (preconditions, constraints, fallbacks, etc.); (2) scans skill files to automatically detect these relations; (3) constructs SLBench, an 86-case executable benchmark from high-confidence, high-impact, locally testable relations; and (4) introduces SLGuard, a lightweight inference-time scaffold that mitigates violations. Evaluation spans six LLM backbones with Codex and Claude Code.
AI.result: Scanning over 5000 public skills shows 70% contain at least one logical relation. On SLBench, unsafe rates reach up to 70%, with violations manifesting as privacy leaks, unsafe configuration changes, and incomplete cleanup. Human audit attributes failures to agent capability gaps and low-salience skill text. SLGuard reduces violations by 63% on targeted cases.
AI.conclusion: Logical-relation following constitutes a distinct and critical reliability challenge for skill-guided agents. The high unsafe rates demonstrate that current LLM agents systematically fail to respect inter-instruction dependencies, and lightweight inference-time scaffolding (SLGuard) offers a viable partial mitigation.

title: L-MAD: A Systematic Evaluation of Multi-Agent Debate Structures in Legal Reasoning
comment: Outstanding paper in the AI4Law Workshop at ICML 2026
summary: While multi-agent debate (MAD) frameworks have shown significant potential in general reasoning, their effectiveness in highly structured, knowledge-heavy legal domains remains under-explored. In this work, we introduce the Legal Multi-Agent Debate (L-MAD) framework to systematically evaluate different debate structures and aggregation methods within Legal Textual Entailment. By assigning distinct expert personas to multiple agents, L-MAD improves upon strong single-agent baselines by up to 8\%. Furthermore, analyzing how debate scales reveals a clear trade-off: increasing the agent population reduces inconsistency and improves accuracy, whereas extending discussion rounds induces a detrimental \textit{over-deliberation drift} where agents reinforce each other's mistakes. Ultimately, our findings outline the practical boundaries and safety margins of deploying collaborative multi-agent systems in high-stakes legal reasoning environments.

AI.tldr: Introduces L-MAD, a legal multi-agent debate framework for textual entailment. Shows multi-agent debate with expert personas improves over single-agent baselines by up to 8%, but reveals a scaling trade-off: more agents help, while more debate rounds cause "over-deliberation drift" where errors are mutually reinforced.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent debate (MAD) frameworks have demonstrated promise in general reasoning tasks, but their applicability to highly structured, knowledge-intensive legal domains remains largely unexamined. The authors aim to fill this gap by systematically investigating whether and how MAD can benefit legal reasoning, specifically Legal Textual Entailment.
AI.method: Proposes the Legal Multi-Agent Debate (L-MAD) framework. Multiple agents are assigned distinct legal expert personas and engage in structured debate. The framework systematically evaluates different debate structures and answer aggregation methods on Legal Textual Entailment tasks. The study also varies agent population size and number of discussion rounds to analyze scaling behavior.
AI.result: L-MAD improves over strong single-agent baselines by up to 8%. Increasing the number of agents reduces inconsistency and boosts accuracy. However, extending discussion rounds induces "over-deliberation drift" — agents begin reinforcing each other's mistakes, degrading performance. This reveals a clear trade-off between agent count and debate depth.
AI.conclusion: Multi-agent debate can substantially benefit legal reasoning when carefully configured, but there are practical boundaries. Over-deliberation poses a safety risk in high-stakes legal settings. The findings define operational margins for deploying collaborative multi-agent systems in legal domains and caution against unbounded debate iterations.

title: HERO: A Heterogeneity-Aware Benchmark Library for Federated Continual Learning
summary: Federated continual learning (FCL) evaluates how distributed clients learn from changing data streams while retaining previously learned knowledge. Existing evaluations are difficult to compare because they often change datasets, task splits, client data splits, task orders, backbones, memory assumptions, and reporting rules simultaneously. We introduce \textbf{HERO}, a heterogeneity-aware benchmark library for FCL. HERO builds benchmark streams by separating three choices that are often coupled, namely the task split, the client data split, and the client task sequence. In HERO-Core, the main comparable benchmark, $α$ controls client data skew and $ρ$ controls task-order mismatch. We evaluate representative FCL methods on CIFAR-100 and TinyImageNet using final average accuracy, average forgetting, and bottom-10\% client accuracy. We also include a graph-based Domain-IL portability case study on OGB-MolPCBA, where scaffold-domain granularity changes the input distribution while the prediction task remains fixed. Our results show that method behavior changes across easy and heterogeneous settings, that average accuracy can hide weak bottom-client performance, that task-order mismatch favors different strategies from synchronized evaluation, and that the same HERO interface can expose domain-shift difficulty beyond image-based FCIL. HERO releases benchmark streams, configurations, method implementations, and reporting scripts to support reproducible and setting-aware FCL evaluation.

AI.tldr: HERO is a benchmark library for Federated Continual Learning (FCL) that disentangles task split, client data split, and client task sequence to enable fair, reproducible comparisons. Evaluations on CIFAR-100, TinyImageNet, and OGB-MolPCBA reveal that method rankings shift under heterogeneous settings, average accuracy masks poor bottom-client performance, and task-order mismatch favors different strategies.
AI.motivation: Existing FCL evaluations are incomparable because they conflate multiple design choices — datasets, task splits, client data splits, task orders, backbones, memory assumptions, and reporting rules — making it impossible to isolate which factors drive performance differences. A standardized, heterogeneity-aware benchmark is needed for reproducible and setting-aware evaluation.
AI.method: HERO separates three typically coupled choices: (1) task split, (2) client data split, and (3) client task sequence. The main benchmark, HERO-Core, uses α to control client data skew and ρ to control task-order mismatch. Representative FCL methods are evaluated using final average accuracy, average forgetting, and bottom-10% client accuracy. A graph-based Domain-IL case study on OGB-MolPCBA extends evaluation beyond image-based Federated Class-Incremental Learning (FCIL).
AI.result: Method behavior varies significantly between easy and heterogeneous settings. Average accuracy can conceal weak performance on bottom clients. Task-order mismatch favors different strategies compared to synchronized evaluation. The HERO interface successfully exposes domain-shift difficulty in non-image domains (molecular property prediction).
AI.conclusion: HERO provides a unified, heterogeneity-aware benchmarking framework that enables reproducible FCL evaluation. The findings underscore that fair comparison requires controlling for heterogeneity axes (data skew, task-order mismatch) and reporting stratified metrics beyond average accuracy. HERO releases all benchmark streams, configurations, method implementations, and reporting scripts publicly.

title: PRecG: Legal Precedent Retrieval with Graph Neural Networks and Rhetorical Role Segmentation
summary:
Legal precedent retrieval is a fundamental task in legal case preparation, planning, litigation strategy, and legal research. Current approaches for automatic precedent retrieval map legal documents to a low-dimensional semantic space and compute similarity based on the proximity of their representations. These approaches treat legal documents as monolithic texts, ignoring the rhetorical organization of the legal technicalities. Ergo, they overlook nuanced legal meanings and fail to distinguish the contextual significance of legal entities and concepts that vary based on their rhetorical roles within the document.
  To address this insufficiency, we propose the PRecG pipeline that computes the similarity between pairs of legal judgments by hierarchically learning their representations. The process begins by decomposing each document into distinct semantic units (segments) based on the rhetorical roles of sentences. For each rhetorical segment, a knowledge graph is constructed to capture the legal entities and their relationships within the segment. Contextual representations of the entities are then learned and aggregated to derive segment-level embeddings. These embeddings are further integrated to produce a unified document-level representation, and finally, the semantic similarity between a pair of documents is computed. We validate the performance of the proposed approach through extensive experiments on a benchmark Indian legal dataset, comparing it against state-of-the-art baselines to demonstrate its effectiveness.

AI.tldr: Current legal precedent retrieval methods treat documents as monolithic texts, ignoring rhetorical structure. The authors propose PRecG, a hierarchical pipeline that segments documents by rhetorical roles, builds knowledge graphs per segment, learns entity representations, and aggregates them to segment and document-level embeddings for similarity computation. Experiments on an Indian legal dataset demonstrate superior performance over baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing legal precedent retrieval methods embed entire documents into a low-dimensional space without accounting for the rhetorical organization of legal texts. This monolithic treatment overlooks nuanced legal meanings and fails to capture how the contextual significance of legal entities and concepts varies depending on their rhetorical role (e.g., facts, arguments, holdings) within the document.
AI.method: PRecG pipeline: (1) Decompose each legal judgment into semantic segments based on rhetorical roles of sentences. (2) For each rhetorical segment, construct a knowledge graph capturing legal entities and their relationships. (3) Learn contextual entity representations and aggregate them into segment-level embeddings. (4) Integrate segment embeddings into a unified document-level representation. (5) Compute semantic similarity between document pairs using these hierarchical representations.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on a benchmark Indian legal dataset demonstrate that PRecG outperforms state-of-the-art baselines for legal precedent retrieval.
AI.conclusion: Hierarchically modeling legal documents — from rhetorical segments to knowledge graphs to segment embeddings to document representations — effectively captures nuanced legal meaning and improves precedent retrieval accuracy compared to monolithic text-based approaches.

title: KnitID: Machine-Knitted RFID Antennas for Battery-Free Authentication, Localization and Interaction
summary: Battery-free RFID systems offer a scalable and maintenance-free approach to interaction. We present KnitID, a machine-knitted textile RFID antenna design that enables on-body authentication, localization, and interaction. Unlike prior antenna designs, KnitID achieves a compact antenna form factor (60mm by 8mm) by integrating magnet wire into the unique loop-over-loop structure of machine knitting. This structure reduces the size of conventional loop antennas by around 90\%, while also providing 30\% longer sensing ranges than standard dipole designs with similar size on the human body. The compact form factor creates new opportunities to embed multiple RFID tags across the human body, enriching backscatter signals and supporting a broader range of battery-free on-body interactions. To demonstrate this capability, we build an interactive sleeve to support wearer authentication, spatial localization, and interaction detection. Through technical evaluations, we show the feasibility of KnitID to provide diverse and battery-free interactions on knitted user interfaces.

AI.tldr: KnitID introduces a compact machine-knitted RFID antenna (60mm×8mm) using magnet wire in a loop-over-loop structure, achieving ~90% size reduction over conventional loops and 30% longer sensing range than similarly-sized dipoles. An interactive sleeve demonstrates on-body authentication, localization, and battery-free interaction.
AI.motivation: Battery-free RFID systems offer scalable, maintenance-free interaction, but existing antenna designs either lack compactness for comfortable on-body integration or suffer from limited sensing range. There is a need for a textile-integrated RFID antenna that is compact, comfortable, and performs well on the human body to enable richer multi-tag on-body interactions.
AI.method: The authors leverage machine knitting to integrate magnet wire into a loop-over-loop knit structure, creating a compact 60mm×8mm RFID antenna. This fabrication technique shrinks the conventional loop antenna footprint by ~90%. Multiple such tags are embedded across a garment (an interactive sleeve) to enrich backscatter signals. Signal processing and sensing pipelines are built to support authentication, spatial localization, and interaction detection from the multi-tag RFID backscatter.
AI.result: The KnitID antenna achieves ~90% size reduction compared to conventional loop antennas while providing 30% longer on-body sensing range versus similarly-sized standard dipole antennas. The interactive sleeve prototype successfully demonstrates wearer authentication, spatial localization, and interaction detection, with technical evaluations confirming feasibility for diverse battery-free knitted user interfaces.
AI.conclusion: KnitID demonstrates that machine-knitted, compact RFID antennas can enable practical on-body authentication, localization, and interaction without batteries. The approach opens new possibilities for embedding multiple RFID tags into everyday garments, supporting richer on-body sensing and interaction modalities.

title: Benchmarking Large Language Models on Repairing Qiskit Programs using Bugs4Q
summary: In quantum programs, Bugs4Q is a widely used benchmark containing real quantum defects. However, its evaluation assumes that benchmark labels remain valid and that generated fixes execute in the target environment. We evaluate two Bugs4Q versions containing 67 unique real Qiskit defects, adding executable tests where missing, and re-run all entries across six pinned Qiskit releases (0.25.0, 0.45.0, 1.0.0, 1.1.1, 2.0.0, and 2.3.1). We find that quantum benchmarks can suffer from silent label inversion: entries become invalid without errors when reference fixes stop executing or buggy programs no longer reproduce failures. Thus, correctness depends on the (benchmark, version) pair rather than the benchmark alone. We evaluate four LLMs (GPT-4o-mini, GPT-5o-mini, GPT-5.4, and GPT-5.4-mini), generating up to 10 repair candidates per defect and testing them across all versions. GPT-5.4 achieves the highest pass@10 (48.8%), followed by GPT-5.4-mini (47.3%), GPT-5o-mini (30.3%), and GPT-4o-mini (22.6%). All models perform best on Qiskit 0.45.0 and decline after the Qiskit 1.0 transition. Many failures arise from deprecated or incompatible APIs rather than incorrect repairs, and 64\% of successful repairs occur on entries invalid under the target version. We release a re-validated, version-pinned Bugs4Q benchmark and show that benchmark validation must precede repair evaluation.

AI.tldr: The Bugs4Q benchmark for quantum program repair suffers from "silent label inversion," where benchmark entries become invalid across Qiskit versions without warning. The authors re-validate Bugs4Q across six Qiskit releases, evaluate four LLMs on repair generation, and find that GPT-5.4 achieves the best pass@10 (48.8%), though most successes occur on entries already invalid under the target version. They release a version-pinned, re-validated benchmark.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations using the Bugs4Q benchmark assume labels remain valid and that generated fixes execute correctly in target environments. The authors hypothesize that quantum software benchmarks degrade silently across API versions, undermining the validity of repair evaluations. They aim to quantify this degradation and reassess LLM-based quantum program repair under controlled, version-pinned conditions.
AI.method: The authors curate two Bugs4Q versions comprising 67 unique real Qiskit defects, add missing executable tests, and re-run all entries across six pinned Qiskit releases (0.25.0 through 2.3.1). They define and detect "silent label inversion," where reference fixes stop executing or buggy programs no longer reproduce failures. Four LLMs (GPT-4o-mini, GPT-5o-mini, GPT-5.4, GPT-5.4-mini) generate up to 10 repair candidates per defect, each tested across all six versions to compute pass@k metrics.
AI.result: Silent label inversion is pervasive: benchmark validity depends on the (benchmark, version) pair. GPT-5.4 achieves the highest pass@10 at 48.8%, followed by GPT-5.4-mini (47.3%), GPT-5o-mini (30.3%), and GPT-4o-mini (22.6%). Performance peaks on Qiskit 0.45.0 and declines after the 1.0 transition. Many failures stem from deprecated or incompatible APIs rather than incorrect logic. Critically, 64% of successful repairs occur on entries that are invalid under the target version, inflating apparent repair efficacy.
AI.conclusion: Benchmark validation must precede repair evaluation in quantum software engineering. The authors release a re-validated, version-pinned Bugs4Q benchmark and caution that unvalidated benchmarks produce misleading assessments of LLM-based program repair. API instability in the quantum computing ecosystem amplifies the benchmark degradation problem.

title: SherAgent: Scaling Attack Investigation in the Wild via LLM-Empowered Iterative Query-Filter Backtracking
summary: Provenance-based attack investigation enables viable automation by standardizing data and query logic; however, it is critically hindered in practice by dependency explosions and fragmented causal chains in the wild. Towards designing a robust and automated investigation tool, we collaborated with the SOC of a major Internet corporation serving billions of users. By engaging in real-world incident response, we are able to evaluate and refine their existing LLM-based investigation workflows, which processes tens of thousands of raw alerts daily, leaving thousands for manual triage, to find out the root causes of investigation failures and major challenges in their existing tools. Motivated by these findings, we propose SherAgent, an LLM-empowered automated investigation system. Operating on an iterative ``query-filter'' backtracking paradigm over provenance graphs, SherAgent leverages the semantic reasoning capabilities of LLMs to process unstructured data, such as investigation context and threat intelligence. To overcome fragmented causal chains caused by missing events, the system dynamically calibrates query conditions to broaden the search scope. Concurrently, it performs precision result filtering and strategic nodes selection for subsequent exploration, thereby mitigating dependency explosions. Extensive evaluations in the wild demonstrate that SherAgent improves the end-to-end investigation success rate by 31.1% and 63.7% compared to both legacy enterprise baselines and SOTA approaches, respectively. Furthermore, it operates with remarkable efficiency, incurring under $0.10 in API costs and requiring less than 4 minutes per investigation. Finally, our user study confirms that SherAgent provides accurate and clear insights, significantly reducing the analytical overhead for security experts.

AI.tldr: SherAgent is an LLM-powered automated attack investigation system that uses an iterative "query-filter" backtracking paradigm over provenance graphs to overcome dependency explosions and fragmented causal chains, achieving 31.1%–63.7% improvement over baselines at under $0.10 and 4 minutes per investigation.
AI.motivation: Provenance-based attack investigation is hampered by two critical practical challenges: (1) dependency explosions that produce overwhelmingly large causal graphs, and (2) fragmented causal chains caused by missing events in real-world telemetry. Existing tools, including LLM-based workflows at a major Internet corporation's SOC, leave thousands of alerts requiring manual triage daily. This motivates the need for a robust, automated system that addresses both root causes of investigation failure.
AI.method: SherAgent employs an iterative "query-filter" backtracking paradigm over provenance graphs. It leverages LLM semantic reasoning to process unstructured context and threat intelligence. To handle fragmented causal chains from missing events, the system dynamically calibrates query conditions to broaden the search scope. Simultaneously, it applies precision result filtering and strategic node selection for subsequent exploration steps to mitigate dependency explosions.
AI.result: In real-world evaluations, SherAgent improved end-to-end investigation success rate by 31.1% over legacy enterprise baselines and by 63.7% over SOTA approaches. Each investigation costs under $0.10 in API calls and completes in less than 4 minutes. A user study confirmed that SherAgent delivers accurate, clear insights and significantly reduces analytical overhead for security experts.
AI.conclusion: SherAgent demonstrates that combining LLM-based semantic reasoning with dynamic provenance graph exploration effectively addresses the dual bottlenecks of dependency explosion and causal chain fragmentation, enabling practical, low-cost, high-accuracy automated attack investigation at scale in real-world SOC environments.

title: MedRealMM: A Real-World Multimodal Benchmark for Chinese Online Medical Consultation
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in online medical consultation, yet existing benchmarks remain poorly aligned with real clinical practice. Many rely on synthetic conversations or patient simulators, omit patient-uploaded medical images, or evaluate open-ended clinical responses using multiple-choice or lexical-overlap metrics that poorly reflect clinical quality. We introduce \textbf{MedRealMM}, a large-scale benchmark for multimodal online medical consultation built from de-identified patient-doctor interactions collected from a nationwide Chinese internet hospital. MedRealMM uses a Multimodal Clinical Challenge Point (MCCP) extraction framework to identify clinically demanding moments in authentic consultation trajectories and converts each into a standardized next-response generation task while preserving the preceding text-image context. Each instance is paired with a case-specific rubric refined by physicians that rewards clinically desirable behaviors and penalizes unsafe, unsupported, or contradictory responses. The current release contains 5,620 real-world multimodal cases spanning 64 clinical departments. We evaluate 19 general-purpose and medical-specialized LLMs, including text-only and multimodal systems. Our results show that image information is critical for reliable clinical performance and that current frontier models remain below the online physician response. Although some frontier models satisfy as many or more positive clinical criteria than physicians, they trigger more negative criteria, indicating that safety-sensitive error avoidance remains a central bottleneck. MedRealMM offers a realistic and reproducible benchmark for evaluating multimodal medical reasoning in real-world online consultation. The dataset will be publicly available on Hugging Face at https://huggingface.co/datasets/jdh-algo/MedRealMM.

AI.tldr: MedRealMM is a large-scale multimodal benchmark for online medical consultation, built from 5,620 real patient-doctor interactions across 64 departments. It uses a Multimodal Clinical Challenge Point framework to create standardized next-response generation tasks with physician-refined rubrics, revealing that current LLMs underperform human doctors and struggle particularly with safety-critical error avoidance.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for medical LLMs are misaligned with real clinical practice: they rely on synthetic conversations, omit patient-uploaded images, and use evaluation metrics (multiple-choice, lexical overlap) that fail to capture genuine clinical quality. A realistic, multimodal benchmark grounded in authentic consultations is needed.
AI.method: MedRealMM is constructed from de-identified records from a Chinese internet hospital. The Multimodal Clinical Challenge Point (MCCP) extraction framework identifies clinically demanding moments in real consultation trajectories, converting each into a next-response generation task with preserved text-image context. Each case is paired with a physician-refined, case-specific rubric that rewards clinically desirable behaviors and penalizes unsafe, unsupported, or contradictory responses. The benchmark encompasses 5,620 cases across 64 departments and is used to evaluate 19 general-purpose and medical-specialized LLMs (both text-only and multimodal).
AI.result: Image information was shown to be critical for reliable clinical performance. Frontier multimodal models achieved comparable or better scores on positive clinical criteria relative to physicians but triggered significantly more negative criteria. No model matched the overall performance of online physicians, with safety-sensitive error avoidance identified as the central bottleneck.
AI.conclusion: MedRealMM provides a realistic, reproducible benchmark for multimodal medical reasoning in online consultation. Current frontier LLMs remain below physician-level performance, and addressing safety-sensitive errors — not just expanding positive clinical behaviors — is the key challenge for future progress.

title: DaDaDa: A Dataset for Data Pricing in Data Marketplaces
summary: High-quality data drives machine learning advances across industries. Recognizing the value of data, data transactions are increasingly common, giving rise to many data marketplaces, e.g., AWS Marketplace, Databricks, and Datarade. However, determining the appropriate prices for data products remains a significant challenge due to the unique properties of data products. Traditional pricing methods in economics can be categorized into the cost approach, the income approach, and the sales comparison approach. The cost approach fails in data pricing due to near-zero marginal cost from data replication, and the income approach fails due to inherently unpredictable data revenue. The sales comparison approach remains viable, yet its application is hindered by the absence of standardized pricing benchmarks for data products across marketplaces. To address this challenge, we introduce \texttt{DaDaDa}, the first dataset for data product pricing, containing metadata for 16,147 data products from 9 major data marketplaces worldwide. \texttt{DaDaDa} enables the training of pricing models, thereby establishing price benchmarks for new data products. In addition, \texttt{DaDaDa} can be utilized for other important tasks in data markets, such as data product classification and retrieval. Experiments and a retrieval prototype demonstrate the effectiveness of \texttt{DaDaDa} for pricing, classification, and retrieval of data products. The dataset and code are available at https://github.com/ZJU-DIVER/DaDaDa.

AI.tldr: Introduces DaDaDa, a dataset of 16,147 data product metadata from 9 marketplaces, enabling machine learning-based pricing models to establish standardized price benchmarks where traditional economic approaches fail, and supporting data product classification and retrieval.
AI.motivation: Data pricing is challenging because traditional economic methods fail: the cost approach fails due to near-zero marginal replication cost, and the income approach fails due to unpredictable data revenue. The sales comparison approach is viable but lacks standardized pricing benchmarks across marketplaces. A dedicated dataset is needed to train pricing models.
AI.method: The authors construct DaDaDa, a dataset comprising metadata for 16,147 data products collected from 9 major global data marketplaces. This dataset enables training machine learning models for pricing data products via the sales comparison approach, and also supports classification and retrieval tasks.
AI.result: Experiments and a retrieval prototype demonstrate the effectiveness of DaDaDa across three tasks: data product pricing, classification, and retrieval.
AI.conclusion: DaDaDa is the first dataset specifically designed for data product pricing and serves as a foundational resource for building pricing benchmarks, with additional utility for classification and retrieval in data marketplaces. The dataset and code are publicly released.

title: Augmenting Fundamental Analysis with Large Language Models: A RAG-Based System for Generating Investor Briefs
summary: In this study, we examine the opportunities brought by Large Language Models (LLMs) to various aspects of fundamental analysis of companies based on their reports as well as data and documents describing macroeconomic situation like GDP and inflation changes as well as documents filled to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) which can be found in EDGAR. We were preprocessing those data and than sending via API to gpt-4o model in a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) like regime. We prepared as well a document describing an exemplar investor knowledge based on Kitchin cycles. We were scanning data important for analysis of 9 companies for 4 weeks. Using LLM we were producing automatic briefs about them. They were sent to nine participants who are individual investors to evaluate usefulness of such approach to data analysis.

AI.tldr: This study explores using GPT-4o with a RAG-like pipeline to automatically generate investment briefs from SEC EDGAR filings and macroeconomic data, guided by an exemplar knowledge base on Kitchin cycles. Nine individual investors evaluated the weekly briefs for nine companies over four weeks to assess practical usefulness.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether LLMs can enhance fundamental analysis by automating the extraction and synthesis of insights from financial filings and macroeconomic indicators, reducing the manual effort required from individual investors.
AI.method: The authors preprocessed SEC EDGAR filings and macroeconomic data (GDP, inflation), then sent them via API to GPT-4o in a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)-like regime. A curated knowledge document based on Kitchin cycles was prepared to guide the LLM's reasoning. Automated briefs were generated weekly for 9 companies over a 4-week period and distributed to 9 individual investor participants for utility evaluation.
AI.result: Not explicitly reported in the abstract; the paper describes sending briefs to nine individual investors for evaluation, but the outcomes of that evaluation are not summarized.
AI.conclusion: Not explicitly stated in the abstract. The study appears to be an exploratory investigation into the feasibility and perceived usefulness of LLM-driven fundamental analysis briefs for retail investors.

title: Indirect and Direct AI Scaffolding for Computational Problem Posing: A Pilot Experience Report
summary: Problem posing is a valuable learning activity in computing education, encouraging learners to actively construct, refine, and reflect on problems rather than simply solving them. This experience report presents the design and pilot deployment of two LLM-powered scaffolding systems for supporting problem posing across two computational scenarios with different levels of task openness. Both systems assessed student-generated problems using Bloom's Taxonomy-based criteria and applied the same assessment framework, differing only in output modality: one provided guiding questions (Indirect scaffolding), while the other offered worked examples (Direct scaffolding). We conducted a within-subjects, counterbalanced pilot study with 20 graduate students and collected problem-quality ratings, user-experience surveys, and post-session interviews. Our deployment showed that both systems supported problem refinement in complementary ways, each offering distinct benefits. Direct scaffolding produced greater immediate improvements, while interviews showed that participants valued Indirect scaffolding for promoting deeper reflection on their own problem design. Based on these findings, we suggest sequencing the two modalities by beginning with Indirect scaffolding to promote reflection, then shifting to Direct scaffolding when learners become stuck. These lessons offer an initial practical strategy for integrating LLM-based scaffolding into computing classrooms.

AI.tldr: A pilot study tested two LLM-powered scaffolding systems for problem posing in computing education—one providing guiding questions (Indirect) and one offering worked examples (Direct). Both used Bloom's Taxonomy for assessment. Direct scaffolding yielded greater immediate improvement, while Indirect scaffolding promoted deeper reflection. The authors recommend sequencing both modalities: Indirect first for reflection, then Direct when learners stall.
AI.motivation: Problem posing is underutilized in computing education despite its pedagogical value for active learning. Learners struggle with constructing quality problems, and LLMs offer a scalable way to scaffold this process. The authors sought to compare two scaffolding modalities (Indirect vs. Direct) to understand their differential effects and inform practical deployment strategies.
AI.method: A within-subjects, counterbalanced pilot study with 20 graduate students across two computational scenarios differing in task openness. Both LLM-powered systems assessed student-generated problems using Bloom's Taxonomy-based criteria. One system delivered Indirect scaffolding (guiding questions); the other delivered Direct scaffolding (worked examples). Data collected included problem-quality ratings, user-experience surveys, and post-session interviews.
AI.result: Both modalities supported problem refinement but in complementary ways. Direct scaffolding produced greater immediate improvements in problem quality. Interviews revealed participants valued Indirect scaffolding for promoting deeper reflection on their own problem design. No single modality was uniformly superior; each offered distinct benefits.
AI.conclusion: The authors recommend a sequenced strategy: begin with Indirect scaffolding to foster reflection, then transition to Direct scaffolding when learners become stuck. This offers a practical, evidence-informed approach for integrating LLM-based scaffolding into computing classrooms.

title: Automating Just-In-Time Python Type Annotation Updating
summary: Type annotations are more and more popular in Python projects to avoid type errors caused by Python's dynamic typing feature. However, when developers change source code, these type annotations are often neglected or overlooked, resulting in outdated and inconsistent type annotations. Such obsolete type annotations can hinder program comprehension, mislead developers, and even introduce bugs in the future. Therefore, it is necessary to avoid and correct these inconsistent type annotations from the very beginning. In this work, we argue that obsolete type annotations can be reduced and even avoided by automatically updating type annotations alongside code changes. We refer to this task as "Just-In-Time (JIT) type annotation updating". To solve this task, we propose a novel LLM-based approach named TypeUp (Type Annotation Updator) to automate this task. TypeUp can automatically generate new type annotations based on the old type annotations and corresponding code changes. Specifically, TypeUp guides LLM to perform type annotation updates by eliciting its knowledge and logical reasoning power and learning from similar code changes. The evaluation results show that TypeUp outperforms state-of-the-art type infer approach (i.e., TypeGen) by 41.9% on our task. Moreover, we conducted an in-the-wild evaluation with real-world software projects, 20 out of 25 type annotation updates generated by our approach have already been confirmed by developers, showing our approach's practical value in real-world environments.

AI.tldr: TypeUp is an LLM-based approach that automatically updates Python type annotations alongside code changes (Just-In-Time updating), outperforming state-of-the-art type inference by 41.9% and achieving 80% developer confirmation rate in real-world projects.
AI.motivation: Python type annotations frequently become outdated and inconsistent when developers change source code, as annotations are often neglected during code modifications. These obsolete annotations hinder program comprehension, mislead developers, and can introduce future bugs. Current approaches lack the ability to automatically update type annotations concurrently with code changes.
AI.method: TypeUp leverages LLMs guided by elicited domain knowledge and logical reasoning, combined with learning from similar code changes. Given old type annotations and corresponding code changes, it automatically generates updated type annotations.
AI.result: TypeUp outperformed TypeGen (SOTA type inference) by 41.9% on the JIT type annotation updating task. In an in-the-wild evaluation across real-world software projects, 20 out of 25 generated type annotation updates were confirmed by developers.
AI.conclusion: JIT type annotation updating is a viable strategy to reduce annotation obsolescence. TypeUp demonstrates strong practical value, validated by real-world developer acceptance, suggesting LLM-based approaches can effectively maintain type annotation consistency during software evolution.

title: Malaika: Understanding Malware through Tri-Grounded Agentic Reasoning
summary: Recent LLM-based systems have shown promising capabilities for security-focused code analysis. Malware understanding, however, poses a distinct challenge: analysts must reconstruct high-level malicious behaviors under partial observability from sparse, dispersed evidence intertwined with benign functionality. While static analysis can expose security-relevant signals, the central challenge is not merely identifying suspicious code, but determining whether the evidence sufficiently supports an auditable behavior-level conclusion. We formulate malware understanding as a grounded reasoning problem and argue that reliable behavior reconstruction requires three complementary forms of grounding. Domain grounding constrains how behavior hypotheses are generated and evaluated, semantics grounding localizes and connects supporting program evidence, and knowledge grounding supports behavioral attribution through externally verifiable threat knowledge. To study this hypothesis, we present Malaika, a multi-agent framework that operationalizes the three grounding mechanisms through analyst-inspired reasoning, tool-mediated evidence localization, and retrieval-based behavioral attribution. We instantiate Malaika for Android malware analysis and evaluate it on malware-understanding tasks. Results show that Malaika improves analysis quality over prior LLM-based malware-analysis frameworks and demonstrate that reliability depends not only on model capability but also on the reasoning process. In particular, comparisons against malware-analysis systems and frontier agentic frameworks show that grounding-aware reasoning produces more precise and auditable conclusions. Ablation studies further support the grounding hypothesis. These findings suggest that grounding-aware reasoning provides a principled foundation for reliable malware understanding and, more broadly, for evidence-grounded software analysis.

AI.tldr: Malaika is a multi-agent framework for malware understanding that uses three grounding mechanisms (domain, semantics, knowledge) to enable reliable, auditable behavior reconstruction from sparse evidence. Evaluated on Android malware, it outperforms prior LLM-based systems, showing that grounding-aware reasoning is key to precise conclusions.
AI.motivation: Malware understanding requires reconstructing high-level malicious behaviors under partial observability from sparse, dispersed evidence. Existing LLM-based systems can identify suspicious code, but the core challenge is determining whether evidence sufficiently supports an auditable behavior-level conclusion. The authors argue that reliable behavior reconstruction demands structured grounding beyond raw model capability.
AI.method: The authors formulate malware understanding as a grounded reasoning problem with three grounding types: (1) domain grounding for hypothesis generation/evaluation, (2) semantics grounding for localizing and connecting program evidence, and (3) knowledge grounding for behavioral attribution via external threat knowledge. They implement Malaika, a multi-agent framework operationalizing these mechanisms through analyst-inspired reasoning, tool-mediated evidence localization, and retrieval-based attribution. The system is instantiated for Android malware analysis.
AI.result: Malaika improves analysis quality over prior LLM-based malware-analysis frameworks. Comparisons against malware-analysis systems and frontier agentic frameworks show that grounding-aware reasoning yields more precise and auditable conclusions. Ablation studies support the grounding hypothesis, demonstrating that reliability depends on both model capability and the reasoning process.
AI.conclusion: Grounding-aware reasoning provides a principled foundation for reliable malware understanding and, more broadly, for evidence-grounded software analysis. The three grounding mechanisms — domain, semantics, and knowledge — are complementary and essential for producing auditable, trustworthy conclusions.

title: KV-PRM: Efficient Process Reward Modeling via KV-Cache Transfer for Multi-Agent Test-Time Scaling
summary: Process Reward Models (PRMs) have been proven to be highly effective in guiding test-time scaling (TTS) methods, which significantly boost the capabilities of LLM-based multi-agent systems. However, existing PRMs are text-based: they re-encode the entire trajectory text from scratch. In long multi-agent rollouts, the scoring cost, growing quadratically with respect to sequence length L, creates a severe computational bottleneck, severely limiting PRMs' application in long-context scenarios. To resolve this, we introduce KV-PRM, a highly efficient process reward model that eliminates the heavy text re-encoding by directly reading the KV cache produced naturally during the LLM's generation phase. By processing a single "verify token" against the pre-existing KV cache, KV-PRM reduces the scoring cost from O(L^2) to O(L). We formally prove that the KV cache contains strictly greater information capacity than text, and is more efficient for downstream reward modeling. Empirically, across the MATH, GSM8K, and AIME benchmarks, KV-PRM matches or strictly outperforms text-PRMs under various TTS methods such as Beam Search, MCTS, and Weighted Voting, with up to a 5,000x reduction in scoring FLOPs, a 37x reduction in latency, and a 34x reduction in per-sequence memory footprint compared to text-based PRMs.

AI.tldr: KV-PRM replaces text-based process reward models by directly reading KV caches from LLM generation, reducing scoring complexity from O(L²) to O(L) while matching or outperforming text-PRMs, achieving up to 5000x FLOP reduction.
AI.motivation: Text-based PRMs re-encode entire trajectory text for scoring, causing quadratic O(L²) computational cost with respect to sequence length. This creates a severe bottleneck for long-context multi-agent rollouts, limiting PRM applicability at scale.
AI.method: KV-PRM reads the KV cache produced during LLM generation directly, avoiding text re-encoding entirely. It processes a single "verify token" against the pre-existing KV cache, reducing scoring cost from O(L²) to O(L). The authors formally prove KV cache contains strictly greater information capacity than text for downstream reward modeling.
AI.result: Across MATH, GSM8K, and AIME benchmarks, KV-PRM matches or outperforms text-PRMs under Beam Search, MCTS, and Weighted Voting. Achieves up to 5000x reduction in scoring FLOPs, 37x latency reduction, and 34x per-sequence memory footprint reduction.
AI.conclusion: KV-PRM demonstrates that leveraging KV caches directly for reward modeling is both theoretically superior (greater information capacity) and practically transformative (orders-of-magnitude efficiency gains), enabling PRM scaling to long-context multi-agent scenarios previously infeasible with text-based approaches.

title: Accelerating GPU Inference of Large Language Models with Moderately Unstructured Sparse Weight Matrices
summary: With the growing deployment of large language models (LLMs), LLM inference cost has become a key challenge. Pruning techniques that introduce sparsity into weight matrices can accelerate inference. However, maintaining model quality typically limits pruning to moderate unstructured sparsity (around 50\%). At these sparsity levels, none of the existing GPU kernels for sparse matrix multiplication (SpMM) can outperform their dense counterparts. This paper proposes an efficient GPU inference method for LLMs with moderate sparsity. We propose a three-layer matrix storage format comprising: (i) a Sparse-TC layer enabling sparse tensor cores to accelerate SpMM; (ii) a Slot-Filling layer using parallel differential distance for matrix compression while supporting low-cost on-chip decoding; (iii) a lightweight Residual Layer ensuring correct SpMM computation. Building on this format, we design a SpMM kernel that jointly utilizes sparse tensor cores and CUDA cores. This design enables an efficient execution pipeline and overlaps on-chip computation with memory access. Evaluations show that our work is the first to outperform dense matrix multiplication on modern GPUs equipped with high-bandwidth memory (HBM). It achieves up to 1.64x kernel-level speedup over SpInfer (EuroSys'25, Best paper) and up to 1.41x end-to-end speedups over FlashLLM (VLDB'24). Our source code: https://github.com/moui0/cudac.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an efficient GPU inference kernel for LLMs with moderate (~50%) unstructured sparsity. It introduces a three-layer matrix storage format (Sparse-TC, Slot-Filling, Residual) and a SpMM kernel that jointly leverages sparse tensor cores and CUDA cores, achieving the first SpMM implementation to outperform dense GEMM on HBM-equipped GPUs — up to 1.64x over SpInfer and 1.41x end-to-end over FlashLLM.
AI.motivation: LLM inference is increasingly costly, and weight pruning can reduce this cost via sparsity. However, at the moderate unstructured sparsity levels (~50%) that preserve model quality, existing sparse matrix multiplication (SpMM) GPU kernels cannot outperform dense matrix multiplication (GEMM). This work aims to bridge that gap — achieving practical speedups from moderate sparsity where prior approaches fail.
AI.method: The authors propose a three-layer matrix storage format: (1) Sparse-TC Layer — enables sparse tensor cores to accelerate SpMM; (2) Slot-Filling Layer — uses parallel differential distance for compression with low-cost on-chip decoding; (3) Residual Layer — a lightweight layer ensuring correct SpMM computation. On top of this format, they design a SpMM kernel that jointly utilizes sparse tensor cores and CUDA cores, creating an efficient execution pipeline that overlaps on-chip computation with memory access.
AI.result: The proposed method is the first to outperform dense matrix multiplication on modern HBM-equipped GPUs under moderate sparsity. It achieves up to 1.64x kernel-level speedup over SpInfer (EuroSys'25 Best Paper) and up to 1.41x end-to-end speedup over FlashLLM (VLDB'24).
AI.conclusion: By combining sparse tensor cores, a novel compressed storage format with efficient decoding, and CUDA core collaboration, the proposed kernel overcomes the long-standing barrier where moderate sparsity fails to yield practical speedups over dense GEMM. This makes weight pruning a viable acceleration strategy for LLM inference on modern GPUs.

title: Complexity-Guided Component-wise Initialization for Language Model Pretraining
summary: Pretrained language models often exhibit structured weight spectra, suggesting that training may repeatedly produce similar layerwise and component-wise organization. We ask whether these recurring spectral patterns can be reused as an initialization signal for GPT-2-style language-model pretraining. First, we analyze eleven pretrained GPT-2-style checkpoints that vary in size, language, tokenizer, and training corpus, measuring Frobenius norm and effective-rank entropy across layers and Transformer subcomponents. The checkpoints show shared depth trends, especially increasing scale and stronger spectral concentration in residual-writing matrices. We then construct initialization schemes that imitate the component-wise magnitudes and spectral profiles of pretrained models, and compare them with several weight initialization methods. These initializers visibly change the model's structural spectral patterns, but the evaluation results do not show a corresponding performance advantage. Pretrained-weight reuse remains competitive, while coarse spectral matching alone is not a reliable optimization strategy. Our results suggest that pretrained spectra are useful diagnostics of trained model structure, but that effective reuse likely requires preserving richer information than component-wise scale and singular-value shape.

AI.tldr: Analysis of GPT-2-style checkpoints reveals recurring spectral patterns (Frobenius norm, effective-rank entropy) across layers and components. Initialization schemes mimicking these spectral profiles alter structural patterns but yield no performance gains, suggesting that coarse spectral matching alone is insufficient for effective weight reuse.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether the recurring structured weight spectra observed in pretrained language models can be repurposed as initialization signals for GPT-2-style pretraining, potentially improving training efficiency or outcomes.
AI.method: The authors analyzed 11 pretrained GPT-2-style checkpoints (varying in size, language, tokenizer, and corpus) using Frobenius norm and effective-rank entropy across layers and Transformer subcomponents. They then constructed initialization schemes that imitate component-wise magnitudes and spectral profiles of pretrained models, comparing them against several existing weight initialization methods.
AI.result: Shared depth trends were observed across checkpoints, notably increasing scale and stronger spectral concentration in residual-writing matrices. The spectral-mimicking initializers visibly altered structural spectral patterns but did not produce corresponding performance advantages. Pretrained-weight reuse remained competitive.
AI.conclusion: Pretrained spectra serve as useful diagnostics of trained model structure, but effective reuse likely requires preserving richer information beyond component-wise scale and singular-value shape. Coarse spectral matching alone is not a reliable optimization strategy.

title: Inside the Skill Market: From Software Engineering Activities to Reusable Agent Skills
summary: Software engineering (abbrev. SE) has continuously evolved through increasingly powerful forms of reuse, from source code and libraries to components and services. Recent advances in AI agents have introduced a potentially new reusable artifact: skills. Emerging agent skill repositories and marketplaces enable developers to package, share, and reuse SE expertise as reusable skills. This trend raises a fundamental question: what SE activities are being encapsulated into reusable skills? Existing studies primarily focus on a broad range of skills acquisition, safety, or benchmarking, while lacking a systematic understanding of SE-specific skills and their coverage across the software development lifecycle. To address this gap, we conduct the first large-scale empirical study of SE skills in public repositories and marketplaces. We collect and analyze a large corpus of SE skills, examining the activities they encapsulate, lifecycle coverage, evolution characteristics, and evaluation mechanisms. Our findings reveal that SE activities are increasingly becoming reusable artifacts via skills and suggest promising research opportunities for skill recommendation and engineering-oriented structuring, as well as the need for mechanisms to encapsulate high-context SE activities into reusable skills. Overall, our study provides the first activity-centric characterization of SE skills and reveals how SE activities are increasingly being transformed into reusable skills. These findings offer new insights into skill reuse, ecosystem development, and the future of agent-centric SE.

AI.tldr: First large-scale empirical study of software engineering (SE) skills in public repositories, analyzing their activity coverage across the development lifecycle, evolution, and evaluation mechanisms. Reveals SE activities are increasingly becoming reusable artifacts, with gaps in high-context activity encapsulation.
AI.motivation: While AI agents have enabled skills as a new form of reusable artifact in SE, existing research focuses on skill acquisition, safety, or benchmarking without systematically understanding which SE activities are encapsulated as skills and their coverage across the software development lifecycle. This gap motivates a systematic, activity-centric empirical investigation.
AI.method: The authors conduct a large-scale empirical study by collecting and analyzing a large corpus of SE skills from public repositories and marketplaces. They examine: (1) the SE activities each skill encapsulates, (2) lifecycle coverage, (3) evolution characteristics, and (4) evaluation mechanisms.
AI.result: Findings show that SE activities are increasingly being transformed into reusable skills. However, gaps exist in encapsulating high-context SE activities. The study reveals patterns in lifecycle coverage and evolution, and identifies research opportunities for skill recommendation, engineering-oriented structuring, and better encapsulation mechanisms.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides the first activity-centric characterization of SE skills, demonstrating how SE activities are transitioning into reusable artifacts. It highlights implications for skill reuse, ecosystem development, and the future of agent-centric software engineering, while identifying open research challenges.

title: Blockchain-Linked Auditable Decision Management for Telecom/IoT Fraud-Control Requests
comment: 16 pages, 5 figures, 10 tables, IEEE Transaction Submission
summary: Telecom fraud-control studies often stop at detector-level classification, but deployment use requires request-level policy resolution, lifecycle traceability, and auditability. This paper reframes fraud control as blockchain-linked auditable decision management for synthetic telecom/IoT fraud-control requests, and its main result is that the QLoRA-tuned LLM branch becomes much more usable than zero-shot prompting but mainly approaches, rather than outperforms, a lower-cost centralized ensemble. The framework maps each synthetic deployment record to a managed request, blocks explicit out-of-boundary cases through a deterministic hard-fraud gate, scores non-hard requests using centralized ML (M1), federated meta-learning (M2), or LLM-family risk sources (M3), and resolves actions through a shared five-state policy, two-zone refinement mechanism, and local Ethereum-compatible audit layer. Evaluation uses separate synthetic training data and a 100,000-record deployment replay corpus, so the study should be read as controlled drift-replay evidence rather than field validation or proof of live deployability. On validation, M1 gives the strongest balance, with legitimate-request FPR 0.0890 under the 0.10 operating cap and soft-fraud recall 0.8341. On labeled deployment replay, however, the legitimate-FPR gap becomes large: M1 rises to 0.1646 and M3-QLoRA to 0.1801, while M3-QLoRA reduces the M3-Base legitimate FPR from 0.3915 and reaches 0.8240 soft-fraud recall. Blockchain telemetry shows that lifecycle gas, cost, latency, and throughput differences are driven by submitted off-chain decision profiles rather than changes in fraud logic.

AI.tldr: This paper reframes telecom fraud control as a blockchain-linked auditable decision management system, comparing centralized ML, federated meta-learning, and QLoRA-tuned LLMs. The QLoRA-tuned LLM significantly improves over zero-shot prompting but mainly approaches rather than surpasses the lower-cost centralized ensemble, with performance gaps widening under deployment replay conditions.
AI.motivation: Current telecom fraud-control research stops at detector-level classification, failing to address request-level policy resolution, lifecycle traceability, and auditability required for real deployment. There is a need to evaluate whether LLM-based approaches can serve as usable risk scorers within a full auditable decision management pipeline.
AI.method: The framework maps synthetic deployment records to managed requests with four components: (1) a deterministic hard-fraud gate blocking explicit out-of-boundary cases; (2) risk scoring via centralized ML (M1), federated meta-learning (M2), or LLM-family sources (M3, including zero-shot and QLoRA-tuned variants); (3) a shared five-state policy with two-zone refinement for action resolution; (4) a local Ethereum-compatible audit layer. Evaluation uses synthetic training data and a 100,000-record deployment replay corpus under controlled drift-replay conditions.
AI.result: On validation data, M1 achieves the best balance (legitimate FPR 0.0890, soft-fraud recall 0.8341). On deployment replay, performance degrades: M1 legitimate FPR rises to 0.1646, M3-QLoRA to 0.1801. However, M3-QLoRA substantially reduces M3-Base legitimate FPR from 0.3915 and reaches 0.8240 soft-fraud recall. Blockchain telemetry indicates lifecycle gas, cost, latency, and throughput differences stem from submitted off-chain decision profiles rather than fraud logic changes.
AI.conclusion: QLoRA-tuned LLMs become much more usable than zero-shot prompting for fraud control but mainly approach rather than outperform a lower-cost centralized ensemble. The paper should be interpreted as controlled drift-replay evidence, not field validation or proof of live deployability.

title: Scoped Verification for Reliable Long-Horizon Agentic Context Evolution under Distribution Shift
summary: Deployed LLM agents rely on agentic context, the model-external textual control content assembled by an operational harness. In this work, the mutable component of that context is a persistent system-level instruction that is updated from operational experience while the model, tools, and harness remain fixed. Over long evolution horizons, flat-text maintenance makes verification increasingly difficult as accumulated instructions grow and interact. We propose Graph-Regularized Agentic Context Evolution (GRACE), which maintains the persistent instruction component as a typed semantic graph and validates proposed updates within the local typed neighborhoods of modified nodes. Accepted graph updates are reconstructed as incremental edits to the textual instruction checkpoint used at deployment. We evaluate GRACE within a fixed telecom agent harness derived from $τ^2$-bench under a controlled distribution-shift protocol. Across five independent replications, GRACE improves strict reliability, measured by pass^3, from the Gemini 2.5 Flash zero-shot value of 0.091 to 0.673$\pm$0.136 at the final checkpoint. This exceeds a Gemini 3.1 Pro zero-shot reference of 0.242 on the same held-out set, while the flat-text HCE baseline finishes at 0.191$\pm$0.051. These results identify two requirements for reliable long-horizon context evolution, a structural substrate that makes verification local and a consolidation mechanism that keeps accumulated instruction content usable.

AI.tldr: GRACE proposes maintaining LLM agent system instructions as a typed semantic graph instead of flat text, enabling local verification of updates. Evaluated on a telecom benchmark, it achieves far higher reliability (0.673) than flat-text baselines (0.191) and zero-shot approaches.
AI.motivation: Deployed LLM agents accumulate persistent system-level instructions over time. With flat-text maintenance, as instructions grow and interact, verification becomes increasingly difficult over long evolution horizons. There is a need for a structural substrate enabling local, tractable verification of updates and a consolidation mechanism to keep accumulated instructions usable.
AI.method: GRACE represents the persistent instruction component as a typed semantic graph. Proposed updates are validated within the local typed neighborhoods of modified nodes. Accepted graph-level changes are then reconstructed as incremental edits to the textual instruction checkpoint used at deployment. The approach is evaluated within a fixed telecom agent harness derived from τ²-bench under a controlled distribution-shift protocol across five independent replications.
AI.result: GRACE improved strict reliability (pass³) from the Gemini 2.5 Flash zero-shot baseline of 0.091 to 0.673 ± 0.136 at the final checkpoint. This exceeded a Gemini 3.1 Pro zero-shot reference of 0.242 on the same held-out set. The flat-text HCE baseline finished at only 0.191 ± 0.051.
AI.conclusion: Reliable long-horizon context evolution requires two key elements: (1) a structural substrate (typed graph) that makes verification local, and (2) a consolidation mechanism that keeps accumulated instruction content usable, avoiding the degradation seen in flat-text approaches.

title: Adaptive Bayes exactly tracks information over intrinsic time
summary: Bayesian and multiplicative-weights updates reweight experts, models, or actions from sequential feedback. We show that the regret of any such update obeys an exact information-accounting identity. On each round, the learner's excess loss to any chosen comparator is the sum of an immediate payment for the uncertainty exposed by the round and a reduction in the information distance from the learner's current weights to the comparator. The cumulative payment defines a pathwise uncertainty clock, the \emph{intrinsic time} of the realized sequence. Summing one-step balances yields two exact adaptive decompositions of cumulative regret, one for each natural way of composing the update across rounds. Because the decompositions are exact rather than upper bounds, favorable stochastic or low-noise regimes appear as self-bounding properties of the realized intrinsic time, not as slack in worst-case analyses. The same calculus covers Hedge, optimistic and side-information variants, continuous priors, boosting, online convex optimization, contextual bandits, and repeated games: the pathwise account is the same in every case.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes an exact information-accounting identity for any Bayesian or multiplicative-weights update, showing that cumulative regret decomposes into an immediate uncertainty payment plus a reduction in information distance to a comparator. This yields a pathwise "intrinsic time" clock and two exact adaptive regret decompositions, with favorable regimes emerging as self-bounding properties rather than slack in worst-case bounds.
AI.motivation: Traditional regret analyses for online learning rely on worst-case upper bounds, where favorable stochastic or low-noise conditions appear merely as slack. The authors aim to provide exact (non-inequality) decompositions of cumulative regret that reveal these favorable regimes as self-bounding properties of the realized data sequence, not artifacts of loose bounding.
AI.method: The authors derive a one-step exact identity relating excess loss to (1) an immediate payment for uncertainty exposure and (2) the reduction in information distance (relative entropy) between the learner's current weights and a chosen comparator. Summing across rounds produces two exact adaptive regret decompositions corresponding to two natural ways of composing updates. The cumulative payments define a pathwise "intrinsic time" clock that measures the actual uncertainty realized along the sequence.
AI.result: The framework yields exact (non-asymptotic, non-inequality) regret decompositions. Stochastic or low-noise regimes manifest as self-bounding properties of the realized intrinsic time, eliminating reliance on worst-case slack. The calculus unifies Hedge, optimistic and side-information variants, continuous priors, boosting, online convex optimization, contextual bandits, and repeated games under a single information-accounting identity.
AI.conclusion: The pathwise information-accounting identity provides a universal lens for understanding Bayesian and multiplicative-weights updates. Exact regret decompositions reveal intrinsic time as a fundamental quantity, and the unification across diverse online learning settings suggests this accounting principle is a deep structural property of these algorithms.

title: Letter Lemmatization: One-to-one and Banded RNNs for Reversing Character-Set Simplification and Abbreviation in Medieval Text
comment: Accepted for publication (after peer review ) in the ICDAR 2026 workshop "VINALDO: 3rd International Workshop on Machine Vision and NLP for Document Analysis"
summary: Medieval document transcribers have very different practices; on top of that, heterogeneous digitization policies have resulted in corpora where the character-set must be viewed as fluid. In this paper we address the problem of changing between character-sets in a flexible manner. We focus on one-to-one character mappings and train characterlevel one-to-one RNNs to undo them with self-supervision; recovering half the CER even with 20 text lines. We analyse the use of these one-to-one networks for HTR post-correction and we see that they obtain significant improvements while totally ignoring ins-dels.
