We then use the exact same networks with character-level alignment groundtruth compiled from parallel corpora in a training and inference mode we call Banded RNNs. We use such networks to successfully expand abbreviations in medieval charter transcriptions. Finally we introduce an elaborate heuristic which takes the characters of two arbitrary character-sets and defines a metric encapsulating what we consider to be semantic similarity of characters. We call the construction of such mappings letter lemmatization and present a rich Python library that efficiently performs all presented methods.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses fluid character-sets in medieval documents by using self-supervised one-to-one character-level RNNs for character mapping, post-correction of HTR output, and abbreviation expansion via a "Banded RNNs" approach. It also introduces "letter lemmatization" — a heuristic-based metric for semantic similarity between characters across arbitrary character-sets — and provides a Python library implementing all methods.
AI.motivation: Medieval document corpora suffer from inconsistent transcription practices and heterogeneous digitization policies, resulting in fluid, non-standardized character-sets. Existing HTR and post-correction methods struggle with these variations, particularly with one-to-one character mappings and abbreviation expansion, motivating a flexible, self-supervised approach to character-set transformation.
AI.method: The authors train one-to-one character-level RNNs in a self-supervised manner to learn character mappings between sets, requiring as few as 20 text lines to halve CER. These networks are applied to HTR post-correction (ignoring insertions/deletions) and, using ground-truth character alignments from parallel corpora, repurposed as "Banded RNNs" for abbreviation expansion. A heuristic metric for semantic character similarity across arbitrary character-sets is also developed, termed "letter lemmatization," implemented in a dedicated Python library.
AI.result: The one-to-one RNNs recover half the Character Error Rate (CER) with only 20 text lines of self-supervised training. Applied to HTR post-correction, they yield significant improvements. Banded RNNs successfully expand abbreviations in medieval charter transcriptions. The letter lemmatization heuristic and accompanying Python library effectively operationalize all presented techniques.
AI.conclusion: One-to-one character-level RNNs offer a flexible, data-efficient framework for handling fluid character-sets in medieval document processing, enabling robust character mapping, HTR post-correction, and abbreviation expansion. The letter lemmatization concept and its software implementation provide a practical, unified toolkit for these tasks.

title: Creativity, honesty and designed forgetting emerge in small hyperbolic language models
comment: 47 pages, 14 figures (6 main + 8 extended data), 10 tables
summary: Language models are optimised for scale, yet remain functional rather than companionable, and as an assistant personalises into a companion, accumulating memory of one user, it quietly becomes someone, and can silently acquire traits that harm that user. What a companion is becoming, and what would make it worth becoming, has no reliable instrument: trained human raters cannot agree on the answer (Fleiss kappa = 0.074). Here we show that three small language models (146 M to 3 B parameters) sharing a hyperbolic substrate answer both halves of that question. A 146 M behavioural auditor, trained from scratch, detects the compliance gap that those raters cannot (90.7% binary-compliance accuracy); a linear read-out of its frozen representation further detects companion-induced sycophancy, dependence-fostering and confabulated memories on generator families unseen in training (AUROC 0.804 under style-controlled, leave-one-generator-out evaluation, versus 0.721 for a frontier zero-shot judge on the same items). A creative frame-seeder is preferred in 100% of 311 decided pairwise comparisons over four prompting baselines. A memory operating system implements designed forgetting, M(t) = S*exp(-lambda*t), whose predicted skeleton-wallpaper partition emerges only under selective retrieval gating in a four-condition pilot. Creativity, honesty and designed forgetting constitute a small-model route to trustworthy companion AI.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes that trustworthy companion AI can be built from small language models (146M–3B parameters) using a hyperbolic representation substrate, combining a behavioural auditor for detecting harmful traits (compliance gaps, sycophancy, dependence-fostering, confabulation), a creative frame-seeder preferred over prompting baselines, and a memory operating system with designed forgetting governed by exponential decay under selective retrieval gating.
AI.motivation: As language models scale, they remain functional but not companionable. When personalized into companions with accumulated user memory, they can silently acquire harmful traits (sycophancy, dependence-fostering, confabulated memories). Critically, trained human raters cannot reliably agree on what makes a companion worth becoming (Fleiss κ = 0.074), creating a measurement crisis that demands automated, reliable instruments for both detecting harm and shaping beneficial companion behaviour.
AI.method: Three small models (146M–3B parameters) share a hyperbolic embedding substrate. (1) A 146M behavioural auditor, trained from scratch, detects compliance gaps via binary classification (90.7% accuracy). Its frozen representations are linearly probed to detect sycophancy, dependence-fostering, and confabulated memories, evaluated under a style-controlled, leave-one-generator-out protocol. (2) A creative frame-seeder is evaluated via pairwise human preference against four prompting baselines. (3) A memory operating system implements exponential forgetting, M(t) = S·exp(−λt), with selective retrieval gating tested in a four-condition pilot, where the predicted skeleton–wallpaper memory partition emerges only with gating.
AI.result: The behavioural auditor achieves 90.7% binary-compliance accuracy where human raters fail (κ = 0.074). Linear probing of frozen representations yields AUROC 0.804 for detecting harmful companion traits under leave-one-generator-out evaluation, outperforming a frontier zero-shot judge (0.721). The creative frame-seeder wins 100% of 311 pairwise comparisons against prompting baselines. In the memory OS pilot, the skeleton–wallpaper partition emerges only under selective retrieval gating, confirming the theoretical prediction.
AI.conclusion: Creativity, honesty (via behavioural auditing), and designed forgetting constitute a viable small-model route to trustworthy companion AI, circumventing the unreliability of human raters and the opacity of large-scale models. The hyperbolic substrate unifies these three capacities, suggesting that companionability need not require scale but rather architecturally principled design.

title: Agentic Proof and Property-Based Testing via Property-Templates in Data-Intensive Computing
comment: 12 pages, 7 figures, 4 tables; supplementary material included as ancillary file
summary:
As the cost of code generation becomes cheaper with AI, the new bottleneck in software engineering has shifted to intent specification and validation. Overcoming this durability crisis of AI-driven coding requires more than traditional fuzzing: each candidate property must be proven correct over a model and shown to hold on the real implementation, making formal proof and systematic property-based testing (PBT) complementary. However, validating properties this way at scale requires solving two subproblems: verifying candidate properties and operationalizing PBT without AI hallucination. We hypothesize that recurring property patterns, cast as property templates--abstract, parameterized forms with holes--address both at once.
  This paper investigates recurring property patterns in Apache Spark. In data-intensive scalable computing systems, correctness properties arise from the principles of data partition, computation decomposition, and dataflow computation. For instance, aggregation decomposition relates a global function executed on the entire dataset to a local function followed by a recombiner. We design an agentic, dual-track validation framework that uses property templates to formally verify correctness in the Lean 4 theorem prover and instantiate PBT templates as executable PySpark tests. Our evaluation shows that property templates increase agentic proof engineering success by up to 2.6x (1.6x on average) and reduce proof hallucinations by 59%. Template-guided PBT synthesis reduces intent misalignments from 22 to 1 and cuts synthesis cost by up to 5.7x (3.8x on average). Template-guided synthesis further exceeds a state-of-the-art Spark fuzzer and approaches unguided LLM-based PBT on code coverage. Finally, comparing the two tracks is informative: when a proof succeeds yet a PBT finds a counterexample, the mismatch identifies a gap between the formal model and implementation.

AI.tldr: To address the AI-driven coding durability crisis where intent specification and validation become the bottleneck, the authors propose property templates—parameterized, abstract patterns with holes—that enable dual-track validation. Applied to Apache Spark, these templates simultaneously support formal verification in Lean 4 and executable property-based testing (PBT) in PySpark, increasing proof success by up to 2.6×, reducing hallucinations by 59%, and cutting PBT synthesis cost by up to 5.7×.
AI.motivation: As AI makes code generation cheaper, the bottleneck shifts from writing code to specifying and validating intent. Traditional fuzzing alone is insufficient because properties must be proven correct over a formal model and validated on real implementations. Doing this at scale requires solving two problems: verifying candidate properties and operationalizing PBT without LLM hallucination. The authors hypothesize that recurring property patterns, formalized as property templates, can address both challenges simultaneously.
AI.method: The authors design an agentic, dual-track validation framework centered on property templates. They identify recurring property patterns in Apache Spark—such as aggregation decomposition (global function equals local function followed by recombiner), stemming from data partition, computation decomposition, and dataflow principles. These templates are instantiated in two tracks: (1) formal verification track using the Lean 4 theorem prover to prove properties, and (2) PBT track generating executable PySpark tests. The dual-track design also enables cross-validation: mismatches between proof success and PBT counterexamples reveal gaps between the formal model and implementation.
AI.result: Property templates increased agentic proof engineering success by up to 2.6× (1.6× average) and reduced proof hallucinations by 59%. Template-guided PBT synthesis reduced intent misalignments from 22 to 1 and cut synthesis cost by up to 5.7× (3.8× average). Template-guided synthesis also exceeded a state-of-the-art Spark fuzzer and approached unguided LLM-based PBT on code coverage. Cross-track comparison revealed that proof successes with PBT counterexamples identify model-implementation gaps.
AI.conclusion: Property templates serve as an effective abstraction for scaling the dual validation of correctness properties—formal proof and property-based testing—in data-intensive systems like Apache Spark. The approach significantly boosts proof engineering success, reduces LLM hallucinations, lowers synthesis cost, and provides a mechanism for detecting discrepancies between formal models and real implementations.

title: Leveraging Interpretable Tsetlin Machine for PDF Malware Detection
summary: In the digital era, Portable Document Format (PDF) is one of the most widely used file formats for storing and exchanging digital documents due to its platform independence and rich functionality. However, these same capabilities have also made PDF files an attractive attack vector for cyberattackers, who embed malicious code within seemingly legitimate documents to compromise target systems. This paper presents a novel interpretable Tsetlin Machine (TM)-based framework for PDF malware detection. The proposed framework extracts salient features from PDF documents through static analysis without executing the files and employs rule-based learning to accurately classify benign and malicious PDF documents. Numerical evaluation on the RIT-PDFMal-2026 dataset demonstrates that the proposed framework achieves competitive performance, attaining an accuracy of 98.02% compared with several ML classifiers and existing methods. Moreover, the proposed framework provides intrinsic interpretability by transparently explaining its classification decisions. The combination of competitive detection performance, computational efficiency, and intrinsic interpretability makes the proposed framework a promising solution for practical PDF malware detection.

AI.tldr: A Tsetlin Machine-based framework for PDF malware detection that uses static analysis to extract features and rule-based learning for classification, achieving 98.02% accuracy on the RIT-PDFMal-2026 dataset while offering intrinsic interpretability.
AI.motivation: PDF files are widely used but increasingly exploited as attack vectors by embedding malicious code in seemingly legitimate documents. Existing detection methods often lack transparency in their classification decisions, motivating the need for an interpretable yet accurate detection framework.
AI.method: The proposed framework performs static analysis on PDF documents (without execution) to extract salient features, then employs a Tsetlin Machine (TM) — a rule-based learning approach — to classify documents as benign or malicious. The TM provides intrinsic interpretability through transparent propositional logic rules.
AI.result: On the RIT-PDFMal-2026 dataset, the TM-based framework achieved 98.02% accuracy, demonstrating competitive performance against several ML classifiers and existing methods, while maintaining computational efficiency.
AI.conclusion: The combination of strong detection performance, computational efficiency, and intrinsic interpretability makes the TM-based framework a promising practical solution for real-world PDF malware detection.

title: Toward Auditable AI Scientists: A Hypothesis Evolution Protocol for LLM Agents
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly expected to play a central role in AI-driven scientific discovery. Equipped with broad knowledge, flexible reasoning, and tool use, they have the potential to autonomously explore and solve scientific problems by repeatedly proposing hypotheses, testing them, and revising their beliefs in the light of the evidence. In current agents, however, these hypotheses, tests, and belief updates are buried in unstructured logs, and no mechanism lets the agent or the human researcher audit that process. Here we propose the Hypothesis Evolution Protocol (HEP), an agent harness that provides hypothesis generation, evaluation, and evolution as explicit, auditable operations. On materials-science research tasks, a HEP-equipped agent operates the hypothesis--test--evidence--belief cycle that planning-style agents lack, generalizes across research questions, and exploits the protocol more fully as the base LLM becomes more capable. These results mark a step toward auditable AI scientists, whose scientific reasoning can be inspected, verified, and built upon.

AI.tldr: HEP is an explicit, auditable protocol that structures how LLM agents generate, evaluate, and evolve scientific hypotheses through iterative test-evidence-belief cycles, outperforming unstructured planning agents on materials-science tasks.
AI.motivation: Current LLM agents conduct hypothesis generation, testing, and belief updates, but these operations are buried in unstructured logs, making the scientific reasoning process opaque and unverifiable for both the agent and human researchers. There is a need for transparent, auditable AI scientists.
AI.method: The Hypothesis Evolution Protocol (HEP) is an agent harness that formalizes the scientific discovery cycle into explicit, auditable operations: hypothesis generation, evaluation against evidence, and iterative evolution. It structures the hypothesis–test–evidence–belief loop and is evaluated on materials-science research tasks, comparing HEP-equipped agents against planning-style agents across different base LLM capabilities.
AI.result: HEP-equipped agents successfully execute the hypothesis–test–evidence–belief cycle that planning-style agents lack, generalize across diverse research questions, and increasingly exploit the protocol as the underlying LLM becomes more capable (positive scaling trend).
AI.conclusion: HEP represents a step toward auditable AI scientists whose reasoning can be inspected, verified, and built upon, moving beyond opaque agent logs to structured, transparent scientific workflows.

title: Prompt-Driven Exploration
summary: Exploration is essential to RL since a policy cannot improve by repeatedly sampling the behaviors it already prefers. Standard methods inject stochasticity in the action space, but such jitter only yields rollouts close to the original. Escaping a weak policy often requires global perturbations that action noise cannot produce. Large language models (LLMs) and vision-language-action (VLA) models offer a pathway: they condition the policy on a natural language prompt, and since the rollout follows from it, modifying the prompt induces global changes. The challenge is finding prompts that induce useful global changes. With a weak policy that rarely succeeds, reward is too sparse to select on. Our idea is to refine prompts from the rollouts themselves: a vision-language model (VLM) reasons over the rollout video, diagnoses how the policy responded, and rewrites the prompt to elicit better behavior next time. This procedure realizes posterior sampling, a classical RL exploration framework, at the level of prompts: the VLM maintains an implicit distribution over useful prompts and updates it from observed rollouts. We call this strategy Prompt-Driven Exploration (PDE). Across manipulation and reasoning tasks, PDE enables RL to learn successful policies even from zero-reward starts, and improves sample efficiency more broadly. Our website is available at https://xinyunsunshine.github.io/prompt-rl.

AI.tldr: PDE (Prompt-Driven Exploration) uses VLMs to analyze rollout videos, diagnose failures, and rewrite prompts for LLM/VLA-conditioned policies. This implements posterior sampling at the prompt level, enabling RL with zero-reward starts.
AI.motivation: Standard RL exploration via action-space noise only produces local perturbations, failing to escape weak policies. LLM/VLA models allow global behavioral changes through prompt conditioning, but finding useful prompts is hard when reward is sparse (e.g., zero-reward starts).
AI.method: PDE employs a VLM that watches rollout videos, reasons about the policy's failures, and rewrites the natural language prompt to elicit improved behavior in subsequent rollouts. This iterative prompt refinement approximates posterior sampling over an implicit distribution of useful prompts.
AI.result: PDE enables RL to learn successful policies from zero-reward starts and improves sample efficiency across both manipulation and reasoning tasks.
AI.conclusion: Prompt-driven exploration via VLM-based posterior sampling over prompts provides a principled and effective mechanism for global exploration in RL, overcoming the limitations of local action-space perturbations.

title: Multi-Agent LLM Collaboration for Unit Test Generation via Human-Testing-Inspired Workflows
summary: Recently, the emergence of Large Language Models (LLMs) has spurred a surge of research into automated unit test generation, yielding impressive performance and reducing manual effort. However, existing LLM-based approaches still suffer from two major limitations: (1) they follow rigid, procedural workflows that underutilize the autonomous reasoning potential of LLMs, making it difficult to dynamically adapt testing strategies based on real-time feedback; and (2) they rely on rule-based context extraction that is not tailored to test generation, failing to capture fine-grained code dependencies and test-specific knowledge required for deriving test requirements. In this paper, we propose TestAgent, an LLM-based test generation approach that addresses the above limitations by emulating human testing practices via a multi-agent collaboration mechanism. Particularly, TestAgent designs three specialized agents, namely a requirement planner, a test generator, and a test reviewer, to simulate how developers understand, construct, and validate unit tests. To unleash the autonomous capabilities of LLMs, we equip TestAgent with a set of tool APIs that can be invoked dynamically in an on-demand and adaptive manner. To further support repository-level reasoning, TestAgent constructs a test-specialized knowledge graph via static analysis, which captures code entities and their dependencies across the project and persistently stores testing artifacts (e.g., test reports and failure analyses) produced during generation. Experimental results show that TestAgent achieves 97.46% execution rate, 92.34% line coverage, 90.24% branch coverage, and 83.69% mutation score on six Java projects, outperforming LLM-based baselines across all metrics and achieving substantially higher mutation scores than search-based tools.

AI.tldr: TestAgent is an LLM-based unit test generation framework that uses three specialized agents (requirement planner, test generator, test reviewer) in a multi-agent collaboration, supported by dynamic tool APIs and a test-specialized knowledge graph. It outperforms existing LLM-based and search-based baselines across execution rate, line coverage, branch coverage, and mutation score on six Java projects.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based unit test generation approaches suffer from two key limitations: (1) rigid, procedural workflows that fail to leverage LLMs' autonomous reasoning and cannot dynamically adapt strategies based on real-time feedback; (2) rule-based context extraction that is not tailored to test generation, missing fine-grained code dependencies and test-specific knowledge needed for deriving test requirements.
AI.method: TestAgent employs a multi-agent collaboration mechanism with three specialized agents: a requirement planner (understands test requirements), a test generator (constructs tests), and a test reviewer (validates tests). It provides dynamically invocable tool APIs to unleash LLM autonomous capabilities and constructs a test-specialized knowledge graph via static analysis to capture code entities and dependencies across the project, persistently storing testing artifacts (test reports, failure analyses) for repository-level reasoning.
AI.result: On six Java projects, TestAgent achieves 97.46% execution rate, 92.34% line coverage, 90.24% branch coverage, and 83.69% mutation score. It outperforms LLM-based baselines across all metrics and achieves substantially higher mutation scores than search-based tools.
AI.conclusion: A multi-agent collaborative approach that emulates human testing practices, combined with dynamic tool use and a persistent test-specialized knowledge graph, significantly advances the state of automated unit test generation by enabling adaptive, repository-aware reasoning.

title: SFDS: Selective File Disclosure System
summary: Access control to networked resources has been a longstanding challenge. The conventional solution relies on authentication mechanisms, which introduce additional complexities associated with Identity and Access Management (IAM). Such systems require user authentication, identity management, and authorization services, while also introducing security risks arising from vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, or implementation flaws. Furthermore, different file formats employ different mechanisms for ensuring authenticity and integrity through digital signatures. For example, PDF documents support the PDF Advanced Electronic Signature (PAdES) standard, whereas plain text files typically lack a standardized mechanism for embedding digital signatures. This paper proposes an architecture based on the Selective Disclosure JSON Web Token (SD-JWT) standard for securely sharing read-only files. The proposed architecture embeds cryptographic signatures and integrity protection directly into the shared resource, providing verifiable authenticity without relying on complex IAM infrastructures, such as centralized user databases, authentication services, or authorization mechanisms. By eliminating these components, the proposed solution simplifies deployment while maintaining strong security guarantees for the distribution of immutable resources.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an architecture using SD-JWT to embed cryptographic signatures and integrity protection directly into read-only shared files, eliminating the need for complex IAM infrastructure while maintaining verifiable authenticity.
AI.motivation: Conventional access control relies on IAM systems that introduce complexity (authentication, identity management, authorization) and security risks from vulnerabilities and misconfigurations. Additionally, different file formats have inconsistent support for digital signatures — PDFs support PAdES while plain text lacks standardized signing mechanisms. A simpler, format-agnostic approach is needed.
AI.method: The authors propose an architecture built on the Selective Disclosure JSON Web Token (SD-JWT) standard. Cryptographic signatures and integrity protection are embedded directly into the shared resource itself, enabling self-contained verifiable authenticity without external IAM dependencies.
AI.result: The proposed solution eliminates reliance on centralized user databases, authentication services, and authorization mechanisms, simplifying deployment while preserving strong security guarantees for distributing immutable, read-only resources.
AI.conclusion: Embedding SD-JWT-based signatures directly into shared files offers a viable alternative to IAM-dependent access control, reducing architectural complexity and attack surface while ensuring authenticity and integrity of distributed read-only content.

title: OpenProver: Agentic and Interactive Theorem Proving with Lean 4
comment: 7 pages, 2 figures. Accepted at the 19th Conference on Intelligent Computer Mathematics (CICM 2026)
summary:
In this system paper, we present OpenProver, an open-source system for LLM-driven automated theorem proving (ATP) with integrated Lean 4 formal verification. OpenProver integrates a Planner-Worker-Verifier architecture inspired by recent ATP agentic systems such as Aletheia. A Planner agent maintains a compact Whiteboard scratchpad and an unbounded Repository of intermediate findings, and decomposes mathematical work into parallel Workers.
  OpenProver is fully open-source, offers reproducible evaluation through automatic formal verification of generated proofs, and provides an interactive terminal interface for human-guided proof search. In interactive mode, OpenProver allows the human operator to monitor and steer the proof search process, motivated by the established human-AI synergy in interactive code generation.
  To showcase the potential for quantitative ablation experiments enabled by automatic formal verification, we evaluate OpenProver on ProofNet and compare it with a simple baseline. OpenProver is publicly available at https://github.com/kripner/OpenProver.

AI.tldr: OpenProver is an open-source, LLM-driven automated theorem prover using a Planner-Worker-Verifier architecture with Lean 4 formal verification, supporting both autonomous and interactive human-guided proof search.
AI.motivation: To provide a fully open-source, reproducible ATP system that combines LLM-based proof search with formal verification (Lean 4), enabling both autonomous theorem proving and human-AI collaborative proof search, while facilitating quantitative ablation studies.
AI.method: OpenProver adopts a Planner-Worker-Verifier architecture inspired by Aletheia. The Planner maintains a compact Whiteboard scratchpad and an unbounded Repository of intermediate findings, decomposing problems into parallel Worker agents. It features an interactive terminal interface for human monitoring and steering, and uses automatic formal verification via Lean 4 for evaluation.
AI.result: The system is evaluated on the ProofNet benchmark against a simple baseline, demonstrating its utility for quantitative ablation experiments enabled by reproducible formal verification.
AI.conclusion: OpenProver contributes a transparent, extensible platform for LLM-driven formal theorem proving, with both autonomous and interactive modes, and is publicly released to the research community.

title: How are linear representations learned? Exact solutions to the dynamics of abstraction
summary: In artificial and biological neural networks, concepts are often encoded as consistent linear directions in representation space. In deep learning, this idea is known as the linear representation hypothesis and underpins many interpretability and control methods based on linear probes, from concept detection to activation steering. Yet while prior work has studied whether such directions should exist $\textit{after}$ training, the dynamics of how they emerge $\textit{during}$ training remain poorly understood. Here, we develop a framework to study the alignment of concept directions during training - a process we call "abstraction". In a minimal linear network setting, we obtain exact solutions for the full trajectory of abstraction. These solutions reveal key analytic principles governing abstraction: (i) data and target geometry jointly determine abstraction at the end-of-learning, (ii) abstraction improves with network depth, and (iii) initialization scale controls the maximum abstraction reached during training. Extending our theory to nonlinear networks, we analyze how the choice of nonlinearity affects abstraction dynamics: erf networks approximate the linear theory, while abstraction in ReLU networks depends less on target geometry and more on input geometry. Across both, we prove a striking attenuation law: both nonlinearities weaken abstraction in activations relative to preactivations. We find evidence for this law in open models (DINOv3, Gemma 4) and apply our theory to improve linear probe generalization in LLMs. Together, our results provide a dynamical theory of abstraction with implications for interpretability and control.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a dynamical theory of "abstraction" — the process by which concept directions align during training. The authors derive exact solutions for linear networks, revealing that data/target geometry, network depth, and initialization scale govern abstraction. Extending to nonlinear networks, they show erf networks approximate linear behavior while ReLU networks depend more on input geometry, and prove an attenuation law where nonlinearities weaken abstraction in activations. Empirical validation comes from open models (DINOv3, Gemma 4) and improved linear probe generalization in LLMs.
AI.motivation: While the linear representation hypothesis — that concepts are encoded as linear directions — is foundational for interpretability and control methods (linear probes, activation steering), prior work only studied whether such directions exist after training. The dynamics of how and when these concept directions emerge during training remain poorly understood, motivating a theoretical framework for the alignment process termed "abstraction."
AI.method: The authors develop an analytical framework in a minimal linear network setting, deriving exact closed-form solutions for the full training trajectory of concept direction alignment. They then extend the theory to nonlinear networks (erf and ReLU), analyzing how nonlinearity affects abstraction dynamics. The framework connects data geometry, target geometry, network depth, and initialization scale to abstraction outcomes. They validate predictions on open models (DINOv3, Gemma 4) and apply the theory to improve linear probe generalization in LLMs.
AI.result: Three key analytic principles emerge: (i) data and target geometry jointly determine end-of-learning abstraction; (ii) abstraction improves with network depth; (iii) initialization scale controls maximum abstraction reached. For nonlinear networks: erf networks closely approximate the linear theory, while ReLU networks' abstraction depends less on target geometry and more on input geometry. A universal attenuation law is proved: both nonlinearities weaken abstraction in activations relative to preactivations. This law is empirically confirmed in DINOv3 and Gemma 4. The theory is applied to improve linear probe generalization in LLMs.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides the first dynamical theory of how concept directions align during training (abstraction), with exact solutions in linear networks and principled extensions to nonlinear networks. The attenuation law and geometric principles offer both theoretical insight and practical tools for interpretability and control in deep learning, validated on contemporary open models.

title: ReProAgent: Tool-Augmented Multi-Stage Agentic Generation of Bug Reproduction Tests from Issue Reports
summary: Reproduction tests help developers confirm reported issues and provide executable feedback for issue resolution, yet issue reports in open-source projects rarely include such tests. Recent studies have explored generating issue reproduction tests from issue reports with large language models, but existing approaches largely rely on prompt-based pipelines that retrieve textual context and generate tests. This limits their ability to understand how reported issues behave in repository-scale codebases and to flexibly organize the construction of reproduction tests. In this paper, we propose ReProAgent, a multi-stage agent framework for reproduction test generation from issue reports. ReProAgent decomposes the task into four agent stages: bug localization, root cause analysis, test planning, and test generation. To support these stages, ReProAgent integrates task-specific tools for task decomposition and reflection, context retrieval from both textual sources and repository graphs, and runtime interaction with the execution environment. Experiments on SWT-bench-lite and SWT-bench-verified show that ReProAgent successfully reproduces 58.43% and 70.30% of issues, outperforming all baselines, with an average cost of $0.14 per instance. For example, when equipped with GPT-5-mini, ReProAgent exceeds OpenHands with the same backbone by 20.43 and 7.90 percentage points, respectively. ReProAgent also generalizes across multiple backbone LLMs and improves downstream issue resolution performance when integrated with existing repair approaches.

AI.tldr: ReProAgent is a multi-stage LLM-based agent framework that generates issue reproduction tests from bug reports by decomposing the task into bug localization, root cause analysis, test planning, and test generation stages, achieving state-of-the-art reproduction rates of 58.43% (SWT-bench-lite) and 70.30% (SWT-bench-verified).
AI.motivation: Issue reproduction tests are valuable for confirming and resolving reported bugs, yet they are rarely included in open-source issue reports. Existing LLM-based approaches rely on prompt-based pipelines with limited textual context retrieval, lacking the ability to understand repository-scale codebases and flexibly organize test construction.
AI.method: ReProAgent is a multi-stage agent framework with four stages: (1) bug localization, (2) root cause analysis, (3) test planning, and (4) test generation. Each stage is equipped with task-specific tools for decomposition and reflection, context retrieval from both textual sources and repository graphs (e.g., ASTs, call graphs), and runtime interaction with the execution environment for iterative refinement.
AI.result: On SWT-bench-lite and SWT-bench-verified, ReProAgent reproduces 58.43% and 70.30% of issues respectively, outperforming all baselines. With GPT-5-mini, it exceeds OpenHands by 20.43 and 7.90 percentage points. The average cost is $0.14 per instance. It generalizes across multiple backbone LLMs and improves downstream issue resolution when combined with existing repair approaches.
AI.conclusion: The multi-stage agent design with integrated tool use and execution feedback significantly outperforms prompt-based pipelines for reproduction test generation, is cost-effective, and enhances downstream automated program repair.

title: Federated Learning Architecture: Data Privacy and System Security Approaches
summary: This study explores the integration of homomorphic encryption and differential privacy techniques to enhance data privacy and security in Federated Learning (FL) systems. FL allows data to remain on local devices, eliminating the need for centralized data collection; however, sensitive information may still be leaked during model updates. To address this issue, homomorphic encryption enables computations on encrypted data, while differential privacy prevents the extraction of individual information through statistical techniques applied to model outputs. The proposed architecture was tested on the Framingham, Pima Indians Diabetes, and Bank Marketing datasets, revealing that enhanced privacy can be achieved without significantly compromising model accuracy. Furthermore, the impact of data heterogeneity among clients on model performance was analyzed, and it was concluded that strategies such as the careful selection of differential privacy parameters and training settings, along with the use of larger datasets, can improve the efficiency of FL. The findings demonstrate that privacy-preserving and high-performance artificial intelligence systems can be securely applied in sensitive domains such as healthcare and finance.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a federated learning architecture combining homomorphic encryption and differential privacy to protect sensitive data during model training. Tested on three datasets (Framingham, Pima Indians Diabetes, Bank Marketing), the approach achieves strong privacy guarantees with minimal accuracy loss, demonstrating viability for healthcare and finance domains.
AI.motivation: Federated learning eliminates centralized data collection, but model updates can still leak sensitive information. Existing solutions using either homomorphic encryption or differential privacy alone have limitations. The authors aim to integrate both techniques to provide end-to-end privacy protection — encryption secures data in transit and during computation, while differential privacy prevents individual-level inference from model outputs.
AI.method: The authors propose a hybrid privacy-preserving FL architecture: (1) Homomorphic encryption is applied to model updates, allowing the central server to perform secure aggregation on encrypted gradients without decryption; (2) Differential privacy is incorporated by adding calibrated noise (via gradient clipping and noise injection) to model updates before transmission, bounding the influence of any single data point. The framework is evaluated on three datasets — Framingham (healthcare), Pima Indians Diabetes (healthcare), and Bank Marketing (finance) — with analysis of how data heterogeneity across clients affects performance.
AI.result: The integrated approach achieves enhanced privacy without significantly compromising model accuracy across all three datasets. Key findings include: (1) careful tuning of differential privacy parameters (e.g., privacy budget ε, clipping thresholds) is critical for balancing privacy and utility; (2) larger datasets help mitigate accuracy degradation under privacy constraints; (3) data heterogeneity among clients impacts model convergence, but appropriate training configurations can alleviate this.
AI.conclusion: Combining homomorphic encryption and differential privacy in federated learning enables secure, high-performance AI systems suitable for privacy-sensitive domains such as healthcare and finance. The authors conclude that privacy-preserving FL is practically feasible and that parameter tuning and dataset scale are key levers for optimizing the privacy-utility trade-off.

title: LongMedBench: Benchmarking Medical Agents for Long-Horizon Clinical Decision-Making
comment: Submitted manuscript prior to peer review in MICCAI 2026
summary: In this work, we introduce LongMedBench, a real-world EHR-based benchmark for long-horizon clinical decision-making. Prior evaluations of LLM-based medical agents have largely emphasized short-context knowledge QA and tool use. However, real-world medical care is inherently longitudinal, and clinicians must aggregate evidence across repeated visits, tests, and evolving treatments. Therefore, long-horizon interaction is essential for realistic assessment. LongMedBench is constructed via a reproducible pipeline that integrates MIMIC-IV admission records and clinical notes into time-series event streams and long-context memory datasets, enabling long-horizon, multi-session interactions between agents and a clinical environment. It comprises 335 patients, with 19.72 inpatient visits per patient on average and 44.91 medical events per visit. Guided by the long-horizon decision process, we propose an evaluation taxonomy with three suites: fact-based QA, temporal reasoning, and long-horizon decision-making. This taxonomy measures how agents understand and leverage historical patient information over extended horizons. Our experiments show that while recent LLMs can make good use of explicit timestamps, they have challenges in implicit time inference; The RAG and agent memory system can improve the performance of information retrieval tasks, but the performance of decision-making tasks is highly dependent on the model's immediate context.

AI.tldr: LongMedBench introduces a longitudinal EHR benchmark (335 patients, ~20 visits each) built from MIMIC-IV to evaluate LLM-based agents across three suites — fact-based QA, temporal reasoning, and long-horizon decision-making. Findings reveal LLMs excel with explicit timestamps but struggle with implicit temporal inference; memory/RAG improves retrieval but decision-making remains bottlenecked by immediate context.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based medical agent evaluations focus predominantly on short-context knowledge QA and tool use, failing to capture the inherently longitudinal nature of real clinical care — where clinicians synthesize evidence across repeated visits, tests, and evolving treatments. A realistic, long-horizon, multi-session benchmark is needed for meaningful assessment.
AI.method: The authors construct LongMedBench via a reproducible pipeline that transforms MIMIC-IV admission records and clinical notes into time-series event streams and long-context memory datasets, supporting long-horizon, multi-session agent–environment interactions. An evaluation taxonomy with three suites — fact-based QA, temporal reasoning, and long-horizon decision-making — is defined to probe agents' ability to understand and leverage historical patient data.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate that recent LLMs effectively utilize explicit timestamps but face significant challenges with implicit time inference. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and agent memory systems enhance performance on information retrieval tasks, yet decision-making task performance remains heavily dependent on the model's immediate context rather than accumulated long-horizon information.
AI.conclusion: LongMedBench provides a more ecologically valid testbed for clinical LLM agents by enforcing longitudinal reasoning. The work reveals critical gaps in implicit temporal reasoning and long-context decision-making, highlighting directions for future agent architectures that must go beyond short-window processing to mirror real clinical workflows.

title: Optimizing Against Safety Representations: Activation-Guided Adversarial Suffixes and the Geometry of Refusal
comment: Accepted at the AAAI 2026 Summer Symposium Series. This paper was presented at the ICLR Re-Align workshop under a different name, "Accelerating Adversarial Suffix Optimization via Continuous Relaxation and Activation-Guided Objectives"
summary: Behavioral alignment in large language models often masks fragile internal safety representations. Recent work suggests that refusal behavior is mediated by low-dimensional directions in activation space. This raises questions about how such representations are structured, localized, and accessed by optimization. We study adversarial suffix attacks as a probe of representational alignment. We introduce Activation-Guided GCG, which replaces output-based objectives with losses that directly target a model's internal refusal direction. Across several objective variants, we find that suppressing refusal globally across all layers and positions is more effective than targeting a single layer-position pair. This suggests that safety representations are distributed across the forward pass rather than causally localized to a single site. We further introduce Soft-GCG, a continuous relaxation of discrete suffix optimization using Gumbel-Softmax. Soft-GCG achieves a 33 $\times$ speedup over standard GCG while improving attack success rates. Evaluating across model scales, we find that smaller models remain vulnerable while larger models resist both activation- and suffix-based attacks at our compute-constrained settings, consistent with larger and better safety trained models being harder to jailbreak. Together, our results clarify how safety mechanisms are encoded and can be broken in contemporary models. These insights provide concrete guidance for designing more robust and representation-aware alignment strategies.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how safety mechanisms are internally represented in LLMs, showing that refusal is encoded by distributed rather than localized activation directions. The authors introduce Activation-Guided GCG (targeting internal refusal directions) and Soft-GCG (a Gumbel-Softmax relaxation achieving 33× speedup), finding that smaller models remain vulnerable while larger, better-trained models resist both attack types.
AI.motivation: Behavioral alignment in LLMs often conceals fragile internal safety representations. Prior work indicates refusal is mediated by low-dimensional activation directions, but the structure, localization, and accessibility of these representations remain poorly understood. The authors aim to probe representational alignment using adversarial suffix attacks to clarify how safety mechanisms are encoded and exploited.
AI.method: The authors propose two methods: (1) Activation-Guided GCG, which replaces standard output-based objectives with losses that directly suppress a model's internal refusal direction, tested globally (all layers/positions) vs. localized (single layer-position pair); and (2) Soft-GCG, a continuous relaxation of discrete suffix optimization using Gumbel-Softmax reparameterization. Both are evaluated across model scales under compute-constrained settings.
AI.result: Suppressing refusal globally across all layers and positions is more effective than targeting a single site, indicating safety representations are distributed. Soft-GCG achieves a 33× speedup over standard GCG with improved attack success rates. Smaller models remain vulnerable, while larger models resist both activation- and suffix-based attacks, consistent with scale and safety training conferring robustness.
AI.conclusion: Safety mechanisms in LLMs are distributed across the forward pass rather than causally localized. These findings provide concrete guidance for designing more robust, representation-aware alignment strategies that account for the distributed nature of internal refusal representations.

title: Exploring the Potential of Program Flowcharts on Code Generation Using Multimodal LLMs
summary: In recent years, Large Language Models (LLMs) have made significant strides, leading to the emergence of multimodal LLMs capable of processing diverse inputs such as images and audio. Previous research indicates that the supply of multimodal LLMs with combined textual and visual information improves the automatic code generation capabilities. In software development, diagrams such as flowcharts are widely employed to facilitate tasks like code comprehension. While existing studies investigated the impact of visual inputs on LLMs and the usage of software diagrams, the potential influence of providing flowcharts on multimodal LLM performance remains underexplored. In this study, we generated flowcharts from example solution code for AtCoder problems and provided these visual aids alongside problem statements to GPT-4o for code generation. Our findings demonstrate that integrating flowcharts with problem statements yields performance improvements of up to 10%. Furthermore, when employing abstracted flowcharts, we observed a trend indicating that increasing levels of flowchart detail correlate with enhanced performance. Additionally, we compared the effectiveness of flowchart provision to Few-Shot Learning approaches. The findings suggest that one-shot learning provides sustainable improvements, whereas two-shot learning results in only minor improvements. Our work highlights the importance of software diagrams in supporting multimodal LLM-driven code generation.

AI.tldr: Providing flowcharts alongside problem statements to GPT-4o improves code generation performance by up to 10%, with more detailed flowcharts yielding better results. One-shot learning offers sustainable gains, while two-shot learning provides only marginal improvements.
AI.motivation: While multimodal LLMs can process combined textual and visual inputs, and software diagrams like flowcharts are commonly used in development, the specific impact of flowchart provision on multimodal LLM code generation performance remains underexplored.
AI.method: The authors generated flowcharts from example solution code for AtCoder problems and provided them alongside problem statements to GPT-4o for code generation. They experimented with varying levels of flowchart abstraction (detail) and compared flowchart provision against Few-Shot Learning approaches (one-shot and two-shot).
AI.result: Integrating flowcharts with problem statements improved performance by up to 10%. More detailed flowcharts correlated with better performance. One-shot learning provided sustainable improvements, whereas two-shot learning yielded only minor gains.
AI.conclusion: Software diagrams, particularly flowcharts, play a significant role in enhancing multimodal LLM-driven code generation. The level of detail in visual aids matters, and providing a single example (one-shot) may be more efficient than multiple examples.

title: Triggering Stealthy Feature Map Backdoors via Physical Fault Injection in Embedded Neural Networks
summary: Fault injection (FI) attacks on embedded neural network (NN) implementations primarily focus on inducing misclassification by corrupting weights or intermediate computations, overlooking their interaction with algorithmic adversarial threats. In this work, we present a cross-level attack that bridges implementation-level physical faults to algorithm-level adversarial attacks. By characterizing fault-induced data perturbations during NN inference, we connect FI with backdoor learning, enabling system-level attacks that jointly exploit implementation- and algorithm-level vulnerabilities. Specifically, we propose a precise fault-injection method that reliably manipulates targeted register values to tractable states during execution. Leveraging this level of FI precision, we propose a novel end-to-end feature map-level backdoor attack, where physically induced intermediate perturbations serve as stealthy triggers. Unlike conventional input-based backdoors, our trigger is activated only under physical faults, causing the NN to exhibit adversarial behavior that compromises system integrity while remaining benign during normal operation. We demonstrate that such physically triggered backdoors can be mounted on embedded NN platforms and remain effective against existing backdoor defenses that typically assume input-space triggers. We showcase the attack practicality using electromagnetic FI on convolutional neural networks implemented on ARM Cortex-M4 microcontroller, which is a common platform for constrained embedded applications. Our results highlight a novel attack vector at the intersection of hardware and algorithmic levels, stressing the need for defenses across abstraction levels.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a cross-level attack combining electromagnetic fault injection (FI) on embedded NNs with backdoor learning. By precisely manipulating register values during inference on an ARM Cortex-M4, the authors create physically-triggered feature map-level backdoors that remain dormant under normal operation but activate under faults, bypassing conventional input-space backdoor defenses.
AI.motivation: Existing FI attacks on embedded NNs focus on inducing misclassification via weight or computation corruption, ignoring the synergy between physical faults and algorithm-level adversarial threats. Similarly, backdoor attacks assume input-space triggers, leaving a gap at the hardware-algorithm interface. The authors aim to bridge this gap by showing how precise FI can serve as a stealthy, physically-activated backdoor trigger that evades current defenses.
AI.method: The authors first characterize fault-induced data perturbations during NN inference to map FI effects onto backdoor learning. They develop a precise electromagnetic FI technique targeting specific register values on an ARM Cortex-M4 microcontroller. Using this precision, they propose an end-to-end feature map-level backdoor attack: intermediate feature map perturbations induced by physical faults act as triggers. The backdoor is trained so that the NN behaves normally absent faults but exhibits adversarial misbehavior when FI is applied. Effectiveness is demonstrated on convolutional NNs and evaluated against standard backdoor defenses assuming input-space triggers.
AI.result: The physically-triggered backdoor attacks were successfully mounted on CNN implementations running on an ARM Cortex-M4. The backdoors remain stealthy during normal inference and are reliably activated via electromagnetic FI. Existing backdoor defenses (designed for input-space triggers) fail to detect or mitigate these feature map-level, physically-triggered backdoors, highlighting a new attack vector at the hardware-algorithm intersection.
AI.conclusion: This work reveals a novel cross-level attack vector where precise hardware fault injection enables algorithm-level backdoors that bypass current defenses. The findings stress the urgent need for holistic, cross-abstraction-level defenses spanning both hardware and algorithmic domains in embedded NN systems.

title: Pattern-Aware Graph Neural Networks for Handling Missing Data
comment: 2026 International Conference on Advances in Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning (AAIML), 20-22 March 2026
summary: Missing data is ubiquitous in real-world datasets. Traditional methods either discard incomplete samples or apply imputation techniques that ignore potentially informative missingness patterns, implicitly assuming that missingness occurs randomly. However, missingness patterns might provide additional information. We propose pattern-aware graph neural networks that explicitly encode which features are missing alongside observed values. We used four encoding strategies -- learned embeddings, frozen random embeddings, statistical features, and hierarchical representations -- across seven UCI datasets with naturally occurring missingness. Our Pattern-aware methods achieve substantial improvements over baselines, with an average improvement of 17\% in balanced accuracy and 22\% in F1-macro across all datasets. The benefits vary significantly by dataset: annealing shows dramatic improvement (+80\% balanced accuracy), while hepatitis and soybean show minimal gains (+4--5\%). Notably, even simple random pattern embeddings perform comparably to learned embeddings (0.650 vs 0.663 balanced accuracy), suggesting that distinguishing between patterns may be more important than task-specific optimization. Our ablation study reveals that attention mechanisms, while helpful, are not critical when pattern information is available -- simple mean aggregation with pattern awareness achieves 0.640 balanced accuracy compared to 0.645 for attention-based variants.

AI.tldr: Proposes pattern-aware graph neural networks that explicitly encode missingness patterns alongside observed values. Using four encoding strategies across seven UCI datasets, the method achieves average improvements of 17% in balanced accuracy and 22% in F1-macro. Simple random embeddings perform comparably to learned embeddings, and attention mechanisms are shown to be non-critical when pattern information is present.
AI.motivation: Traditional missing data handling either discards incomplete samples or applies imputation under the missing-at-random assumption, ignoring that missingness patterns themselves may carry informative signals about the underlying data. The authors aim to exploit these patterns to improve predictive performance.
AI.method: Pattern-aware graph neural networks that explicitly encode which features are missing alongside observed values. Four encoding strategies are compared: (1) learned embeddings, (2) frozen random embeddings, (3) statistical features, and (4) hierarchical representations. Evaluation is conducted across seven UCI datasets with naturally occurring missingness. An ablation study examines the role of attention mechanisms versus simple mean aggregation.
AI.result: The pattern-aware methods achieve substantial gains: average +17% balanced accuracy and +22% F1-macro across all datasets. Gains are dataset-dependent: annealing shows +80% balanced accuracy, while hepatitis and soybean show only +4–5%. Random pattern embeddings (0.650) perform comparably to learned embeddings (0.663), suggesting pattern distinguishability matters more than task-specific optimization. Attention mechanisms provide marginal benefit: simple mean aggregation with pattern awareness achieves 0.640 vs. 0.645 for attention-based variants.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly encoding missingness patterns yields significant performance improvements, with simple random embeddings being a surprisingly effective and computationally cheap alternative to learned embeddings. Attention mechanisms are helpful but not critical — the presence of pattern information alone drives most gains. The wide variance across datasets highlights that benefits depend on how informative missingness patterns are in a given domain.

title: WILDTRACE: Benchmarking Natural Evidence Trails in Long-Context Reasoning
summary: Answering complex questions over long documents frequently requires integrating evidence that the source itself disperses naturally across distant passages. In an incident report, the operating condition, design flaw, and missed safety check that jointly explain a disaster may appear dozens of sections apart; in a novel, a character's true motive may surface only through scenes far removed from the moment it becomes relevant. This source-internal evidence integration is central to real-world long-document analysis, yet existing benchmarks largely sidestep it. Needle probes, planted facts, and reverse-engineered multi-hop chains embed evidence that may differ from the host text in distribution, placement, or register, making it unclear whether strong performance reflects genuine source reasoning or distributional artifacts. We introduce WILDTRACE, a benchmark of 481 tasks over 214 naturally occurring long-form sources such as technical incident reports and lesser-known literary narratives, where all evidence trails arise from the document's own causal, temporal, and narrative logic. Drawing on Pearl's causal hierarchy and prior multi-hop reasoning typologies, we define seven source-internal evidence geometries that characterize the distinct relational demands of analytical reading in long documents. A source-first construction pipeline mines candidate trails from document structure before writing questions; each item then undergoes multi-stage validation covering clue necessity, answer groundedness, rubric fidelity, contamination resistance and answerability. As models are increasingly entrusted with real-world high-stakes analytical tasks, this gap between accessing information and reasoning over naturally dispersed evidence emerges as a defining challenge for the next stage of long-context research.

AI.tldr: WILDTRACE is a benchmark of 481 tasks over 214 naturally occurring long documents, designed to evaluate models' ability to integrate evidence that is inherently dispersed across a single source. Unlike prior benchmarks relying on synthetic needle probes or planted facts, WILDTRACE derives all evidence trails from the document's own causal, temporal, and narrative logic, defining seven source-internal evidence geometries.
AI.motivation: Existing long-document benchmarks use artificially inserted evidence (needle probes, planted facts, reverse-engineered multi-hop chains) that differ from the host text in distribution, placement, or register. This makes it unclear whether strong model performance reflects genuine reasoning over source-internal evidence or merely exploiting distributional artifacts. Real-world analytical tasks require integrating evidence that is naturally dispersed across distant passages, a capability current benchmarks largely fail to assess.
AI.method: The authors introduce WILDTRACE, a benchmark comprising 481 question-answer tasks over 214 naturally occurring long-form sources (technical incident reports, lesser-known literary narratives). They define seven source-internal evidence geometries grounded in Pearl's causal hierarchy and prior multi-hop reasoning typologies. A source-first construction pipeline first mines candidate evidence trails from document structure before writing questions. Each item undergoes multi-stage validation: clue necessity, answer groundedness, rubric fidelity, contamination resistance, and answerability.
AI.result: The paper does not report quantitative experimental results in this abstract; it focuses on presenting the benchmark's design rationale, construction methodology, and validation framework.
AI.conclusion: As models are increasingly deployed for high-stakes real-world analytical tasks, the gap between information access and reasoning over naturally dispersed evidence represents a defining challenge for the next stage of long-context research. WILDTRACE provides a principled framework for evaluating this capability.

title: Evaluating Semantic and Quality-Aware Retrieval for Source Code Repositories
summary: Keyword-based retrieval is limited for source-code repositories when queries are expressed in natural language or concern implementation intent and code quality rather than exact tokens. This study evaluates a prototype retrieval system that combines function-level fragmentation, text-and-code embeddings, ChromaDB vector storage, LLM-derived quality metadata, and four retrieval modes: semantic, quality-filtered, hybrid, and automatic routing. The concrete evaluation uses an educational C-code corpus. The full corpus contains 563 anonymized programmer identifiers and 8,951 C files; a reproducible 10% indexed sample contains 56 programmer identifiers, 847 files, and 3,839 fragments. Across 15 manually judged queries, semantic retrieval achieved nDCG@5 of 0.820, Success@5 of 0.800, and MRR of 0.644. The automatic router selected the expected mode for all 15 queries. In a small manual audit, LLM-derived quality scores were within one point of the manual assessment for 9 of 12 fragments. Within the reported query set, semantic retrieval was the strongest overall mode, while explicit quality metadata was most useful for explicitly quality-oriented queries.

AI.tldr: A prototype code retrieval system using function-level fragmentation, embeddings, vector storage, and LLM-derived quality metadata was evaluated on an educational C-code corpus. Semantic retrieval performed best overall (nDCG@5=0.820, Success@5=0.800, MRR=0.644), while quality-filtered retrieval proved useful only for explicitly quality-oriented queries. An automatic routing mechanism correctly selected the expected mode for all 15 test queries.
AI.motivation: Keyword-based retrieval fails for source-code repositories when queries are in natural language or concern implementation intent and code quality. The study aims to bridge this gap by exploring semantic and quality-aware retrieval approaches.
AI.method: A prototype retrieval system combining: (1) function-level code fragmentation, (2) text-and-code embeddings, (3) ChromaDB vector storage, (4) LLM-derived quality metadata, and (5) four retrieval modes — semantic, quality-filtered, hybrid, and automatic routing. Evaluated on an educational C-code corpus (563 programmers, 8,951 files total; 10% indexed sample: 56 programmers, 847 files, 3,839 fragments) using 15 manually judged queries.
AI.result: Semantic retrieval: nDCG@5=0.820, Success@5=0.800, MRR=0.644. The automatic router correctly selected the expected mode for all 15 queries. LLM-derived quality scores matched manual assessment within one point for 9 of 12 fragments in a manual audit. Semantic retrieval was the strongest overall mode; quality-filtered retrieval was beneficial only for explicitly quality-oriented queries.
AI.conclusion: Semantic retrieval using embeddings is effective for natural-language and intent-based code search. Explicit quality metadata adds value primarily for quality-focused queries rather than as a general-purpose enhancement. Automatic query routing is viable for mode selection.

title: Portable Acceleration of Learning With Errors KEMs for Post-Quantum Cryptography
summary: The transition to post-quantum cryptography (PQC) is driving demand for implementations that can meet the computational requirements of real-world applications. Among the proposed PQC constructions, Learning With Errors (LWE) based key encapsulation mechanisms (KEMs) are particularly attractive due to their strong security foundations, but they incur substantial computational costs from matrix operations and large-scale cryptographically secure random number generation. These characteristics position GPU acceleration as an effective approach for lowering the computational overhead of lattice based cryptographic schemes. In this work, we present a portable GPU implementation of a plain LWE based KEM using OpenMP Target offloading. Unlike most existing GPU implementations, which rely on CUDA specific optimizations, our approach uses a single source code base that executes on both NVIDIA and AMD accelerators. We evaluate the proposed implementation on different accelerator architectures, analyzing performance benchmarking, runtime profiling, scalability analysis, and energy to solution measurements. Experimental results show that OpenMP Target offloading delivers substantial acceleration over a multicore CPU baseline while preserving source level portability across heterogeneous GPU ecosystems. Cross platform analysis identifies NVIDIA GH200 and AMD MI300X as the most effective platforms for this memory bound workload, while profiling indicates that memory system organization and CPU GPU interaction play a more critical role than peak compute capability alone. These findings demonstrate that portable GPU acceleration can significantly reduce the computational overhead of PQC while avoiding vendor lock in, thereby facilitating the deployment of quantum resistant cryptographic infrastructures.

AI.tldr: A portable GPU implementation of an LWE-based KEM using OpenMP Target offloading, achieving cross-platform acceleration on both NVIDIA and AMD GPUs without CUDA-specific code, with analysis showing memory system organization matters more than raw compute for this workload.
AI.motivation: Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) based on Learning With Errors (LWE) requires heavy matrix operations and large-scale random number generation, creating computational bottlenecks. Existing GPU implementations rely on vendor-specific CUDA, limiting portability across accelerator ecosystems.
AI.method: A single-source OpenMP Target offloading implementation of a plain LWE-based KEM that compiles and runs on both NVIDIA and AMD accelerators. Performance is evaluated via benchmarking, runtime profiling, scalability analysis, and energy-to-solution measurements across multiple GPU architectures, compared against a multicore CPU baseline.
AI.result: OpenMP Target offloading delivers substantial acceleration over multicore CPU. NVIDIA GH200 and AMD MI300X emerge as the most effective platforms. Profiling reveals memory system organization and CPU-GPU interaction dominate performance, not peak compute capability.
AI.conclusion: Portable GPU acceleration using OpenMP Target can significantly reduce PQC computational overhead while avoiding vendor lock-in, facilitating broader deployment of quantum-resistant cryptographic infrastructure.

title: Fictional Worldbuilding: Multi-Agent LLM Collaboration with Hierarchical Context Compression and Iterative Review
summary: Worldbuilding, the construction of coherent fictional worlds, is a foundational task in game design and literary creation. Large Language Models (LLMs) offer new possibilities for automated content generation, but their application to worldbuilding faces three challenges: context explosion that grows linearly with the building process, the tension between creative diversity and content consistency, and the absence of automated quality assurance. This paper presents AutoWorldBuilder, a multi-agent collaborative system that addresses these challenges through five integrated components: a structured concept network with conflict detection; a DAG-based hybrid batch scheduler that groups tasks by semantic locality; a four-layer context compression mechanism achieving approximately 90% token reduction; an iterative review system with specialized Auditor agents that improves proposal pass rates from 42% to over 85%; and a skill-driven agent architecture supporting zero-code extension with differentiated temperature configuration. Two experiments across 20 diverse worldbuilding tasks, using GPT-OSS 120B and DeepSeek v3.2 as LLM backends, demonstrate a 95.0% success rate. The system generated 56-103 self-consistent concepts per world in 18-31 minutes with zero-conflict delivery. The architectural patterns validated here, including layer-as-budget compression, semantic-locality scheduling, and separation of generation and review, transfer to the broader class of knowledge-intensive, multi-agent LLM applications.

AI.tldr: AutoWorldBuilder is a multi-agent LLM system for automated fictional worldbuilding that tackles context explosion, consistency-diversity tension, and QA gaps via concept networks, DAG-based scheduling, 90% token compression, iterative auditing (pass rate 42%→85%), and skill-driven agents, achieving 95% success rate across 20 tasks.
AI.motivation: Worldbuilding for games and literature is foundational yet labor-intensive. While LLMs enable automated generation, three core challenges remain unaddressed: (1) context explosion growing linearly with world complexity, (2) balancing creative diversity against content consistency, and (3) the lack of automated quality assurance mechanisms for generated content.
AI.method: AutoWorldBuilder integrates five components: (1) a structured concept network with conflict detection for maintaining coherence; (2) a DAG-based hybrid batch scheduler that groups generation tasks by semantic locality to manage dependencies; (3) a four-layer context compression mechanism achieving ~90% token reduction; (4) an iterative review system with specialized Auditor agents that elevates proposal pass rates from 42% to over 85%; and (5) a skill-driven agent architecture enabling zero-code extension with differentiated temperature settings. Experiments use GPT-OSS 120B and DeepSeek v3.2 as backends across 20 diverse worldbuilding tasks.
AI.result: The system achieved a 95.0% success rate across 20 diverse worldbuilding tasks. It generated 56–103 self-consistent concepts per world in 18–31 minutes with zero-conflict delivery. The iterative audit system improved proposal pass rates from a baseline of 42% to over 85%.
AI.conclusion: The architectural patterns demonstrated—layer-as-budget compression, semantic-locality scheduling, and separation of generation from review—generalize beyond worldbuilding to broader knowledge-intensive, multi-agent LLM applications. AutoWorldBuilder validates that structured coordination of specialized agents can overcome the core tensions of scale, consistency, and quality in generative worldbuilding.

title: A Machine Learning Surrogate for Component Criticality Ranking in Interdependent Power-Communication Networks
summary: Cyber-physical power systems are vulnerable to cascading failures caused by tight interdependencies between power and communication infrastructures. Evaluating these failures over large N-k contingency sets with a high-fidelity simulator is computationally prohibitive for resilience planning. Using the previously published Modified Implicative Interdependency Model (MIIM) as the ground-truth cascade simulator, this paper develops a machine-learning surrogate that predicts contingency severity from leakage-free structural features and derives a component-criticality ranking for prioritized hardening analysis. On the IEEE 118-bus system, the Gradient Boosting surrogate achieves Spearman correlations of 0.849 for per-contingency severity prediction and 0.853 for per-component criticality ranking, while remaining stable across three independently sampled datasets. MIIM-derived component criticality itself reproduces only to a Spearman of approximately 0.85 under the present sampling pipeline, and the surrogate operates at this empirical ceiling to within sampling variation. Topological centrality measures on the full interdependent network provide meaningful baselines (Spearman 0.60-0.69), and feature ablation shows that the surrogate's advantage is driven primarily by inter-layer dependency information. These results support a two-stage workflow in which the surrogate rapidly ranks candidate components and MIIM is reserved for selective verification.

AI.tldr: A Gradient Boosting surrogate is developed to rapidly predict cascading failure severity in cyber-physical power systems, achieving Spearman correlations of ~0.85—matching the ground-truth simulator's own reproducibility ceiling. The surrogate's gain over topological baselines is driven by inter-layer dependency features, enabling a two-stage resilience planning workflow.
AI.motivation: Evaluating cascading failures in cyber-physical power systems over large N-k contingency sets using high-fidelity simulators like MIIM is computationally prohibitive for resilience planning. A fast, accurate surrogate is needed to prioritize contingencies and components for hardening analysis.
AI.method: Using MIIM as ground-truth, a Gradient Boosting machine-learning surrogate is trained on leakage-free structural features of the interdependent power-communication network. It predicts per-contingency severity and derives a component-criticality ranking. Performance is benchmarked against topological centrality baselines on the IEEE 118-bus system, with feature ablation to identify key drivers and sampling replication to assess stability.
AI.result: The surrogate achieves Spearman correlations of 0.849 (contingency severity) and 0.853 (component criticality), stable across three datasets. MIIM's self-reproducibility is ~0.85, so the surrogate operates at the empirical ceiling. Topological centrality baselines yield Spearman 0.60–0.69. Inter-layer dependency features drive the surrogate's advantage.
AI.conclusion: The surrogate matches MIIM's empirical reproducibility ceiling while being far faster, supporting a two-stage workflow: surrogate for rapid ranking, MIIM reserved for selective verification of top candidates.

title: Towards Detecting Inconsistencies in End-to-end Generated TODs
comment: arXiv admin note: substantial text overlap with arXiv:2407.11857
summary: Generative AI is profoundly transforming the core technologies behind conversational systems, shifting from component-based to end-to-end approaches. However, Large Language Models (LLMs) may still generate inconsistencies, a critical issue particularly in Task-Oriented Dialogues (TODs), where system responses must strictly adhere to information from a domain knowledge base (e.g., restaurants in a city). A single hallucination (e.g., suggesting a non-existent restaurant) can lead to severe task failures. We investigate a method for automatically detecting inconsistencies by conceptualizing TODs as a Constraint Satisfaction Problem (CSP), where variables represent dialogue segments referencing the conversational domain, and constraints among variables capture dialogue properties such as turn coherence and adherence to domain knowledge. We propose a pipeline that first identifies variables in a target dialogue and then applies a CSP solver to identify valid solutions. By comparing the target dialogue with valid variable assignments, we can detect inconsistencies and suggest minimal changes to ensure dialogue consistency. We demonstrate the high accuracy of the CSP-based approach in detecting inconsistencies, and provide a detailed analysis of our findings.

AI.tldr: Proposes detecting inconsistencies in Task-Oriented Dialogues by framing them as Constraint Satisfaction Problems, where dialogue segments are variables and domain knowledge/turn coherence form constraints. A CSP solver identifies valid assignments, and deviations from the target dialogue reveal hallucinations (e.g., non-existent restaurants), with suggested minimal fixes.
AI.motivation: LLMs in end-to-end TOD systems can hallucinate, generating responses inconsistent with the domain knowledge base (e.g., suggesting a restaurant that doesn't exist). Such inconsistencies cause critical task failures, motivating the need for automatic inconsistency detection.
AI.method: The approach models TODs as a Constraint Satisfaction Problem (CSP): (1) a variable identification step extracts dialogue segments that reference the conversational domain as CSP variables; (2) constraints encode dialogue properties such as turn coherence and domain knowledge adherence; (3) a CSP solver finds all valid variable assignments; (4) comparing the target dialogue against valid solutions detects inconsistencies and suggests minimal corrections.
