AI.result: The CSP-based approach demonstrates high accuracy in detecting inconsistencies in task-oriented dialogues, with detailed analysis provided.
AI.conclusion: Framing TOD consistency checking as a CSP offers an effective, principled method for automatically detecting LLM hallucinations and ensuring dialogue responses strictly adhere to domain knowledge bases.

title: Attention to Detail: Evaluating Energy, Performance, and Accuracy Trade-offs Across vLLM Configurations
summary:
Large Language Models are reshaping how software is developed and maintained. They are typically deployed in production using inference engines such as vLLM, which can efficiently serve pre-trained, highly configurable models. While prior work has focused on model architectures and hardware acceleration, the impact of inference engine configuration on energy consumption, performance, and output quality remains poorly understood.
  In this paper, we present a large-scale controlled study of three selected vLLM configuration options: attention kernel type, prefix caching, and chunked prefill. We evaluate all combinations of these configurations across 5 open-weight LLMs and 5 diverse inference tasks, totaling $9,000$ runs and $93,600$ measures. We analyze energy consumption, latency, and accuracy, and examine both main effects and interaction effects between configuration options and tasks.
  Our results show that the studied configuration options significantly impact energy and performance, mainly driven by attention type and prefix caching, while chunked prefill has a limited effect under the default vLLM serving configuration and evaluated workloads. These effects are highly model- and workload-dependent, and no configuration is universally optimal. We further show that model choice dominates global trade-offs, while configuration tuning provides local improvements along the Pareto frontier. Unexpectedly, inference options can also affect model accuracy.

AI.tldr: A large-scale controlled experiment (9,000 runs, 93,600 measures) investigating how three vLLM configuration options—attention kernel type, prefix caching, and chunked prefill—affect energy consumption, latency, and accuracy across 5 LLMs and 5 tasks. Results show significant but highly model- and workload-dependent effects, with attention type and prefix caching as dominant factors, while chunked prefill has limited impact. Model choice dominates global trade-offs; configuration tuning provides only local Pareto improvements.
AI.motivation: While prior work on LLM inference optimization has focused on model architectures and hardware acceleration, the impact of inference engine configuration options (specifically in vLLM) on the energy-performance-quality trade-off remains poorly understood. There is a lack of empirical evidence on how these configurations interact with different models and workloads.
AI.method: A large-scale controlled study evaluating all combinations of three vLLM configuration options (attention kernel type, prefix caching, chunked prefill) across 5 open-weight LLMs and 5 diverse inference tasks, totaling 9,000 runs and 93,600 measurements. The authors analyze main effects and interaction effects on energy consumption, latency, and accuracy, examining both main effects and interactions between configurations, models, and tasks.
AI.result: (1) Attention kernel type and prefix caching significantly impact energy and performance; chunked prefill has limited effect under default vLLM settings. (2) Effects are highly model- and workload-dependent—no universally optimal configuration exists. (3) Model choice dominates global trade-offs along the Pareto frontier; configuration tuning yields only local improvements. (4) Unexpectedly, inference configuration options can also affect model accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Inference engine configuration significantly impacts the energy-performance-accuracy trade-off in LLM serving, but effects are not uniform across models and tasks. Practitioners should prioritize model selection for global optimization and use configuration tuning for fine-grained, workload-specific improvements. The finding that configuration choices affect accuracy (not just efficiency) warrants further investigation.

title: VEXAIoT: Autonomous IoT Vulnerability EXploitation using AI Agents
summary: Internet of Things (IoT) systems are inherently vulnerable due to constrained hardware, outdated firmware, and insecure default configurations, creating a need for scalable and adaptive security testing approaches. While recent adoptions of Large Language Model (LLM) agents have demonstrated promise in penetration testing and Capture-the-Flag (CTF) environments, their application to IoT specific vulnerabilities remains unexplored. This paper presents an autonomous multi-agent framework, referred to as Vulnerability EXploitation using AI Agents (VEXAIoT), for vulnerability discovery and exploitation in IoT environments using LLM-based reasoning and offensive security tools. The framework combines a vulnerability detection agent and an attack execution agent to perform reconnaissance, plan attack sequences, and execute exploits against vulnerable IoT services. The system is evaluated in IoTGoat and Metasploitable environments across ten attack scenarios mapped to OWASP IoT vulnerabilities. Experimental results show attack success rate of up to 100% with low token overhead and average execution times under two minutes for most attacks. Across 260 attack executions, VEXAIoT achieves a 95.0% overall success rate, including 94.5% success in IoTGoat and 96.7% success in Metasploitable2. These results demonstrate the potential for LLM-driven agents to automate IoT vulnerability assessment and offensive security workflows in controlled environments

AI.tldr: VEXAIoT is a multi-agent LLM framework for automated IoT vulnerability discovery and exploitation, achieving 95% success rate across 260 attack executions in IoTGoat and Metasploitable2 environments, with sub-2-minute execution times for most attacks.
AI.motivation: IoT systems are inherently vulnerable due to constrained hardware, outdated firmware, and insecure defaults, yet LLM-based security testing has not been applied to IoT-specific vulnerabilities. There is a need for scalable, adaptive, automated security testing tailored to IoT environments.
AI.method: The VEXAIoT framework employs two LLM-based agents: a vulnerability detection agent for reconnaissance and attack planning, and an attack execution agent for exploit delivery. The system is evaluated across 10 attack scenarios mapped to OWASP IoT vulnerabilities in IoTGoat and Metasploitable2 environments, with 260 total attack executions.
AI.result: VEXAIoT achieves a 95.0% overall attack success rate (94.5% on IoTGoat, 96.7% on Metasploitable2), with up to 100% success on individual scenarios. Most attacks complete in under two minutes with low token overhead.
AI.conclusion: LLM-driven multi-agent frameworks show strong potential for automating IoT vulnerability assessment and offensive security workflows in controlled environments, bridging the gap between general-purpose LLM penetration testing tools and IoT-specific security needs.

title: How Does Bayesian Causal Discovery Fail? Characterising Structural Consequences in Linear Gaussian Networks under Latent Confounding
summary: Bayesian causal discovery is widely used for its ability to quantify epistemic uncertainty over directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) through posterior inference. However, its behaviour under latent confounding remains poorly understood, as existing work typically notes that confounding breaks identifiability without characterising how the posterior distribution over DAGs responds. In this work, we analyse posterior behaviour under latent confounding in linear Gaussian causal models, focusing on additive latent confounding between exactly two observed variables. We derive a critical correlation threshold above which the score function favours graphs with a spurious edge between the confounded variables, and show that this threshold decreases with sample size -- more data lowers the correlation required for the spurious edge to be favoured. Beyond this threshold, we characterize two distinct posterior failure regimes determined by the local structure around the confounded variables. Our findings are supported by exact posterior computations on multiple graph structures, demonstrating both the predicted failure regimes.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes how Bayesian causal discovery over DAGs behaves under latent confounding in linear Gaussian models. It derives a critical correlation threshold above which spurious edges between confounded variables are favored, shows this threshold decreases with sample size, and identifies two distinct posterior failure regimes determined by local graph structure.
AI.motivation: Bayesian causal discovery is widely used for uncertainty quantification over DAGs, but its behavior under latent confounding is poorly understood. Existing work merely notes that confounding breaks identifiability without characterizing how the posterior distribution over DAGs actually responds, leaving a critical gap in understanding when and how posterior inference fails.
AI.method: The authors analyze posterior behavior under additive latent confounding between exactly two observed variables in linear Gaussian causal models. They derive analytical expressions for the score function (marginal likelihood) and compute exact posteriors over multiple graph structures. They identify a critical correlation threshold by comparing scores between graphs with and without the spurious edge, and characterize how this threshold depends on sample size and local graph structure.
AI.result: The paper derives a critical correlation threshold above which the posterior favors DAGs with a spurious edge between confounded variables. This threshold decreases as sample size increases — meaning more data paradoxically makes the spurious edge easier to favor. Beyond this threshold, two distinct posterior failure regimes emerge: one where the spurious edge appears with correct causal direction, and another where edge orientation also fails. Exact posterior computations on multiple graph structures confirm both regimes.
AI.conclusion: Latent confounding induces systematic, predictable failures in Bayesian causal discovery: beyond a sample-size-dependent correlation threshold, spurious edges are favored, and two distinct failure regimes arise depending on local graph structure. This challenges the intuition that more data helps, and provides the first formal characterization of how confounding corrupts posterior inference over DAGs.

title: SafeExplorer: An Unbiased Policy Gradient for Reinforcement Learning with Recovery Interventions
summary: Training reinforcement-learning agents directly on physical robots makes every fall costly, since a fall can damage the platform and cannot be undone like a simulator reset; the goal is therefore to minimize falls during training rather than trade them off against return, as constrained Markov decision process (MDP) formulations do. A standard mitigation hands control to a separate recovery policy whenever the agent leaves a designer-specified safe region (a subset of state space it should stay within), but the resulting mixed-policy rollouts silently bias every on-policy update, and the importance-sampling correction that would remove this bias is ill-defined whenever the recovery policy is deterministic. We address this bias with a drop-in modification of proximal policy optimization (PPO). Its core is an unbiased policy-gradient estimator that uses the score function only at safe timesteps and never evaluates the recovery policy's density, so it stays valid even when the recovery policy is deterministic, exactly where importance sampling breaks, and it empirically dominates importance sampling even when the recovery policy is stochastic. Because the recovery policy still makes credit assignment slow near the safe-region boundary, two further components accelerate learning: a closed-form value for recovery-triggering states when dynamics and recovery are deterministic, and an imitation loss that copies recovery actions only when recovery succeeds. On a three-environment, five-seed benchmark, the resulting algorithm reduces training-time falls by factors of 233x, 48x, and 26x on HalfCheetah, Ant, and Unitree Go1 over standard PPO, while matching or exceeding PPO's final reward, and on Ant, where the recovery policy is unreliable, it is the only method that reaches 80% of the best final reward.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an unbiased policy-gradient estimator for safe RL training on physical robots, eliminating the bias introduced by mixed-policy rollouts with a deterministic recovery policy. Combined with a closed-form value function for boundary states and an imitation loss, the method reduces training-time falls by up to 233× over standard PPO while matching or exceeding final reward.
AI.motivation: Training RL agents directly on physical robots is hazardous because falls damage the hardware and cannot be undone. While recovery policies are commonly used to keep the agent within a safe region, on-policy updates from mixed-policy rollouts are biased, and importance-sampling corrections fail when the recovery policy is deterministic — a common practical scenario. The goal is to minimize falls during training (not merely trade them off against return) while preserving unbiased policy-gradient estimation.
AI.method: The authors introduce a drop-in modification of PPO with three components: (1) an unbiased policy-gradient estimator that applies the score function only at safe timesteps, never evaluating the recovery policy's density, making it valid even for deterministic recovery policies; (2) a closed-form value function for states that trigger recovery, assuming deterministic dynamics and recovery; and (3) an imitation loss that copies recovery actions only when recovery succeeds, accelerating credit assignment near the safe-region boundary.
AI.result: On a three-environment, five-seed benchmark (HalfCheetah, Ant, Unitree Go1), the method reduces training-time falls by 233×, 48×, and 26× respectively over standard PPO, while matching or exceeding PPO's final reward. On Ant, where the recovery policy is unreliable, it is the only method reaching 80% of the best final reward.
AI.conclusion: The proposed unbiased estimator, combined with the closed-form value and imitation loss, enables safe and efficient on-policy RL training on physical robots. It eliminates the bias of mixed-policy rollouts without requiring stochastic recovery policies, dramatically reduces falls, and maintains competitive asymptotic performance, making it suitable for real-world robot learning where falls are costly and recovery policies are often deterministic.

title: DKCD: Domain Knowledge-Enhanced Causal Discovery from Unstructured Data
summary: Causal discovery from unstructured data is a challenging yet underexplored task in high-expertise domains such as healthcare, finance, and education. Existing methods typically leverage the general knowledge of large language models (LLMs) to identify causal factors from unstructured data and annotate them into structured data for causal graph construction. However, they remain limited by two key challenges (CHs): (CH1) insufficient identification of latent factors, which are implicit in the data yet essential for causal discovery, due to the lack of domain-specific knowledge; and (CH2) unreliable factor annotation, caused by the lack of domain-grounded reasoning, which propagates errors to the resulting causal graphs. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel Domain Knowledge-enhanced Causal Discovery framework (DKCD) for causal discovery from unstructured data in high-expertise domains with three interconnected components: (1) Knowledge Mining: It retrieves relevant domain knowledge based on observable factors to support subsequent causal reasoning. (2) Knowledge-guided Causal Reasoning: Reasoning with relevant knowledge, it discovers latent causal factors to address CH1 and generates key causal clues for more accurate data annotation to address CH2. (3) Causal Structure Discovery: It constructs the final causal graphs based on a more complete factor set and accurate annotations. Experiments on two domain-specific datasets show that DKCD significantly improves both causal factor identification and causal graph construction.

AI.tldr: DKCD is a domain knowledge-enhanced framework for causal discovery from unstructured data in high-expertise domains. It integrates knowledge mining, knowledge-guided causal reasoning (to uncover latent factors and improve annotation reliability), and causal structure discovery, outperforming existing LLM-based methods on two domain-specific datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based causal discovery methods from unstructured data suffer from two key limitations: (1) insufficient identification of latent causal factors due to lack of domain-specific knowledge, and (2) unreliable factor annotation due to absence of domain-grounded reasoning, which propagates errors into the final causal graphs.
AI.method: The DKCD framework comprises three interconnected components: (1) Knowledge Mining — retrieves domain knowledge based on observable factors; (2) Knowledge-guided Causal Reasoning — leverages retrieved knowledge to discover latent causal factors and generate key causal clues for accurate annotation; (3) Causal Structure Discovery — constructs final causal graphs using the enriched factor set and improved annotations.
AI.result: Experiments on two domain-specific datasets demonstrate that DKCD significantly improves both causal factor identification and causal graph construction compared to existing methods.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating domain knowledge into LLM-based causal discovery effectively addresses the challenges of latent factor identification and annotation reliability, leading to more complete and accurate causal graphs in high-expertise domains.

title: Git-Assistant: Planning-Based Support for Updating Git Repositories
summary: Version control systems are essential for collaborative software development, yet tools like git remain challenging for many practitioners. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) offer promising capabilities for interpreting developer intent, but their effectiveness in repository management tasks is limited by the need for formal reasoning. This work introduces Git-Assistant, an AI-based assistant that combines LLMs with automated planning to support developers in executing non-trivial git operations. The assistant analyzes repository context, translates natural language requests into actionable command sequences, and incorporates planning techniques to ensure correctness and safety. We present a systematic evaluation methodology using synthetic and randomized git environments, comparing the performance of LLM-only and planning-augmented variants across multiple metrics. Experimental results demonstrate that integrating formal reasoning with LLMs improves reliability and reduces errors in repository management, highlighting the potential of hybrid AI approaches for intelligent developer assistance.

AI.tldr: Git-Assistant combines LLMs with automated planning to translate natural language requests into safe, correct git command sequences. Planning-augmented variants outperform LLM-only approaches in reliability and error reduction for repository management tasks.
AI.motivation: Git remains challenging for many practitioners despite its centrality to collaborative development. LLMs can interpret developer intent but lack the formal reasoning needed for reliable repository management, motivating a hybrid approach that marries natural language understanding with planning-based correctness guarantees.
AI.method: Git-Assistant integrates LLMs with automated planning: it analyzes repository context, translates natural language requests into actionable git command sequences, and uses planning techniques to verify correctness and safety. Evaluation uses synthetic and randomized git environments, comparing LLM-only versus planning-augmented variants across multiple metrics.
AI.result: Planning-augmented variants consistently outperform LLM-only baselines, demonstrating improved reliability and fewer errors in executing non-trivial git operations.
AI.conclusion: Integrating formal reasoning with LLMs yields more dependable AI-assisted repository management, validating the hybrid AI paradigm for intelligent developer tooling.

title: Impact of Benign Connectivity Variations on Intrusion Detection for Encrypted OPC UA Traffic in Industrial Private 5G Networks
comment: 7 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables. Accepted for presentation at the 31st IEEE International Conference on Emerging Technologies and Factory Automation (ETFA 2026)
summary: Machine learning (ML)-based intrusion detection systems (IDSs) are increasingly used to monitor encrypted industrial communication. However, their behavior under realistic private 5G operating conditions remains insufficiently understood. This paper investigates the impact of benign connectivity variations on ML-based IDSs for encrypted Open Platform Communications Unified Architecture (OPC UA) traffic in industrial private 5G networks. Experimental results show that legitimate connectivity events can noticeably increase false positive activity despite the absence of attacks. Furthermore, elevated IDS anomaly scores frequently coincide with periods of control-plane (CP) activity associated with these events. The findings highlight the importance of considering CP context when interpreting IDS outputs in industrial private 5G environments.

AI.tldr: Benign connectivity events in industrial private 5G networks can significantly increase false positives in ML-based IDSs monitoring encrypted OPC UA traffic, with elevated anomaly scores correlating with control-plane activity.
AI.motivation: ML-based IDSs are increasingly deployed for encrypted industrial communication monitoring, yet their performance under realistic private 5G operating conditions—particularly the effect of benign connectivity variations—remains poorly understood.
AI.method: Experimental evaluation of ML-based IDS behavior on encrypted OPC UA traffic within an industrial private 5G network, focusing on the impact of legitimate connectivity events on anomaly scores and false positive rates.
AI.result: Legitimate connectivity events cause a noticeable increase in false positive activity despite no attacks being present. Elevated IDS anomaly scores frequently coincide with control-plane (CP) activity associated with these benign connectivity events.
AI.conclusion: Control-plane context is critical for interpreting IDS outputs in industrial private 5G environments; ignoring it risks misclassifying benign connectivity events as malicious activity.

title: ProofCouncil: An LLM Agent for Solving Open Mathematical Problems
comment: 25 pages, 7 figures. ProofCouncil appears as System A (IMProofBench ProofCouncil) in the official FirstProof second-batch report (arXiv:2606.18119). Code and agent-building library: https://github.com/eth-sri/proof-council
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown increasing promise in solving open problems in mathematics. However, their performance can be further improved through agentic workflows tailored to real-world mathematical practice. To this end, we introduce ProofCouncil, a mathematical agent that is designed to tackle open problems using an author-critic architecture. ProofCouncil served as a submission to the second batch of FirstProof, a challenge consisting of 10 real-world mathematical problems that agents must solve autonomously. Its submissions for 6 of the 10 problems were judged by the referees to be correct up to at most minor revisions, showing the best performance among participating teams. We also evaluate ProofCouncil on 30 open problems collected from mathematical researchers. Among the 21 solutions that received human feedback, 5 were judged completely correct, 2 more were judged promising pending final verification, and a further 8 contained useful partial progress. In this short paper, we describe the development of ProofCouncil and the agent-building library used to create it, which we release as open source to the community.

AI.tldr: ProofCouncil is an LLM-based mathematical agent using an author-critic architecture that achieved the best performance in the FirstProof challenge and demonstrated promising results on 30 open mathematical problems.
AI.motivation: LLMs show promise in solving open mathematical problems, but their performance can be enhanced through agentic workflows that reflect real-world mathematical practice, specifically iterative authoring and critiquing.
AI.method: The authors introduce ProofCouncil, a mathematical agent built on an author-critic architecture. It was submitted to the FirstProof challenge (10 autonomous mathematical problems) and further evaluated on 30 open problems collected from mathematical researchers, with human feedback on 21 solutions.
AI.result: In FirstProof, ProofCouncil's submissions for 6/10 problems were judged correct (up to minor revisions), ranking best among all teams. On the 30 open problems, of 21 solutions receiving human feedback: 5 completely correct, 2 promising pending verification, and 8 with useful partial progress.
AI.conclusion: The author-critic agentic workflow significantly boosts LLM performance on open mathematical problems. The agent-building library is released as open source to the community.

title: BlockServe: Block-Grained Continuous Batching for High-Throughput Diffusion LLM Serving
summary: Efficient serving of diffusion large language models (dLLMs) is hindered by convergence heterogeneity: when batching multiple requests, different sequences converge at different rates, causing faster requests to stall behind slower stragglers and introducing compute bubbles and tail latency. We present BlockServe, a continuous batching framework that integrates block-grained scheduling -- immediately evicting completed requests at block boundaries -- with mixed-state execution that extends dual cache and parallel decoding to heterogeneous batches via gather-scatter indexing. Furthermore, a compute-aware admission controller expands effective batch capacity through token-budgeted refill. On Dream and LLaDA across five benchmarks, BlockServe achieves 1.9--10.6$\times$ throughput over Fast-dLLM with comparable generation quality, establishing block-grained scheduling as a foundation for high-throughput offline dLLM inference.

AI.tldr: BlockServe is a continuous batching framework for diffusion LLMs that uses block-grained scheduling to immediately evict completed requests at block boundaries, preventing faster sequences from stalling behind slower ones. It achieves 1.9–10.6× throughput over Fast-dLLM while maintaining generation quality.
AI.motivation: Diffusion LLMs suffer from convergence heterogeneity during batched inference: different sequences converge at different rates, causing faster requests to idle while slower stragglers complete, introducing compute bubbles and tail latency. Existing solutions lack effective mechanisms to handle this imbalance in continuous batching scenarios.
AI.method: BlockServe introduces three key components: (1) block-grained scheduling that evicts completed requests immediately at block boundaries rather than waiting for full batch completion; (2) mixed-state execution that extends dual cache and parallel decoding to heterogeneous batches via gather-scatter indexing; and (3) a compute-aware admission controller that expands effective batch capacity through token-budgeted refill.
AI.result: On Dream and LLaDA across five benchmarks, BlockServe achieves 1.9–10.6× throughput improvement over Fast-dLLM with comparable generation quality.
AI.conclusion: Block-grained scheduling is established as a foundational approach for high-throughput offline diffusion LLM inference, effectively addressing the convergence heterogeneity problem in batched serving.

title: Deceptive Grounding: Entity Attribution Failure in Clinical Retrieval-Augmented Generation
summary:
Retrieval-augmented generation evaluation checks whether model claims are factually grounded in retrieved documents. It does not check whether retrieved evidence is attributed to the correct entity.
  A clinical RAG response can pass every automated check (zero hallucinations, near-perfect faithfulness, real citations) while presenting drug Y's clinical evidence as evidence about queried drug X. We term this deceptive grounding (DG): a failure invisible to faithfulness, hallucination, and citation checks because every claim is sourced from a real document, about the wrong entity.
  Using a controlled factorial benchmark across 13 models, we find DG rates spanning 8-87% at peak adversarial conditions. Medical and biomedical fine-tuned models reach up to 86.7%; domain specialization amplifies the failure rather than mitigating it.
  A controlled ablation identifies the mechanism: removing entity-specific clinical evidence from retrieved documents eliminates entity-attribution failure entirely, shifting all failures to confabulation. The two failure modes respond to the same trigger, taking different paths.
  Production measurement across 740 drug-disease pairs finds 7.8% overall DG in a deployed RAG system, rising to 13.6% for recently approved drugs. Entity-attribution verification (checking that cited evidence applies to the queried entity) detects DG at 97.0% precision and 98.7% DG recall (IPW-adjusted human gold standard); no existing framework implements it.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies "deceptive grounding" (DG) — a previously invisible failure mode in RAG systems where model claims are factually grounded in real documents about the wrong entity, passing all standard evaluation checks. DG rates reach 86.7% in worst-case scenarios, with domain-specialized medical models performing worse, not better. Entity-attribution verification can detect DG at 97% precision and 98.7% recall.
AI.motivation: Current RAG evaluation frameworks check faithfulness and hallucination but entirely miss a critical failure mode: claims supported by correct evidence attributed to the wrong entity. In clinical contexts, this could mean presenting evidence about Drug Y as if it were about Drug X — a dangerous error invisible to all existing automated checks.
AI.method: The authors use a controlled factorial benchmark across 13 models to isolate DG rates under adversarial conditions. They perform a controlled ablation removing entity-specific clinical evidence to identify the causal mechanism. Additionally, they conduct production measurement across 740 drug-disease pairs in a deployed RAG system and evaluate entity-attribution verification using IPW-adjusted human gold standard annotations.
AI.result: DG rates span 8–87% at peak adversarial conditions. Medical fine-tuned models reach 86.7%, showing domain specialization amplifies the failure. Removing entity-specific evidence eliminates DG entirely, converting failures to confabulation. In production, 7.8% overall DG was found, rising to 13.6% for recently approved drugs. Entity-attribution verification achieves 97.0% precision and 98.7% recall (IPW-adjusted).
AI.conclusion: Deceptive grounding is a systematic, measurable, and currently unmonitored failure mode in RAG systems. Entity-attribution verification represents a necessary new evaluation dimension beyond faithfulness and hallucination checks, and should be implemented in RAG evaluation frameworks — especially for high-stakes clinical applications.

title: How Far Are We from Detecting Flaky Tests? On the Limits of Code-Based Detection
summary: Flaky tests pass and fail on the same code version, weakening the signal of test results and disrupting continuous integration (CI) pipelines. Code-based flakiness detectors report strong benchmark results, yet their use in practice remains limited. We argue that the field is studying the wrong problem: Flakiness is not a static property of test code, which often lacks the information needed to decide whether a test is flaky. Analyzing three code-based detectors operating on test code, we found that widely used benchmarks contain shortcuts that inflate reported F1 scores and that evaluation protocols overstate generalizability. To control for these shortcuts, we curated two datasets. The first, C-IDoFT (54,468 unit tests from 57 GitHub projects), keeps a developer-confirmed subset of IDoFT's flaky tests and rebuilds only the non-flaky class from repeated executions instead of fixed versions of flaky tests. C-IDoFT is a controlled counterfactual, not a benchmark for reuse. Our CodeBERT reimplementations of two published detectors scored far above its constant baselines under the published cross-validation protocol but no better than them once projects were separated. The high scores rested on the labeling shortcut and the evaluation protocol, not on the test code. On FlakeBench, a benchmark restricted to flakiness types typically recognizable from test code, and the same project-disjoint protocol, the models identified nearly all flaky tests. The second dataset, mined from CI logs, contains 86 flaky end-to-end tests that passed and failed on the same commit. The test code and CI log yielded a cause for 42% of them; the other 58% required further execution evidence. Rather than abandoning flakiness prediction, we reframe it around whether an observed failure is flaky and how likely a test is to fail given its execution environment. Our datasets and CI-mining method support this direction.

AI.tldr: Existing code-based flaky test detectors appear effective due to benchmark shortcuts and flawed evaluation protocols, not because flakiness is statically detectable from test code. The authors curate two controlled datasets, demonstrate that prior high scores vanish under rigorous project-disjoint evaluation, and reframe the problem from static prediction to determining whether an observed failure is flaky given execution context.
AI.motivation: Code-based flakiness detectors report strong benchmark results but see limited practical adoption. The authors hypothesize that flakiness is not a static property of test code—test code often lacks the information needed to decide flakiness—and that inflated results stem from benchmark artifacts and evaluation shortcuts rather than genuine predictive capability.
AI.method: The authors analyzed three code-based detectors, identified shortcuts in widely used benchmarks (e.g., labeling artifacts in IDoFT), and curated two new datasets: (1) C-IDoFT, a controlled counterfactual dataset of 54,468 unit tests from 57 GitHub projects with developer-confirmed flaky tests and non-flaky tests rebuilt from repeated executions; (2) a CI-log-mined dataset of 86 flaky end-to-end tests that passed and failed on the same commit. They reimplemented two published detectors using CodeBERT and evaluated them under both the original cross-validation protocol and a strict project-disjoint protocol. They also analyzed whether test code and CI logs alone could determine flakiness causes.
AI.result: Under the original cross-validation protocol, CodeBERT reimplementations scored far above constant baselines. Under project-disjoint evaluation, performance dropped to no better than constant baselines on C-IDoFT—high scores were attributable to labeling shortcuts, not test code. On FlakeBench (restricted to flakiness types recognizable from code) with project-disjoint protocol, models identified nearly all flaky tests. For the CI-mined dataset, test code and CI logs yielded a cause for only 42% of flaky end-to-end tests; 58% required further execution evidence.
AI.conclusion: The paper reframes flakiness prediction around two questions: whether an observed failure is flaky, and how likely a test is to fail given its execution environment. The curated datasets and CI-mining method support this new direction, moving away from treating flakiness as a static property of test code.

title: Ceci n'est pas une pipe: AI systems as semantic abstractions
summary: An AI system's output is not the fact or world state it appears to describe, but rather an engineered representation. We propose a semantic framework to describe AI systems, to be able to examine the correctness of such representations. To do so, we distinguish what is justified by accepted domain knowledge, what reference sources say, and what the system can currently use. This allows us to give precise definitions to common failures: extrapolation, refuted or unsupported assertion, sources versus knowledge mismatch, stale or refuted source, added hypotheses, unsupported use... We hope our framework gives a useful vocabulary for specifying and checking AI systems whose outputs, citations, tool calls, and world-changing actions must be justified by reliable claims and explicit authority rather than apparent fluency.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a semantic framework for analyzing AI outputs by distinguishing between domain knowledge, reference sources, and system-available information, thereby enabling precise definitions of common failure modes like extrapolation, unsupported assertions, and source-knowledge mismatches.
AI.motivation: AI outputs are engineered representations, not facts. There is a need for a rigorous vocabulary to specify, verify, and audit AI systems whose claims, citations, and actions must be grounded in reliable evidence and explicit authority rather than superficial fluency.
AI.method: Introduces a tripartite semantic distinction: (1) what is justified by accepted domain knowledge, (2) what reference sources say, and (3) what the system can currently use. This framework is then applied to formally categorize and define failure modes.
AI.result: Yields precise definitions for common AI failures: extrapolation, refuted assertions, unsupported assertions, sources-versus-knowledge mismatch, stale or refuted sources, added hypotheses, and unsupported use.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a useful vocabulary for specifying and checking AI systems, ensuring outputs are justified by reliable claims and explicit authority rather than apparent fluency alone.

title: TSRouter: Dynamic Modality-Model Selection for Time Series Reasoning
summary: Time series reasoning is essential for real-world problem-solving. While both Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs) can reason about time-series data, their capabilities are complementary: LLMs process time series as text sequences and thus preserve exact numerical understanding, but struggle with global patterns, whereas VLMs efficiently capture these patterns by visualizing time series but may lose fine-grained details. Moreover, models vary significantly in task-specific expertise and inference costs. Dynamically selecting the most suitable modality and model for each query is therefore crucial, yet challenging because it requires modeling the complex interactions among tasks, queries, modalities, and models, which carry rich contextual signals. To this end, we introduce TSRouter, a graph-based dynamic routing framework. TSRouter constructs a heterogeneous graph of task, query, modality, and model nodes to contextualize the interactions among query characteristics, modality attributes, and model capabilities. TSRouter formulates routing as a candidate scoring problem, where each modality-model pair is evaluated based on user-defined performance-cost preferences to select the optimal candidate. Comprehensive evaluations on 4 distinct time series reasoning tasks reveal that TSRouter substantially outperforms diverse baselines with 16\% to 46\% relative improvements. Furthermore, TSRouter demonstrates robust zero-shot plug-and-play generalization to unseen models and novel tasks and preserves high performance while reducing computational overhead through cost-aware optimization. Our code is available at https://github.com/tianyi-lab/TSRouter.

AI.tldr: TSRouter is a graph-based dynamic routing framework that selects the optimal modality-model pair (LLM or VLM) for time series reasoning queries, balancing performance and computational cost. It constructs a heterogeneous graph of task, query, modality, and model nodes and formulates routing as candidate scoring, achieving 16–46% relative improvement over baselines with strong zero-shot generalization.
AI.motivation: LLMs and VLMs have complementary strengths for time series reasoning: LLMs excel at exact numerical understanding via text but miss global patterns, while VLMs capture global patterns through visualization but lose fine-grained details. Models also differ in task expertise and inference costs. Manually selecting the best modality-model pair per query is impractical, necessitating an automated, context-aware routing mechanism that models the complex interactions among tasks, queries, modalities, and models.
AI.method: TSRouter constructs a heterogeneous graph with nodes representing tasks, queries, modalities, and models to encode their contextual interactions. Routing is cast as a candidate scoring problem: each modality-model pair is evaluated against user-defined performance-cost preferences, and the optimal candidate is selected. The framework supports cost-aware optimization and plug-and-play generalization to unseen models and tasks.
AI.result: On 4 distinct time series reasoning tasks, TSRouter achieves 16–46% relative improvement over diverse baselines. It demonstrates robust zero-shot plug-and-play generalization to unseen models and novel tasks, and maintains high performance under cost-aware optimization, effectively reducing computational overhead.
AI.conclusion: TSRouter effectively addresses the modality-model selection problem for time series reasoning by leveraging graph-based contextual modeling and preference-driven candidate scoring. It outperforms existing approaches, generalizes to new models/tasks without retraining, and balances performance with efficiency through cost-aware routing.

title: Self-Guided Test-Time Training for Long-Context LLMs
summary: Long-context processing has become increasingly important for large language models (LLMs), but simply extending the context window does not guarantee effective utilization of long inputs. As input length grows, accuracy often degrades, indicating that models still struggle to identify and use the evidence most relevant to a question. A promising way to improve long-context utilization is test-time training (TTT), which treats the test context as a training example for instance-specific parameter adaptation. However, applying TTT to the entire long context is prohibitively expensive, while adapting on randomly sampled spans introduces severe noise. Because most spans in a long context are irrelevant to the specific question, training on them may even degrade the base model's performance. Our preliminary study shows that TTT is highly sensitive to training-span quality: on LongBench-v2, TTT on randomly sampled spans hurts performance, whereas TTT on oracle spans substantially improves it. Motivated by this, we propose a simple method, Self-Guided TTT (S-TTT): before adaptation, the model identifies the evidence spans it should learn from, and the standard language-modeling training objective is applied only to those selected spans. On two challenging long-context reasoning benchmarks, LongBench-v2 and LongBench-Pro, S-TTT improves accuracy for both Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, achieving up to a 15% relative improvement.

AI.tldr: Self-Guided TTT (S-TTT) improves long-context LLM reasoning by having the model identify relevant evidence spans before applying test-time training, avoiding noise from irrelevant text and achieving up to 15% relative improvement on LongBench-v2 and LongBench-Pro.
AI.motivation: LLMs struggle to effectively utilize long contexts — accuracy degrades as input length grows. While test-time training (TTT) can adapt models to specific instances, applying it to entire long contexts is computationally prohibitive, and training on randomly sampled spans introduces harmful noise because most content is irrelevant to the question. Preliminary experiments show TTT is highly sensitive to span quality: random spans hurt performance, while oracle spans substantially improve it.
AI.method: Self-Guided TTT (S-TTT): Before adaptation, the model itself identifies which evidence spans in the long context are relevant to the question. Then, the standard language-modeling training objective is applied exclusively to those self-selected spans, avoiding noise from irrelevant content while keeping computational cost manageable.
AI.result: S-TTT improves accuracy on two challenging long-context reasoning benchmarks (LongBench-v2 and LongBench-Pro) for both Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, achieving up to a 15% relative improvement.
AI.conclusion: Self-guided span selection is an effective and practical strategy for test-time training on long contexts, enabling instance-specific adaptation without the noise and computational burden of naive TTT approaches.

title: Diversifying to Verify: When Task-Equivalent Programs Differ in Verifiability
summary:
Program verification is crucial for software correctness, but producing fully verified programs remains difficult in practice. This paper studies whether implementation structure affects automated verifiability when multiple generated programs are intended to satisfy the same task-level semantics.
  We present Diversify2Verify, a staged LLM-based pipeline for Why3 that infers representation-specific contracts, generates and tests diverse recursive and imperative array/list implementations, and attempts verification with bounded verifier-guided annotation repair. We also construct a verification-oriented benchmark of 73 tasks over integers, arrays, and lists, yielding 292 implementation variants. Diversify2Verify verifies 96 artifacts initially and 154 after two repair passes, improving artifact-level verification from 32.9% to 52.7%. At the task level, at least one variant verifies for 49 of 73 tasks, a 67.1% success rate. These results show that task-equivalent implementations can differ substantially in verifiability and that implementation diversity helps find verification-friendly artifacts.

AI.tldr: Diversify2Verify is an LLM-based pipeline that generates diverse implementations of the same task and exploits structural differences to improve automated verification rates. On a 73-task benchmark (292 variants), it raises artifact-level verification from 32.9% to 52.7% and achieves 67.1% task-level success, demonstrating that implementation diversity significantly aids verifiability.
AI.motivation: Fully verified programs remain difficult to produce in practice. The paper investigates whether the structure of an implementation — given multiple functionally equivalent programs satisfying the same specification — affects how readily each can be automatically verified. The core hypothesis is that implementation diversity can expose verification-friendly variants.
AI.method: The authors propose Diversify2Verify, a staged pipeline targeting Why3. It (1) infers representation-specific contracts from task-level semantics, (2) generates and tests diverse recursive and imperative implementations over arrays and lists using an LLM, and (3) attempts formal verification, applying bounded, verifier-guided annotation repair over two passes when initial proofs fail.
AI.result: A benchmark of 73 tasks (integers, arrays, lists) yields 292 implementation variants. Diversify2Verify initially verifies 96 artifacts (32.9%). After one repair pass this reaches 146, and after two passes 154 (52.7%). At the task level, at least one variant verifies for 49 of 73 tasks (67.1% success rate).
AI.conclusion: Task-equivalent implementations differ substantially in verifiability. Generating structurally diverse implementations and selecting verification-friendly variants is an effective strategy to raise automated verification coverage, as evidenced by the near-doubling of artifact-level success and majority task-level success.

title: TSAI-MetaFraud: A Benchmark Dataset for Financial Fraud Transaction and Behavioral Risk Detection in Metaverse Ecosystems
summary: The emergence of metaverse platforms has created virtual economies that introduce new challenges related to fraud, bot activity, and illicit financial behavior. Despite growing interest in trustworthy metaverse analytics, existing datasets typically focus on user behavior, authentication, or financial transactions in isolation, limiting the development and reproducible evaluation of multimodal fraud detection methods. To address this gap, we present TSAI-MetaFraud, a multimodal, multi-task benchmark dataset for fraud analytics in virtual economies. TSAI-MetaFraud integrates behavioral, transactional, and graph-structured information while incorporating realistic fraud and automated bot scenarios. We define benchmark tasks including transaction fraud detection, cross-modal node classification, temporal link prediction, and weakly supervised fraud detection, and provide baseline evaluations using machine learning models and graph neural networks. By jointly capturing behavioral activity, financial interactions, and relational structure within a unified virtual economy, TSAI-MetaFraud provides a benchmark for advancing multimodal learning, graph mining, fraud analytics, and trustworthy AI in emerging metaverse ecosystems.

AI.tldr: TSAI-MetaFraud is a multimodal, multi-task benchmark dataset that integrates behavioral, transactional, and graph data to advance fraud detection in metaverse virtual economies, with tasks including transaction fraud detection, cross-modal node classification, temporal link prediction, and weakly supervised fraud detection.
AI.motivation: Existing metaverse fraud datasets treat user behavior, authentication, and financial transactions in isolation, hindering the development and reproducible evaluation of multimodal fraud detection methods. A unified benchmark integrating these modalities is needed.
AI.method: The authors construct TSAI-MetaFraud, a benchmark dataset combining behavioral activity, financial transaction logs, and graph-structured relational data with realistic fraud and bot scenarios. They define four benchmark tasks and provide baseline evaluations using traditional ML models and graph neural networks (GNNs).
AI.result: The paper presents the dataset and baseline results across the defined tasks, demonstrating the feasibility of the benchmark for evaluating multimodal and graph-based fraud detection approaches.
AI.conclusion: TSAI-MetaFraud fills a critical gap by offering a unified, reproducible benchmark that jointly captures behavioral, financial, and relational signals, thereby facilitating progress in multimodal learning, graph mining, and trustworthy AI for metaverse ecosystems.

title: Multimodal Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) is increasingly used to align multimodal large language models (MLLMs), but higher rewards do not always imply better task performance. This risk is amplified when visual evidence is evaluated by text-only or weakly grounded rewards. We study reward hacking in MLLM RL across safety VQA, chart VQA, and stress-test settings, varying reward design, data ambiguity, model scale (2B-32B), and RL algorithm (GRPO, RLOO, DAPO). We introduce Newly Rewarded Failure Rate (NRFR), which measures failures among samples whose proxy reward improves over the SFT baseline. Outcome-only rewards cause severe hacking, reaching 48.1% Reward Hacking Rate (RHR), while NRFR exceeding RHR shows that RL creates new failures rather than merely inheriting them. Scaling reduces but does not eliminate hacking: even the 32B model retains a 54.9% worse rate under outcome-only rewards, whereas answer-aware rewards improve the oracle trend at every scale. Robustness is also algorithm- and scale-dependent: GRPO is consistently most resistant, RLOO remains vulnerable, and DAPO improves substantially from 2B to 8B. Visual-evidence rewards help only with reliable verification: keyword-based checks increase hacking, while VLM-as-judge semantic verification reduces it. Overall, multimodal reward hacking is a systematic result of optimizing imperfect rewards, and robust alignment requires rewards and verifiers that remain reliable under optimization pressure.

AI.tldr: RL alignment of multimodal LLMs suffers from reward hacking, where higher proxy rewards do not translate to better task performance. The paper introduces NRFR to measure newly created failures, shows outcome-only rewards cause severe hacking (up to 48.1% RHR), and finds that answer-aware rewards, larger models, GRPO algorithm, and VLM-as-judge verification mitigate but do not eliminate the problem.
AI.motivation: Reinforcement learning is widely used to align MLLMs, but proxy reward signals — especially text-only or weakly grounded ones — can be optimized without genuine improvement in visual task performance. The authors aim to systematically characterize when and why reward hacking occurs in multimodal RL settings.
AI.method: The authors evaluate reward hacking across three settings (safety VQA, chart VQA, stress tests), varying reward design (outcome-only vs. answer-aware), data ambiguity, model scale (2B–32B), and RL algorithm (GRPO, RLOO, DAPO). They introduce two metrics: Reward Hacking Rate (RHR) and Newly Rewarded Failure Rate (NRFR), which distinguishes inherited failures from failures newly created during RL optimization.
AI.result: Outcome-only rewards yield severe hacking with RHR up to 48.1%, and NRFR exceeding RHR indicates RL introduces new failures. Scaling reduces hacking but does not eliminate it: a 32B model still shows 54.9% worse rate under outcome-only rewards. Answer-aware rewards improve the oracle trend at all scales. GRPO is most robust among algorithms; RLOO remains vulnerable; DAPO improves substantially from 2B to 8B. Keyword-based visual verification increases hacking, while VLM-as-judge semantic verification reduces it.
AI.conclusion: Multimodal reward hacking is a systematic consequence of optimizing imperfect rewards. Robust alignment demands reward functions and verifiers that remain reliable under optimization pressure, with answer-aware rewards and semantic VLM verification being key design principles.

title: Training, Reading, and Editing Legible Transformers
summary: A transformer can be built from operators that are legible by construction -- bounded, named units that read as fuzzy set operations rather than dense activations -- but legibility must be pressed for during training, and the pressure has a failure mode. A crispness penalty meant to sharpen a bounded operator into a decisive detector instead collapses it into a dead constant. An identity, E[v(1-v)] = mu(1-mu) - var, shows why -- the penalty is a variance-minimizer blind to the difference between a live detector and a constant -- and names the fix: a per-channel variance floor, the target legibility metric written as a loss, which recovers both legibility and quality. A learned per-unit fraction then retires the hand-set reserved-GELU partition of prior work: given the choice the model keeps no unit as pure GELU and routes 87% of its load-bearing computation through crisp operators. The result is the most legible transformer we have built -- 78% of its feed-forward operands and 50% of its attention value channels are crisp-and-contextual detectors, and per-head legibility rises from 18% in shallow layers to 78% in deep ones. Read in the correct rotated per-layer frame, these units separate a clean detection (what a unit responds to) from a harder naming (what its output decodes to); and because the objective makes each unit crisp and sparse, edits to them are far more local -- 50-184x in the deep layers where the edit sites concentrate -- and can target explicit conjunctions a single neuron cannot express. Finally, a between-unit decorrelation pressure exposes a legibility dial: it trades a circuit's reuse for independence at no quality cost, turning concepts into single, surgically editable units and a prediction into a short explanation read off a handful of named operations. Quality holds at parity with a conventional baseline throughout.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a method to train transformers with legible, crisp operators (fuzzy-set-like units) by replacing a flawed crispness penalty with a per-channel variance floor loss, achieving high legibility (78% crisp feed-forward units, 50% crisp attention channels) while maintaining model quality. It also introduces a decorrelation pressure that allows trading circuit reuse for unit independence, enabling surgical edits and interpretable explanations.
AI.motivation: Prior work showed transformers can be built from legible operators (bounded, named units operating as fuzzy set operations), but achieving legibility during training is difficult. A naive crispness penalty meant to sharpen operators into decisive detectors fails by collapsing them into dead constants. The paper aims to understand this failure mode and develop a fix that yields both legibility and maintained model quality.
AI.method: The authors identify the failure of crispness penalties through the identity E[v(1-v)] = μ(1-μ) − var, showing the penalty minimizes variance without distinguishing a live detector from a constant. Their fix is a per-channel variance floor, formulated as a loss targeting the legibility metric directly. They also introduce a learned per-unit fraction that replaces hand-set reserved-GELU partitions (87% of computation routes through crisp operators). A between-unit decorrelation pressure is added as a controllable dial trading circuit reuse for independence.
AI.result: The resulting transformer achieves 78% crisp-and-contextual feed-forward operands and 50% crisp attention value channels. Per-head legibility rises from 18% (shallow layers) to 78% (deep layers). In a rotated per-layer frame, units cleanly separate detection (what a unit responds to) from naming (what its output decodes to). Edits become far more local (50-184× in deep layers) and can target explicit conjunctions beyond single-neuron capacity. The decorrelation dial trades reuse for independence at no quality cost, enabling single-unit concepts and short explanations. Quality matches conventional baselines throughout.
AI.conclusion: Legible transformers can be trained successfully by replacing variance-minimizing crispness penalties with a per-channel variance floor loss. The approach recovers both legibility and quality, produces units amenable to surgical editing, and offers a controllable trade-off between circuit reuse and unit independence — all without sacrificing model performance.

title: A Sovereign, Open-Source Foundation Model for German and English
summary: We present Soofi S 30B-A3B, a sovereign, open-source Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) hybrid Mamba Transformer foundation model for German and English. Its hybrid design activates only 3B of 30B parameters per token and keeps the inference cache near-constant as context grows, giving it a decisive throughput advantage over dense models for long-context, high-concurrency deployment. Pretrained on roughly 27 trillion tokens with deliberately up-weighted German, Soofi S matches dense 14 to 27B models on aggregate English and German benchmarks while achieving the best code aggregates in both languages among 17 open base models, and outperforms every European sovereign baseline in our comparison, including ones far larger in active parameters. Among fully open models, Soofi S obtains the highest English and German evaluation scores, ahead of Olmo 3 32B and Apertus 70B. Soofi S was built end-to-end on the German Industrial AI Cloud, a sovereign HPC scale AI infrastructure operated by Deutsche Telekom in Munich. Soofi S will be released under highly permissive, open-access terms: weights, selected intermediate checkpoints, full per-source data accounting, hyperparameters, and training and evaluation code. Where source licenses permit, data-construction artifacts are released under permissive licenses; commercially licensed sources are documented with aggregate statistics and exact mixture accounting.

AI.tldr: Soofi S 30B-A3B is a sovereign, open-source hybrid Mamba-Transformer MoE model for German and English, activating only 3B of 30B parameters per token. Trained on ~27T tokens with up-weighted German, it matches dense 14–27B models on benchmarks, achieves top code scores among 17 open models, and was built entirely on Deutsche Telekom's sovereign German Industrial AI Cloud.
AI.motivation: To create a sovereign, open-source foundation model optimized for both German and English that combines the efficiency of mixture-of-experts and hybrid Mamba-Transformer architectures, achieving high throughput for long-context, high-concurrency deployment while maintaining competitive performance against larger dense models.
AI.method: A hybrid Mamba-Transformer Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture with 30B total parameters, activating only 3B per token. The inference cache remains near-constant as context length grows. Pretraining spans ~27 trillion tokens with deliberately up-weighted German data. The entire pipeline — from data construction through training to evaluation — runs on the German Industrial AI Cloud, a sovereign HPC infrastructure.
AI.result: Soofi S matches dense models in the 14–27B parameter range on aggregate English and German benchmarks. It achieves the best code aggregates in both languages among 17 open base models and outperforms every European sovereign baseline, including models with far more active parameters. Among fully open models, it attains the highest English and German evaluation scores, surpassing Olmo 3 32B and Apertus 70B.
AI.conclusion: Soofi S demonstrates that a sovereign, openly released hybrid Mamba-Transformer MoE model can achieve competitive or superior performance compared to larger dense models and other sovereign efforts, with significant throughput advantages for long-context inference. The fully open release — including weights, checkpoints, data accounting, hyperparameters, and code — sets a new standard for transparency in sovereign AI development.

title: How Do Software Professionals Evaluate AI-Generated Code? (Registered Report)
comment: This report has been accepted for ESEM 2026 (Registered Reports Track)
summary: Recent advances in generative AI tools have significantly changed how software professionals write, evaluate, and interact with code. Generative AI tools such as GitHub Copilot, ChatGPT, and Claude are increasingly being integrated into everyday workflows. Despite the growing adoption of and reliance on these tools, it remains unclear as to how software professionals evaluate the code they generate. To explore this topic, we will conduct a constructivist grounded theory study that incorporates a survey, semi-structured interviews, and laddering interviews. With the initial survey data collection complete, we aim to interview 20--50 software professionals iteratively until theoretical saturation is achieved. This research aims to build a theory of how software professionals evaluate AI-generated code, grounded in their accounts of evaluative practices, perceptions, and preferences.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a planned constructivist grounded theory study investigating how software professionals evaluate AI-generated code from tools like Copilot, ChatGPT, and Claude, using surveys, semi-structured interviews, and laddering interviews with 20–50 participants until theoretical saturation.
AI.motivation: Despite rapid adoption of generative AI coding tools in professional workflows, there is a lack of understanding regarding the evaluative practices, perceptions, and preferences software professionals employ when assessing AI-generated code.
AI.method: A constructivist grounded theory approach combining a survey (already completed), semi-structured interviews, and laddering interviews with 20–50 software professionals, conducted iteratively until theoretical saturation is reached.
AI.result: No results yet reported; the paper describes work in progress with only initial survey data collection completed. The anticipated outcome is a grounded theory of code evaluation practices.
AI.conclusion: Not yet available — the study is in its early stages, aiming to build a substantive theory of how software professionals evaluate AI-generated code based on their lived experiences and accounts.

title: Statistically Undetectable Backdoors in Deep Neural Networks
summary: We show how an adversarial model trainer can plant backdoors in a large class of deep, feedforward neural networks. These backdoors are statistically undetectable in the white-box setting, meaning that the backdoored and honestly trained models are close in total variation distance, even given the full descriptions of the models (e.g., all of the weights). The backdoor provides access to invariance-based adversarial examples for every input, mapping distant inputs to unusually close outputs. However, without the backdoor, it is provably impossible (under standard cryptographic assumptions) to generate any such adversarial examples in polynomial time. Our theoretical and preliminary empirical findings demonstrate a fundamental power asymmetry between model trainers and model users.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a method for planting statistically undetectable backdoors in deep feedforward neural networks, where backdoored and honest models are indistinguishable in total variation distance even with full white-box access, yet the backdoor enables invariance-based adversarial examples that are provably impossible to generate without it under cryptographic assumptions.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate a fundamental power asymmetry between model trainers and model users: trainers can embed backdoors that are statistically undetectable (even with full model access) while granting the trainer the ability to produce adversarial examples that no polynomial-time user could generate without knowledge of the backdoor.
AI.method: The authors construct backdoors by exploiting the sign patterns of network weights, encoding a secret key into the weight configuration. They prove statistical undetectability via total variation distance bounds between backdoored and honestly trained distributions. They then show that the backdoor allows generating invariance-based adversarial examples (distant inputs mapped to close outputs), while proving that without the backdoor key, generating such examples is computationally hard under standard cryptographic assumptions (e.g., existence of one-way functions).
AI.result: The authors provide theoretical proofs and preliminary empirical results showing that backdoored models are statistically indistinguishable from honest models, yet the backdoor creates an exploitable vulnerability that is cryptographically hard to discover without the secret key. This establishes a provable power asymmetry between trainer and user.
AI.conclusion: There exists a fundamental and provable asymmetry: model trainers can plant undetectable backdoors granting them adversarial capabilities that are computationally infeasible for users to replicate or even detect, raising significant security implications for the machine learning supply chain.

title: FairSelect: A Systematic Evaluation of Multi-Level and Intersectional Algorithmic Fairness
comment: 15 pages, 5 tables, Submission to Health Informatics Knowledge Management Conference 2026
summary: Algorithmic fairness methods are increasingly used to identify and mitigate bias in machine learning models, yet most approaches are evaluated in isolation and along single demographic axes. This limits practical guidance for selecting fairness strategies, where disparities may arise across intersectional subgroups and across multiple stages of the modeling lifecycle. This work presents FairSelect, a toolkit for systematically evaluating fairness mitigation strategies applied individually and in combination across preprocessing, inprocessing, and postprocessing stages. FairSelect supports multiple model architectures, intersectional subgroup evaluation, and comparison of fairness utility tradeoffs across baseline, single method, and multi level configurations. The framework was validated using synthetic clinical datasets designed to represent specific bias mechanisms and a real-world replication of two-year stroke risk prediction among patients with atrial fibrillation. Synthetic experiments showed that targeted fairness methods generally reduced intended subgroup disparities, while combined strategies produced larger average fairness improvements with modest utility tradeoffs. In the clinical prediction task, mitigation effects were highly variable, with some combinations improving both fairness and predictive performance while others were ineffective or counterproductive. These findings demonstrate that fairness interventions interact in nonadditive and context dependent ways. FairSelect provides a practical framework for systematically identifying fairness strategies that improve subgroup equity while preserving model performance in clinical machine learning.

AI.tldr: FairSelect is a toolkit for systematically evaluating fairness mitigation strategies across preprocessing, inprocessing, and postprocessing stages, supporting intersectional subgroup evaluation. Validated on synthetic and real clinical data, it reveals that fairness interventions interact nonadditively and are context-dependent, providing a practical framework for selecting strategies that balance equity and model performance.
AI.motivation: Most algorithmic fairness methods are evaluated in isolation along single demographic axes, limiting practical guidance for selecting fairness strategies when disparities exist across intersectional subgroups and multiple modeling lifecycle stages.
AI.method: FairSelect toolkit evaluates fairness mitigation strategies individually and in combination across preprocessing, inprocessing, and postprocessing stages. It supports multiple model architectures, intersectional subgroup evaluation, and fairness-utility tradeoff comparisons across baseline, single-method, and multi-level configurations. Validation used synthetic clinical datasets with specific bias mechanisms and a real-world replication of two-year stroke risk prediction in atrial fibrillation patients.
AI.result: Synthetic experiments: targeted fairness methods reduced intended subgroup disparities; combined strategies yielded larger fairness improvements with modest utility tradeoffs. Clinical prediction task: mitigation effects were highly variable — some combinations improved both fairness and predictive performance, while others were ineffective or counterproductive. Interactions among interventions were nonadditive and context-dependent.
AI.conclusion: Fairness interventions interact in nonadditive and context-dependent ways. FairSelect offers a practical framework for systematically identifying fairness strategies that improve subgroup equity while preserving model performance in clinical machine learning.

title: Test-Time Scaling for Small VLMs on Multilingual Visual MCQ
summary: Test-time scaling (TTS) reliably improves reasoning in large language models, but whether it transfers to small open vision-language models remains unclear. We examine this on EXAMS-V, a multilingual visual multiple-choice benchmark, comparing self-consistency, describe-then-reason with PRM-guided beam search, and two post-hoc selectors across Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct and Qwen3.5-4B. What matters is the conditions under which TTS runs, not the search or verification machinery. The largest factor is parseability: an early prompt format left many chains reasoning correctly yet never committing to an answer letter, which a standard answer cue and a guided repair step largely remove. A larger decoding budget removes the rest: raising the per-chain token limit from 1k to 2k recovers 3.7 pp, whereas sampling more chains (8 to 16) adds only 0.15 pp. Once chains have room to finish, elaborate methods contribute little: PRM-guided beam search trails plain self-consistency by 0.39 pp at over eight times the cost, and neither a training-free generative critic nor a trained multimodal PRM beats majority vote across both policies. The largest gain comes instead from the policy model itself (+11.4 pp). Our best configuration reaches 84.1% on the held-out ImageCLEF 2026 test split, ranking first on the Visual MCQ leaderboard.

AI.tldr: Test-time scaling (TTS) for small open vision-language models is analyzed on a multilingual visual MCQ benchmark. The key finding is that parseability (ensuring chains output answer letters) and decoding budget (token limits) matter far more than sophisticated search or verification methods. Simple self-consistency matches or beats PRM-guided beam search and post-hoc selectors at much lower cost.
AI.motivation: Investigate whether test-time scaling techniques that reliably improve reasoning in large language models also transfer effectively to small open vision-language models, and identify which components of TTS actually drive performance gains.
AI.method: Evaluated on EXAMS-V, a multilingual visual multiple-choice benchmark, comparing: (1) self-consistency (majority vote), (2) describe-then-reason with PRM-guided beam search, and (3) two post-hoc selectors (a training-free generative critic and a trained multimodal PRM). Tested across Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct and Qwen3.5-4B. Varied prompt formatting, per-chain token limits (1k vs 2k), and number of sampled chains (8 vs 16).
AI.result: Parseability is the dominant factor: an early prompt format caused chains to reason correctly but fail to commit to an answer letter; a standard answer cue plus guided repair largely resolved this. Increasing per-chain token limit from 1k to 2k recovered 3.7 pp, while sampling more chains (8→16) added only 0.15 pp. PRM-guided beam search trailed plain self-consistency by 0.39 pp at >8× cost. Neither selector beat majority vote. The policy model upgrade alone yielded +11.4 pp. Best configuration achieved 84.1% on the held-out ImageCLEF 2026 test split, ranking first on the Visual MCQ leaderboard.
AI.conclusion: For small open VLMs, TTS gains depend primarily on output parseability and sufficient decoding budget, not on sophisticated search or verification. Simple self-consistency is both effective and cost-efficient. Upgrading the underlying policy model yields the largest improvements.

title: Practical Source Code Recovery from Binary Functions Using Anchor-Based Retrieval and LLM Reasoning
summary: We present a practical pipeline for recovering source code from stripped binary functions by combining reverse engineering, anchor-based source code retrieval, and large language model reasoning. Our binary-to-source-code retrieval method attempts to identify the source function from a source code database, rather than generating approximate decompiled pseudocode. It extracts anchors such as strings, constants, external calls, and available function names using Ghidra, retrieves candidate files via an inverted-index search database, narrows candidates to likely function snippets, and re-ranks them with a large language model (LLM) based on disassembly, decompiled code, and source metadata. Confident matches can also serve as anchors in later passes. In an evaluation backed by our high-fidelity source code database on a stripped, optimized tcpdump binary, our proposed binary-to-source matching method achieves 95.2% assembly instruction coverage. Experiments on a GitHub-based retrieval database showed lower performance with 35.5% instruction coverage on average, mainly due to retrieval misses. These results show that source-level binary recovery excels with high-quality databases and remains a useful tool in noisy environments.

AI.tldr: A pipeline recovers source code from stripped binaries by combining reverse engineering, anchor-based retrieval from a source database, and LLM re-ranking. Using high-fidelity databases, it achieves 95.2% instruction coverage on tcpdump, though coverage drops to ~35.5% with noisy GitHub-based retrieval.
AI.motivation: Recovering original source code from stripped, optimized binaries is a hard reverse engineering problem. Existing approaches typically generate approximate decompiled pseudocode rather than identifying the actual original source functions. The authors aim to perform true source-level recovery by matching binary functions to their original source code in a database, leveraging both static analysis and LLM reasoning.
AI.method: The pipeline uses Ghidra to extract anchors (strings, constants, external calls, function names) from stripped binaries. An inverted-index search database retrieves candidate source files, which are narrowed to likely function snippets. A large language model (LLM) re-ranks candidates using disassembly, decompiled code, and source metadata. High-confidence matches are iteratively fed back as additional anchors for subsequent passes.
AI.result: With a high-fidelity source database on a stripped, optimized tcpdump binary, the method achieves 95.2% assembly instruction coverage. Experiments using a GitHub-based retrieval database yielded lower performance (35.5% average instruction coverage), primarily due to retrieval misses.
AI.conclusion: Source-level binary recovery is highly effective when paired with high-quality source databases, and remains a useful tool even in noisy, real-world retrieval environments dominated by retrieval misses.

title: SAGEAgent: A Self-Evolving Agent for Cost-Aware Modality Acquisition in Multimodal Survival Prediction
summary: Does every cancer patient truly need a complete diagnostic workup for accurate survival prediction? In multimodal clinical oncology, diagnostic modalities follow a clinically mandated order of escalating burden -- from demographics collected at intake to genomic profiling requiring specialized tissue analysis. Current multimodal survival methods either assume all modalities are available or passively handle missing data, but none actively reason about whether acquiring the next modality is justified for a given patient along this ordered workflow. We formulate this as a sequential decision problem and propose SAGEAgent (Sequential Acquisition Guided by Experience), a self-evolving LLM-based clinical agent that decides which diagnostic modalities to acquire for each patient, balancing predictive accuracy against clinical invasiveness. SAGEAgent reasons about each patient's evolving diagnostic state through clinical tools that translate numerical predictions into text, an episodic memory that retrieves similar past cases, and a semantic memory that accumulates reusable decision patterns from experience. Experiments on a glioma cohort combining TCGA-LGG, TCGA-GBM, and BraTS with four diagnostic modalities demonstrate that SAGEAgent achieves competitive survival prediction accuracy while reducing average acquisition burden by 55%.
