AI.tldr: SAGEAgent is a self-evolving LLM-based clinical agent that sequentially decides which diagnostic modalities to acquire per patient, balancing survival prediction accuracy against clinical invasiveness. It reduces average acquisition burden by 55% while maintaining competitive accuracy on a glioma cohort.
AI.motivation: Current multimodal survival prediction methods either assume all modalities are available or passively handle missing data. However, clinical diagnostics follow an ordered workflow of escalating burden (from basic demographics to invasive genomic profiling), and no existing approach actively reasons about whether acquiring the next modality is justified for a given patient.
AI.method: The authors formulate modality acquisition as a sequential decision problem. SAGEAgent uses an LLM-based agent with three key components: (1) clinical tools that translate numerical predictions into interpretable text, (2) episodic memory that retrieves similar past cases, and (3) semantic memory that accumulates reusable decision patterns from prior experience. The agent reasons about each patient's evolving diagnostic state to decide whether to stop or acquire the next modality.
AI.result: Evaluated on a glioma cohort combining TCGA-LGG, TCGA-GBM, and BraTS with four diagnostic modalities, SAGEAgent achieves competitive survival prediction accuracy while reducing the average acquisition burden by 55% compared to using all modalities.
AI.conclusion: SAGEAgent demonstrates that adaptive, patient-specific modality acquisition can dramatically reduce diagnostic burden without sacrificing predictive performance, suggesting a paradigm shift from universal complete workup to personalized sequential diagnostic decision-making in clinical oncology.

title: Eluna: An Agentic LLM System for Automating Warehouse Operations with Reasoning and Task Execution
summary: Warehouse operations are governed by Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) that encode complex, multi-system decision logic, which must be executed reliably under strict time constraints, yet LLM agents lack mechanisms to enforce procedural compliance and degrade under the context overload full SOP specifications introduce. We present Eluna, a production-deployed agentic system for reliable SOP execution. Eluna is a graph-guided, multi-agent framework that encodes SOPs as directed acyclic graphs with progressive disclosure and delegates independent tasks to parallel sub-agents, each with persistent code execution and live data access. To meet production latency and accuracy needs, we use asymmetric episodic distillation where a strong teacher is improved through episodic error memories, then a smaller student is fine-tuned on the corrected trajectories with memory stripped, internalizing corrections without inference-time overhead. On a 13-task benchmark and two production applications, our fine-tuned models match or exceed their teacher, beat all larger off-the-shelf baselines, and reach 94% expert agreement on the ticket processing application.

AI.tldr: Eluna is a production-deployed, graph-guided multi-agent system that enforces SOP compliance via DAG-based progressive disclosure and parallel sub-agents, using asymmetric episodic distillation to fine-tune a compact student model that matches or exceeds larger teacher models on warehouse automation tasks.
AI.motivation: Warehouse SOPs require complex, multi-system decision logic under strict time constraints, but LLM agents lack procedural compliance mechanisms and degrade under the context overload of full SOP specifications.
AI.method: Eluna encodes SOPs as directed acyclic graphs with progressive disclosure, delegates independent tasks to parallel sub-agents with persistent code execution and live data access, and applies asymmetric episodic distillation: a strong teacher model is improved via episodic error memories, then a smaller student model is fine-tuned on corrected trajectories with memories stripped out, internalizing corrections without inference-time overhead.
AI.result: On a 13-task benchmark and two production applications, the fine-tuned models match or exceed the teacher model, outperform all larger off-the-shelf baselines, and achieve 94% expert agreement on the ticket processing application.
AI.conclusion: Graph-guided multi-agent architecture combined with asymmetric episodic distillation enables reliable, production-grade SOP execution with smaller, efficient models that rival or surpass larger counterparts.

title: Normalisation-Based Likelihood Ratio Estimation for Forensic Authorship Verification
summary: Authorship verification (AV) is the task of determining whether two texts were written by the same author. In a forensic context, the strength of AV evidence can be quantified using likelihood ratios. Most AV methods are score-based and deriving well-calibrated likelihood ratios from these scores requires a separate calibration model. This, in turn, requires additional amounts of case-relevant data, which is often time-consuming to obtain and prepare. This study proposes two novel normalisation techniques, the Square Root Correction and the Hapax Correction, for deriving likelihood ratios from the AV method LambdaG without the need of a calibration model (Nini et al. 2026). These corrections are designed to mitigate the overestimation of evidential strength that may result from long or highly repetitive texts. Performance is evaluated against logistic regression calibration across fifteen corpora and a range of text lengths (100-9,500 tokens), using the log-likelihood ratio cost (Cllr). The proposed methods achieve performance comparable to logistic regression calibration, with the Hapax Correction outperforming it in approximately 45% of tests (weighted by corpora). Furthermore, performance was more frequently close (within 5%) when the Hapax Correction was outperformed by logistic regression calibration, compared with the reverse comparison. Eliminating the need to train a calibration model reduces data-requirements, time and complexity, thereby increasing the accessibility and transparency of forensic text comparison. This combination of empirical performance and practical advantages supports the adoption of the proposed methods in forensic settings.

AI.tldr: Two novel normalization techniques—Square Root Correction and Hapax Correction—are proposed for deriving well-calibrated likelihood ratios from the LambdaG authorship verification method without a separate calibration model. The Hapax Correction matches or outperforms logistic regression calibration in ~45% of tests and offers comparable overall performance, reducing data requirements and complexity in forensic text comparison.
AI.motivation: Most score-based authorship verification methods require a separate calibration model to derive well-calibrated likelihood ratios, which demands additional case-relevant data that is time-consuming to obtain and prepare. There is a need for methods that yield calibrated likelihood ratios directly without this calibration step, particularly to address overestimation of evidential strength from long or highly repetitive texts.
AI.method: The authors propose two normalization corrections—Square Root Correction and Hapax Correction—applied to the LambdaG AV method (Nini et al. 2026). These corrections mitigate evidential strength overestimation due to text length and repetitiveness. Performance is benchmarked against logistic regression calibration across 15 corpora and text lengths from 100 to 9,500 tokens, using log-likelihood ratio cost (Cllr) as the evaluation metric.
AI.result: Both proposed corrections achieve performance comparable to logistic regression calibration. The Hapax Correction outperforms logistic regression calibration in approximately 45% of tests (weighted by corpora). When logistic regression outperforms the Hapax Correction, the margin is more frequently within 5%, whereas the reverse is less common, indicating the Hapax Correction is rarely substantially worse.
AI.conclusion: Eliminating the calibration model reduces data requirements, time, and complexity, increasing accessibility and transparency in forensic text comparison. The combination of strong empirical performance and practical advantages supports adopting the proposed normalization methods in forensic settings.

title: Failure as a Process: An Anatomy of CLI Coding Agent Trajectories
summary: Large language model (LLM) coding agents are increasingly deployed to autonomously perform software engineering tasks in terminal-based environments, making their reliability a growing concern. Existing empirical studies investigate why coding agents fail, yet they largely treat failure as a final outcome rather than a temporal process, providing limited insight into how failures emerge, evolve, and become unrecoverable. We present the first large-scale empirical study of CLI coding-agent failure trajectories, introducing a process-oriented framework that analyzes failure through its onset, evolution, and recovery across execution trajectories. We first collect 3,843 execution trajectories generated by seven frontier models across three coding-agent scaffolds (OpenHands, MiniSWE, and Terminus2) on Terminal-Bench, then carefully filter them to obtain 1,794 complete and valid trajectories for manual annotation (over 63,000 execution steps), from which we derive 14 findings spanning failure occurrence, root causes, recovery, and cross-system consistency. Our findings show that coding-agent failures are predominantly driven by epistemic errors, typically begin within the first few execution steps, and often remain hidden until recovery is no longer possible, suggesting that improving coding-agent reliability requires earlier validation and intervention rather than relying solely on final-outcome evaluation.

AI.tldr: A large-scale empirical study analyzing 1,794 CLI coding-agent failure trajectories across seven frontier models and three scaffolds, introducing a process-oriented framework that examines failure onset, evolution, and recovery. Key findings: failures are predominantly epistemic, begin early in execution, and remain hidden until unrecoverable, suggesting the need for early validation rather than final-outcome evaluation.
AI.motivation: Existing studies treat coding-agent failures as final outcomes rather than temporal processes, providing limited insight into how failures emerge, evolve, and become unrecoverable. Understanding failure trajectories is critical as LLM coding agents are increasingly deployed autonomously in terminal-based software engineering tasks.
AI.method: Collected 3,843 execution trajectories from seven frontier models across three coding-agent scaffolds (OpenHands, MiniSWE, Terminus2) on Terminal-Bench. Filtered to 1,794 complete/valid trajectories comprising over 63,000 execution steps. Conducted manual annotation within a process-oriented framework categorizing failure by onset, evolution, and recovery stages, yielding 14 empirical findings.
AI.result: Coding-agent failures are predominantly driven by epistemic errors; failures typically begin within the first few execution steps; errors often remain hidden until recovery becomes impossible. Cross-system consistency was observed in failure patterns. The findings suggest that final-outcome evaluation alone is insufficient for ensuring reliability.
AI.conclusion: Improving coding-agent reliability requires earlier validation and intervention mechanisms rather than relying solely on final-outcome evaluation. The process-oriented failure trajectory framework provides a more nuanced lens for understanding and mitigating autonomous coding agent failures.

title: Beyond Fixed Representations: The Vocabulary and Verifier Gaps in Open-Ended AI
summary:
Modern AI systems are increasingly being evaluated for their ability to reason, code, prove theorems, use tools, and long-horizon research tasks. These are powerful capabilities, but they share a structural limitation: the representational frame within which the model operates, including its conceptual vocabulary, the space of admissible solutions it can search, and the criteria by which success is evaluated, is typically fixed and supplied in advance. This paper argues that building stronger intelligent systems capable of open-ended innovation requires additional classes of operations: the creation, stabilization, and reuse of new representational primitives, which alter the space being searched rather than simply searching within it.
  We characterize the distance between current AI systems and genuinely open-ended intelligence through two gaps. The first is the vocabulary gap, the difficulty of inventing and stabilizing new representational primitives rather than merely recombining existing ones. The second is the verifier gap, the difficulty of judging the value of a new primitive when its full payoff may be visible only after future reuse. We interpret both gaps through a unified framework of intelligence as cognitive discrepancy reduction. By viewing intelligent behaviors as a sequence of cognitive transformations, we distinguish intra-space transformations which operate within a fixed representational frame, from generative transformations which may modify the frame itself. On this basis, we propose a ladder of innovation autonomy and outline several directions for advancing open-ended AI, including objectives that reward useful representational change, persistent memory architectures for invented primitives, and adaptive verification mechanisms capable of evolving alongside the representations they evaluate.

AI.tldr: The paper argues current AI systems are limited by fixed representational frames and proposes that true open-ended intelligence requires operations that create, stabilize, and reuse new representational primitives. It identifies two key gaps—the vocabulary gap (inventing new primitives) and the verifier gap (judging their value before future reuse)—and frames them through a cognitive discrepancy reduction lens, distinguishing intra-space from generative transformations.
AI.motivation: Modern AI systems excel at reasoning, coding, and tool use but operate within pre-supplied representational frames—fixed conceptual vocabularies, solution spaces, and success criteria. For open-ended innovation, systems must go beyond searching within existing spaces and instead alter those spaces through new representational primitives. The paper aims to characterize what is missing and provide a unified framework for addressing it.
AI.method: The authors reframe intelligence as cognitive discrepancy reduction, decomposing intelligent behavior into sequences of cognitive transformations. They distinguish between (1) intra-space transformations operating within a fixed representational frame, and (2) generative transformations that modify the frame itself. Using this framework, they diagnose two gaps: the vocabulary gap and the verifier gap, then propose a ladder of innovation autonomy and architectural directions.
AI.result: The paper yields a conceptual framework rather than empirical results. Key contributions include: the vocabulary-verifier gap diagnosis, the intra-space vs. generative transformation distinction, a ladder of innovation autonomy, and design directions such as objectives rewarding useful representational change, persistent memory for invented primitives, and adaptive verification mechanisms.
AI.conclusion: Building AI capable of open-ended innovation requires systems that can create, stabilize, and reuse new representational primitives, not merely optimize within fixed frames. Bridging the vocabulary and verifier gaps demands rethinking objectives, memory architectures, and verification to support generative transformations that expand the space of what can be represented and evaluated.

title: NL-PAC: Specification Ambiguity and Certified Minimax Risk Floors in LLM-Mediated Supervision
summary: Large language models increasingly provide labels, evaluations, and feedback for tasks specified in natural language. When a specification admits multiple readings but the supervision channel does not reveal which is operative, additional labels reduce sampling error without resolving the resulting identification problem. We introduce Natural Language PAC (NL-PAC), a framework that uses a fixed model's thresholded decoding law to define admissible labels and candidate targets. The probability that multiple labels are admissible equals the diameter of the pointwise-admissible target class, and under target-blind supervision every learner incurs worst-case risk of at least half this diameter, at every sample size; the exact randomized minimax risk over this class is attained by a data-independent strategy. Finite-sample confidence bounds make these quantities certifiable from held-out unlabeled inputs. In a frozen Qwen~2.5--3B audit, one prespecified prompt yields a positive model-relative certificate, whereas a paraphrase and exact-rule controls yield zero. A held-out bridge audit finds that supplied candidate reading clauses fail the admissibility condition needed to transfer the certificate to coherent readings. The guarantee is specific to the audited model, prompt, threshold, and input distribution; extending it to human interpretations requires external validation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Natural Language PAC (NL-PAC), a framework that quantifies identification risk when large language models provide supervision for ambiguously specified natural language tasks. Using a fixed model's thresholded decoding law, it defines admissible labels and shows that worst-case risk is bounded below by half the diameter of the admissible target class. The framework is demonstrated through an audit of Qwen 2.5-3B, revealing that certification is prompt-specific and requires external validation for human interpretation.
AI.motivation: When natural language task specifications admit multiple interpretations (readings) and the supervision channel does not disambiguate which reading is operative, collecting additional labeled data reduces sampling error but cannot resolve the fundamental identification problem. Existing PAC frameworks do not account for this ambiguity arising from natural language specifications in LLM-based supervision.
AI.method: The authors propose the NL-PAC framework, which uses a fixed model's thresholded decoding law to (1) define admissible labels and candidate target functions, (2) characterize the pointwise-admissible target class diameter, (3) prove that every learner under target-blind supervision incurs worst-case risk of at least half this diameter at any sample size, (4) establish that the exact randomized minimax risk is attained by a data-independent strategy, and (5) provide finite-sample confidence bounds certifiable from held-out unlabeled inputs. The framework is validated through a frozen Qwen 2.5-3B audit examining prespecified prompts, paraphrases, and exact-rule controls, plus a held-out bridge audit for reading clause admissibility.
AI.result: Under target-blind supervision, the worst-case risk lower bound equals half the diameter of the pointwise-admissible target class for all sample sizes. The randomized minimax risk is achieved by a data-independent strategy. In the Qwen 2.5-3B audit, one prespecified prompt yields a positive model-relative certificate, while a paraphrase and exact-rule controls yield zero. The bridge audit finds that supplied candidate reading clauses fail the admissibility condition needed for certificate transfer to coherent readings. The guarantee is specific to the audited model, prompt, threshold, and input distribution.
AI.conclusion: The NL-PAC framework provides a principled way to quantify and certify the risk arising from ambiguous natural language specifications in LLM supervision. However, the guarantees are inherently model-specific and prompt-specific; extending them to human interpretations requires external validation beyond the proposed framework.

title: FreyaTTS Technical Report
summary: We introduce Freya-TTS, a compact, tokenizer-free, Turkish-first text-to-speech model designed for highly reliable and efficient conversational synthesis. Freya-TTS is a 183.2M-parameter non-autoregressive conditional flow-matching Diffusion Transformer (DiT) that operates in the frozen continuous latent space of AudioVAE2 (16 kHz encode, 48 kHz decode), allowing the model to focus its capacity on text-to-latent mapping while inheriting high-quality 48 kHz reconstruction. We advance the framework along three key dimensions: (1) rule-free end-to-end modeling from a 92-symbol Turkish character vocabulary without a phonemizer, grapheme-to-phoneme frontend, or discrete speech tokenizer; (2) non-autoregressive parallel denoising, which predicts the entire latent sequence simultaneously over a predicted duration; and (3) a production-oriented two-stage post-training recipe consisting of single-speaker voice locking and short-utterance coverage, improving speaker consistency and robustness on short inputs. On the Freya-TR-Eval benchmark, Freya-TTS achieves a band-matched word error rate (WER) of 8.0% and character error rate (CER) of 3.0%, outperforming substantially larger open-source systems while using a fraction of their parameters. The model achieves a real-time factor of 0.11 on consumer GPUs and runs faster than real time on a laptop CPU, making it well suited for resource-constrained edge deployment. We release the model weights, training and inference code, and evaluation benchmark under the Apache-2.0 license.

AI.tldr: Freya-TTS is a compact (183.2M params), tokenizer-free Turkish TTS model using flow-matching Diffusion Transformers in AudioVAE2's latent space. It achieves 8.0% WER / 3.0% CER with 0.11 RTF on consumer GPUs, outperforming larger systems while running faster than real-time on CPU.
AI.motivation: To build a highly reliable, efficient, Turkish-first TTS system that eliminates reliance on phonemizers, G2P frontends, and discrete speech tokenizers, while being deployable on resource-constrained edge devices without sacrificing output quality (48 kHz).
AI.method: A non-autoregressive conditional flow-matching Diffusion Transformer (DiT) operating in the frozen continuous latent space of AudioVAE2 (16 kHz encode, 48 kHz decode). It uses end-to-end modeling from raw Turkish characters (92-symbol vocabulary), parallel denoising over predicted durations, and a two-stage post-training pipeline: single-speaker voice locking followed by short-utterance coverage training.
AI.result: On Freya-TR-Eval: 8.0% WER, 3.0% CER — outperforming larger open-source TTS systems. Real-time factor of 0.11 on consumer GPUs; runs faster than real-time on a laptop CPU.
AI.conclusion: Freya-TTS demonstrates that a compact, tokenizer-free, fully non-autoregressive DiT with targeted post-training can achieve state-of-the-art Turkish TTS with extremely low latency, enabling practical edge deployment. All artifacts are open-sourced under Apache 2.0.

title: Balancing Usefulness and Naturalness: An LLM-based Curation Pipeline for Code Review Comments
comment: arXiv admin note: substantial text overlap with arXiv:2502.03425
summary:
Code review is a cornerstone of software development, where reviewers provide feedback through written comments to ensure code quality, maintainability, and correctness. The effectiveness of this process hinges on the quality of review comments. As large language models (LLMs) gain traction in automating code review tasks, the utility of these systems is directly limited by the quality of the datasets on which they are trained. Unfortunately, existing code review datasets are often noisy, inconsistent, or poorly structured, which hinders the ability of LLMs to learn to generate accurate, helpful, and human-like review comments.
  To overcome these limitations, we propose two different curation pipelines designed to improve both the quality and the utility of large-scale code review datasets. In the first pipeline, all review comments are systematically reformulated by an LLM to improve their clarity, conciseness, and civility while preserving their semantic intent. The curated dataset resulting from this approach, called CuREV, offers cleaner, higher-quality, and easier-to-learn-from comments that lead to measurable improvements in downstream automation tasks, namely review comment generation and code refinement. Building on this, we propose an improved pipeline, guided by high-quality exemplars, that enhances the realism and diversity of curated review comments. This method first separates the dataset into high-quality and low-quality reviews, based on a systematic quality assessment using an evaluation framework. High-quality comments are preserved in their original form and further used as in-context exemplars to inspire the reformulation of low-quality comments. By varying the exemplars provided, the reformulated comments are not only clearer and more actionable but also exhibit a broader range of writing styles, making them more realistic and human-like.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes two LLM-based curation pipelines to improve noisy code review datasets. The first (CuREV) systematically reformulates all comments for clarity. The second uses high-quality exemplars to guide reformulation of low-quality comments, enhancing realism and stylistic diversity. Both pipelines demonstrably improve downstream tasks like review comment generation and code refinement.
AI.motivation: Existing code review datasets are noisy, inconsistent, and poorly structured, limiting the ability of LLMs to learn to generate accurate, helpful, and human-like review comments for automated code review tasks.
AI.method: Two curation pipelines are proposed: (1) CuREV — all review comments are reformulated by an LLM to improve clarity, conciseness, and civility while preserving semantic intent; (2) An improved pipeline that splits the dataset into high- and low-quality reviews via a systematic quality assessment framework, preserves high-quality comments as-is, and uses them as in-context exemplars to guide LLM reformulation of low-quality comments, with varying exemplars to promote stylistic diversity.
AI.result: The curated datasets lead to measurable improvements in downstream automation tasks, specifically review comment generation and code refinement. The exemplar-guided pipeline additionally produces comments that are more realistic, actionable, and diverse in writing style.
AI.conclusion: LLM-driven curation pipelines can significantly enhance the quality and utility of code review datasets. The exemplar-guided approach offers particular advantages in realism and diversity, suggesting that selective reformulation guided by high-quality references is superior to wholesale rewriting.

title: Knowledge Graphs and Explainable AI as Complementary Resources for Urban Mining
comment: Accepted for presentation at the AISE Workshop @ IJCAI-ECAI 2026
summary: Pre-demolition assessment, the regulated audit process at the heart of urban mining, is an information process in which AI support must serve qualified auditors who remain accountable for the decisions taken. The relevant unit of value is not prediction accuracy alone, but the defensibility of the supported decisions: their legibility, plausibility, sourcing, and contestability. Explainable AI techniques and domain knowledge graphs each address parts of this requirement, and existing taxonomies have catalogued their integration. The literature is descriptively rich but structurally under-specified: what remains less developed is a structural account of why specific integrations produce artefacts neither resource can provide alone. This paper offers a complementarity-theoretic interpretation grounded in the IS resource-based tradition. We propose four consolidated KG-XAI integration modes (Lifting, Constraining, Typing, and Revising), each defined as a typed operation over XAI artefacts and knowledge-graph substrate structures. Each mode unlocks a distinct property of defensibility and contributes to the kind of regulatory artefact pre-demolition assessment demands. A fire-door example from the urban-mining process illustrates the modes using the W3C Linked Building Data stack and valuation extensions.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a structural framework defining four integration modes (Lifting, Constraining, Typing, Revising) for combining Explainable AI (XAI) with Knowledge Graphs (KG) to produce regulatory-grade artefacts for pre-demolition audits, where defensibility — not just accuracy — is the core value.
AI.motivation: Pre-demolition assessment in urban mining requires AI-supported decisions that are defensible (legible, plausible, sourced, contestable), not merely accurate. While XAI and KGs each address parts of this need and their integration has been catalogued taxonomically, the literature lacks a structural explanation of why specific integrations yield unique artefacts neither resource can produce alone.
AI.method: The paper adopts a complementarity-theoretic interpretation grounded in IS resource-based theory. It defines four consolidated KG-XAI integration modes — Lifting, Constraining, Typing, and Revising — each formalized as a typed operation over XAI artefacts and KG substrate structures. The framework is illustrated through a fire-door example using the W3C Linked Building Data stack with valuation extensions.
AI.result: Each integration mode unlocks a distinct defensibility property: Lifting enhances legibility, Constraining ensures plausibility, Typing provides sourcing, and Revising enables contestability. Together they produce regulatory artefacts that satisfy the accountability requirements of pre-demolition audits.
AI.conclusion: A structural, operationally-typed account of KG-XAI integration fills the gap left by descriptive taxonomies, showing how complementarity between the two resources generates defensible decision-support artefacts essential for regulated urban-mining processes.

title: Stochastic Linear Bandits with Partially Observed Actions
summary: The stochastic linear bandit, where actions are represented as vectors and rewards are linear, is a central paradigm for sequential decision making. We study a partially observed variant of this problem in which the learning agent only sees a random subset of coordinates for each action. Such partial observability arises naturally in settings like recommendation and healthcare, where full action descriptions can be expensive or even impossible to obtain. In general, this makes sublinear regret information-theoretically impossible. However, we show that this barrier can be overcome when the action vectors have low intrinsic dimension. We propose an algorithm, TOFU-POV, that estimates the latent action subspace using the masked actions, imputes current actions using an epoch-wise frozen representation, and runs OFUL in the resulting low-dimensional coordinates. Our theory shows that TOFU-POV enjoys a $\sqrt{T}$ regret that scales with the intrinsic action subspace dimension as opposed to the ambient dimension and quantifies the interaction between these quantities and the missingness, decision set size, and subspace conditioning. We also devise a rank-adaptive algorithm that does not require the knowledge of the intrinsic dimension. We complement these guarantees with a lower bound based on a novel product construction that separates usual reward-learning uncertainty from a missingness-dependent cost intrinsic to partial observation. Synthetic and real data experiments support our theory and show that TOFU-POV can substantially improve upon natural baselines in this challenging problem.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the stochastic linear bandit problem under partial observability, where only a random subset of action coordinates is observed. The authors propose TOFU-POV, an algorithm that estimates a low-dimensional latent subspace from masked actions, imputes missing coordinates, and applies OFUL in the reduced space. They prove a √T regret bound scaling with intrinsic dimension rather than ambient dimension, provide a rank-adaptive variant, establish a matching lower bound, and validate results with synthetic and real data experiments.
AI.motivation: In many real-world sequential decision-making settings (e.g., recommendation systems, healthcare), obtaining full feature descriptions of actions is expensive or infeasible — only partial coordinates are observed. This partial observability generally makes sublinear regret information-theoretically impossible. The authors aim to show that when action vectors lie in a low-dimensional subspace, this barrier can be overcome.
AI.method: The authors propose TOFU-POV (Truncated Observations For Uncertainty reduction with Partial Observed Vectors). The algorithm operates in epochs: (1) estimates the latent action subspace from historically observed masked action vectors, (2) imputes missing coordinates of current actions by projecting onto this subspace, and (3) runs the OFUL (Optimism in the Face of Uncertainty for Linear bandits) algorithm in the resulting low-dimensional representation. They also provide a rank-adaptive variant that estimates the intrinsic dimension rather than requiring it as input. For lower bounds, they devise a novel product construction that separates standard reward-learning uncertainty from a missingness-dependent cost.
AI.result: TOFU-POV achieves a √T regret that scales with the intrinsic action subspace dimension rather than the ambient dimension, with explicit dependence on missingness rates, decision set size, and subspace conditioning. The rank-adaptive variant maintains similar guarantees. The lower bound demonstrates a fundamental cost of partial observation that is unavoidable. Synthetic and real-data experiments show TOFU-POV substantially outperforms natural baselines.
AI.conclusion: Partial observability in stochastic linear bandits is surmountable when actions have low intrinsic dimensionality. TOFU-POV bridges subspace recovery, imputation, and optimistic exploration to achieve regret that depends only on the latent dimension, with both upper and lower bounds characterizing the fundamental trade-offs. The approach is practically effective as demonstrated by experimental results.

title: Conceptual Networks for Cross-Linguistic Idiomatic Expressions:A Feature-Based Graph Approach
summary: We present an interpretable network-based framework for representing idiomatic and figurative meaning across eight typologically diverse languages, totaling 160 conventional expressions, the large majority of which are idiomatic. Each expression is annotated with binary conceptual features (containment, concealment, emotional, social, etc.) derived from cognitive-linguistic theory, and pairwise Jaccard similarities define a weighted graph. Community detection reveals that idioms cluster by conceptual schema rather than by language, producing a structure consistent with cognitive-linguistic predictions. The conceptual network captures unique semantic information not present in distributional embeddings, can be scaled via automatic annotation with LLMs, improves downstream idiom detection, and remains robust when enriched with corpus frequencies. Cross-lingual transfer experiments show that conceptual proximity alone can identify acceptable translation equivalents across five language families, with substantial gains over embedding-based baselines. Ablation studies demonstrate that all three feature dimensions -- schemas, roles, and valence -- contribute non-redundantly to both the network's organizational properties and its performance on idiom detection, and that specific graph-derived signals (community membership, neighbor similarity) are particularly informative. The framework offers an interpretable, cross-linguistically stable representation of idiomatic meaning, combining theoretical grounding with practical utility.

AI.tldr: A graph-based framework using cognitive-linguistic conceptual features to represent idiomatic meaning across 8 languages; communities cluster by schema not language, the network captures semantics absent from embeddings, and conceptual proximity enables cross-lingual idiom translation surpassing embedding baselines.
AI.motivation: Idiomatic expressions pose challenges for NLP because their meanings are non-compositional and highly language-specific. Existing distributional embeddings fail to capture the conceptual underpinnings of figurative meaning, and there is no interpretable, cross-linguistically stable representation of idiomatic semantics grounded in cognitive-linguistic theory.
AI.method: 160 conventional expressions across 8 typologically diverse languages are annotated with binary conceptual features (containment, concealment, emotional, social, etc.) derived from cognitive-linguistic theory. Pairwise Jaccard similarities define a weighted graph. Community detection is applied to examine clustering structure. The network is evaluated on idiom detection tasks, scaled via automatic LLM annotation, enriched with corpus frequencies, and tested in cross-lingual transfer experiments across five language families against embedding-based baselines. Ablation studies isolate contributions of schema, role, and valence feature dimensions, as well as graph-derived signals (community membership, neighbor similarity).
AI.result: Idioms cluster by conceptual schema rather than by language, aligning with cognitive-linguistic predictions. The conceptual network captures unique semantic information not present in distributional embeddings. It improves downstream idiom detection, remains robust with corpus frequency enrichment, and scales via LLM-based automatic annotation. Cross-lingual transfer shows that conceptual proximity alone identifies acceptable translation equivalents across five language families, with substantial gains over embedding baselines. All three feature dimensions (schemas, roles, valence) contribute non-redundantly; graph-derived signals (community membership, neighbor similarity) are particularly informative.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework provides an interpretable, cross-linguistically stable representation of idiomatic meaning that combines theoretical grounding from cognitive linguistics with practical utility for NLP tasks, demonstrating that conceptual structure transcends language boundaries in figurative expressions.

title: Writing Bug Reports for Software Repair Agents: What Information Matters Most?
summary: Software development is increasingly moving toward agentic-first workflows. This includes AI agents responsible for generating initial fixes for submitted issue reports. In this setting, issue reports are no longer merely documentation for human maintainers; they become the primary task specification for the agent. However, little is known about how such reports should be written to maximize the agent's chances of producing a correct fix. We study what makes a bug report agent-ready. Starting from the SWE-bench Verified benchmark (i.e., a collection of 500 real repository issues with human-written gold patches and test suites for evaluating generated fixes) we manually classify each issue by change type (e.g., bug fix vs refactoring) and annotate each sentence with its information type, such as observed behavior, expected behavior, reproduction steps, localization cues, and suggested fixes. We focus on the 441 issues representing bug reports, and we run on them mini-swe-agent using three LLM backbones (i.e., GPT-5-mini, MiniMax M2.5, and Gemini 3 Flash). We then fit a binomial regression model to estimate the incremental association between each information type and agent success, controlling for confounding factors. Our results suggest that agentic-first reports benefit most from information that narrows the agent's search and repair space. Localization cues, such as references to affected code areas, are positively associated with successful repairs, while suggested fixes, expressed either in code or natural language, show some of the strongest positive associations with pass probability. An ablation study removing selected information types confirms that agents benefit less from information traditionally useful to humans, such as reproduction steps, and more from sentences that expose a repair direction, either through bug localization or a suggested fix.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates what makes a bug report "agent-ready" for AI-driven software repair. Using 441 bug reports from SWE-bench Verified, the authors annotate sentences by information type and run repair agents with three LLMs, then fit a binomial regression model. Key finding: localization cues and suggested fixes are the strongest positive predictors of repair success, while traditional human-oriented information like reproduction steps is less beneficial.
AI.motivation: As software development shifts toward agentic-first workflows where AI agents automatically generate fixes from issue reports, there is no empirical guidance on how to write bug reports that maximize agent repair success. Existing issue reports are optimized for human maintainers, not AI agents.
AI.method: (1) Manually classify 500 SWE-bench Verified issues by change type and annotate each sentence with information types (observed behavior, expected behavior, reproduction steps, localization cues, suggested fixes). (2) Run mini-swe-agent with three LLM backbones (GPT-5-mini, MiniMax M2.5, Gemini 3 Flash) on the 441 bug-report subset. (3) Fit a binomial regression model to estimate the incremental association between each information type and agent success, controlling for confounders. (4) Perform an ablation study removing selected information types to confirm findings.
AI.result: Localization cues (references to affected code areas) are positively associated with successful repairs. Suggested fixes (in code or natural language) show some of the strongest positive associations with pass probability. Conversely, reproduction steps — traditionally valuable for humans — provide comparatively less benefit to agents. The ablation study confirms that agents benefit more from information exposing a repair direction than from human-oriented details.
AI.conclusion: Agentic-first bug reports should prioritize information that narrows the search and repair space — specifically localization cues and suggested fixes — rather than traditional human-oriented elements like reproduction steps. This has implications for how issue reporting practices should evolve in agent-driven development workflows.

title: TrustX Agent Risk Classification Framework (ARC): Risk-Tiering Internally Created Agentic AI Systems
comment: This is a working paper on our risk classification tool, with iterations currently underway
summary: The proliferation of agentic AI systems across enterprise and public-sector contexts has outpaced the capacity of general-purpose AI risk frameworks to classify and govern them. In this paper, we introduce the TrustX Agent Risk Classification Framework, a structured, repeatable instrument that can be applied to seven types of agentic AI systems and is grounded in foundational pre-existing AI governance frameworks. At the core of the framework is a twelve-dimension scoring rubric that robustly quantifies the risk. This rubric is combined with other components, such as the GPA + IAT classification model and the five-level autonomy framework derived from existing literature. These inputs produce a three-tier governance output with mapped control recommendations. A specialised Coding Assistant extension is also included to account for nuances specific to this type of agentic AI system. We then use an illustrative example to show our framework in practice. ARC is intended for AI governance practitioners, risk officers, developers, and regulators, and it will regularly undergo iteration as we continue to expand it and make it more robust. The community can access the interactive framework here: https://arc.responsible.ai/

AI.tldr: The TrustX Agent Risk Classification Framework (ARC) is a structured, repeatable tool for classifying and governing seven types of agentic AI systems, featuring a 12-dimension scoring rubric, a GPA+IAT classification model, a five-level autonomy framework, and a three-tier governance output with control recommendations.
AI.motivation: General-purpose AI risk frameworks have not kept pace with the rapid proliferation of agentic AI systems in enterprise and public-sector contexts, creating a gap in classification and governance capabilities.
AI.method: The framework integrates three components: (1) a 12-dimension scoring rubric for risk quantification, (2) a GPA+IAT classification model, and (3) a five-level autonomy framework from prior literature. These inputs produce a three-tier governance output with mapped control recommendations. A specialized Coding Assistant extension addresses domain-specific nuances. An illustrative example demonstrates practical application.
AI.result: The framework produces a three-tier governance classification with corresponding control recommendations. The authors provide an interactive implementation accessible at https://arc.responsible.ai/.
AI.conclusion: ARC provides a practical, structured instrument for AI governance practitioners, risk officers, developers, and regulators. The framework is designed for iterative refinement and ongoing expansion to enhance robustness over time.

title: Federated Low-Rank Koopman Learning for Multivariate Time-Series Anomaly Detection in IoT Systems
summary: Distributed IoT systems generate multivariate time-series streams for monitoring physical assets, servers, and embedded sensing platforms. Detecting abnormal temporal behavior is critical for fault diagnosis, predictive maintenance, and security. However, practical IoT anomaly detection is hindered by decentralized and non-IID data, limited bandwidth, and the constrained computation and memory of edge devices. This paper proposes FedKAD, a resource-efficient federated Koopman anomaly detection framework for distributed IoT multivariate time series. Unlike deep-learning-based anomaly detectors that require training and communicating large neural models, FedKAD learns normal temporal dynamics through lightweight sliding-window Koopman representations. Federated training is formulated as a low-rank consensus problem, where raw sensor streams and local reduced dynamics remain on device while only compact subspace variables are exchanged with the server. To optimize the shared representation under orthonormality constraints, we develop a federated Stiefel-ADMM algorithm and provide convergence and stationarity analysis under partial client participation. During inference, each client detects anomalies locally by measuring the prediction residual between observed future trajectories and the learned Koopman dynamics. Experiments on four widely used multivariate time-series anomaly detection benchmarks show that FedKAD maintains or improves detection performance compared with federated deep-learning baselines. More importantly for IoT deployment, FedKAD provides up to $2.1\times10^3$ faster training, $80\times$ lower communication, and $79\times$ lower inference latency than neural baselines, confirming its suitability for resource-constrained edge devices.

AI.tldr: FedKAD is a lightweight federated anomaly detection framework for IoT multivariate time series that uses Koopman operator theory instead of deep learning. It achieves comparable or better detection performance while reducing training time by up to 2100×, communication by 80×, and inference latency by 79× compared to neural baselines.
AI.motivation: Practical IoT anomaly detection faces four key challenges: (1) data is decentralized and non-IID across edge devices, (2) limited communication bandwidth prevents transmitting raw data, (3) edge devices have constrained computation and memory, and (4) deep-learning-based detectors require training and communicating large models, which is infeasible in resource-constrained IoT settings.
AI.method: FedKAD employs lightweight sliding-window Koopman representations to learn normal temporal dynamics. Federated training is cast as a low-rank consensus problem where raw sensor data and local reduced dynamics stay on-device, and only compact subspace variables are exchanged with the server. A federated Stiefel-ADMM algorithm is developed to optimize the shared representation under orthonormality constraints, with convergence and stationarity guarantees under partial client participation. At inference, each client locally detects anomalies by measuring prediction residuals between observed future trajectories and the learned Koopman dynamics.
AI.result: Experiments on four benchmark multivariate time-series anomaly detection datasets show FedKAD matches or exceeds the detection performance of federated deep-learning baselines. In terms of resource efficiency, it achieves up to 2.1×10³ faster training, 80× lower communication overhead, and 79× lower inference latency.
AI.conclusion: FedKAD demonstrates that Koopman-based representations offer a compelling alternative to deep learning for federated anomaly detection on edge devices, delivering strong detection accuracy with drastically reduced computational and communication costs, making it well-suited for real-world IoT deployments.

title: Tokenizer Transplantation: Mitigating Autoregressive Collapse in Edge-Efficient Bengali ASR
comment: 5 pages, 2 figures. Accepted as a poster at the MusIML Workshop, ICML 2026
summary: Lightweight speech recognition models are critical for edge deployment, yet highly optimized architectures like Moonshine often fail on morphologically rich, non-Latin languages such as Bengali. This study identifies the root cause of this failure as the model's English-centric byte-level tokenizer, which fragments Bengali words into high-fertility byte chains and triggers catastrophic autoregressive collapse during inference. To resolve this, a novel vocabulary transplantation pipeline is proposed to replace the decoder vocabulary with the native-script BanglaBERT WordPiece vocabulary and resize the corresponding token embedding matrix. Experimental results demonstrate a reduction in token fertility from 9.16 to 1.30. By decreasing autoregressive sequence length by 85.8%, decoding instability is entirely mitigated. When evaluated on the 882-hour Lipi-Ghor dataset, the modified architecture achieves a competitive 21.54% Word Error Rate (WER) and a Real-Time Factor (RTF) of 0.0053. Ultimately, this research provides a scalable, reproducible blueprint for cross-script adaptation of compact ASR models without the need for resource-intensive pre-training.

AI.tldr: Lightweight ASR models like Moonshine fail on Bengali due to English-centric byte-level tokenization causing decoding collapse. A vocabulary transplantation method using BanglaBERT WordPiece reduces token fertility from 9.16 to 1.30, cutting sequence length by 85.8% and achieving 21.54% WER with 0.0053 RTF on a 882-hour dataset—offering a scalable cross-script adaptation blueprint without retraining.
AI.motivation: Lightweight speech recognition models optimized for edge deployment (e.g., Moonshine) catastrophically fail on morphologically rich, non-Latin languages like Bengali. The root cause is identified as the English-centric byte-level tokenizer, which fragments Bengali words into excessively long byte chains (high token fertility), leading to autoregressive decoding collapse during inference.
AI.method: A vocabulary transplantation pipeline is proposed: the decoder's vocabulary and token embedding matrix are replaced with the native-script BanglaBERT WordPiece vocabulary, preserving the encoder while adapting the decoder to Bengali's linguistic structure without resource-intensive pre-training.
AI.result: Token fertility dropped from 9.16 to 1.30, autoregressive sequence length decreased by 85.8%, fully eliminating decoding instability. On the 882-hour Lipi-Ghor dataset, the modified model achieved 21.54% WER and 0.0053 RTF.
AI.conclusion: Vocabulary transplantation offers a scalable, reproducible blueprint for adapting compact ASR models to non-Latin, morphologically rich languages without costly retraining, enabling effective cross-script deployment on edge devices.

title: Agora: Enhancing LLM Agent Reasoning Via Auction-Based Task Allocation
summary: Enhancing the reasoning capabilities of large language model (LLM) agents requires effective orchestration of diverse expert models and tools. However, existing frameworks typically call APIs based on coarse-grained matching between tasks and the functions of expert models or tools, while overlooking critical factors such as performance variability and cost efficiency among functionally similar alternatives. To address this, we propose Agora, a framework that introduces an incentive-compatible auction mechanism for dynamically allocating tasks to expert models and tools. By treating reasoning steps as tradeable items, Agora enables agents to bid based on their rectified competence-ensuring that critical logic is routed to the most capable solver rather than the most overconfident one. Evaluations across five benchmarks show that Agora improves over matched single-model, routing, and cascade baselines under comparable candidate pools, while exposing a controllable cost-quality trade-off through a single auction parameter.

AI.tldr: Agora introduces an incentive-compatible auction mechanism for LLM agents to dynamically allocate reasoning tasks among expert models and tools, routing critical logic to the most capable solver based on rectified competence rather than overconfidence, achieving improved performance with controllable cost-quality trade-offs.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agent frameworks rely on coarse-grained task-function matching for expert model/tool selection, ignoring performance variability and cost efficiency among functionally similar alternatives. This leads to suboptimal routing where overconfident but less capable models may be selected for critical reasoning steps.
AI.method: Agora frames reasoning steps as tradeable items in an incentive-compatible auction. Expert models and tools bid on tasks based on their rectified competence (calibrated self-assessment rather than raw confidence), enabling dynamic allocation that routes critical logic to the most capable solver. The mechanism exposes a single tunable auction parameter for controlling the cost-quality trade-off.
AI.result: Evaluations across five benchmarks demonstrate that Agora outperforms matched single-model, routing, and cascade baselines under comparable candidate pools, while the auction parameter provides explicit control over the cost-quality trade-off.
AI.conclusion: Agora demonstrates that market-based mechanisms, specifically incentive-compatible auctions with rectified competence bidding, offer a principled and effective approach to orchestrating heterogeneous expert models and tools in LLM agent systems.

title: Optimal Top-$k$ Identification from Pairwise Comparisons
summary: We study the active learning problem of fixed-confidence top-$k$ identification from noisy pairwise comparisons. In this problem, an algorithm sequentially chooses pairs of items to compare, observes the outcomes, and stops when it can return the set of top-$k$ items with error probability at most $δ$. The objective is to design such a $δ$-correct procedure that minimizes the expected number of comparisons (the sample complexity). This problem falls within the broader literature on fixed-confidence pure exploration in bandit models, where a common target is asymptotic optimality: the algorithm's expected sample complexity matches the information theoretic lower bound as $δ\to 0$. Asymptotically optimal procedures have been developed for a range of fixed-confidence pure-exploration problems, however to the best of our knowledge, for top-$1$, or more generally top-$k$ identification from pairwise comparisons under latent utility models an asymptotically optimal algorithm has not been established. In this setting, we develop such an algorithm. We characterize the structure of the lower bound and formulate it as a saddle-point problem. This structure enables a computationally efficient primal-dual procedure that learns the asymptotically optimal comparison allocation online. We then construct an adaptive comparison-allocation algorithm that tracks the allocation learned by the primal-dual procedure and prove it is asymptotically optimal.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first asymptotically optimal algorithm for fixed-confidence top-k identification from noisy pairwise comparisons under latent utility models, achieving sample complexity that matches the information-theoretic lower bound as δ→0 through a novel saddle-point formulation and an online primal-dual allocation tracking procedure.
AI.motivation: While asymptotically optimal procedures exist for many pure-exploration bandit problems, no such algorithm has been established for top-k identification from pairwise comparisons under latent utility models (e.g., Bradley-Terry, Thurstone). This gap motivates the development of an algorithm that achieves the fundamental sample complexity limit.
AI.method: The authors characterize the information-theoretic lower bound as a saddle-point problem, which reveals structural properties enabling computationally efficient optimization. They design a primal-dual online learning procedure that learns the asymptotically optimal comparison allocation during the sampling process. An adaptive algorithm is then constructed to track this allocation and is proven to achieve asymptotic optimality (matching the lower bound as δ→0).
AI.result: The proposed algorithm is proved to be δ-correct (error probability ≤ δ) and asymptotically optimal, meaning its expected sample complexity matches the information-theoretic lower bound in the limit δ→0. The saddle-point formulation yields a computationally tractable approach to the otherwise intractable optimal allocation problem.
AI.conclusion: This work resolves the open problem of asymptotic optimality for top-k identification from pairwise comparisons, providing both theoretical guarantees and a practical algorithm. The primal-dual framework for online allocation learning may also prove useful for related pure-exploration problems.

title: Toward Real-Time Sentence-Level Sign Language Translation
summary: Most sign language understanding systems operate at the level of isolated signs, limiting their usefulness in natural communication. We study sentence-level sign language translation (SLT) with the primary goal of real-time deployment rather than proposing a new translation architecture. We fine-tune a SHuBERT-ByT5 translation stack on a uniformly sampled 9,872-example subset of How2Sign, selected because of compute and storage constraints, using QLoRA while keeping SHuBERT frozen. The model obtains a validation BLEU of 16.7 and, on the test split, BLEU 15.9 and BLEURT 44.7. The main contribution is a hardware-aware streaming system: a Raspberry Pi 4B reference client provides camera capture, local text display, and speech output, while compute-intensive perception and translation run on a CPU/GPU backend. The capture protocol remains client-agnostic, so the same backend can serve a browser, phone, or laptop. Chunked ingestion, bounded queues, parallelized perception, temporal reordering, and a sentence-boundary state machine reduce mean post-finalization response latency from 1.873 to 1.354 seconds (27.71%) and P95 latency from 2.919 to 2.130 seconds (27.03%) over the complete 9,872-example working subset.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a real-time, hardware-aware streaming system for sentence-level sign language translation. Using a fine-tuned SHuBERT-ByT5 model (QLoRA, frozen SHuBERT) on a 9,872-example subset of How2Sign, they achieve BLEU 15.9 on the test set. The key contribution is a low-latency streaming pipeline deployed across a Raspberry Pi client and a CPU/GPU backend, reducing mean post-finalization latency by 27.71% through chunked ingestion, parallelized perception, and a sentence-boundary state machine.
AI.motivation: Most sign language understanding systems operate only on isolated signs, limiting their usefulness for natural, continuous communication. The authors aim to enable sentence-level SLT with a focus on real-time deployability across heterogeneous hardware, rather than proposing a novel translation architecture.
AI.method: A SHuBERT-ByT5 translation stack is fine-tuned using QLoRA (with SHuBERT frozen) on a uniformly sampled 9,872-example subset of How2Sign due to compute/storage constraints. The streaming system uses a Raspberry Pi 4B as the reference client for camera capture, local text display, and speech output, while perception and translation run on a backend CPU/GPU. Optimizations include chunked ingestion, bounded queues, parallelized perception, temporal reordering, and a sentence-boundary state machine to reduce latency.
AI.result: The model achieves validation BLEU 16.7, test BLEU 15.9, and BLEURT 44.7. The streaming optimizations reduce mean post-finalization response latency from 1.873s to 1.354s (27.71% reduction) and P95 latency from 2.919s to 2.130s (27.03% reduction) over the full 9,872-example working subset.
AI.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that a client-agnostic, hardware-aware streaming architecture can make sentence-level sign language translation practical for real-time deployment, with significant latency reductions achieved through system-level optimizations rather than model architecture changes.

title: ConceptSMILE: Auditing the Trustworthiness of Concept-Based Explainable AI
summary: Concept-based explainable artificial intelligence (AI) can make model reasoning more human-understandable, but concept-level outputs are not automatically trustworthy. We introduce ConceptSMILE, a model-agnostic perturbation-based auditing framework for evaluating the reliability of concept-based explanations. Rather than replacing SMILE, ConceptSMILE extends its perturbation-based logic from feature- or region-level attribution to the auditing of human-understandable concept explanations. The framework perturbs input regions, measures concept-response shifts, applies locality weighting, and fits an XGBoost surrogate to approximate local concept behaviour. Reliability is assessed through attribution accuracy, surrogate fidelity, faithfulness, stability, and consistency. We evaluate ConceptSMILE on retinal fundus images by comparing MedSAM-derived visual concepts with VLM-based semantic concepts. Results show that reliability varies across concepts and pathways: MedSAM achieves stronger spatial attribution and the highest surrogate fidelity ($R^2 = 0.8503$, $R_w^2 = 0.8465$), while the VLM pathway shows stronger vessel faithfulness and stronger stability under selected artefact conditions. ConceptSMILE provides an independent audit layer for evaluating the trustworthiness of concept-based XAI.

AI.tldr: ConceptSMILE is a model-agnostic perturbation-based auditing framework that evaluates the reliability of concept-based XAI explanations by measuring attribution accuracy, surrogate fidelity, faithfulness, stability, and consistency, demonstrated on retinal fundus images comparing MedSAM visual concepts against VLM semantic concepts.
AI.motivation: Concept-based explainable AI can make model reasoning more human-understandable, but concept-level outputs lack automatic trustworthiness guarantees. There is a need for an independent audit mechanism to assess whether concept-based explanations are reliable.
AI.method: ConceptSMILE extends perturbation-based logic from feature/region-level attribution to concept-level auditing. The framework: (1) perturbs input regions, (2) measures shifts in concept responses, (3) applies locality weighting, and (4) fits an XGBoost surrogate model to approximate local concept behavior. Reliability is quantified along five dimensions: attribution accuracy, surrogate fidelity, faithfulness, stability, and consistency.
AI.result: Evaluated on retinal fundus images comparing MedSAM-derived visual concepts with VLM-based semantic concepts. MedSAM achieved stronger spatial attribution and the highest surrogate fidelity (R²=0.8503, R_w²=0.8465). The VLM pathway exhibited stronger vessel faithfulness and greater stability under selected artefact conditions. Reliability varied significantly across different concepts and pathways.
AI.conclusion: ConceptSMILE provides an effective, independent audit layer for evaluating concept-based XAI trustworthiness. The variation in reliability across concepts and explanation pathways underscores the importance of auditing concept-level explanations before relying on them in practice.

title: AlphaZero in Sparsely Rewarded Games: Limits and Auxiliary Supervision
summary: AlphaZero has demonstrated that a neural-guided Monte Carlo Tree Search can achieve superhuman performance, but strong play does not necessarily imply perfect play. We study this gap in two oracle-evaluable domains with contrasting structure: Connect Four, a solved partisan game with exact game-theoretic values, and Chomp, an impartial game whose optimal play is governed by Grundy-number structure. Under a unified self-play $+$ MCTS pipeline, we compare vanilla AlphaZero, a multi-frame variant (limited to Chomp), and an AlphaZero Auxiliary Loss (AZAL) that adds oracle-derived policy supervision. We find that vanilla AlphaZero achieves strong play across both domains but cannot preserve the exact trajectories required for optimal play: in Connect Four, it fails to maintain the optimal line of play, while in Chomp, it fails to consistently restore the $g=0$ invariant. On rectangular Chomp boards, multi-frame inputs alone do not remove this gap. Nevertheless, AZAL substantially improves oracle consistency across multi-seeded full-game traces and sampled-state evaluations. On Chomp, AZAL reaches perfect full-game oracle consistency on 10x11 and high but not complete consistency on 9x10; on Connect Four, AZAL improves oracle-match rate and delays the first oracle mistake, but does not reach perfect play.

AI.tldr: AlphaZero plays strongly but not perfectly in oracle-evaluable games. Vanilla AlphaZero fails to preserve optimal trajectories in Connect Four and Grundy invariants in Chomp. Adding oracle-derived policy supervision (AZAL) significantly improves oracle consistency and achieves near-perfect play on Chomp but falls short of perfection on Connect Four.
AI.motivation: Strong play does not imply perfect play. The gap between superhuman performance and truly optimal (perfect) play is underexplored. The authors aim to quantify and close this gap using two oracle-evaluable domains — Connect Four (solved, partisan) and Chomp (impartial, Grundy-based) — where ground-truth optimal actions are known.
AI.method: A unified self-play + MCTS pipeline is used across both domains. Three variants are compared: (1) vanilla AlphaZero, (2) a multi-frame input variant (Chomp only), and (3) AlphaZero Auxiliary Loss (AZAL), which augments the policy head with an auxiliary loss using oracle-derived policy supervision. Evaluation uses multi-seeded full-game traces and sampled-state evaluations to measure oracle consistency.
AI.result: Vanilla AlphaZero achieves strong play in both domains but cannot preserve exact optimal trajectories: it loses the optimal line in Connect Four and fails to consistently restore the g=0 invariant in Chomp. Multi-frame inputs alone do not close the gap on rectangular Chomp boards. AZAL substantially improves oracle consistency: on Chomp 10x11, it reaches perfect full-game oracle consistency; on 9x10, high but incomplete; on Connect Four, AZAL improves oracle-match rate and delays first oracle mistakes but does not achieve perfect play.
AI.conclusion: Neural-guided MCTS alone is insufficient for perfect play even in modestly sized oracle-evaluable games. Incorporating oracle supervision via an auxiliary policy loss significantly narrows the gap, achieving perfect play on some Chomp boards. However, the structural differences between partisan (Connect Four) and impartial (Chomp) games may affect the difficulty of reaching perfect play, and further work is needed to close the gap entirely.

title: Task-Specific Multimodal Question Answering Agents via Confidence Calibration and Incremental Reasoning for QANTA 2026
comment: 10 pages, 1 figure. Accepted at the EMM-QA 2026 Workshop, ICML 2026 (Non-Archival). Rank #1 overall system in the QANTA 2026 Challenge
summary: We present our submission to the QANTA 2026 shared challenge at the ICML 2026 Workshop on Efficient Multimodal Question Answering (EMM-QA). Quanta evaluates multimodal quizbowl systems that answer pyramid-style questions from incrementally revealed text and accompanying images while operating under realistic efficiency constraints. The challenge consists of two distinct tasks: Tossup questions, which require deciding when to answer under uncertainty, and Bonus questions, which emphasize accurate answer selection and human adoption. To address these differing objectives, we develop a task-specific two-agent architecture. Our Tossup agent utilizes a GPT-4o-mini-class model (referred to as GPT-4.1-mini in the competition logs) with confidence-calibrated answering and a domain-specific numeric reasoning policy that reduces overconfident predictions from isolated quantitative clues. Our Bonus agent uses GPT-4o-class model (referred to as GPT-4.1) with leadin-aware reasoning, structured relational reasoning, and multimodal evidence integration to improve exact answer selection. Rather than relying on a retrieval pipeline or model ensembles, our approach emphasizes efficient reasoning policies and confidence calibration within a hosted-only environment. Our system achieved the highest overall leaderboard score of 0.402, including a Tossup score of 0.238 and a Bonus Effect score of 0.164. The results demonstrate that lightweight, task-specific reasoning strategies can provide strong performance on resource-constrained multimodal question answering benchmarks.

AI.tldr: A two-agent architecture using GPT-4o-class models with task-specific reasoning policies (confidence-calibrated answering for Tossup, leadin-aware multimodal reasoning for Bonus) achieved the highest overall score (0.402) at the QANTA 2026 shared challenge, demonstrating that lightweight reasoning strategies can excel under efficiency constraints without retrieval pipelines or ensembles.
AI.motivation: The QANTA 2026 challenge requires multimodal quizbowl systems to answer pyramid-style questions from incrementally revealed text and images under strict efficiency constraints. The two tasks — Tossup (deciding when to answer under uncertainty) and Bonus (accurate answer selection for human adoption) — have divergent objectives that a single monolithic approach cannot optimally satisfy. Prior systems often rely on retrieval pipelines or model ensembles, which are computationally expensive and may exceed the hosted-only resource constraints of the challenge.
AI.method: The authors propose a task-specific two-agent architecture: (1) A Tossup agent employing a GPT-4o-mini-class model (GPT-4.1-mini) with confidence-calibrated answering, using a domain-specific numeric reasoning policy to mitigate overconfident predictions from isolated quantitative clues; (2) A Bonus agent using a GPT-4o-class model (GPT-4.1) with leadin-aware reasoning, structured relational reasoning, and multimodal evidence integration for precise answer selection. The system operates entirely within a hosted-only environment, eschewing retrieval pipelines and model ensembles in favor of efficient reasoning policies and calibration.
AI.result: The system achieved the highest overall leaderboard score of 0.402, comprising a Tossup score of 0.238 and a Bonus Effect score of 0.164, ranking first among all submissions to the QANTA 2026 shared challenge.
AI.conclusion: Lightweight, task-specific reasoning strategies paired with confidence calibration can deliver state-of-the-art performance on resource-constrained multimodal QA benchmarks, outperforming approaches that depend on retrieval augmentation or ensembling. The two-agent design effectively addresses the distinct demands of Tossup and Bonus question formats.

title: REFORGE: A Method for Benchmarking LLMs' Reverse Engineering Capabilities in Decompiled Binary Function Naming
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures; accepted for publication to the 23rd International Conference on Applied Computing 2026, Lisbon October 24-26,2026
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to reverse-engineering tasks, and recent threat-intelligence reporting shows them operating inside live offensive-security workflows. Claims about their capability, however, outpace our ability to measure it. Existing benchmarks for LLM-assisted binary analysis treat the construction of function-level ground truth as a solved pre-processing step and report accuracy without disclosing how many functions were reliably evaluable. We argue that the principal obstacle to fair evaluation is not model capability but the reliability of binary-to-source alignment under compiler optimization. This paper presents Reforge, a provenance-tracked pipeline that constructs function-level ground truth from C source through compilation, DWARF and syntactic extraction, alignment, and decompilation, and that operationalizes alignment uncertainty as an eight-gate confidence funnel with three-tier stratification. On a controlled micro-benchmark, high-confidence yield falls from 87.2% to 65.9% across optimization levels, and unpaired comparisons overstate optimization-induced performance decay through survivorship bias. A proof-of-concept evaluation of seven contemporary LLMs on function naming demonstrates the substrate and motivates uncertainty-aware benchmarking practice

AI.tldr: Current LLM-assisted binary analysis benchmarks are unreliable because they ignore the difficulty of aligning decompiled functions with source-level ground truth under compiler optimization. Reforge introduces a provenance-tracked pipeline with an eight-gate confidence funnel to quantify alignment uncertainty, revealing that survivorship bias inflates perceived model performance and advocating for uncertainty-aware evaluation.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for LLM-assisted reverse engineering treat function-level ground truth construction as trivial and report accuracy without disclosing alignment reliability. The authors argue that binary-to-source alignment under compiler optimization is the true bottleneck, and that ignoring alignment uncertainty leads to survivorship bias that overstates the effect of optimization on model performance decay.
AI.method: Reforge is a provenance-tracked pipeline that constructs function-level ground truth by compiling C source, extracting syntactic information via DWARF debug data, performing decompilation, and aligning functions across representations. It operationalizes alignment uncertainty through an eight-gate confidence funnel with three-tier stratification (high-confidence, medium-confidence, low-confidence), and uses both paired (same-function) and unpaired comparisons to quantify survivorship bias in optimization-induced performance estimates.
AI.result: On a controlled micro-benchmark, high-confidence alignment yield drops from 87.2% to 65.9% as compiler optimization increases. Unpaired comparisons (which ignore alignment uncertainty) overstate the apparent performance degradation caused by optimization — a survivorship bias effect. A proof-of-concept evaluation on function naming with seven contemporary LLMs validates the substrate.
AI.conclusion: Fair evaluation of LLMs on binary analysis tasks requires explicit handling of alignment uncertainty. Benchmarks should report confidence-stratified results and account for survivorship bias rather than treating ground truth alignment as a solved pre-processing step.

title: Group Invariant Spectral Embedding
summary: Spectral embedding methods are widely used for dimensionality reduction and clustering of high-dimensional datasets with intrinsic low-dimensional structures. Although many datasets of practical interest exhibit invariance under symmetries such as rotations, standard spectral embedding methods do not account for this, treating symmetry-related data points as unrelated. Our approach to this problem is to incorporate the symmetries directly into the affinity kernels used for spectral embedding. We analyze the case of a Riemannian data manifold $M$ with symmetries given by a compact Lie group~$G$ and prove that, under suitable conditions, graph Laplacians constructed from three types of invariant kernels converge pointwise to explicit second-order differential operators on the quotient space $M/G$. Our analysis implies improved convergence rates, as the effective dimension drops according to the dimension of the group. We validate our approach on datasets with $\mathrm{SO}(2)$ or $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ symmetry, and show that $G$-invariant spectral embedding recovers the intrinsic geometry of the data, in contrast to standard spectral embedding, which fails to do so even in the limit of infinite data.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes incorporating symmetries (given by a compact Lie group G) directly into affinity kernels for spectral embedding. The authors prove that graph Laplacians from three types of G-invariant kernels converge pointwise to differential operators on the quotient space M/G, yielding improved convergence rates due to reduced effective dimension. Experiments on SO(2) and SO(3) symmetric datasets validate the approach.
AI.motivation: Standard spectral embedding methods treat symmetry-related data points as unrelated, ignoring invariances (e.g., rotational symmetries) common in real-world datasets. This degrades performance and fails to recover intrinsic geometry, even with infinite data.
AI.method: The authors construct affinity kernels that are explicitly invariant under a compact Lie group G acting on a Riemannian data manifold M. They analyze three types of invariant kernels and prove pointwise convergence of the resulting graph Laplacians to second-order differential operators on the quotient M/G, leveraging the reduced effective dimension.
AI.result: Theoretical results establish pointwise convergence to explicit differential operators on M/G, with convergence rates improving as the group dimension increases. Empirically, G-invariant spectral embedding successfully recovers intrinsic geometry on datasets with SO(2) and SO(3) symmetry, whereas standard spectral embedding fails even in the infinite-data limit.
AI.conclusion: Encoding symmetries directly into the spectral embedding kernel yields both theoretical guarantees (convergence to quotient-space operators, improved rates) and practical benefits (faithful recovery of intrinsic geometry), outperforming standard approaches that ignore known invariances.

title: Sensitivity-Aware Thresholding and Token Routing for Activation Sparsification in Large Language Models
summary: Efficient inference in Large Language Models (LLMs) requires deciding where computation can be reduced while preserving model quality.
