We study this problem through multilayer perceptron (MLP) activation sparsification and token-level conditional routing. We first propose Sensitivity-Aware Thresholding for Sparsity (SATS), a threshold calibration method to choose layerwise gate thresholds using a local MLP output sensitivity proxy rather than calibrating thresholds directly from activation percentiles. While SATS retains the existing mechanism of sparsifying MLP activations by thresholding gate activations, it replaces percentile-based calibration with a sensitivity-aware selection rule. We then introduce a lightweight token routing framework that dynamically selects between a base path and a modified path on a per-token basis, rather than applying the modified computation uniformly to all tokens. We evaluate both methods on multiple recent open-weight LLMs. Our results show that SATS improves over the threshold-based sparsification baseline at matched actual sparsity and that token routing yields a more favorable quality-throughput trade-off than static activation modification baselines. Overall, our results suggest that improved threshold calibration and token routing can improve the quality-throughput trade-off in LLMs.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SATS, a sensitivity-aware threshold calibration method for MLP activation sparsification, and a token-level conditional routing framework. Both methods improve the quality-throughput trade-off in LLM inference compared to static baselines.
AI.motivation: Efficient LLM inference requires selectively reducing computation without degrading model quality. Existing methods either use percentile-based thresholding for MLP sparsification (suboptimal) or apply modified computation uniformly across tokens (wasteful). The authors aim to address both limitations.
AI.method: (1) SATS: calibrates layerwise gate thresholds using a local MLP output sensitivity proxy rather than activation percentiles, retaining the gating mechanism but replacing the selection rule. (2) Token routing: a lightweight framework that dynamically selects between a base path and a modified path on a per-token basis instead of uniform application.
AI.result: SATS outperforms the threshold-based sparsification baseline at matched actual sparsity levels. Token routing achieves a more favorable quality-throughput trade-off than static activation modification baselines. Both evaluated on multiple recent open-weight LLMs.
AI.conclusion: Improved threshold calibration via sensitivity-aware selection and per-token conditional routing can meaningfully enhance the quality-throughput trade-off in LLM inference.

title: Model Agnostic Graph Prompt Learning for Crystal Property Prediction
summary: Graph Neural Networks have emerged as a powerful tool for the fast and accurate prediction of various crystal properties. These models often encode domain-specific knowledge into their graph encoding modules, which increases their parameter size and makes their performance heavily dependent on domain expertise. Added to this, explicitly incorporating all chemical and structural features, that might influence a specific crystal property into the GNN encoder, is a challenging task. In this work, we propose a soft prompt learning framework that captures latent features essential for property prediction, which are not explicitly provided to the GNN. We introduce a novel multilevel graph prompt learning framework comprising both node-level and graph-level soft prompts. At the node level, we capture the local chemical semantics of different atom types, while at the graph level, we encode the global structural symmetry of the crystal graph. Our proposed prompt learning framework is lightweight and seamlessly integrates with any existing GNN encoder. Extensive experiments on popular benchmark datasets show that incorporating prompt learning significantly improves (3\% - 15\%) the performance of state-of-the-art GNN models in crystal property prediction tasks. Furthermore, the learned soft prompts enable cross-property knowledge transfer, enhancing prediction performance for properties with limited training data. Code is available at https://github.com/shrimonmuke0202/Prompt.git

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a lightweight, multilevel soft prompt learning framework for crystal property prediction that captures latent features (local chemical semantics at the node level and global structural symmetry at the graph level) not explicitly encoded in GNNs, yielding 3–15% performance improvements and enabling cross-property knowledge transfer.
AI.motivation: Existing GNNs for crystal property prediction rely heavily on domain-specific feature engineering, increasing parameter size and requiring expert knowledge. Explicitly encoding all relevant chemical and structural features into the GNN encoder is inherently challenging, motivating a prompt-based approach to capture latent predictive features without modifying the base GNN architecture.
AI.method: The authors propose a multilevel graph prompt learning framework with two types of soft prompts: (1) node-level prompts that capture local chemical semantics of different atom types, and (2) graph-level prompts that encode global structural symmetry of the crystal graph. The framework is designed to be lightweight and plug-and-play, integrating seamlessly with any existing GNN encoder without architectural modification. Soft prompts are learned during training to supplement the explicit features already provided to the GNN.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on popular crystal property benchmark datasets demonstrate that incorporating the proposed prompt learning framework improves state-of-the-art GNN model performance by 3% to 15% across crystal property prediction tasks. Additionally, the learned soft prompts facilitate cross-property knowledge transfer, boosting prediction accuracy for properties with limited training data.
AI.conclusion: Soft prompt learning is an effective and efficient paradigm for crystal property prediction, capturing complementary latent features that explicit GNN encoders may miss. The multilevel design (node + graph) proves synergistic, and the approach enables valuable transfer learning across different crystal properties, particularly benefiting data-scarce scenarios.

title: Correlation-Aware Contextual Bandits with Surrogate Rewards for LLM Routing
summary: We study contextual bandit problems with correlated arms and access to surrogate reward signals produced by a machine learning model, motivated by applications such as large language model (LLM) routing. Unlike classical contextual bandits that rely solely on bandit feedback and assume conditional independence across arms, our setting allows context-dependent inter-arm correlations and auxiliary reward information that may be noisy or misspecified. We propose algorithms that leverage such surrogate rewards through two complementary designs. A coupled reward-mixing approach pools true and surrogate rewards to accelerate learning when surrogate signals are reliable, while a decoupled prediction-mixing approach maintains separate estimators for bandit feedback and surrogate rewards and adaptively combines their predictions. This decoupling yields robustness to surrogate misspecification, recovering regret guarantees comparable to reward-only bandit methods in the worst case, while achieving improved regret when surrogate predictions are sufficiently informative. We provide theoretical regret analyses for both approaches and evaluate them on LLM routing benchmarks under varying accuracy versus cost trade-offs. The results demonstrate improved sample efficiency and consistently better accuracy-cost trade-offs compared to standard contextual bandit baselines and strong static routing methods.

AI.tldr: This paper studies contextual bandits with inter-arm correlations and auxiliary surrogate rewards (e.g., from ML models). It proposes two algorithms: (1) a coupled reward-mixing approach that pools true and surrogate rewards for fast learning when surrogates are reliable, and (2) a decoupled prediction-mixing approach that maintains separate estimators and adaptively combines them, ensuring robustness to surrogate misspecification. Theoretical regret bounds are provided, and experiments on LLM routing benchmarks show superior accuracy-cost trade-offs over standard baselines.
AI.motivation: Real-world applications like LLM routing require selecting among correlated models under cost constraints, where surrogate reward signals (e.g., from a cheaper model or heuristic) are available but potentially noisy or misspecified. Classical contextual bandits assume conditional independence across arms and only bandit feedback, which fails to exploit these auxiliary signals and inter-arm correlations.
AI.method: Two complementary algorithmic designs are proposed. The coupled reward-mixing approach directly pools true bandit feedback with surrogate rewards into a combined reward signal to accelerate learning. The decoupled prediction-mixing approach maintains separate reward estimators for bandit and surrogate signals, then adaptively combines their predictions — yielding robustness when surrogates are misspecified while still benefiting from informative surrogates. Both approaches are analyzed theoretically for regret guarantees.
AI.result: Theoretical regret bounds show that the coupled approach excels with reliable surrogates, while the decoupled approach matches standard bandit regret in worst-case misspecification and improves regret with informative surrogates. Experiments on LLM routing benchmarks demonstrate improved sample efficiency and consistently better accuracy-cost trade-offs compared to standard contextual bandit baselines and strong static routing methods.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging inter-arm correlations and surrogate reward signals — even noisy ones — can significantly improve contextual bandit learning in applications like LLM routing. The decoupled prediction-mixing design offers a practical, robust solution that gracefully degrades under misspecification while accelerating learning under favorable conditions.

title: Variable-Length Generative Protein Design via Generalized Poisson Flow
summary: The ability to generate variable-length proteins is crucial in protein design, where the optimal length is often unknown and tightly coupled to designability. Current diffusion- and flow-based generative models typically require the protein length to be specified before sampling, limiting their flexibility in exploring the feasible design space. To address this limitation, we introduce Generalized Poisson Flow (GPFlow), a variable-length generative framework that learns the rate function of an inhomogeneous generalized Poisson process by minimizing its negative log-likelihood. We establish population-level guarantees for recovering the joint multimodal distribution and derive an upper bound on the KL divergence between the data and generated distributions. We comprehensively evaluate GPFlow across structure and sequence design, motif scaffolding, and peptide co-design, spanning Euclidean, categorical, and Riemannian modalities to fully validate its variable-length generation quality. In unconditional design, GPFlow improves structural designability and achieves the best distributional fitness for sequence design compared to their corresponding fixed-length baselines, while perfectly recovering the length distribution. In conditional motif scaffolding, GPFlow ranks first on 10 of 16 structure-based design tasks with significantly more unique successes and also achieves more passed tasks in sequence-based design. In peptide co-design, GPFlow remains competitive even without access to a native-length oracle.

AI.tldr: GPFlow is a variable-length generative framework for protein design that models an inhomogeneous generalized Poisson process, enabling sampling without pre-specifying protein length. It achieves strong performance across structure/sequence design, motif scaffolding, and peptide co-design, often outperforming fixed-length baselines while recovering native length distributions.
AI.motivation: Current diffusion- and flow-based protein generative models require the protein length to be specified before sampling, which is limiting because optimal length is often unknown a priori and tightly coupled to designability. A flexible framework capable of generating variable-length proteins is needed to fully explore the feasible design space.
AI.method: GPFlow learns the rate function of an inhomogeneous generalized Poisson process by minimizing its negative log-likelihood. The framework provides population-level guarantees for recovering the joint multimodal distribution and derives an upper bound on the KL divergence between data and generated distributions. It spans Euclidean, categorical, and Riemannian modalities.
AI.result: In unconditional design, GPFlow improves structural designability and achieves best distributional fitness for sequence design over fixed-length baselines while perfectly recovering length distribution. In motif scaffolding, it ranks first on 10/16 structure-based tasks with more unique successes and more passed tasks in sequence-based design. In peptide co-design, GPFlow remains competitive even without a native-length oracle.
AI.conclusion: GPFlow successfully enables variable-length protein generation with theoretical guarantees, demonstrating superior or competitive performance across diverse protein design tasks. Its ability to model length as an integral part of the generative process removes a key limitation of prior fixed-length approaches.

title: Learning More from Less: Reinforcement Learning from Hindsight
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) is increasingly used to post-train vision-language-action (VLA) models, but every update consumes robot rollouts that are slow and costly to collect, making sample efficiency a central concern. Manipulation tasks typically provide only sparse rewards, so a weak policy fails almost every rollout early in training and has little to learn from, even when those failures execute coherent behavior. Such a failure, however, is a success at a different task. We present Learning from Hindsight (LfH), which brings hindsight relabeling to RL post-training of VLAs by scoring failed rollouts against the tasks they actually achieved. A single vision-language model relabels both the instruction and the reward, proposing a hindsight instruction for a group of failed rollouts and scoring how well each satisfies it, and the policy trains on the relabeled and original rollouts jointly. Because VLAs generalize across language, relabeling in language lets the policy learn more from the same trajectories. On out-of-distribution LIBERO-PRO tasks, where standard RL improves only slowly, LfH achieves $5\times$ improvement in sample efficiency, and outperforms a dense progress-reward baseline. The gains hold across VLA backbones and on a physical Franka robot.

AI.tldr: LfH applies hindsight relabeling to RL post-training of VLA models: a VLM relabels failed rollouts with the tasks they actually achieved, enabling joint training on original and relabeled data. This yields 5× sample efficiency gains on LIBERO-PRO tasks and outperforms dense reward baselines, across VLA backbones and on real robots.
AI.motivation: RL post-training of VLA models suffers from severe sample inefficiency because manipulation tasks provide only sparse rewards. Early in training, weak policies fail on nearly every rollout and learn little, despite often executing coherent behavior that constitutes success at a different, unlabeled task. Collecting robot rollouts is slow and costly, making this a critical bottleneck.
AI.method: Learning from Hindsight (LfH) uses a single vision-language model to perform dual relabeling on failed rollouts: (1) it proposes a hindsight instruction describing what the robot actually accomplished, and (2) it scores each failed rollout against that relabeled instruction. The policy then trains jointly on both original (sparse-reward) and relabeled rollouts. Because VLAs generalize across language, language-space relabeling enables more learning from the same trajectories.
AI.result: On out-of-distribution LIBERO-PRO tasks, LfH achieves 5× improvement in sample efficiency over standard RL and outperforms a dense progress-reward baseline. Gains hold across multiple VLA backbones and on a physical Franka robot.
AI.conclusion: Hindsight relabeling in language space is an effective, general strategy for improving sample efficiency in RL post-training of VLAs, turning previously wasted failed rollouts into valuable training signal.

title: COBS: Cumulant Order Block Sparse Attention
summary: Block sparse attention is a hardware friendly way to alleviate the key-value (KV) cache read bottleneck in large language models (LLMs). However, it is not prevalent among leading open-weight LLMs, which rely instead on dense attention or fine-grained selection, thereby motivating our analysis. We study DeepSeek's Native Sparse Attention (NSA) as a representative method, whose three-branch design lets us isolate block selection, the most challenging and consequential stage. We formalize selection and reduce it to ranking blocks by a single quantity, the attention mass: the sum of a block's attention scores. We show that if selection retrieves the blocks with the largest attention mass, block sparse attention can match the quality of dense attention. However, computing the exact attention mass requires reading every key, so the problem of block selection ultimately reduces to approximating this mass from a compact summary instead of the full keys. Via a cumulant expansion, we show why existing methods falter: their selection strategies attempt to estimate the attention mass, but are confined to a first-order approximation. Therefore, we propose COBS (Cumulant Order Block Sparse Attention), an attention method that builds on NSA, incorporating a novel selector that stores a compressed second-order statistic per block. On the 32k RULER long-context retrieval benchmark, COBS raises the NSA baseline's mean score from 0.2999 to 0.8195, approaching dense attention at 0.9040 and closing about 86% of the gap, while using only 1.21x the KV cache read traffic of the NSA baseline and 15.15x less read traffic than dense. The same model preserves short-context behavior and attains lower position-wise negative log-likelihood (NLL) than dense attention in our comparison.

AI.tldr: COBS improves block sparse attention by using a second-order cumulant expansion to better approximate attention mass per block, closing ~86% of the quality gap to dense attention on long-context retrieval while maintaining near-sparse read efficiency.
AI.motivation: Block sparse attention is hardware-efficient for reducing KV cache read bottlenecks in LLMs, but leading open-weight models still prefer dense or fine-grained attention. Existing sparse methods fail because their block selection strategies rely on first-order approximations of attention mass, motivating a more accurate, compact summary statistic.
AI.method: The authors formalize block selection as ranking by attention mass (sum of attention scores per block) and analyze NSA's three-branch design. Using a cumulant expansion, they show existing selectors are limited to first-order approximation. COBS extends NSA with a selector that stores a compressed second-order statistic (quadratic form) per block, enabling better attention mass estimation without reading full keys.
AI.result: On the 32k RULER benchmark, COBS improves the NSA baseline mean score from 0.2999 to 0.8195 (dense: 0.9040), closing ~86% of the gap. It uses only 1.21x the KV cache read traffic of NSA and 15.15x less than dense attention. It also preserves short-context performance and achieves lower position-wise NLL than dense attention.
AI.conclusion: Second-order cumulant-based block selection substantially bridges the quality gap between sparse and dense attention while retaining the efficiency benefits of block-sparse methods. COBS demonstrates that compact higher-order statistics are a viable path toward practical sparse attention for long-context LLMs.

title: EvoLP: Self-Evolving Latency Predictor for Model Compression in Real-Time Edge Systems
comment: Author's accepted version. Published in IEEE Embedded Systems Letters
summary: Edge devices are increasingly utilized for deploying deep learning applications on embedded systems. The real-time nature of many applications and the limited resources of edge devices necessitate latency-targeted neural network compression. However, measuring latency on real devices is challenging and expensive. Therefore, this letter presents a novel and efficient framework, named EvoLP, to accurately predict the inference latency of models on edge devices. This predictor can evolve to achieve higher latency prediction precision during the network compression process. Experimental results demonstrate that EvoLP outperforms previous state-of-the-art approaches by being evaluated on three edge devices and four model variants. Moreover, when incorporated into a model compression framework, it effectively guides the compression process for higher model accuracy while satisfying strict latency constraints. We open source EvoLP at https://github.com/ntuliuteam/EvoLP.

AI.tldr: EvoLP is a novel framework that accurately predicts inference latency of deep learning models on edge devices and evolves during network compression to improve prediction precision, outperforming prior SOTA across three edge devices and four model variants.
AI.motivation: Edge devices are widely used for deep learning inference but have strict real-time requirements and limited resources. Latency-targeted compression is essential, yet measuring actual latency on real devices is difficult and costly. A reliable, evolving latency predictor is needed to guide compression without expensive on-device measurements.
AI.method: EvoLP is an efficient latency prediction framework that evolves during the network compression process to achieve progressively higher prediction accuracy. It learns to map model architectures to inference latency on target edge devices, with an evolving mechanism that refines predictions as compression alters the model structure.
AI.result: EvoLP outperforms prior state-of-the-art latency predictors when evaluated on three different edge devices and four model variants. When integrated into a model compression framework, it effectively guides compression to achieve higher model accuracy while satisfying strict latency constraints.
AI.conclusion: EvoLP provides an accurate, evolving latency predictor that significantly improves latency-guided model compression for edge deployment, with the code publicly released to facilitate further research.

title: Super-Tuning: From Activation-Aware Pruning to Sparse Fine-Tuning
summary: Large language models (LLMs) remain expensive to fine-tune because full-parameter updates require substantial memory, compute, and per-task storage. We study whether saliency signals originally developed for pruning can be reused to choose where a model should adapt. We propose Super, a sparse parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) method that fixes a small trainable support using a Wanda-style activation-weighted magnitude score [Sun et al., 2023] computed from a calibration pass. We then introduce Supra, a hybrid adapter that combines this sparse update with LoRA while preserving a matched trainable-parameter budget through a simple budget-splitting rule. In single-seed Math17K arithmetic experiments on Llama-3.2-1B and Meta-Llama-3-8B, the best Super/Supra variants achieve the highest average accuracy among the tested schedule-selected adapter configurations. We also include a PaFi-style magnitude-only support as a closest training-free sparse baseline and find that low-score supports under both magnitude and Wanda-style orderings can be effective. These results suggest that simple pruning-inspired orderings can provide useful fixed sparse supports for PEFT, especially when combined with low-rank adapters.

AI.tldr: Super/Supra repurposes pruning-inspired saliency scores (Wanda-style activation-weighted magnitude) to select fixed sparse trainable parameters for parameter-efficient fine-tuning, and Supra combines this with LoRA under a matched budget. On Llama models with Math17K arithmetic tasks, these methods achieve top average accuracy among schedule-selected adapters, showing that pruning orderings can effectively guide sparse PEFT.
AI.motivation: Full-parameter fine-tuning of LLMs is prohibitively expensive in memory, compute, and per-task storage. While PEFT methods like LoRA exist, the authors investigate whether saliency signals originally designed for model pruning can be repurposed to intelligently select which parameters to fine-tune, potentially offering a simpler and more effective sparse adaptation strategy.
AI.method: The authors propose two methods: (1) **Super** — a sparse PEFT method that uses a Wanda-style activation-weighted magnitude score (computed via a single calibration pass) to fix a small subset of trainable parameters, freezing all others. (2) **Supra** — a hybrid adapter that combines Super's sparse update with LoRA, using a budget-splitting rule to maintain a matched total trainable-parameter count between the sparse and low-rank components. A PaFi-style magnitude-only support is included as a training-free sparse baseline for comparison.
AI.result: On single-seed Math17K arithmetic experiments with Llama-3.2-1B and Meta-Llama-3-8B, the best Super and Supra variants achieve the highest average accuracy among all tested schedule-selected adapter configurations. Notably, even low-score supports under both magnitude-based and Wanda-style orderings prove effective, and the PaFi-style magnitude-only baseline performs competitively.
AI.conclusion: Simple, pruning-inspired parameter importance orderings can provide useful fixed sparse supports for PEFT. The combination of sparse updates with low-rank adaptation (Supra) is particularly effective, suggesting that hybrid approaches leveraging pruning saliency signals are a promising direction for efficient LLM adaptation.

title: Pitfalls and Remedies for Multi-Task Bayesian Optimization
summary: Bayesian optimization routinely warm-starts a target experiment with data from related source tasks, and the multi-task Gaussian process is the textbook surrogate for the job. We revisit this default in a controlled setting and find that it misestimates the cross-task correlation even in the simplest non-trivial case, affinely related source and target tasks, where a working transfer learning method should obviously succeed. We trace the failure to two independent structural mechanisms. Per-task standardization, the textbook fix for the affine slice ambiguity, propagates a finite-sample alignment error into the recovered correlation. The marginal likelihood itself identifies the correlation only at a per-sample rate that a Gaussian process at non-overlapping designs further dilutes. We propose three conservative remedies that follow from the analysis: promoting per-task means and scales to model parameters, restricting the task covariance to non-negative correlations, and co-locating part of the source and target designs. Across synthetic multi-task problems and surrogate-based hyperparameter tuning transfer, these remedies recover the target-only baseline on the simple instances, while the broader failure persists on harder instances and across most rank-based and latent-context variants.

AI.tldr: Bayesian optimization with multi-task Gaussian processes fails to recover cross-task correlation even in simple affine source–target settings due to per-task standardization errors and slow statistical identification rates; three conservative fixes are proposed.
AI.motivation: Warm-starting Bayesian optimization with data from related source tasks is standard practice, with the multi-task Gaussian process (MTGP) as the default surrogate. However, the authors observe that MTGP fails to correctly estimate cross-task correlation even in the simplest non-trivial case — affinely related tasks — where transfer learning should trivially succeed. This motivates a rigorous diagnosis of why the default fails.
AI.method: The authors conduct a controlled theoretical-empirical analysis of MTGP failure modes. They identify two structural mechanisms: (1) per-task input/output standardization, the standard fix for affine slice ambiguity, propagates finite-sample alignment error into the recovered cross-task correlation; (2) the marginal likelihood identifies the correlation parameter at a slow, per-sample rate, further diluted when source and target designs are non-overlapping. Three conservative remedies are proposed: (a) promoting per-task means and scales to explicit model parameters rather than pre-processing steps, (b) restricting the task covariance matrix to non-negative correlations, and (c) co-locating a portion of source and target design points. Evaluation spans synthetic multi-task problems and surrogate-based hyperparameter tuning transfer.
AI.result: The three remedies successfully recover target-only baseline performance on simple affine instances where the vanilla MTGP fails. However, on harder transfer problems and across most rank-based and latent-context MTGP variants, the broader failure persists, indicating a more fundamental limitation of current multi-task surrogate formulations for warm-starting Bayesian optimization.
AI.conclusion: The default MTGP warm-starting procedure in Bayesian optimization is flawed due to identifiable structural issues in correlation estimation. The proposed conservative fixes help in simple settings but do not fully resolve the problem in complex scenarios, suggesting that more fundamental advances in multi-task surrogate modeling are needed for reliable transfer in Bayesian optimization.

title: Mach-Mind-4-Flash Technical Report
summary: We present Mach-Mind-4-Flash, a 35B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) agentic model with 3B activated parameters. Through post-training optimization alone without scaling pre-training compute, the model achieves performance on par with or surpassing that of 100B-parameter-class models. By introducing scalable agentic interaction environments for large-scale reinforcement learning, the model attains significant performance gains on real-world application tasks. Our pipeline comprises three stages: (1) a unified RL/OPD training infrastructure with dynamic multi-teacher scheduling and operator-level acceleration, delivering 17\% end-to-end training speedup; (2) multiple domain-specific RL experts trained in parallel across Reasoning, General, and Agent tracks, then fused into a single generalist via Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD) -- a routed reverse-KL objective that eliminates the see-saw degradation of mixed-reward RL; (3) Hybrid Median-length Policy Optimization (HMPO), a single-stage token-efficiency method that compresses reasoning chains by 19--46\% with $\le$0.7 percentage-point accuracy loss. Mach-Mind-4-Flash scores 92.70 on AIME'26, 82.82 on IFBench, 80.74 on Behavioral-SafetyBench, 75.80 on BFCL-v4, 72.31 on BrowseComp-zh, and 84.20 on ClawBench -- leading or matching models with 10--30$\times$ its activated size at a fraction of the inference cost.

AI.tldr: Mach-Mind-4-Flash is a 35B MoE model (3B activated) that, through post-training RL optimization alone, matches or exceeds 100B-class models. Key innovations include Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD) to fuse domain-specific RL experts without degradation, and Hybrid Median-length Policy Optimization (HMPO) for compressing reasoning chains by 19–46% with minimal accuracy loss.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that post-training optimization (RL) alone, without scaling pre-training compute, can elevate a relatively small MoE model (35B total / 3B activated) to performance levels competitive with models 10–30× its activated parameter count. The work also aims to solve two practical RL challenges: the "see-saw degradation" from mixed-reward RL training and the token-inefficiency of long reasoning chains.
AI.method: Three-stage pipeline: (1) Unified RL/OPD training infrastructure with dynamic multi-teacher scheduling and operator-level acceleration yielding 17% speedup. (2) Parallel training of domain-specific RL experts across Reasoning, General, and Agent tracks, fused via Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD) — a routed reverse-KL objective that prevents the see-saw degradation typical of mixed-reward RL. (3) Hybrid Median-length Policy Optimization (HMPO), a single-stage token-efficiency method compressing reasoning chains by 19–46% with ≤0.7pp accuracy loss.
AI.result: Mach-Mind-4-Flash achieves: AIME'26: 92.70, IFBench: 82.82, Behavioral-SafetyBench: 80.74, BFCL-v4: 75.80, BrowseComp-zh: 72.31, ClawBench: 84.20 — leading or matching models with 10–30× its activated parameters at a fraction of the inference cost.
AI.conclusion: Post-training RL optimization with MOPD and HMPO enables a 35B/3B-activated MoE model to rival or surpass much larger models. The MOPD fusion strategy successfully mitigates mixed-reward interference, and HMPO provides substantial token reduction without meaningful accuracy degradation, making the approach both performant and cost-efficient.

title: A Survey on the Green Development of Large Models: From Resource-Efficient Architectures to Hardware-Software Co-Design
comment: This paper has been accepted by CJE (2026), paper homepage: https://cje.ejournal.org.cn/article/doi/10.23919/cje.2025.00.438
summary: The rapid expansion of large-scale AI models has led to significant performance breakthroughs across diverse domains, yet it has also raised critical concerns regarding computational costs, energy consumption, and environmental sustainability. This survey provides a comprehensive overview of the green development of large models, emphasizing resource-efficient architectures and full-stack hardware-software co-design. We systematically review recent advances in efficient model construction, including attention operator optimization, linear-complexity architectures, and model sparsification and merging, as well as training and deployment strategies such as data-efficient learning, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, and computational compression. Beyond algorithmic improvements, we explore energy-efficient AI hardware, including mainstream AI chips, memory optimization, cross-platform deployment, and sustainable infrastructure. Furthermore, we examine how large models are being applied to sustainability-critical domains such as DeepSeek, remote sensing interpretation, national-scale infrastructure, and global initiatives. Finally, we discuss key challenges and future directions, highlighting the need for continual learning paradigms, memory-centric hardware, and standardized evaluation protocols. This survey aims to offer a holistic roadmap toward sustainable, scalable, and socially responsible development of large models. Paper homepage: https://cje.ejournal.org.cn/article/doi/10.23919/cje.2025.00.438

AI.tldr: A comprehensive survey on making large-scale AI models more resource-efficient and environmentally sustainable through algorithmic innovations, hardware-software co-design, and applications in sustainability-critical domains.
AI.motivation: The rapid scaling of large AI models has yielded breakthrough performance but at the cost of enormous computational demands, energy consumption, and environmental impact, creating an urgent need for "green" development strategies.
AI.method: The survey systematically reviews three broad categories: (1) efficient model construction techniques including attention operator optimization, linear-complexity architectures, model sparsification, and model merging; (2) training and deployment strategies such as data-efficient learning, parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), and computational compression; and (3) energy-efficient AI hardware covering mainstream AI chips, memory optimization, cross-platform deployment, and sustainable infrastructure. It also examines real-world applications and discusses future directions.
AI.result: The paper provides a holistic taxonomy of green AI techniques spanning the full stack — from algorithms to hardware — and highlights application cases in domains like DeepSeek, remote sensing interpretation, and national-scale infrastructure. Key challenges identified include the need for continual learning paradigms, memory-centric hardware, and standardized evaluation protocols for sustainable AI.
AI.conclusion: Achieving sustainable, scalable, and socially responsible large models requires a full-stack, hardware-software co-design approach. The survey calls for continued innovation in continual learning, memory-centric architectures, and standardized green AI benchmarks to guide future development.

title: Neural Collapse Is Forbidden: Information Floors in Language Models
summary: Within-class variance in language-model representations is commonly read as incomplete neural collapse. We argue it is allocated information storage, and that the allocation obeys a law. A one-line centering identity voids a family of simplex equiangular-tight-frame claims, including our own earlier ones; in dimensionless variance shares across 14 models, macro-category structure carries only 4-12% of representational variance and within-token context carries 79-91%, stable across a 100x parameter range. On the theory side, token-level weight decay penalizes a category in proportion to its type count, not its occurrence mass, reducing next-token prediction to an imbalanced K-class problem whose optimum orders category norms by type count. A converse floor, proved for binary categories, forces within-category dispersion to be at least proportional to the conditional mutual information I(token; context | category). The law holds: identity dispersion, not total variance, tracks this information across every tested model and partition, under a model-free estimate and even across models, where one model's information predicts another's dispersion; and over pretraining the category share overshoots, decays, and partially recovers, because the information it must carry never left.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that within-class variance in language model representations is not "incomplete neural collapse" but rather allocated information storage governed by a law. A centering identity disproves simplex ETF claims, shows category structure carries only 4-12% of variance while within-token context carries 79-91%, and proves a theoretical floor linking within-category dispersion to conditional mutual information I(token; context | category), which holds empirically across models and training.
AI.motivation: Prior work interprets within-class variance in language model representations as incomplete neural collapse toward simplex equiangular tight frames (ETF). The authors challenge this view, proposing instead that this variance constitutes allocated information storage obeying a principled relationship between dispersion and information-theoretic quantities.
AI.method: A one-line centering identity is used to decompose representational variance and void simplex ETF claims. Variance shares are measured across 14 models spanning a 100x parameter range. Theoretically, token-level weight decay is analyzed to show it reduces next-token prediction to an imbalanced K-class problem where category norms are ordered by type count. A converse bound is proved for binary categories, establishing that within-category dispersion is lower-bounded proportionally to I(token; context | category). The relationship is tested using model-free estimates of conditional mutual information.
AI.result: Macro-category structure accounts for only 4-12% of representational variance, while within-token context accounts for 79-91%, stable across the 100x parameter range. Identity dispersion, not total variance, tracks I(token; context | category) across every tested model and partition. One model's information predicts another's dispersion. Over pretraining, category variance share overshoots, decays, and partially recovers, consistent with the information it must carry.
AI.conclusion: Within-class variance in language model representations is functionally allocated information storage rather than a deficiency in neural collapse. The proposed law—linking dispersion to conditional mutual information—holds robustly across models, partitions, and training dynamics, reframing how representational structure in language models should be understood.

title: EXHOLD: Experience-Aware Real-Time Hold Control for Large-Scale Ride-Hailing Matching at DiDi
summary:
In large-scale ride-hailing, hold control is a critical mechanism for improving passenger-driver experience. By selectively delaying certain driver-order pairs, the system waits for better opportunities, reduces cancellations, and mitigates wasted driver effort. However, existing industrial hold strategies often rely on heuristic thresholding over multiple predictive models, which can be brittle under non-stationary traffic and hard to optimize for multi-objective experience signals.
  We propose EXHOLD, a deployable two-stage framework decoupling experience-aware pair assessment from hold-time execution. In Stage I, we learn a decision model assigning each driver-order pair to discrete, interpretable experience tiers by optimizing a unified objective that aggregates satisfaction signals across the matching funnel. In Stage II, we solve for a monotone hold-time schedule via constrained optimization over empirical quantiles. This explicitly enforces service guardrails bounding the unnecessary holding of promising matches while maximizing overall experience improvement.
  We evaluate EXHOLD through randomized A/B experiments in DiDi's production system in Brazil. Results show consistent gains in marketplace efficiency and experience: EXHOLD increases trip completion and driver income, significantly reduces passenger cancellations, and improves funnel efficiency. Ablations and behavioral analyses confirm both stages are essential and that the policy makes calibrated decisions under spatiotemporal heterogeneity. EXHOLD is currently deployed, serving production traffic in Brazil.

AI.tldr: EXHOLD is a two-stage framework for ride-hailing hold control that decouples experience-aware pair assessment from hold-time execution. Stage I assigns driver-order pairs to interpretable experience tiers via a unified optimization objective. Stage II computes a monotone hold-time schedule using constrained optimization over empirical quantiles. Deployed and A/B tested in DiDi's Brazil production system, it improves trip completion, driver income, reduces passenger cancellations, and enhances funnel efficiency.
AI.motivation: Existing industrial hold strategies in large-scale ride-hailing rely on heuristic thresholding over multiple predictive models, which is brittle under non-stationary traffic and difficult to optimize for multi-objective experience signals. There is a need for a principled, deployable framework that jointly considers passenger and driver experience while respecting operational guardrails.
AI.method: EXHOLD is a two-stage framework. Stage I learns a decision model that assigns each driver-order pair to discrete, interpretable experience tiers by optimizing a unified objective aggregating satisfaction signals across the matching funnel. Stage II solves for a monotone hold-time schedule via constrained optimization over empirical quantiles, enforcing service guardrails that bound unnecessary holding of promising matches while maximizing overall experience improvement.
AI.result: Randomized A/B experiments in DiDi's production system in Brazil show: increased trip completion and driver income, significantly reduced passenger cancellations, and improved funnel efficiency. Ablation studies and behavioral analyses confirm both stages are essential, and the policy makes calibrated decisions under spatiotemporal heterogeneity.
AI.conclusion: EXHOLD provides a principled, deployable solution for ride-hailing hold control that moves beyond heuristic thresholding. Its two-stage design effectively balances multi-objective experience signals with operational constraints, demonstrating consistent production gains and is currently deployed serving live traffic in Brazil.

title: Quantum Circuits in Diffusion Models: A Fair-Comparison Study and a Mechanistic Analysis of Angle-Embedding Failures
summary: We study the integration of variational quantum circuits (VQCs) into diffusion models through a squeeze-and-excitation (SE) channel-modulation scaffold that isolates the quantum contribution. Using a role-matched classical control and multi-seed significance testing across DDPM and latent diffusion on MNIST and CIFAR-10, with a score-based NCSN study on MNIST, we find that quantum cores achieve comparable mean FID to the classical control across DDPM and latent diffusion, while paired sampling-seed tests for EfficientSU2 detect no statistically significant difference. Although the quantum cores use $4.5$--$9\times$ fewer core parameters than the role-matched control, parameter-matched classical controls attain comparable mean FID, so the experiments do not establish a quantum parameter-efficiency advantage. We further identify a structural failure in score-based NCSN: the unbounded score target, proportional to $1/σ$, drives angle-embedding inputs far beyond the $2π$ period of rotation gates, causing phase aliasing and collapse of the quantum modulator. A bounding transformation, $θ\leftarrow π\tanh(\cdot)$, maps inputs to the non-aliasing domain and substantially improves both quantum cores. Since all circuits are classically simulated at a few-qubit scale, we do not claim quantum advantage. Instead, the study provides a fair-comparison protocol for quantum-enhanced generative models and a mechanistic account of when and why angle embeddings fail.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates integrating variational quantum circuits into diffusion models via an SE channel-modulation framework. Using rigorous classical controls and statistical testing, it finds no significant FID improvement or parameter-efficiency advantage for quantum cores. A critical failure mode in score-based models due to phase aliasing from unbounded inputs is identified and mitigated with a bounding transformation.
AI.motivation: To rigorously evaluate whether variational quantum circuits provide any generative performance advantage when integrated into classical diffusion models, using fair comparison protocols that isolate the quantum contribution and account for parameter counts and statistical significance.
AI.method: A squeeze-and-excitation (SE) channel-modulation scaffold integrates VQCs into DDPM, latent diffusion, and score-based (NCSN) generative models. The quantum contribution is isolated by role-matching with a classical MLP control. Multi-seed FID evaluation and paired sampling-seed significance testing are performed on MNIST and CIFAR-10. Parameter-matched classical controls are also tested. A bounding transformation (θ ← π tanh(·)) is introduced to prevent phase aliasing in angle embeddings for NCSN.
AI.result: Quantum cores achieve comparable mean FID to classical controls in DDPM and latent diffusion; paired-seed tests (EfficientSU2) show no statistically significant difference. Quantum cores use 4.5–9× fewer parameters, but parameter-matched classical controls match performance, negating a quantum parameter-efficiency claim. In NCSN, unbounded score targets cause phase aliasing and modulator collapse; the proposed bounding transformation substantially improves both quantum cores.
AI.conclusion: No quantum advantage is demonstrated at few-qubit scale. The study provides a robust fair-comparison protocol for quantum-enhanced generative models and identifies a fundamental failure mechanism of angle embeddings in score-based diffusion models, with an effective mitigation strategy.

title: Power Flow Feasibility Assessment Using Variational Graph Autoencoders
summary: Data-driven methods, including graph neural networks, have been studied for accelerating power flow calculations in recent years, but very little attention has been paid to the solution feasibility, which can be obtained by traditional solvers. This paper presents a Variational Graph Autoencoder (VGAE) that detects the power flow solution feasibility, using the IEEE 118-bus case, to assess the validity of the solutions provided by AI-driven solvers.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a Variational Graph Autoencoder (VGAE) to detect power flow solution feasibility, addressing a gap in AI-driven solvers where feasibility verification is typically neglected. The model is evaluated on the IEEE 118-bus system.
AI.motivation: Data-driven methods, particularly graph neural networks, have been increasingly applied to accelerate power flow calculations. However, these AI-driven solvers lack the inherent feasibility-checking capability of traditional numerical solvers. No prior work has adequately addressed how to verify whether solutions produced by AI-driven power flow solvers are actually valid/feasible.
AI.method: The authors employ a Variational Graph Autoencoder (VGAE) — a generative graph neural network architecture — to perform binary classification of power flow solution feasibility. The VGAE learns a latent representation of the power grid (IEEE 118-bus case) and reconstructs or predicts whether a given operating point yields a feasible power flow solution.
AI.result: The VGAE-based approach successfully detects power flow solution feasibility on the IEEE 118-bus test case, providing a mechanism to validate solutions generated by AI-driven solvers.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating feasibility detection via VGAE is essential for making AI-driven power flow solvers practically reliable, bridging a critical gap between data-driven acceleration and the feasibility guarantees traditionally offered by conventional solvers.

title: Present but Rescaled: Chat-to-Agent Transfer of Additive Activation Steering
summary: Additive activation steering (injecting a scaled residual-stream direction during generation) is calibrated almost entirely in single-turn chat, yet the models it targets are increasingly deployed as tool-using ReAct agents. We present the first systematic chat-to-agent transfer study of additive steering, coupling behavioral measurement with a representation read-out in a matched-information design: the same items rendered as plain chat or as a ReAct tool-use episode, with matched-norm random-direction controls and the transcript re-encoded every turn to exclude KV-cache contamination. Transfer is real but rescaled, and the right description is a dissociation: the injected direction reaches the late layers at near-full strength in every setting and model tested (install-site agent-over-chat ratios 0.83-1.16 across three families), while the behavioral coupling is reset per model and context. On Qwen2.5-7B a refusal bypass vector amplifies in the agent (T = 1.45, CI [1.20, 1.78], N = 300); across a powered uniform-protocol distribution the coupling spans amplification (Gemma-2-9B T = 2.00) to attenuation (Yi-1.5-9B T = 0.43, CI [0.29, 0.60]), with no universal constant and a single clean attenuator against a universal sign. Directional ablation of the same axis does not amplify (T = 0.93, CI including 1) while additive injection amplifies (T = 1.50), a 20.1-point gain difference (CI [13.4, 26.8]) that identifies an additive-specific mechanism. Two pre-registered instruments converge to localize the rescaling to the ReAct format scaffold, before any tool observation, rather than to the observation boundary where a dilution account would predict it. The safety implication is immediate and unpredictable: agentic deployment amplifies steering-based refusal bypass by up to 2.00x on some models while others attenuate, so a deployment cannot assume a given model is safe under additive steering.

AI.tldr: Additive activation steering vectors, calibrated in single-turn chat, transfer imperfectly to ReAct agent settings. While the injected direction reaches late layers at near-full strength across all tested models and contexts, the behavioral effect is rescaled unpredictably — some models show amplification (up to 2×), others attenuation — with rescaling localized to the ReAct format scaffold rather than tool observations. This poses an immediate safety concern for agentic deployments.
AI.motivation: Additive activation steering methods (e.g., refusal bypass vectors) are calibrated almost exclusively in single-turn chat, yet modern LLMs are increasingly deployed as tool-using ReAct agents. No prior work has systematically studied whether and how these steering vectors transfer from chat to agent contexts, creating a blind spot for both capability and safety evaluations.
AI.method: The authors conduct a systematic chat-to-agent transfer study using a matched-information design: identical items are presented either as plain chat or as a ReAct tool-use episode. Random-direction vectors with matched norms serve as controls, and transcripts are re-encoded every turn to prevent KV-cache contamination. The study couples behavioral measurement with a representation read-out to track whether injected directions reach late layers. Two pre-registered instruments localize the rescaling effect to either the ReAct format scaffold or the tool-observation boundary. The design spans three model families (Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Yi-1.5-9B) with a powered uniform-protocol distribution.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) Injected directions reach late layers at 83–116% of chat strength across all settings — the representation transfers nearly fully. (2) Behavioral coupling, however, is rescaled per model and context: Qwen2.5-7B shows amplification (T=1.45), Gemma-2-9B amplifies (T=2.00), while Yi-1.5-9B attenuates (T=0.43). No universal rescaling constant exists. (3) Directional ablation does not amplify (T=0.93, CI includes 1), while additive injection does (T=1.50), a 20.1-point gain difference identifying an additive-specific mechanism. (4) Rescaling is localized to the ReAct format scaffold, not the observation boundary. (5) Safety implication: agentic deployment can amplify steering-based refusal bypass by up to 2× on some models.
AI.conclusion: Chat-to-agent transfer of additive steering is real but rescaled, characterized by a dissociation between near-full representation transfer and unpredictable behavioral rescaling. Because some models amplify steering effects (including refusal bypass) in agent contexts while others attenuate, no deployment can assume a model is safe under additive steering without model-specific agentic evaluation. The rescaling originates in the ReAct format scaffold itself, meriting further mechanistic investigation.

title: A Personalized Computational Framework for Assessing the Sufficiency of Partially Observed Data in Healthcare AI models
summary: Achieving early and timely diagnosis and treatment for disease is a major challenge. Recent applications of machine learning (ML) algorithms trained on patient data have shown promise in many different settings for predicting the patient health state. A challenge often faced when applying these ML algorithms is that at any given time, not all clinical variables (features) needed as input to perform prediction tasks are available. We define the concept of full-feature-capacity (FFC) to refer to prediction performance when such algorithms make use of all features on which they were trained. We then introduce Feature Sufficiency Analysis (FSA) - an analysis for determining whether a subset of all clinical features needed by an AI model is sufficient to achieve FFC. FSA estimates the underlying distributions of missing variables conditioned on features that are available. FSA provides a patient-specific assessment of whether the existing set of measured features achieves FFC. If yes, then there is no need to acquire further inputs and a ML-based prediction. We provide two case studies: prediction of need for postoperative prolonged ventilation in patients recovering from heart surgery; 10-year mortality prediction in an outpatient cohort. We also demonstrate that FSA also provides a clinically interpretable feature-ranking methodology based on prediction sufficiency, identifies intrinsically hard-to-predict patient populations, and has the potential to perform cost-aware optimization for clinical data acquisition. FSA provides a generic computational approach for determining whether incomplete clinical information is sufficient to support trustworthy AI-assisted clinical decision-making, thereby facilitating the prospective deployment of healthcare AI systems across diverse clinical settings.

AI.tldr: FSA is a method to determine whether a subset of available clinical features is sufficient for an ML model to achieve performance equivalent to using all features (full-feature-capacity). It estimates missing variable distributions conditioned on available features, provides patient-specific assessments, and offers interpretable feature ranking, with applications demonstrated in postoperative ventilation prediction and 10-year mortality prediction.
AI.motivation: In real-world clinical settings, not all variables required by ML prediction models are available at decision time. This incompleteness undermines model reliability and hinders deployment. The authors aim to address the gap between trained-model feature requirements and real-world data availability by determining when a partial feature set is "good enough."
AI.method: The authors introduce Feature Sufficiency Analysis (FSA), which estimates the conditional distribution of missing features given observed features. FSA then evaluates whether the available feature subset achieves full-feature-capacity (FFC) — i.e., prediction performance indistinguishable from using all features. The method yields patient-specific sufficiency assessments, a sufficiency-based feature ranking, identification of hard-to-predict subgroups, and can incorporate cost-aware optimization for data acquisition.
AI.result: FSA was validated in two case studies: (1) predicting need for postoperative prolonged ventilation after heart surgery, and (2) 10-year mortality prediction in an outpatient cohort. Results demonstrate FSA's ability to assess per-patient feature sufficiency, rank features by their contribution to prediction sufficiency, and identify intrinsically difficult-to-predict patient populations.
AI.conclusion: FSA offers a generic, interpretable computational framework for assessing whether incomplete clinical data can still support trustworthy AI-assisted decisions. It facilitates prospective deployment of healthcare AI by reducing unnecessary data acquisition and enabling cost-efficient, context-aware clinical decision-making.

title: COAST: Context-Aware Differential Learning for Gene Expression Prediction in Spatial Transcriptomics
summary: Spatial transcriptomics enables profiling of spatial gene expression but is limited by high cost and low throughput, motivating prediction from H&E histopathology images. Existing context-aware methods mainly supervise absolute expression, while relative expression relationships between spots are rarely used explicitly. We propose COAST, a context-aware differential learning framework for spatial gene expression prediction. COAST conditions the local and global context features with type-specific modulation and aggregates the target and context spot tokens using a Transformer encoder to capture both fine-grained local patterns and slide-level structure. It is trained with a joint objective that combines absolute expression regression with signed differential regression between the target and context spots. Experiments on multiple spatial transcriptomics datasets show consistent improvements in correlation- and distribution-based metrics, demonstrating the effectiveness of context-aware differential learning for histology-based spatial gene expression prediction.

AI.tldr: COAST is a context-aware framework that predicts spatial gene expression from H&E images by combining absolute expression regression with signed differential regression between target and context spots, achieving consistent improvements across multiple datasets.
AI.motivation: Spatial transcriptomics is costly and low-throughput. Existing prediction methods from histopathology images only supervise absolute expression, ignoring the relative expression relationships between spatially adjacent spots, which provide valuable contextual information.
AI.method: COAST uses type-specific modulation to condition local and global context features, aggregates target and context spot tokens via a Transformer encoder to capture fine-grained local patterns and slide-level structure, and trains with a joint objective combining absolute expression regression and signed differential regression between target and context spots.
AI.result: Experiments on multiple spatial transcriptomics datasets demonstrate consistent improvements in both correlation-based and distribution-based metrics.
AI.conclusion: Context-aware differential learning, which explicitly models relative expression relationships between spots, is an effective strategy for improving histology-based spatial gene expression prediction.

title: Understanding Schedule-Free Methods in Nonconvex Optimization: Rate Guarantees and Escaping Saddles
summary: Schedule-Free methods have attracted growing interest for alleviating the burden of designing and tuning a learning rate scheduler, while matching and sometimes even outperforming optimizers with tuned schedulers. Despite their strong empirical results, their convergence theory in nonconvex optimization, where modern machine learning objectives typically arise, has remained largely unexplored. In this paper, we provide worst-case analyses of Schedule-Free gradient descent and Schedule-Free stochastic gradient descent, in their standard form and without auxiliary modifications or restrictive conditions, for smooth but possibly nonconvex objectives. Based on a Lyapunov analysis derived from the continuous-time limiting ordinary differential equation associated with these methods, we show that Schedule-Free gradient descent and Schedule-Free stochastic gradient descent achieve the optimal worst-case convergence rates attainable among first-order methods. We further formulate Schedule-Free gradient descent as a nonautonomous dynamical system and prove strict-saddle avoidance under an arbitrarily small one-time perturbation. These theoretical results provide a better understanding of the strong performance that Schedule-Free methods demonstrate.

AI.tldr: This paper provides the first rigorous worst-case convergence analysis for Schedule-Free gradient descent (SF-GD) and SF-SGD in smooth nonconvex optimization, proving they achieve optimal rates among first-order methods, and establishes strict-saddle avoidance under arbitrarily small perturbation.
AI.motivation: Schedule-Free methods have demonstrated impressive empirical performance, matching or exceeding tuned-scheduler optimizers while eliminating scheduler design burden. However, their convergence theory in nonconvex settings—where modern ML objectives lie—remained unexplored. The authors aim to fill this theoretical gap and explain the strong empirical results.
AI.method: The authors employ Lyapunov analysis derived from the continuous-time limiting ODE associated with SF methods to establish worst-case convergence rates. They also formulate SF-GD as a nonautonomous dynamical system and prove strict-saddle avoidance via an arbitrarily small one-time perturbation argument.
AI.result: SF-GD and SF-SGD achieve the optimal worst-case convergence rates attainable among first-order methods for smooth nonconvex objectives. Additionally, SF-GD provably avoids strict saddles under minimal perturbation, characterizing its escape behavior from undesirable stationary points.
AI.conclusion: The theoretical results offer a principled understanding of why Schedule-Free methods perform so strongly in practice, validating their design and providing convergence guarantees that match the best possible rates for first-order methods in nonconvex optimization.

title: Application of machine learning to monster level prediction in tabletop RPG game design
summary: Designing balanced adversaries is a central but labor-intensive task in tabletop role-playing game (TTRPG) development. In systems such as Pathfinder, each monster is described by many numerical attributes that jointly determine its power, summarized as an ordinal level. We investigate whether machine learning can support designers by predicting this level from a monster's attributes, framing the task as tabular ordinal regression. We introduce what is, to our knowledge, the first dataset built specifically for TTRPG monster-level prediction, derived from publicly available Pathfinder Second Edition data. Using it, we compare classical regression models with rounding schemes, dedicated tabular ordinal regression algorithms, and neural networks with ordinal-aware losses. To mirror real design workflows, we evaluate all models under chronological and expanding-window protocols with several complementary metrics. Results show that tree-based ensembles outperform linear models and neural approaches, achieving near-perfect ordinal ranking and high predictive accuracy. Explainable AI analyses, such as feature importance and error distributions, show that the model is aligned with human intuition and follows patterns grounded in game rules. Together, these results show that machine learning can reliably approximate designer judgments and serve as an effective computer-aided tool for monster balancing and broader TTRPG system design.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the first dataset for predicting monster levels in Pathfinder 2e using tabular ordinal regression. Tree-based ensembles outperform linear and neural models, achieving near-perfect ranking accuracy, with explainability analyses confirming alignment with human designer intuition.
AI.motivation: Designing balanced adversaries (monsters) in TTRPGs like Pathfinder is a central, labor-intensive task requiring designers to manually tune many numerical attributes to achieve a target power level. The authors investigate whether machine learning can automate monster-level prediction to serve as a computer-aided design tool, reducing designer workload.
AI.method: The authors construct a novel dataset from Pathfinder Second Edition public data. They frame the task as tabular ordinal regression and compare classical regression with rounding, dedicated ordinal regression algorithms (e.g., CORAL, CORN), and neural networks with ordinal-aware losses. Evaluation uses chronological and expanding-window protocols with complementary metrics, plus explainable AI analyses (feature importance, error distributions).
AI.result: Tree-based ensemble methods (e.g., gradient boosting, random forests) significantly outperform linear models and neural approaches, achieving near-perfect ordinal ranking and high predictive accuracy. Explainable AI reveals that the model's feature importance and error patterns align with human intuition and established game rules.
AI.conclusion: ML can reliably approximate designer judgments for monster balancing in TTRPGs. The approach serves as an effective computer-aided tool for monster design and has broader implications for TTRPG system development.

title: Interference and Retention in Continual Learning
summary:
Continual learning commonly relies on post-hoc mechanisms such as replay, elastic regularization, or distillation. This work argues that forgetting should instead be modeled directly as interference between tasks. In the frozen-feature regime, forgetting from learning a new task is exactly the interference energy induced on the old task. In deep networks, the same quantity is recovered through path-averaged curvature with minimal additional forward passes.
  When task supports are disjoint, forgetting can be eliminated structurally and when task supports overlap in conflicting directions, a non-zero distortion floor is unavoidable. The same geometry optimally merges models through task-aware orthogonalization. From this analysis we derive Interference-Gated Functional Allocation (IGFA), a replay-free, Fisher-free method that shares directions when tasks align and protects them when they conflict. Across benchmarks, IGFA achieves lossless retention when tasks are structurally separable and moves unavoidable cost from irreversible forgetting into deferred but recoverable plasticity when they are not. It matches the strongest replay-free structural baselines on dissimilar-task streams and improves on unconditional projection when similarity makes transfer worth preserving.

AI.tldr: The paper models forgetting in continual learning as task interference energy, derives geometric conditions for lossless retention, and proposes IGFA—a replay-free method that shares directions when tasks align and protects them when they conflict, achieving lossless retention for separable tasks and deferred recoverable plasticity otherwise.
AI.motivation: Existing continual learning methods rely on post-hoc mechanisms (replay, elastic regularization, distillation) rather than directly modeling forgetting. The authors argue that forgetting should be understood and addressed at its root: as interference between tasks, which can be quantified and structurally managed through geometric principles.
AI.method: The paper formalizes forgetting as task interference energy. In frozen-feature regimes, this is exact; in deep networks, it is recovered via path-averaged curvature with minimal extra forward passes. From the geometry of task supports, two regimes emerge: (1) disjoint supports allow structural elimination of forgetting, (2) overlapping conflicting directions impose an unavoidable distortion floor. This geometry yields optimal model merging through task-aware orthogonalization. The resulting method, Interference-Gated Functional Allocation (IGFA), is replay-free and Fisher-free: it shares parameter directions when tasks are aligned and protects them via orthogonalization when they conflict.
AI.result: IGFA achieves lossless retention when tasks are structurally separable. For non-separable tasks, it shifts unavoidable cost from irreversible forgetting into deferred but recoverable plasticity. It matches the strongest replay-free structural baselines on dissimilar-task streams and outperforms unconditional projection when task similarity makes transfer beneficial.
AI.conclusion: Forgetting can be directly modeled as interference, enabling principled continual learning without replay or Fisher information. IGFA demonstrates that by respecting the geometry of task supports—sharing when aligned, protecting when conflicting—one can achieve lossless retention where possible and graceful degradation where not.

title: Temporal Knowledge Graph Forecasting under Distribution Shifts: A Synthetic Evaluation
summary: Temporal knowledge graphs (TKGs) represent evolving relational systems, whose underlying data-generating processes often change over time. Yet, TKG forecasting models are commonly evaluated only on empirical benchmark datasets that provide limited insight into the models' robustness to such distribution shifts. Recognising this issue, we study TKG forecasting under controlled shift environments using a synthetic TKG generator that encodes three temporal and structural properties -- recurrence, homophily, and periodicity -- as data-generating mechanisms. This allows us to evaluate seven forecasting architectures under stationary and shifting regimes. Our experiments suggest that robustness in TKG forecasting is highly signal-dependent. Recurrence-based and periodic regularities are largely recoverable under stationary conditions, and simple memory-based baselines can be competitive when recurrence dominates the data. However, structural breaks reveal limitations in model adaptivity, with shifts in latent entity-community structure posing the strongest challenge in our study. Overall, our findings improve the understanding of the capabilities and limitations of current TKG models confronted with temporal distribution shifts.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically evaluates temporal knowledge graph (TKG) forecasting models under distribution shifts using a synthetic generator that encodes recurrence, homophily, and periodicity. Experiments across seven architectures reveal that robustness is signal-dependent: recurrence and periodicity are recoverable under stationary conditions, but structural breaks—especially shifts in latent entity-community structure—severely challenge model adaptivity.
AI.motivation: TKG forecasting models are predominantly evaluated on empirical benchmarks that offer limited insight into robustness against temporal distribution shifts, despite real-world relational systems frequently undergoing such changes. The authors aim to fill this gap by studying model behavior under controlled, synthetic shift environments.
AI.method: The authors design a synthetic TKG generator encoding three data-generating mechanisms: recurrence (repetitive relational patterns), homophily (latent entity-community structure), and periodicity (time-dependent regularities). They instantiate both stationary and shifting regimes (e.g., structural breaks in community assignments, changes in periodicity) and benchmark seven forecasting architectures—including memory-based baselines, graph neural networks, and temporal reasoning models—under these controlled conditions.
AI.result: Under stationary conditions, recurrence-based and periodic regularities are largely recoverable, and simple memory-based baselines perform competitively when recurrence dominates. However, under distribution shifts—particularly shifts in latent entity-community structure—all models exhibit significant limitations in adaptivity, revealing that current architectures struggle with structural breaks.
AI.conclusion: Robustness in TKG forecasting is highly signal-dependent. While current models handle recurrence and periodicity well in stationary settings, they lack adaptivity when confronted with structural distribution shifts. The findings underscore the need for more adaptive TKG architectures and advocate for evaluating models under controlled shift environments beyond standard empirical benchmarks.

title: All you need is SAMPAT
summary: The current state of the art in AI/ML rests on deep neural architectures, which, in general, suffer from a lack of interpretability. Interpretability is crucial to gleaning insights while analyzing experimental data, where quantitative predictions may not be adequate for a scientist. We present a three layer neural architecture, SAMPAT (Smooth Approximation via Multivariate Polynomials and Analytic Transformations), that can provably learn a continuous, everywhere differentiable function, that can approximate any smooth function arbitrarily closely. SAMPAT's approximant can be expressed as a closed and compact algebraic, analytic expression, providing complete interpretability. Experiments on synthetic and benchmark datasets indicate that SAMPAT yields competitive performance with simpler representations. For many tasks, a two layer SAMPAT suffices. By imposing restrictions on the connectivity between neurons, SAMPAT may be used to provide a range of approximants, including regular and trigonometric polynomials, rational expressions, Gaussians, mixtures of Gaussians, as well as arbitrary combinations of the same; without restrictions, it learns a suitable structure. SAMPAT may be used to factorize polynomials and model nonlinear systems. With the addition of skip connections, a 4 to 6 layer SAMPAT is adequate to represent a substantive range of methods widely used in AI/ML, allowing the choice of a model's family, not just its parameters, to also be optimized as part of the learning process.

AI.tldr: SAMPAT is a three-layer neural architecture that provably learns smooth functions with closed-form algebraic expressions, offering complete interpretability while maintaining competitive performance, and can represent a wide range of model families when extended with skip connections.
AI.motivation: Deep neural networks lack interpretability, which is critical for scientific data analysis where quantitative predictions alone are insufficient. Scientists need to glean insights from models, motivating the need for an architecture that is both expressive and fully interpretable.
AI.method: The authors propose SAMPAT (Smooth Approximation via Multivariate Polynomials and Analytic Transformations), a three-layer neural architecture that provably learns continuous, everywhere differentiable functions. The learned approximant is expressible as a closed, compact algebraic analytic expression. By constraining inter-neuron connectivity, SAMPAT can yield specific forms such as polynomials, trigonometric polynomials, rational expressions, Gaussians, and mixtures thereof. Skip connections extend it to 4–6 layers, enabling optimization over model families alongside parameters.
AI.result: Experiments on synthetic and benchmark datasets show SAMPAT achieves competitive performance with simpler representations. A two-layer variant suffices for many tasks. SAMPAT can also factorize polynomials and model nonlinear systems.
AI.conclusion: SAMPAT provides a provably interpretable alternative to deep neural networks, capable of approximating arbitrary smooth functions while yielding compact algebraic expressions. With skip connections, it subsumes many AI/ML methods, allowing joint optimization of model family and parameters.

title: Forget Narrowly, Retain Broadly: Unlearning as an Asymmetric Generalization Problem
summary: Machine unlearning in LLMs is the targeted removal of specific knowledge while preserving all other capabilities, critical for privacy and safety. Yet existing benchmarks measure it unreliably. They miss knowledge that resurfaces under paraphrased or indirect queries, a failure we call under-forgetting, and lack the semantic, syntactic, and lexical probes needed to verify that unrelated knowledge is preserved, a failure we call over-forgetting. Both failures reflect an asymmetric generalization problem. Forget evaluation must cover diverse query formulations of the same target facts, testing whether forgetting holds beyond exact training prompts. Retain evaluation must probe a far larger and implicitly defined set, namely every fact disjoint from the forget target. The retain set thus defines the effective forget set, yet current datasets provide no fine-grained annotation of this forget-retain boundary. We address this with SUITE, an evaluation protocol and training corpus that captures forget-retain structure for real-world factual domains. Methods trained on SUITE improve substantially, showing that training data is as important as algorithmic design.
