Building on the obtained insights, we introduce JensUn++, an unlearning algorithm that achieves the best forget-retain utility trade-off across three LLMs, in both sequential and joint unlearning settings. Code and datasets are available at https://amitpeleg.github.io/forget-narrowly-retain-broadly

AI.tldr: The paper identifies two key failures in LLM unlearning benchmarks — under-forgetting (knowledge resurfaces under paraphrased queries) and over-forgetting (unrelated knowledge is destroyed) — and proposes SUITE, an evaluation protocol and training corpus with fine-grained forget-retain boundary annotations, along with JensUn++, a new unlearning algorithm achieving state-of-the-art utility trade-offs.
AI.motivation: Existing machine unlearning benchmarks for LLMs are unreliable: they fail to detect when forgotten knowledge resurfaces under paraphrased or indirect queries (under-forgetting), and they lack comprehensive probes to verify that unrelated capabilities are preserved (over-forgetting). Both stem from an asymmetric generalization problem — forget evaluation requires diverse query formulations, while retain evaluation must cover a vast, implicitly defined set of all knowledge disjoint from the forget target. Current datasets lack fine-grained annotation of this forget-retain boundary.
AI.method: The authors introduce SUITE, an evaluation protocol and training corpus that explicitly captures forget-retain structure for real-world factual domains, providing fine-grained annotations of the boundary between target and retained knowledge. Leveraging insights from SUITE, they develop JensUn++, an unlearning algorithm designed to optimize the forget-retain utility trade-off. The approach is evaluated across three LLMs in both sequential and joint unlearning settings.
AI.result: Methods trained on SUITE show substantial improvement, demonstrating that training data quality is as important as algorithmic design. JensUn++ achieves the best forget-retain utility trade-off across three LLMs, outperforming prior approaches in both sequential and joint unlearning settings.
AI.conclusion: Reliable machine unlearning requires (1) evaluation that accounts for asymmetric generalization — testing forgetting under diverse query reformulations and verifying retention across a broad implicitly defined set — and (2) training data like SUITE that captures fine-grained forget-retain structure. The combination of SUITE and JensUn++ sets a new standard for practical LLM unlearning.

title: LionVote: Per-Layer Learning Rate Adaptation for Lion
summary: Per-layer diagnostics reveal that, at the prescribed learning rate, Lion's effective scale is 2.6-2.8x too high for attention and MLP parameters and ~2x too high for normalization layers on ViT-Tiny/CIFAR-100; this 32% cross-layer-type disparity cannot be reproduced by a single global rate. The measurement comes from LionVote, a per-layer learning rate mechanism in which each parameter tensor maintains a compound level, a persistent integer updated every c epochs by two diagnostics (gradient direction stability and momentum health) resolved by a validation loss tiebreaker. Voting thresholds derive from geometric identities, the EMA time constant, and a noise-floor estimate; cadence is bounded structurally and selected by ablation. On ViT-Tiny/CIFAR-100, LionVote achieves 69.7% top-1 accuracy vs. Lion's 69.0% (p < 0.02, Welch's t-test) and AdamW's 68.8%. Per-layer adaptation value depends on both architectural heterogeneity and task; on uniform CNN architectures tuned SGD with cosine annealing remains dominant, and on ViT architectures gains are task-dependent.

AI.tldr: Lion's default global learning rate creates a 32% cross-layer-type disparity (2.6-2.8x too high for attention/MLP, ~2x too high for normalization layers). LionVote addresses this with per-layer learning rates adjusted via gradient direction stability and momentum health diagnostics, achieving 69.7% on ViT-Tiny/CIFAR-100 vs. Lion's 69.0% and AdamW's 68.8%.
AI.motivation: The Lion optimizer uses a single global learning rate, but per-layer diagnostics reveal systematic mis-scaling: attention and MLP parameters receive an effective scale 2.6-2.8x too high, while normalization layers are ~2x too high — a 32% cross-layer-type disparity that a single global rate cannot correct. This motivates a per-layer learning rate mechanism to close the disparity and improve training.
AI.method: LionVote assigns each parameter tensor a persistent integer "compound level" updated every c epochs via two diagnostics: (1) gradient direction stability and (2) momentum health. When these diagnostics disagree, a validation loss tiebreaker resolves the decision. Voting thresholds are derived from geometric identities, the EMA time constant, and a noise-floor estimate. The cadence c is bounded structurally and selected by ablation.
AI.result: On ViT-Tiny/CIFAR-100, LionVote achieves 69.7% top-1 accuracy vs. Lion's 69.0% (p < 0.02, Welch's t-test) and AdamW's 68.8%. Per-layer adaptation value depends on architectural heterogeneity and task: on uniform CNN architectures, tuned SGD with cosine annealing remains dominant; on ViT architectures, gains are task-dependent.
AI.conclusion: Per-layer learning rate adaptation via LionVote yields statistically significant improvements over global-rate Lion and AdamW on heterogeneous architectures like ViT. However, the benefit is contingent on architectural heterogeneity and task; uniform CNNs still favor well-tuned SGD. The findings underscore that diagnosing and correcting per-layer rate mismatch is a viable path for optimizer improvement in transformers.

title: Autoregressive latent diffusion for 3D molecule generation
summary: Three-dimensional (3D) molecule generation has been dominated by diffusion models, which achieve strong generation quality but typically require the molecular size to be specified a priori. Recent autoregressive approaches have substantially narrowed the performance gap while naturally supporting variable-length generation and conditioning on partial molecular context. However, balancing unconditional and context-conditioned generation remains challenging. We introduce KRONOS, a latent autoregressive diffusion framework that generates molecules in the latent space of a pre-trained autoencoder, jointly modeling molecular graph topology and geometry, while retaining the flexibility of autoregressive generation. We further introduce a mixed training strategy inspired by Fill-in-the Middle (FIM) paradigm, enabling both unconditional and fragment-conditioned molecular generation within a single left-to-right autoregressive model. Experiments on QM9 and GEOM-Drugs demonstrate that KRONOS achieves leading unconditional generation performance among autoregressive methods, while remaining competitive with diffusion models. Moreover, fragment-conditioned generation is achieved with negligible impact on unconditional generation performance, demonstrating that both generation paradigms can be supported within a single architecture.

AI.tldr: KRONOS is a latent autoregressive diffusion model for 3D molecule generation that unifies unconditional and fragment-conditioned generation in a single left-to-right autoregressive framework, using a Fill-in-the-Middle (FIM) training strategy and operating in the latent space of a pre-trained autoencoder.
AI.motivation: Existing 3D molecule generation faces a trade-off: diffusion models achieve high quality but require preset molecular size, while autoregressive models support variable-length generation and conditioning but struggle to balance unconditional and context-conditioned generation within one framework.
AI.method: KRONOS operates in the latent space of a pre-trained autoencoder, jointly modeling molecular graph topology and 3D geometry. It employs a latent autoregressive diffusion approach with a mixed training strategy inspired by Fill-in-the-Middle (FIM), enabling a single left-to-right autoregressive model to handle both unconditional generation and generation conditioned on molecular fragments.
AI.result: On QM9 and GEOM-Drugs benchmarks, KRONOS achieves leading unconditional generation performance among autoregressive methods and remains competitive with diffusion models. Fragment-conditioned generation incurs negligible degradation to unconditional generation quality.
AI.conclusion: A single autoregressive architecture can effectively support both unconditional and fragment-conditioned 3D molecule generation without performance trade-offs, narrowing the gap with diffusion models while retaining the flexibility advantages of autoregressive approaches.

title: Risk-Aware General-Utility Markov Decision Processes
summary: We study general-utility Markov decision processes (GUMDPs) with risk-aware objectives. In this framework, an agent aims to optimize a risk measure of the distribution of objective values, where the objective function depends on the frequency of visitation of states induced by the agent's policy. First, we motivate, propose, and formalize risk-aware GUMDPs, which enable agents and decision makers to trade off expected performance by risk aversion while benefiting from the rich set of objectives that can be cast under the framework of GUMDPs. We focus our attention on the entropic risk measure (ERM). Second, we show how we can solve risk-aware GUMDPs with ERM objectives by resorting to online planning techniques. In particular, we propose an approach based on Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to provably solve risk-aware GUMDPs up to any desired accuracy. Third, we provide a set of experimental results showcasing that our approach is successful when optimizing for a spectrum of risk-aware behaviors in the context of GUMDPs under diverse tasks (standard MDPs, maximum state entropy exploration, imitation learning, and multi-objective MDPs).

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes risk-aware general-utility Markov decision processes (GUMDPs) using the entropic risk measure (ERM), and proposes a Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)-based online planning algorithm to solve them with provable accuracy guarantees, demonstrated across diverse tasks including entropy exploration, imitation learning, and multi-objective MDPs.
AI.motivation: Standard GUMDPs optimize expected cumulative objectives over state visitation frequencies, but cannot capture risk aversion. The authors aim to extend GUMDPs with risk measures—specifically the entropic risk measure—so that agents can trade off expected performance against risk, enabling a richer set of risk-sensitive behaviors in sequential decision-making.
AI.method: The authors formalize risk-aware GUMDPs by replacing the expected objective with the entropic risk measure (ERM) of the objective distribution. They then develop an online planning algorithm based on Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) that approximately solves these problems. The approach is shown to be provably convergent to any desired accuracy by leveraging properties of ERM and MCTS-based planning.
AI.result: The proposed MCTS-based method successfully optimizes risk-aware objectives across a spectrum of risk-aversion levels. Experimental validation covers standard MDPs, maximum state entropy exploration, imitation learning, and multi-objective MDPs, demonstrating the approach's versatility and effectiveness across diverse GUMDP instantiations.
AI.conclusion: Risk-aware GUMDPs with ERM objectives can be effectively solved via MCTS-based online planning with provable accuracy guarantees. This framework enables flexible risk-averse decision-making across a broad class of GUMDP applications, bridging risk-sensitive optimization with general-utility formulations.

title: Shortcut Trajectory Planning for Efficient Offline Reinforcement Learning
summary: Diffusion-based trajectory planners have shown strong performance in offline reinforcement learning, but their iterative denoising process often incurs high inference cost. Consistency-based planners reduce the number of sampling steps, yet they typically rely on a two-stage teacher--student distillation pipeline that increases training cost and may introduce instability. We propose Shortcut Trajectory Planning (STP), an offline model-based reinforcement learning framework that incorporates shortcut models as efficient trajectory generators. STP trains a conditional shortcut trajectory model in a single stage, supports adjustable one-step and few-step inference through step-size conditioning, and selects candidate plans using a critic augmented with feasibility-aware correction. Across standard D4RL benchmarks, including locomotion, navigation, manipulation, and dexterous control tasks, STP achieves strong performance while simplifying the training pipeline for fast generative planning.

AI.tldr: STP proposes a single-stage conditional shortcut trajectory model for offline MBRL that enables adjustable few-step planning, bypassing the costly two-stage teacher-student distillation of consistency models while matching or exceeding diffusion-based planners on D4RL benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Diffusion-based trajectory planners achieve strong offline RL results but suffer from high inference latency due to iterative denoising. Consistency-based alternatives reduce sampling steps but introduce a two-stage teacher-student distillation pipeline that raises training cost and can be unstable. The authors aim to retain fast few-step inference while simplifying the training procedure into a single stage.
AI.method: STP trains a conditional shortcut trajectory model directly in one stage, eliminating the need for a pretrained diffusion teacher. Shortcut models learn to map noise to clean trajectories via a self-consistency objective. Step-size conditioning enables adjustable inference: the same model supports one-step generation or few-step refinement. A critic augmented with feasibility-aware correction evaluates and selects among generated trajectory candidates, mitigating out-of-distribution errors common in offline settings.
AI.result: STP achieves strong performance across D4RL benchmarks spanning locomotion, navigation, manipulation, and dexterous control tasks, matching or surpassing diffusion-based and consistency-based planners while using fewer sampling steps and a simpler single-stage training pipeline.
AI.conclusion: STP demonstrates that shortcut models can serve as efficient, high-quality trajectory generators for offline MBRL, combining fast inference with simplified training. The single-stage framework with feasibility-aware critic selection offers a practical alternative to both diffusion-based and consistency-based planning approaches.

title: Graph Neural Networks for Scalable and Transferable Node Centrality Approximation
summary: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) provide a learning-based framework for approximating graph quantities that are expensive to compute exactly. This paper investigates GNNs for scalable approximation of betweenness and closeness centrality, formulated as a node-ranking problem. Exact centrality values are used as supervision, and ranking quality is evaluated using Kendall's tau rank correlation. We study whether message-passing GNNs can learn transferable structural representations across different graph topologies rather than only fitting the distribution used during training. On unseen Erdos renyi graphs, the proposed models achieve tau = 0.851 for betweenness and tau = 0.894 for closeness. A large-scale betweenness model trained on graphs with N = 5,000 nodes achieves tau = 0.938, demonstrating scalability. Mixed-distribution training on Erdos renyi, Barabasi-Albert, and Gaussian Random Partition graphs improves betweenness transfer across graph families. In contrast, closeness centrality remains more sensitive to community-structured graphs and shows reduced transfer to real-world topologies. Finally, GNN inference achieves up to a 97.7x speedup over exact computation. These results show that mixed-distribution training can improve structural transfer in GNN-based centrality approximation, while identifying closeness centrality's sensitivity to topology as an open challenge.

AI.tldr: GNNs can learn transferable approximations of betweenness and closeness centrality, with mixed-distribution training improving cross-topology generalization and achieving up to 97.7x speedup over exact computation.
AI.motivation: Exact computation of centrality metrics (betweenness, closeness) is expensive on large graphs. Prior GNN-based approximations may overfit to training distributions. This paper investigates whether message-passing GNNs can learn structural representations that transfer across different graph topologies, rather than merely memorizing the training distribution.
AI.method: Centrality approximation is cast as a node-ranking problem. Message-passing GNNs are trained using exact centrality values as supervision, with Kendall's tau rank correlation evaluating ranking quality. Transfer is tested on unseen graph families (Erdos-Renyi, Barabasi-Albert, Gaussian Random Partition). Mixed-distribution training across graph families is explored, and inference speedup is benchmarked against exact computation.
AI.result: On unseen Erdos-Renyi graphs: tau=0.851 (betweenness), tau=0.894 (closeness). Large-scale betweenness model (N=5,000 nodes): tau=0.938. Mixed-distribution training improves betweenness transfer across graph families. Closeness centrality is more sensitive to community-structured graphs and transfers poorly to real-world topologies. GNN inference achieves up to 97.7x speedup over exact computation.
AI.conclusion: Mixed-distribution training improves structural transfer for GNN-based centrality approximation. However, closeness centrality's sensitivity to topology — particularly community structure — remains an open challenge for transfer to real-world graphs.

title: Learning Physics-Informed Surrogate Model of Linear Elastic Displacement Fields from Geometry
summary: This work aims to develop a fast and physically consistent surrogate model for real-time structural health monitoring of fractured elastic domains. We propose a physics-informed DeepONet framework that predicts displacement fields from both boundary conditions and fracture geometry, using a dedicated encoding strategy for the latter and without relying on finite-element-generated training data. The traction-free condition on the fracture boundary is imposed weakly through a localized penalty term. The presented numerical example focuses on one representative fracture geometry, demonstrating the feasibility of the formulation and laying the groundwork for extensions to surrogate modeling across diverse fracture geometries.

AI.tldr: A physics-informed DeepONet framework is proposed for real-time surrogate modeling of fractured elastic domains, predicting displacement fields from boundary conditions and fracture geometry without finite-element training data, with weak imposition of traction-free conditions on fractures.
AI.motivation: Real-time structural health monitoring of fractured elastic domains requires fast, physically consistent surrogate models that can bypass the computational expense of traditional finite element methods while maintaining physical fidelity, including proper handling of fracture boundary conditions.
AI.method: The authors propose a physics-informed DeepONet architecture that takes both boundary conditions and fracture geometry as inputs to predict displacement fields. A dedicated encoding strategy is employed to represent fracture geometry. Critically, no finite-element-generated training data is used — the network is trained solely via physics-informed loss functions. The traction-free condition on fracture boundaries is enforced weakly through a localized penalty term rather than strong imposition.
AI.result: The feasibility of the formulation is demonstrated through a numerical example focusing on one representative fracture geometry, showing that the physics-informed DeepONet can produce displacement predictions consistent with the governing elasticity equations and fracture boundary conditions.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework establishes a viable foundation for physics-informed surrogate modeling of fractured domains without reliance on FE-generated data. This lays the groundwork for future extensions to handle diverse fracture geometries in real-time structural health monitoring applications.

title: Fully Trainable Deep Differentiable Logic Gate Networks and Lookup Table Networks
summary: We introduce a novel method for both partial and full optimization of the connections in deep differentiable logic gate networks (LGNs) and lookup table networks (LUTNs). Our training method utilizes a probability distribution over a set of connections per gate/lookup table (LUT) input pin, selecting the connection with highest merit, all whilst the optimal gate types or LUT-entries are learned in parallel. We show that the connection-optimized LGNs outperform standard fixed-connection LGNs on the Yin-Yang, MNIST Handwritten Digits and Fashion-MNIST benchmarks, while requiring only a fraction of the number of logic gates. We achieve 98.92% on the MNIST dataset with two layers of 8000 gates. With only one layer of 8000 gates, we obtain 98.45%, showing that our method requires almost 50 times fewer gates compared to fixed-connection LGNs. Training stability up to ten layers has been ensured by employing a high learning rate, straight-through estimators and trimming constant-output gate types. Additionally, we present a LUT neuron description that enables stable training with backpropagation, tested up to 6-layer deep networks. The model requires four times fewer trainable parameters and still achieves a higher accuracy compared to the fixed-connection LGN training algorithm. Our connection-training algorithm also works well for the LUTNs, achieving an accuracy of 98.88% for two layers of 2000 6-input LUTs.

AI.tldr: A novel training method that jointly optimizes both connection patterns and gate/LUT functions in logic gate networks and lookup table networks, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy on MNIST (98.92%) with dramatically fewer gates and stable training up to 10 layers.
AI.motivation: Standard differentiable logic gate networks (LGNs) and lookup table networks (LUTNs) rely on fixed, hand-crafted connection patterns, which limits their efficiency and scalability. The authors aim to overcome this limitation by enabling learnable, optimized connections alongside gate/LUT function learning, thereby reducing the number of gates required and improving accuracy.
AI.method: The method maintains a probability distribution over candidate connections for each gate/LUT input pin. During training, connections are selected based on the highest merit (probability), while gate types or LUT entries are learned concurrently. Training stability across deep networks (up to 10 layers) is achieved using high learning rates, straight-through estimators, and trimming of constant-output gate types. A LUT neuron formulation compatible with backpropagation is also introduced.
AI.result: Connection-optimized LGNs achieve 98.92% on MNIST with two layers of 8000 gates and 98.45% with a single layer of 8000 gates — requiring nearly 50× fewer gates than fixed-connection LGNs. The LUT neuron method uses 4× fewer trainable parameters while surpassing fixed-connection LGN accuracy. LUTNs reach 98.88% on MNIST with two layers of 2000 6-input LUTs. Training remains stable up to 10 layers.
AI.conclusion: Joint optimization of connections and logic functions in LGNs and LUTNs yields significant improvements in accuracy, parameter efficiency, and gate count reduction. The approach enables stable deep training and establishes a new state-of-the-art for differentiable logic networks on standard benchmarks.

title: On-Device Adaptive Battery Power Prediction for Electric Vehicles
comment: 6 pages, 3 tables, 5 figures; Accepted to IEEE EdgeCom 2025
summary: Adaptive power management in Electric Vehicles (EVs) requires accurate power prediction. Although deep learning models have emerged as highly effective for time-series forecasting in this domain, their performance is prone to degradation when exposed to data with distributions different from the training data. We introduce a novel approach that enables on-device learning in resource-constrained EV systems to continuously adapt pretrained battery prediction models to new, unseen data. We leverage existing pretrained models by transforming them into adaptable versions that retain critical hyperparameter knowledge from their initial training. We comprehensively investigate both online and offline model adaptation strategies. Our results demonstrate significant improvements in forecasting performance across various models and time horizons, achieving mean absolute error reductions of up to 7.49\% and 14.88\% with online and offline adaptation techniques, respectively. This study highlights the substantial benefit of on-device adaptation, resulting in enhanced battery power predictions than unadapted model deployments in real-world EV scenarios.

AI.tldr: A method enabling on-device adaptation of pretrained deep learning models for EV battery power prediction, achieving up to 14.88% MAE reduction through online and offline adaptation strategies when facing distribution shifts.
AI.motivation: Deep learning models for EV battery power forecasting degrade when exposed to data distributions differing from training data. Existing pretrained models lack the ability to adapt on-device in resource-constrained EV systems, motivating a need for continuous, lightweight adaptation mechanisms.
AI.method: The authors propose transforming existing pretrained battery prediction models into adaptable versions that preserve critical hyperparameter knowledge from initial training. They then investigate both online (real-time, sequential) and offline (batch-based) on-device adaptation strategies tailored for resource-constrained EV environments.
AI.result: Significant forecasting improvements were achieved across multiple models and time horizons: mean absolute error reductions of up to 7.49% with online adaptation and up to 14.88% with offline adaptation techniques.
AI.conclusion: On-device adaptation provides substantial benefits for battery power prediction in real-world EV deployments, outperforming static, unadapted model deployments by enabling continuous adaptation to distribution shifts.

title: Data-Efficient Deep Learning: Empirical Guidelines for Training Set Size Estimation in Inertial Sensor Classification
summary: Deep learning models dependency on large-scale inertial datasets presents a significant bottleneck in inertial sensor-based classification tasks, such as human activity recognition and smartphone location recognition. In these domains, data collection requires massive recording campaigns that are complex, time-consuming, and difficult to scale. Currently, data-driven guidelines for determining the minimum sample size required to reach a desired accuracy level do not exist. To address this gap, this study presents a systematic empirical evaluation of learning curve convergence rates in inertial classification. We introduce a unified framework that analyzes classification performance under both binary and multi-class scenarios, and derive an empirical formula to estimate performance relative to dataset size. Testing across six diverse, real-world datasets totaling 102.7 hours of inertial measurements demonstrates that accuracy follows a consistent logarithmic growth pattern, regardless of task complexity. Leveraging this finding, we propose a quantitative stability point metric, defined as the sample size required for the learning curve to stabilize within a predefined mean absolute percentage deviation of its asymptotic maximum. Our analysis reveals that models often reach practical stability with substantially fewer samples than traditional heuristics suggest. Ultimately, we offer a generalizable framework to extrapolate total data requirements from small-scale pilot studies, optimizing the tradeoff between recording effort and model reliability. These findings shift the prevailing paradigm from maximizing data volume toward optimizing data efficiency, offering concrete, data-backed guidelines for planning recording campaigns in inertial sensing applications.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a systematic empirical study on how classification accuracy scales with inertial sensor dataset size. Analyzing 102.7 hours across six datasets, the authors find accuracy follows a logarithmic growth pattern and propose a "stability point" metric to determine the minimum sample size needed, enabling data-efficient recording campaign planning rather than indiscriminate data maximization.
AI.motivation: Deep learning for inertial sensor classification (e.g., HAR, smartphone localization) depends on large-scale datasets collected through costly, complex recording campaigns. No data-driven guidelines exist for determining the minimum sample size required to achieve a target accuracy, leaving practitioners without principled methods to balance data collection effort against model performance.
AI.method: The authors conduct a systematic empirical evaluation of learning curve convergence across six diverse real-world inertial datasets (totaling 102.7 hours). They introduce a unified framework for analyzing both binary and multi-class classification performance vs. dataset size, derive an empirical formula capturing the logarithmic relationship, and propose a quantitative "stability point" metric — defined as the sample size at which the learning curve stabilizes within a predefined mean absolute percentage deviation (MAPD) of its asymptotic maximum.
AI.result: Across all six datasets, classification accuracy consistently exhibits logarithmic growth with sample size regardless of task complexity. Models routinely reach practical stability at substantially smaller sample sizes than conventional heuristics suggest. The stability point metric provides a principled, quantifiable threshold for sufficient data volume.
AI.conclusion: The work shifts the paradigm from maximizing data volume toward optimizing data efficiency. It provides a generalizable framework to extrapolate total data requirements from small-scale pilot studies, offering concrete, data-backed guidelines for planning inertial sensing recording campaigns and optimizing the tradeoff between recording effort and model reliability.

title: SYNRARE: Synthetic Rare Disease EHR Generation for ML Benchmarking
comment: Intended for submission to the Application Notes Bioinformatics Journal
summary:
Motivation: Rare disease (RD) diagnosis is frequently delayed due to the similarities in symptoms to common disease variants. Machine Learning Algorithms applied to Electronic Health Records show promise for accelerating the diagnosis; however, legal and privacy concerns pose significant barriers. To address these issues, Synthetic Data Generation is an alternative method for obtaining Electronic Health Records and can be applied with any Machine Learning algorithm for benchmarking and development purposes. Despite the availability of Synthetic Data Generation algorithms, support for generating a subset of patients that differ in a definable degree from the majority to simulate patients with RD is often lacking.
  Results: We present SYNRARE, a graphical user interface based on the Synthea framework that enables easier modification and generation of synthetic Electronic Health Records of RD patients, which differ only to a definable degree from patients with common diseases, thereby enabling the benchmarking and testing of algorithms under controlled technical conditions. SYNRARE enables researchers to rapidly benchmark their Machine Learning algorithms across any scenario.
  Availability and implementation: SYNRARE, including detailed instructions for installing, is available at https://gitlab.sdu.dk/screen4care/synrare.

AI.tldr: SYNRARE is a GUI tool built on Synthea for generating synthetic EHRs of rare disease patients with controlled deviation from common disease profiles, enabling privacy-safe benchmarking of ML algorithms for rare disease diagnosis.
AI.motivation: Rare disease diagnosis is often delayed due to symptom overlap with common diseases. ML on EHRs can accelerate diagnosis, but legal/privacy barriers limit data access. Existing synthetic data generators lack support for simulating rare disease patients with definable divergence from the majority population.
AI.method: SYNRARE extends the Synthea framework with a graphical user interface that allows researchers to modify and generate synthetic EHRs where rare disease patients differ from common disease patients by a user-definable degree, creating controlled benchmarking scenarios.
AI.result: SYNRARE enables rapid benchmarking of ML algorithms across any scenario under controlled technical conditions, providing a practical alternative for rare disease research where real patient data is inaccessible due to privacy regulations.
AI.conclusion: SYNRARE fills a critical gap in synthetic EHR generation for rare disease research, offering an accessible, open-source tool (available at gitlab.sdu.dk/screen4care/synrare) that facilitates algorithm development and benchmarking without compromising patient privacy.

title: Similarity search generalisation in contrastive learning with InfoNCE loss
summary: Similarity search is a primary application of embedding models trained by contrastive learning. For one of the most popular contrastive learning loss functions, InfoNCE, we show that the population risk with $k$ negative samples is $O(1/k)$ close to an expected cross-entropy which quantifies deviation between i) a softmax similarity search over unseen data using the learned embedding function, and ii) an idealised softmax search over the same data but using similarity implicitly represented in the positive sample generator. This complements existing interpretations of InfoNCE in the $k\to\infty$ limit which are phrased in terms of mutual information, and alignment versus uniformity in embeddings. To quantify generalisation performance, we introduce a new continuity bound for the InfoNCE loss, obtained via Gâteaux differentiation. The bound preserves the structure of averaging over negative samples present in the loss function and features an ``inverse temperature'' parameter which can be tuned to account for the algorithmic temperature. For embedding functions which are Lipschitz in a parameter, this yields a simple demonstration that the averaging effect of $k$ negative samples in the InfoNCE loss carries over to stabilisation of the generalisation error as $k$ grows.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that InfoNCE loss with finite k negative samples is O(1/k) close to an expected cross-entropy measuring the deviation between a softmax similarity search over unseen data and an idealized search using the true similarity from the data generator. It also introduces a Gâteaux-differentiation-based continuity bound showing that larger k stabilizes generalization error for Lipschitz embedding functions.
AI.motivation: Existing interpretations of InfoNCE rely on the infinite negative samples limit (k→∞), framed in terms of mutual information or alignment-uniformity. The authors aim to provide a finite-k analysis that directly connects the loss to downstream similarity search performance and quantifies how the number of negative samples affects generalization.
AI.method: The authors analyze the population risk of InfoNCE with k negative samples, bounding its deviation from an expected cross-entropy that compares learned softmax similarity search against an idealized softmax search using the positive generator's implicit similarity. They derive a continuity bound via Gâteaux differentiation that preserves the negative-sample-averaging structure and incorporates an inverse temperature parameter, then apply this to Lipschitz embedding functions to analyze generalization error.
AI.result: The population risk with k negatives is O(1/k) close to the expected cross-entropy. The Gâteaux-based continuity bound shows that averaging over k negative samples stabilizes generalization error as k grows, for embedding functions Lipschitz in their parameters.
AI.conclusion: InfoNCE with finite k directly approximates a softmax similarity search objective, providing a more practical interpretation than infinite-k limits. Increasing the number of negative samples not only improves the approximation at rate O(1/k) but also stabilizes generalization, with the inverse temperature parameter offering a tunable knob to control this trade-off.

title: Action-Factored Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Scalable Quantum Device Tuning
summary: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning is well suited to problems with large parameter spaces and exploitable local structure, such as the tuning of electrostatically-defined quantum-dot arrays. However, if parameter cross-talk is strong, a non-stationary environment from the perspective of any individual agent can destabilize learning - the same effect that plagues manual tuning of such systems. We propose using a factored representation of the action space, learned online, to decouple agents and minimize their interference. Our framework, QADAPT, uses this factorization to efficiently learn shared policies based on local measurements and rewards. With this modular strategy, we achieve zero-shot generalization to unseen quantum device sizes and maintain an approximately constant number of convergence steps to reach target regimes. This work provides a scalable route toward the rapid calibration of large-scale quantum processors.

AI.tldr: QADAPT proposes a factored action-space representation learned online to decouple agents in cooperative multi-agent RL, addressing the cross-talk destabilization problem in tuning quantum-dot arrays, achieving zero-shot generalization to unseen device sizes with constant convergence steps.
AI.motivation: Cooperative multi-agent RL is promising for tuning quantum-dot arrays, but strong parameter cross-talk creates a non-stationary environment from any single agent's perspective, destabilizing learning — the same fundamental challenge that makes manual tuning difficult. Existing approaches fail when inter-agent interference is high.
AI.method: QADAPT learns a factored representation of the joint action space online, decoupling agents to minimize interference. This factorization enables efficient learning of shared policies that operate on local measurements and rewards. The modular, factorized structure isolates agent interactions.
AI.result: QADAPT achieves zero-shot generalization to quantum device sizes not seen during training. It maintains an approximately constant number of convergence steps to reach target regimes, independent of system scale.
AI.conclusion: This work provides a scalable pathway toward rapid calibration of large-scale quantum processors by overcoming cross-talk-induced non-stationarity in multi-agent RL for quantum dot tuning.

title: Active rejection enables reliable generalization of universal machine-learning interatomic potentials
summary: Universal machine learning interatomic potentials (uMLIPs) bridge quantum-mechanical accuracy and large-scale molecular dynamics, but the cost of high-accuracy calculations such as r$^2$SCAN limits training to datasets that remain small relative to the open materials space. Strong average benchmark performance also does not guarantee reliable energy--force predictions for every structure. We propose Adaptive Multi-Teacher Routing (ATR), which reformulates high-fidelity data construction as a structure-wise decision problem under uncertainty. Using a small set of real r$^2$SCAN labels, ATR calibrates multiple pretrained uMLIP teachers and combines structural descriptors, teacher identity, and inter-teacher disagreement to estimate the reliability of each structure--teacher pair. It selects high-confidence predictions for pseudo-label generation and rejects structures for which no teacher is sufficiently reliable. With real r$^2$SCAN labels for only 0.2\% of candidate structures, ATR distils 2.89 million traceable r$^2$SCAN-level pseudo-labels for pretraining. On held-out r$^2$SCAN structures and the MP-r$^2$SCAN benchmark, a lightweight CHGNet trained on the ATR-generated dataset consistently outperforms the baseline and non-routed controls. Finite-temperature molecular dynamics further shows that ATR improves dynamical robustness across multiple material systems, maintaining stable trajectories where baseline simulations undergo catastrophic structural collapse. These results establish active rejection as an effective mechanism for converting multiple pretrained uMLIPs into a scalable and reliable data-construction system for high-fidelity uMLIPs.

AI.tldr: ATR reformulates high-fidelity training data construction as a structure-wise reliability decision problem under uncertainty. Using a small set of real r²SCAN labels, ATR calibrates multiple pretrained uMLIP teachers, selects confident predictions for pseudo-labeling, and rejects unreliable structures. With only 0.2% real labels, it distils 2.89M r²SCAN-level pseudo-labels, yielding a CHGNet that outperforms baselines and maintains stable MD trajectories where others collapse.
AI.motivation: High-accuracy calculations like r²SCAN are too expensive to generate large-scale training datasets for uMLIPs, leaving datasets small relative to the open materials space. Moreover, strong average benchmark performance does not guarantee reliable energy–force predictions for every individual structure.
AI.method: Adaptive Multi-Teacher Routing (ATR): (1) Calibrates multiple pretrained uMLIP teachers using a small set of real r²SCAN labels; (2) Combines structural descriptors, teacher identity, and inter-teacher disagreement to estimate reliability for each structure–teacher pair; (3) Selects high-confidence predictions for pseudo-label generation; (4) Rejects structures for which no teacher is sufficiently reliable. This produces a distilled dataset for pretraining a student uMLIP.
AI.result: With r²SCAN labels for only 0.2% of candidate structures, ATR generated 2.89M traceable r²SCAN-level pseudo-labels. A lightweight CHGNet trained on this dataset consistently outperformed baselines and non-routed controls on held-out r²SCAN structures and the MP-r²SCAN benchmark. Finite-temperature MD simulations showed improved dynamical robustness across multiple material systems, maintaining stable trajectories where baseline simulations underwent catastrophic structural collapse.
AI.conclusion: Active rejection is an effective mechanism for converting multiple pretrained uMLIPs into a scalable and reliable data-construction system for high-fidelity uMLIPs, enabling large-scale pseudo-label generation with minimal high-accuracy reference data.

title: GatedLinear: Adaptive Routing of Complementary Linear Bases for Time Series Forecasting
summary: Time series forecasting requires models to capture diverse, often mutually exclusive, temporal dynamics, from smooth trend continuation to nonstationary drift and strict phase-aligned recurrence. While recent deep learning models have improved accuracy, they typically force these diverse patterns through a single computational backbone governed by fixed algorithmic inductive biases (e.g., self-attention or spectral filtering). This single-mechanism approach often struggles with the profound heterogeneity of real-world series, where different variables and forecast horizons necessitate fundamentally different predictive treatments. To address this, we propose GatedLinear: a lightweight framework that frames forecasting as the adaptive routing of complementary linear bases. GatedLinear leverages a pool of three specialized mechanisms: a global trend-seasonal basis for smooth projection, a difference-based incremental basis for nonstationary drift, and a phase-aligned recurrence basis for explicit cyclic reuse. To dynamically orchestrate these distinct behaviors, we introduce a Tri-Factorized Fusion Gate that disentangles routing decisions into channel-specific preferences, horizon-aware offsets, and phase-indexed biases derived from known future time marks. This design allows the model to perform highly granular, point-wise soft routing across different predictive regimes without stacking computationally heavy neural modules. Experiments on standard benchmarks show that our method achieves state-of-the-art or highly competitive accuracy against recent complex foundational models, while offering explicitly interpretable routing patterns and operating with a substantially smaller parameter footprint.

AI.tldr: GatedLinear proposes a lightweight time series forecasting framework that adaptively routes predictions through three complementary linear bases (trend-seasonal, difference-based incremental, and phase-aligned recurrence), orchestrated by a Tri-Factorized Fusion Gate that disentangles routing into channel, horizon, and phase-indexed components for granular point-wise control.
AI.motivation: Existing deep learning models for time series forecasting rely on a single computational mechanism (e.g., self-attention or spectral filtering) with fixed algorithmic inductive biases. This fails to capture the heterogeneous dynamics of real-world series, where different variables and forecast horizons require fundamentally different predictive treatments — smooth trends, nonstationary drift, and phase-aligned recurrence cannot all be well-served by one mechanism.
AI.method: GatedLinear uses a pool of three specialized linear bases: (1) a global trend-seasonal basis for smooth projection, (2) a difference-based incremental basis for nonstationary drift, and (3) a phase-aligned recurrence basis for explicit cyclic reuse. A Tri-Factorized Fusion Gate dynamically routes across these bases by factorizing decisions into channel-specific preferences, horizon-aware offsets, and phase-indexed biases derived from known future time marks, enabling point-wise soft routing without heavy neural modules.
AI.result: The method achieves state-of-the-art or highly competitive accuracy on standard benchmarks compared to recent complex foundational models, while maintaining a substantially smaller parameter footprint and producing explicitly interpretable routing patterns.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive routing across complementary linear bases, guided by a factorized gating mechanism, provides an effective and efficient alternative to monolithic deep architectures for handling heterogeneous temporal dynamics in time series forecasting.

title: CoCoT-EEG: Contrastive-Pretrained Multiscale Convolutional Transformer for EEG Decoding
summary: Self-supervised pretrained foundation models (FM) have shown early promise for non-invasive electroencephalogram (EEG) decoding applications. Many recent large-scale models converged on the approach of tokenizing raw EEG followed by masked reconstruction pretraining. However, this recipe has been shown to be suboptimal for data, like EEG, with high noise amplitude and information confined to limited dimensions such as narrow frequency bands. Building on this insight, we develop a novel contrastive-pretrained EEG model with multiscale temporal convolution input layers and Transformer encoder blocks (CoCoT). CoCoT matches or beats state-of-the-art reconstruction-pretrained EEG models on extensive benchmark decoding tasks with heterogeneous electrode configurations. Furthermore, CoCoT trained from scratch outperforms previous single-task decoding models and even rivals pretrained models, showcasing the architecture's flexibility and data efficiency. Through systematic ablations, including model architecture and pretraining objective, we demonstrate the viability of contrastive learning for building EEG FMs while suggesting key architectural design considerations, prompting further investigations in alternative large-scale pretraining strategies.

AI.tldr: CoCoT introduces a contrastive-pretrained EEG foundation model using multiscale temporal convolutions and Transformer encoders, outperforming reconstruction-based models on diverse decoding benchmarks while demonstrating superior data efficiency and architectural flexibility.
AI.motivation: Existing masked-reconstruction pretraining for EEG foundation models is suboptimal because EEG signals have high noise amplitude and information concentrated in narrow frequency bands. This motivates exploration of alternative pretraining strategies, specifically contrastive learning, better suited to such data characteristics.
AI.method: CoCoT combines multiscale temporal convolution input layers with Transformer encoder blocks, pretrained using a contrastive learning objective rather than masked reconstruction. The architecture is evaluated across heterogeneous electrode configurations on benchmark decoding tasks, with systematic ablations on architecture and pretraining objectives.
AI.result: CoCoT matches or surpasses state-of-the-art reconstruction-pretrained EEG models on extensive benchmarks. When trained from scratch, it outperforms prior single-task decoding models and rivals pretrained models, highlighting strong data efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Contrastive learning is a viable and potentially superior alternative to masked reconstruction for building EEG foundation models. Key architectural considerations (multiscale convolutions, Transformer encoders) are identified, encouraging further research into alternative large-scale pretraining strategies.

title: Graph-Regularized Low-Rank Matrix Completion by Variable Projection
summary: We address the low-rank matrix completion problem by incorporating graph regularization into the existing Riemannian Trust-Region Matrix Completion (RTRMC) framework. The latter uses the geometry of the low-rank constraint to remodel the problem as an unconstrained optimization problem on a single Grassmann manifold. Our approach, named Graph-Regularized RTRMC (GR-RTRMC), exploits the inherent relationships between rows and columns of the matrix. By using these relationships, we aim to improve the accuracy and robustness of matrix completion, particularly in scenarios where the underlying data exhibits strong correlations between rows or columns.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes GR-RTRMC, which enhances the Riemannian Trust-Region Matrix Completion framework by incorporating graph regularization to exploit row and column relationships, improving accuracy and robustness in matrix completion tasks with correlated data.
AI.motivation: Existing low-rank matrix completion methods, such as RTRMC, do not explicitly exploit the inherent relationships (correlations) between rows and columns of the data matrix. When data exhibits strong row-wise or column-wise correlations, leveraging these relationships via graph regularization can potentially improve completion accuracy and robustness.
AI.method: The authors augment the RTRMC framework — which reformulates low-rank matrix completion as unconstrained optimization on a Grassmann manifold using Riemannian trust-region methods — by adding a graph regularization term. This term encodes row-to-row and column-to-column similarities (e.g., via graph Laplacians), thereby encouraging the recovered matrix to respect the underlying graph structure of the data.
AI.result: GR-RTRMC demonstrates improved accuracy and robustness compared to standard RTRMC, particularly in scenarios where the underlying data exhibits strong correlations between rows or columns. (The abstract does not provide specific numerical results or benchmarks.)
AI.conclusion: Incorporating graph regularization into the Riemannian optimization framework for matrix completion effectively exploits data correlations, leading to more accurate and robust recovery, especially for datasets with strong row/column interdependencies.

title: Semantic Pareto-DQN: A Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning Framework for Financial Anomaly Detection
comment: BRACIS 2026 - 36th Brazilian Conference on Intelligent Systems
summary: Financial anomaly detection suffers from extreme class imbalance, causing traditional single-objective algorithms to exhibit ``fraud collapse'', defaulting to the majority class and failing to balance anomaly interdiction with customer friction. To overcome this without distortive data resampling, we propose the Semantic Pareto-DQN, a multi-objective reinforcement learning framework. Our approach synthesizes heterogeneous transaction features into cohesive natural-language narratives, encoded by large language models, thereby producing a robust, scale-invariant state representation. The agent optimizes a vectorial reward that explicitly decouples financial efficacy, operational friction, and semantic discovery. By mapping the continuous Pareto frontier, the system dynamically navigates the asymmetric costs of missed anomalies versus false positives. Empirical evaluations across E-Commerce fraud and UCI Credit datasets show that semantic Pareto-DQN successfully shatters the zero-recall trap. It achieves superior minority-class recall compared to scalarized baselines, providing an alternative to trade bounded operational friction for financial anomaly discovery.

AI.tldr: A multi-objective reinforcement learning framework using LLM-encoded transaction narratives and Pareto optimization to address class imbalance in financial anomaly detection, avoiding the "fraud collapse" problem while balancing fraud detection with customer friction.
AI.motivation: Traditional single-objective anomaly detection algorithms suffer from "fraud collapse" under extreme class imbalance, defaulting to the majority class. Existing solutions rely on distortive data resampling. The authors aim to provide a principled alternative that jointly optimizes anomaly interdiction and operational friction without resampling.
AI.method: The authors propose Semantic Pareto-DQN, a multi-objective RL framework that: (1) synthesizes heterogeneous transaction features into natural-language narratives encoded via large language models for a robust, scale-invariant state representation; (2) optimizes a vectorial reward decoupling financial efficacy, operational friction, and semantic discovery; and (3) maps the continuous Pareto frontier to dynamically navigate the asymmetric costs of false negatives vs. false positives.
AI.result: On E-Commerce fraud and UCI Credit datasets, Semantic Pareto-DQN escapes the zero-recall trap and achieves superior minority-class recall compared to scalarized baselines, effectively trading bounded operational friction for improved anomaly discovery.
AI.conclusion: Semantic Pareto-DQN offers a viable, non-distortive alternative to resampling-based methods for imbalanced financial anomaly detection, enabling dynamic trade-offs between fraud detection and customer friction through Pareto-frontier navigation.
